Open the workbook to page 40. City council members are elected leaders who make decisions for their town or city. One of their main jobs is creating and voting on local laws, called ordinances. Read the workbook's three example decisions aloud and ask the class to guess which way a council would vote on each:

  • Community spaces: Can the new skatepark stay open until 10 PM, or does it have to close at sunset?
  • Public safety: What is the speed limit in front of the middle school? Are electric scooters allowed on the sidewalks?
  • Business rules: Where are food trucks allowed to park, and what kind of permits do they need?

The workbook makes the point that council members do not guess what people want. They hold public meetings and listen: residents complaining about dangerous potholes, students asking for a new basketball court. Then they debate and solve.

Post the workbook's three tests for a strong law where students can see them all period. A strong law is clear so people understand it, fair so it applies equally to everyone, and realistic so it can actually be enforced.

Pre-teach three legal terms in 60 seconds using the vocabulary list from the overview: ordinance, which students use today; due process and probable cause, which return in tomorrow's legal review. Students write all three on a vocabulary card they keep for Day 4.

Facilitation Tip

The skatepark-hours question usually splits the room. Let students argue it for 30 seconds, then point back to the three tests they must use to settle the ordinance: clear, fair, and enforceable.

docs.title: Activity 2: Design Your Town, Find the Problems, Write the Laws (30 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 41-42: "City Council in Action", Steps 2-4)

Step 2: Design Your Town (10 min). Students write or sketch a basic plan for their town on page 41 or on chart paper. The workbook asks six questions:

  • What type of town is it? A busy city, a rural community, a beach town, a growing suburb?
  • What is the weather and climate? Humid rainforest, hot and dry desert, snowy mountains?
  • How do people get from one place to another? Public transportation, snowmobiles, cars, walkways?
  • What makes your town special?
  • What types of jobs are available?
  • What is the name of your town?

Step 3: Think Ahead, What Could Go Wrong? (8 min). Students fill in the workbook's problem table (FYF p. 42) with at least one possible problem per row. The workbook's own examples: a snowy town has to keep the roads clear, and a beach town has to keep trash from building up on the sand.

Area Possible Problems Safety (crime, accidents, etc.) Climate, Weather, and Environment Transportation Other (come up with your own idea)

Step 4: Create Your Town Laws (12 min). Students draft two ordinances that solve problems they just named. Each law answers the workbook's three questions on page 42:

  • What is the law?
  • Why is this law needed?
  • What happens if someone breaks the law?

Every law gets checked against the three tests from Activity 1 before it counts as a draft.

Active Monitoring: Walk the room three times, once per step. Lap 1 target: every town has a name, a climate, and a stated way people get around. Lap 2 target: all four rows of the problem table are filled. Lap 3 target: both laws carry a what, a why, and a consequence. Two misconceptions to have an answer ready for: a "law" written as a wish ("everyone should be nice at the skatepark") rather than a rule, and a consequence nobody could actually enforce. If most students miss the lap 2 target, stop and model one problem row on the projector rather than coaching desk by desk.

DOK 3: Two of your laws could conflict with each other. Pick one law you wrote and name a group in your town it would be hardest on. Would you change the law, or keep it and explain why the cost is worth it?

Facilitation Tip

Students who cannot start the town plan almost always need one constraint instead of six questions. Give them the climate and let them build outward, because the climate generates the problems and the problems generate the laws. A town with no climate produces two laws about phones at school.

docs.title: Activity 3: Review the Laws (5 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 43: "City Council in Action", Step 5 and Class Discussion)

Council members review and improve proposed laws before anyone votes. Students trade drafts with a partner and take turns working the workbook's four review questions:

  • Is the law clear and easy to understand?
  • Is the law fair for everyone in the town?
  • Does the law address the problem effectively?
  • Is anything unclear, missing, or unrealistic?

Each student then uses the feedback to improve one law and records what changed on page 43.

Class Discussion. Close with the workbook's prompts: what was the hardest part of writing laws that are fair and realistic for everyone? How did your partner's feedback change your idea? Which of your laws would be difficult to enforce in a real town, and why?

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Decision Tree / Branching Prompt) · Printable PDF:

The name of my town: _____

My Law #1, in one sentence: _____________

Step 1: A resident breaks Law #1 for the first time. What does my law say happens?

Step 2: Branch on fairness.

IF the resident did not know the law existed, what should the council do next? _____________

IF the resident knew the law and broke it anyway, what should the council do next? _____________

Step 3: One legal or public safety career that would have to help enforce my law, and what that person would do:

Career: _____

What they do: _________

(d(1)(C))

Submit your town plan and both drafted laws with this ticket.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a town-plan template with the six Design Your Town questions already printed and one problem row filled in as a model. Sentence frames for the law drafts: "In the town of _, no one may because __. Anyone who breaks this law must _____."
  • Extension: Students who finish early draft a third law that would be genuinely unpopular but necessary (a water restriction, a curfew, a fee) and write two sentences on how they would explain it at a public meeting. A second option: play an iCivics government game ("Counties Work" or "Do I Have a Right?") and compare the decisions the game forces to the laws they just drafted.
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Ordinance = Ordenanza, Council = Concejo, Law = Ley, Fair = Justo, Enforce = Hacer cumplir, Problem = Problema. Allow students to sketch the town instead of writing it and to draft laws in Spanish first. The workbook page reads above grade level, so read the Step 1 role description aloud.

docs.title: Day 4: Policy Showdown — AI in the Courts + Legal Entrepreneurship
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Work the "Policy Showdown" legal review protocol; use a controlled evidence bank to argue for or against a hypothetical court-tool policy; identify one entrepreneurial opportunity and one professional association in the legal field TEKS d(3)(I), d(3)(H) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: Legal Review Team roles and the model policy · Extend: Prepared arguments applied to AI in the courts · Explore: Legal entrepreneur research · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Argument sheet (opening, 3 pieces of evidence, closing) + position statement (5-7 sentences) + Legal Entrepreneur Card (1 career, 4 fields completed) Materials Find Your Future workbook pp. 44-47, Legal Review Argument and Evidence Sheet, Legal Entrepreneur and Association Card, teacher-approved career/association sources, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Should a computer program be allowed to decide whether someone goes to jail? Write your initial reaction in one sentence.

Take 2-3 responses without arguing the question yet. Note who says "yes" and who says "no", you will use this to assign the two lawyer roles in Activity 1.

docs.title: Activity 1: Set Up the Legal Review Team (8 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 44-45: "Policy Showdown", Steps 1-2)

Open the workbook to page 44 and read the frame: before a new policy is approved, it is reviewed by legal experts who examine it from different sides. Some lawyers argue in support, others argue against, and that back-and-forth is what makes a policy clear, realistic, and effective before it takes effect. Students are joining a City Legal Review Team.

Read the workbook's own case as the model so students see what a policy looks like on paper (FYF pp. 44-45). The city problem is rising trash in public parks. The proposed rule requires reusable containers and bottles where possible and discourages single-use plastics. Point at the three parts every policy has: who it applies to (park visitors, food vendors, city-run events), key requirements (vendors offer reusable or compostable alternatives, trash and recycling stations at every main entrance, educational signs), and enforcement (warnings, then fines or loss of permits for repeat vendor violations, no fines for visitors).

Then put today's live policy in front of them, the one this class reviews:

Proposed policy: Courts in this state may use an AI tool to recommend bail amounts and to flag which cases a judge should review first. A judge may follow the recommendation or set it aside. The tool's scoring method is not released to the public.

Treat this as a hypothetical policy for classroom review. Students use the controlled evidence bank rather than making claims about a real court, tool, person, or case.

Students pair up and choose roles (FYF p. 45):

Supporting Lawyer (in favor of the policy) Opposing Lawyer (against the policy) Argues why the policy should be approved Argues why the policy should NOT be approved, or needs major changes Highlights benefits and positive impacts Identifies risks, unfair impacts, or unintended consequences Defends how it helps solve the problem Questions how realistic or effective the policy is

Use the warm-up reactions to assign roles, giving students the side OPPOSITE their initial reaction. Arguing a side you disagree with is the skill the workbook is after.

Sentence stems (project on the board):

  • "I believe AI should/should not be used in the legal system because _____."
  • "One piece of evidence that supports my position is _____."
  • "A real legal career affected by this would be _ because ___."

Facilitation Tip

Tell students upfront: arguing a side you disagree with is a lawyer skill. Lawyers must understand the opposing side's argument to win. This frames the review as practice, not personal opinion.

Frame the debate at the system level, not the personal level

Before the debate starts, name the lens explicitly: today's question is about the technology and system design: whether an AI tool is accurate and fair enough to be part of legal decision-making at all. It is not about any specific case, any specific person, or any student's family. Students in this class may have family members who have interacted with courts, police, or immigration enforcement; keep the debate on the tool, not on who deserves an outcome.

docs.title: Activity 2: Prepare and Present Arguments (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 46-47: "Policy Showdown", Steps 3-4)

Step 3: Prepare Your Arguments. Each lawyer plans a 1-2 minute argument on the printed argument sheet. The workbook's spec has three parts:

  • Opening statement: the main point, and whether the policy should be approved
  • 3 pieces of evidence: each with a specific detail attached, not a general claim
  • Closing statement: a summary and a recommendation to the judge

The workbook's guiding questions transfer directly to today's policy (FYF p. 46):

Supporting Lawyer Opposing Lawyer Why does this policy improve the courts? What problems could this policy create? Who benefits from it and how? Who could it unfairly impact? What parts of the policy make it realistic and fair? What parts make it unrealistic or unfair? Why is a judge keeping the final say enough of a safeguard? Why is a judge keeping the final say not enough of a safeguard?

Step 4: Present Your Argument. Two pairs join up. The second pair acts as the panel of judges. The Supporting Lawyer presents, the Opposing Lawyer presents, and the judges rule: policy is approved, policy needs revision, or policy is rejected. Judges must explain which argument was most convincing and which concerns were most important. Then the two pairs swap so every student both presents and judges.

Time, Voice, Body: Voice 1 for pair preparation, Voice 3 for the lawyer presenting, Voice 0 while the judges confer. Run a visible 6 minute countdown for preparation, then 90 seconds per presenter and 1 minute per ruling, which is the short end of the workbook's 1 to 2 minute range and the only way both pairs get a turn inside the block. Judging pairs sit facing the presenters, and finished argument sheets go in the tray so the desk stays clear.

After the rulings, students write their personal position, which can match or differ from the side they argued.

DOK 4: What criteria would you use to evaluate whether AI should be used in a specific part of the legal system, like determining bail amounts? Consider fairness, accuracy, and ethics in your answer.

docs.title: Activity 3: Legal Entrepreneurship Research (15 min)
docs.text:
Pivot to the Day 4 secondary objective: legal entrepreneurship. Many legal professionals run their own businesses, solo-practice attorneys, mediators, legal consultants, private investigators.

Students complete the Legal Entrepreneur Card (4 fields):

Field Example (Solo-Practice Family Lawyer) Career name Solo-Practice Family Lawyer What the business does Helps families with divorces, custody, adoption Startup needs Law degree, bar license, office space, malpractice insurance One professional association they would join Texas Bar Association or American Bar Association Family Law Section

Each student picks ONE legal career that could include self-employment, contract work, or a small business and completes the card with a teacher-approved source. H&L may supplement the research, but no student needs an open Google search or vendor login to complete the card.

DOK 3: What conclusions can you draw about the risks and rewards of starting your own law practice versus working for a large firm?

docs.title: Exit Ticket (7 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Short Constructed Response — position paper draft) · Printable PDF:

Draft your AI ethics position paper (5-7 sentences). This is a STRUCTURED short response; each numbered point must appear as at least one sentence in your draft.

  1. Position: I believe AI should / should not be used in legal decisions. (Circle one.)

  2. Evidence that supports my position (one piece from today's Policy Showdown or from my Day 1 career research):

  1. One legal career that would be affected by this choice and WHY:
  1. One professional association that might weigh in on this issue (from my Entrepreneur Card research):

(d(3)(I), d(3)(H))

You will polish this draft into the final submission tomorrow.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Pre-filled argument sheets with 2 pieces of evidence already attached per side, so the student supplies the third. Sentence stems posted on each table. Position paper template with fill-in blanks.
  • Extension: Students argue BOTH sides in two separate paragraphs and identify which side has the stronger evidence. They also research a real court case where AI was used (e.g., COMPAS recidivism tool). A second option: run the workbook's own case as written (FYF pp. 44-47), the city park plastic-waste policy, with its full requirements and enforcement rules.
  • ELL: Bilingual argument sentence stems and entrepreneur card. Pre-teach: Policy = Política, Evidence = Evidencia, Judge = Juez, Entrepreneur = Empresario, Association = Asociación. Pair ESL students with bilingual peers, and let the pair prepare in Spanish before presenting.

docs.title: Day 5: Cluster Wrap-Up + Xello Life Experience
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Submit the legal-policy position evidence; complete the required Xello Life experiences task; connect one lived experience to a legal career task TEKS d(1)(C), d(3)(H) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: Position paper polish and submission · Explore: Pathway Possibilities and Law favorites · Extend: Xello Life Experience connections · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Final legal-policy position + Legal Entrepreneur Card + at least one saved Xello Life experience + paper career connection Materials Chromebooks, Xello accounts, position-paper rubric, Xello Life Experience Connection sheet; H&L and eDynamic optional

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: After this week, could you see yourself working in the legal field? Why or why not?

Take 3-4 responses from both sides. A well-supported "no" is useful career information, so ask each student what fact from the week shaped the answer.

docs.title: Activity 1: Polish + Submit Position Paper (10 min)
docs.text:
Students open their AI Ethics Position Paper draft from Day 4. They polish it using a 4-point checklist projected on the board:

  1. Did I clearly state my position in the first sentence?
  2. Did I include at least one piece of evidence?
  3. Did I name at least one specific legal career?
  4. Did I name at least one professional association?

Students submit the polished paper (digital or paper). This is the summative assessment for Week 1.

docs.title: Activity 2: Optional Pathway Browse + Current Career Choice (7 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 58: "App Exploration"), the Pathway Possibilities step

Students name one legal career they want to investigate, or state that none is a current fit, and cite one job detail. If H&L is available, students may use Pathway Possibilities and favorite careers. The platform action is supplemental and is not graded.

Name where this goes next. These favorites and the pathway rating are the top Hats students draw on in the Capstone, where they choose one Hat as a career goal and write why (FYF p. 283: "Rung 2: Career Goal"). The Irving side of the same question is Dual Credit (FYF p. 56), where a Paralegal Associate of Applied Science or a Junior Legal Assistant Certificate at Singley Academy can start in high school.

Circulate and ask each student, "Which legal career did you favorite, and why?" Check that the answer names a specific job detail rather than only "it sounds cool."

Facilitation Tip

Watch for students who favorite a career just because it pays well. Push back: "What about the daily work attracts you?" The Climber Profile is a personal record. Students should be honest, not strategic.

docs.title: Activity 3: Required Xello Life Experiences (10 min)
docs.text:
Open Xello and direct students to the required Grade 8 Life experiences task. The configured minimum is one saved experience. Students may choose an experience from home, school, a club, a team, a hobby, or volunteering without disclosing private details.

Students complete the activity in Xello and answer the reflection prompts. They look for connections between their lived experiences and the legal careers they explored this week, for example, a student who has resolved sibling arguments has experience with mediation; a student who reads carefully has experience that connects to paralegal work.

After completing the Xello activity, each student writes one sentence in their notebook: "One life experience I have that connects to a legal career is _ because ___."

DOK 3: Think about your finished Position Paper. Which single revision from today would most change how a skeptical reader, someone who disagrees with your position, evaluates your argument? Explain why that revision is more persuasive than the others you made.

docs.title: Activity 4: Experience-to-Career Connection and Catch-Up (15 min)
docs.text: Students complete the paper connection: what they did or learned, one legal career, and the specific career task that connects. Check the Xello Completion Standards report. Students with an access issue submit the paper connection now and complete the required save in the next supervised catch-up block.

docs.title: Optional Extension: eDynamic Unit 5.1 Preview
docs.text:
Use this only inside the Activity 4 catch-up block after all core evidence is complete.

Direct students to eDynamic Learning Unit 5.1: Law & Order. Have them open the unit and read the introduction (5 minutes). This is a preview only. They will not complete the unit today. Tomorrow's class (Wk 2) will pick up first responders using the same workbook chapter, with the "Clinton Lake Case" and "Injured on the Trail" activities (FYF pp. 48-49 and 52-55), and eDynamic 5.1 supports that content.

[VERIFY IN eDynamic] Confirm the title of Unit 5.1 in eDynamic Learning is "Law & Order" and that it covers law enforcement, courts, and corrections topics suitable for 7th-grade Health Science / Law cluster framing.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Concept Map / Connection Diagram) · Printable PDF:

The legal career I favorited in H&L this week: _____

Connect this career to THREE things:

1. A professional association this career would join (Texas Bar Association, American Bar Association, NALA for paralegals, NCRA for court reporters, or other)

My association: _____. In one sentence, why would this career join that specific association?

2. One of MY Xello Life Experience connections from today (a real experience I have that connects to legal work)

My experience: _____. In one sentence, how does this experience prepare me for the favorited career?

3. An Irving ISD program of study that connects (Legal Studies at Singley, Criminal Justice, or another Irving ISD program that touches the legal field)

My program of study: _____. In one sentence, does the Irving ISD program lead DIRECTLY to my favorited career, or is it a STEPPING STONE? Explain.

(d(1)(C), d(3)(H))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a sentence-completion handout for the Xello reflection: "A life experience I have is _. This connects to the career of because __."
  • Extension: Students draft a 4-year high school plan for the Singley Academy Legal Studies program of study, listing the courses they would take in 9th-12th grade and where a Dual Credit course could fit (FYF p. 56).
  • ELL: Pair ESL students with bilingual peers for the Xello Life Experience. Pre-teach: Experience = Experiencia, Volunteer = Voluntario, Skill = Habilidad. Xello has built-in Spanish translation for activity prompts.

docs.title: Week 1: Order in the Court — Legal Careers
docs.text: 2nd Six Weeks | Law, Public Safety, Corrections & Security Cluster | 5 class periods (50 min each)

docs.title: Lesson Objective
docs.text:
Students explore the Law, Public Safety, Corrections & Security career cluster through the Hats & Ladders app and the Find Your Future workbook, investigate legal careers and their education pathways, design a 10-item emergency kit in "Emergency Essentials: Kit Design," draft and revise town ordinances as a council member in "City Council in Action," and use the "Policy Showdown" legal review protocol to argue a position on artificial intelligence in the courts. Students connect legal careers to Irving ISD's Legal Studies program of study at Singley Academy.

Learning Target: I can name at least three legal careers and the training each one needs, design an emergency kit and defend my choices, write two town laws that are clear, fair, and realistic, and argue a position on AI in the courts using evidence.

Success Criteria: I will know I am successful when my career research worksheet lists the job, the training, the pay, and the tools for one legal career, when my emergency kit shows 10 labeled items with a reason for my top 3, when both of my town laws answer what the law is, why it is needed, and what happens if someone breaks it, and when my position paper names one legal career and one professional association affected by AI in the courts.

docs.title: Demonstration of Learning
docs.text: "I can describe at least three careers in the legal field, explain the education pathway from middle school to becoming a lawyer or paralegal, design an emergency kit using critical thinking, draft a town law that is clear, fair, and realistic, and argue a position on AI in the legal system using evidence."

docs.title: TEKS Alignment
docs.text:
• d(1)(B): Explore and describe the CTE career clusters (Day 1).
  • d(1)(C): Identify various career opportunities within one or more career clusters (Days 1-3, 5).
  • d(3)(I): Define entrepreneurship and identify entrepreneurial opportunities within a field of personal interest (Day 4 Legal Entrepreneur Card).
  • d(3)(H): Identify professional associations affiliated with a particular career pathway (Days 4-5).

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Chromebooks with internet access (1 per student)
  • Hats & Ladders student accounts + Find Your Future workbook, Law and Public Safety chapter (printed pp. 39-58)
  • Printed Career Research Worksheet
  • Printed Emergency Kit Decision Plan
  • Printed City Council Town and Ordinance Plan
  • Printed Legal Review Argument and Evidence Sheet
  • Printed Legal Entrepreneur and Association Card
  • Printed Legal Policy Position Paper Rubric
  • Printed Xello Life Experience Connection
  • BLS, Lawyers: bls.gov/ooh/legal/lawyers.htm
  • BLS, Paralegals: bls.gov/ooh/legal/paralegals-and-legal-assistants.htm
  • iCivics free games (Day 3 extension and support option): icivics.org
  • eDynamic Learning Unit 5.1: Law & Order
  • Xello accounts (Life Experience activity)
  • Projector for video and discussion

docs.title: Career Connection
docs.text:
The legal field includes courtroom attorneys, paralegals who prepare case documents, mediators, consultants, and attorneys who run solo practices. The Law and Public Safety cluster reaches beyond the courtroom to city council members who write local law, firefighters and paramedics who respond to emergencies, and wardens who enforce environmental rules. That range is why this week includes both a law-drafting activity and an emergency kit design.

What is Happening at Irving ISD? The workbook's district pages (FYF pp. 56-57: "What is Happening at My District?") name two Irving ISD programs of study for this cluster. Legal Studies builds legal research, legal writing, rules of procedure, case management, law office technology, and legal ethics, with concentrations in criminal, family, and workplace law. Criminal Justice builds criminal law, investigation, and appropriate legal response to violations, and covers the history, organization, and functions of local, state, and federal law enforcement. Students in the Legal Studies program at Singley Academy work in a replica courtroom and run mock trials as defense attorneys, prosecutors, and judges. The related industry certification is Non-Commissioned Security Officer Level 2, and the student organizations are Explorers and Mock Trial. The district pages also introduce Dual Credit, which lets a high school student earn college credit in the same course. Two local dual credit options are the Paralegal Associate of Applied Science and the Junior Legal Assistant Certificate, both at Singley Academy.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text:
• Paralegal: A professional who assists lawyers with legal research, document preparation, and case management. Does not require a law degree.
  • Probable Cause: A reasonable basis to believe a crime may have been committed, allowing legal action like an arrest or search.
  • Due Process: The legal requirement that the government must respect all legal rights owed to a person.
  • Bar Association: A professional association for lawyers. Most states require lawyers to pass the Bar Exam to practice law.
  • Entrepreneur (Legal): A person who starts their own legal business, solo practice, mediation firm, or legal consulting.
  • Emergency Kit: A pre-packed set of essential supplies designed to help people survive a disaster or emergency for 72 hours.
  • Ordinance: A local law passed by a city or town council. A strong ordinance is clear, fair, and realistic enough to enforce (FYF p. 40).
  • Policy: A written rule an organization or a city adopts to solve a problem. Legal review teams argue for and against a policy before it is approved (FYF p. 44).

docs.title: Bridge to Theory (Hats & Ladders)
docs.text:
The Find Your Future workbook gives Law and Public Safety printed pages 39-58. The chapter opener (FYF p. 39: "Exploring the World of LAW AND PUBLIC SAFETY") frames the cluster as fast action paired with careful decision-making: some roles respond in the moment during emergencies, while others investigate, analyze, and piece together what happened. Three Hats appear on the opener page, Judge, Firefighter, and Fish and Game Warden, above a "Be the Decision Maker" prompt that puts students in a city safety inspector's shoes on the opening night of a music festival. The chapter prints no pathway list. Students meet the pathways in the Hats & Ladders app through the Pathway Possibilities step on the App Exploration page (FYF p. 58: "App Exploration"), and they meet Irving ISD's own programs of study on the district pages (FYF pp. 56-57).

This week uses three chapter activities:

  • Emergency Essentials: Kit Design (Day 2): Career Climb activity. Students are a firefighter building a kit citizens can grab during an emergency. They choose an earthquake, fire, or flood scenario, select exactly 10 items from the workbook's 24-item list, draw and label the kit, and share the design with a partner who chose a different scenario (FYF pp. 50-51: "Emergency Essentials: Kit Design").
  • City Council in Action (Day 3): Career Climb activity. Students are a council member for a brand new town. They design the town, scan it for problems in four areas, draft two ordinances that each answer what the law is, why it is needed, and what happens if someone breaks it, then peer-review a partner's laws and revise one (FYF pp. 40-43: "City Council in Action").
  • Policy Showdown (Day 4): Career Climb activity. Students join a City Legal Review Team, split into a Supporting Lawyer and an Opposing Lawyer, prepare a one to two minute argument built from an opening statement, three pieces of evidence, and a closing statement, then present to a peer pair acting as judges who approve the policy, send it back for revision, or reject it (FYF pp. 44-47: "Policy Showdown").

The chapter's other two activities, Clinton Lake Case (FYF pp. 48-49) and Injured on the Trail (FYF pp. 52-55), belong to Wk 2 First Responders, which shares this chapter. Preview them on Day 5 rather than running them here. The Law and Public Safety chapter carries no Powerskill lesson.

docs.title: IISD Instructional Strategies
docs.text:
• Think-Pair-Share: Day 1, Activity 1, the "Be the Decision Maker" prompt on the chapter opener (FYF p. 39), where a city safety inspector must let a music festival start, delay it, or shut it down after the main stage begins shaking. Distinguished: pose it to the whole group, hold a silent 30 second Think, then time Partner A for 30 seconds and Partner B for 30 seconds, and post two stems at different levels: "I would _ because " and "Delaying costs the city __, but letting the show go on risks _____." Ask two pairs to share, not one. Listen while pairs talk for who names what information they would go get before deciding, and pick your share-out pairs from what you heard rather than from raised hands. Close by asking who would rather argue the call in front of a crowd and who would rather be the one who checked the paperwork beforehand, which is the first sort students make between courtroom and behind-the-scenes legal work.
  • Stop and Jot: Day 1, Activity 2, the two pauses during the Law and Public Safety cluster tour video. Distinguished: name both stop points before the video starts, give 45 seconds per jot with the prompt on screen, and offer two stems: "One legal or public safety career I had never heard of is _" and "One thing I still want to know about is __." Read jots over shoulders during both pauses and track which careers get named. If most jots say Lawyer only, steer the Hat browse that follows toward Court Reporter, Paralegal, 911 Dispatcher, and Fish and Game Warden so the research worksheets are not four copies of the same career.
  • Active Monitoring: Day 3, Activity 2, the three stages of "City Council in Action." Distinguished: walk a fixed pathway three times, one lap per stage, each lap with a single target (town named with a climate and a way people get around, all four rows of the problem table filled, both laws carrying a what, a why, and a consequence), marking a clipboard roster as you go. Have the feedback ready for the two known misconceptions before class starts: a "law" written as a wish rather than a rule ("everyone should be nice at the skatepark"), and a consequence nobody could actually enforce. If more than a handful of students miss the second target, pivot and model one problem row on the projector for the whole room instead of coaching desk by desk.
  • Chunking: Day 2, Activities 1 through 3, the four steps of "Emergency Essentials: Kit Design." Distinguished: release one step at a time, say what each step is for before releasing it (the scenario decides the kit, the list decides the trade-offs, the drawing proves a stranger could use it, the partner share tests it), and close each chunk with a quick check before the next one opens. Read the 10-item lists after the second chunk. If most kits are stacked with comfort items, re-teach with the workbook's own line that an item helping in one scenario may not be as effective in another, then reopen the list before students start drawing.
  • Time, Voice, Body (TVB): Day 4, Activity 2, the prepare-and-present rotation. Distinguished: post the three blocks before the first pair prepares, Voice 1 for partner prep, Voice 3 for the lawyer presenting, and Voice 0 while the judging pair confers, with a visible 6 minute countdown for preparation, then 90 seconds per presenter and 1 minute per ruling. Post the two position stems from the plan where every pair can see them, and define where the judging pair sits and where finished argument sheets go so transitions do not eat presenting time. Narrate the pairs who are meeting the expectation rather than correcting the ones who are not. If the first rotation runs long, cut the judges to one question each and announce the change before the next pair starts.

docs.title: Week at a Glance
docs.text: Day Focus Key Activities Deliverable 5E 1 Law and Public Safety Cluster Tour Chapter opener read-along + Be the Decision Maker pair talk + Law cluster app exploration + legal career research Career research worksheet (1 legal career) + Stop and Jot notes Engage · Explain · Explore · Evaluate 2 Emergency Essentials Kit Design "Emergency Essentials: Kit Design" (FYF pp. 50-51): 10-item kit, labeled design, partner share Completed Emergency Kit design Engage · Explore · Explain · Evaluate 3 City Council in Action "City Council in Action" (FYF pp. 40-43): town design, problem scan, two drafted ordinances, partner review Town plan + 2 drafted laws + 1 revised law Engage · Explain · Explore · Evaluate 4 Policy Showdown + Legal Entrepreneurship Legal Review Team roles + argument judged by a peer pair + Legal Entrepreneur Card Argument sheet + Legal Entrepreneur Card + position paper draft Engage · Explain · Extend · Explore · Evaluate 5 Cluster Wrap-Up + Xello Life Experience Position paper polish + Pathway Possibilities + Law favorites + Xello Life Experience + eDynamic 5.1 preview Final Position Paper + updated Climber Profile + Xello reflection Engage · Explain · Explore · Extend · Evaluate

docs.title: Formative Assessment
docs.text:
• Legal career research worksheet + Comparison Matrix exit ticket (2 legal careers x education/salary/task). Day 1, d(1)(B), d(1)(C)
  • Emergency Kit design + Ranked Justification exit ticket (top 3 items ranked by criticality). Day 2, d(1)(C)
  • Two drafted ordinances + one revised law + Decision Tree exit ticket (enforcement branch). Day 3, d(1)(C)
  • Prepared legal argument + judges' ruling + SCR position paper draft (position, evidence, affected career, association). Day 4, d(3)(I), d(3)(H)
  • H&L Favorites + Xello Life Experience + Concept Map exit ticket (career + association + Life Experience + Irving ISD program of study). Day 5, d(1)(C), d(3)(H)

docs.title: Summative Assessment
docs.text: Legal Policy Position Evidence (Day 4-5): Students use a controlled hypothetical and evidence bank to write a 5-7 sentence position, explain one affected legal career, and complete a Legal Entrepreneur and Association Card. One 16-point rubric scores the durable written evidence. Assigned-side speaking, H&L access, and Xello login success are not part of the major grade.

docs.title: Scaffolded Learning
docs.text:
• Pre-filled legal career research worksheet with one career (Court Reporter) modeled
  • Emergency Kit worksheet with the 3 workbook scenarios listed and 3 items pre-suggested
  • Town-plan template for Day 3 with the six Design Your Town questions already printed and one problem row filled in as a model
  • Sentence stems for the Day 4 legal review and the position paper

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
• Research a famous Supreme Court case and identify the different legal professionals who contributed
  • Build a 4-year plan for the Singley Academy Legal Studies program of study
  • Compare the 10-item Emergency Kit for two different scenarios (earthquake vs. flood): what changes and why?
  • Compare salaries of three legal careers across Texas, California, and New York using BLS state data
  • Run the workbook's own Policy Showdown case as written (FYF pp. 44-47): the city park plastic-waste policy, with its own requirements and enforcement rules
  • Play an iCivics courtroom or county-government game ("Do I Have a Right?", "Argument Wars", "Counties Work") and compare the decisions the game forces to the laws drafted on Day 3

docs.title: ELL Language Support
docs.text:
• Pre-teach: Lawyer = Abogado, Paralegal = Asistente Legal, Judge = Juez, Due Process = Debido Proceso, Ordinance = Ordenanza, Emergency = Emergencia, Kit = Equipo
  • Bilingual emergency kit item list (Flashlight = Linterna, First Aid Kit = Botiquín, Whistle = Silbato)
  • Bilingual law-drafting and argument sentence stems
  • The workbook reads well above grade level, so read the scenario paragraphs aloud on Days 2, 3, and 4 and encourage browser translation for any independent reading

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objective Compare daily work and preparation for five first-responder careers; connect two careers to current Singley Academy pathways TEKS d(1)(B), d(1)(C), d(2)(A) Deliverable Three completed comparison rows and two evidence-based responses Materials First Responder Route Guide, FYF pp. 56-58, current Singley Academy CTE page, optional Xello/H&L

docs.title: Before Class
docs.text: Open the dated route guide and the current Irving ISD Singley Academy page. If offering Xello or H&L, preflight it on the student network. Do not make a vendor login the only research route.

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text: If someone calls 911, which workers may be involved before, during, and after responders reach the scene? Students list roles, then sort them into call-taking, response, care, investigation, and documentation.

docs.title: Activity 1: Read the Numbers Correctly (8 min)
docs.text:
Model the difference between a national median, a local estimate, and a starting salary. Students annotate the route guide:

  1. circle the data year;
  2. underline the geography;
  3. box the word median; and
  4. write “not a starting-pay promise” beside the table.

docs.title: Activity 2: Compare Three Careers (22 min)
docs.text:
Students choose three careers and complete the table. Pause after the first row to check that each student has one daily task, one preparation step, and an accurate explanation of what the median does and does not show.

Active monitoring: reject fixed promises such as “every academy lasts six months” or “all EMT programs take twelve weeks.” Accept routes that preserve the source language: requirements vary by agency, state, or locality.

docs.title: Activity 3: Connect to Irving (10 min)
docs.text:
Students use the current district page and FYF district spread to connect Law Enforcement and Emergency Medical - EMT to one career each. Make clear that a program is an opportunity to investigate, not a guaranteed job or credential.

Optional Xello extension: add one current local figure with career, geography, date checked, and whether the display is a range, median, or another measure.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Ranked Justification) · Printable PDF:

Rank the three careers from most to least preparation after high school. Defend the top ranking with one route-guide detail.

docs.title: Supports and Fallbacks
docs.text:
• Pre-teach route, academy, license, certification, median, and locality.
  • Use the frame: “This career commonly requires ; the source says requirements vary by .”
  • Students may compare two careers first, then add the third.
  • If all sites are unavailable, the route guide contains the complete required evidence.

docs.title: Day 2: Clinton Lake — Weigh the Evidence
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objective Separate observations from claims, assess source limits, and write a conclusion that uses three files and names an uncertainty TEKS d(1)(C), d(4)(F) Deliverable Clinton Lake Evidence Tracker Materials FYF pp. 48-49; Climber Notes “Clinton Lake Case,” slides 2-7, embedded in locked Canvas

docs.title: Before Class
docs.text: Open all six Canvas evidence images. Keep the teacher guidance below out of the student page. Students need readable individual images or text descriptions; a single projected montage is not sufficient.

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text: A lake is polluted. Which question must investigators answer before naming a cause? Sort responses into harm, timing, source, and missing test.

docs.title: Activity 1: Evidence Routine (7 min)
docs.text: Teach four questions: What does the file directly show? Who produced it? What can it not prove? How strongly does it address the case question?

docs.title: Activity 2: Six-File Review (23 min)
docs.text: Students review each Canvas image and complete one tracker row at a time. Pause after Files 2 and 4 so students do not treat an inspection note or public statement as independent proof.

docs.title: Activity 3: Careful Conclusion (10 min)
docs.text: Students choose the two strongest harm files, one source-related file, and one evidence gap. Their conclusion may support a landfill cause, an outside cause, mixed causes, or insufficient evidence.

docs.title: Teacher Answer Guidance
docs.text:
• Files 1 and 6 strongly show serious pollution/ecological harm.
  • File 3 documents a major storm; File 5 raises possible illegal dumping. Both support plausible outside or mixed causes, not certainty.
  • File 2 reports routine landfill conditions but is limited and partly relies on an older major check.
  • File 4 is the City's own statement. Its lack of confirmed containment testing weakens confidence but does not prove leakage.
  • No file directly documents a containment failure. A defensible conclusion must preserve that gap.

Integrity here means reporting inconvenient evidence and source limits. Do not tell students that one classroom rule settles every real legal disclosure duty.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Mini-Case) · Printable PDF:

An investigator omits File 5 because it complicates the team's theory. Identify the integrity problem and the professional next step.

docs.title: Supports and Fallbacks
docs.text:
• Pre-teach evidence/evidencia, claim/afirmación, source/fuente, reliable/confiable, uncertain/incierto.
  • Read each file aloud and let students highlight before paraphrasing.
  • A private written conclusion is equal to discussion. An absent student uses all six embedded files independently.

docs.title: Day 3: Injured on the Trail — Controlled Simulation
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objective Describe SAR/WFR responsibilities and demonstrate safe communication, consent, observation, and documentation in a career simulation TEKS d(1)(C) Deliverable Injured on the Trail Simulation Record Materials FYF pp. 52-53; Climber Notes slides 2-3; optional triangular bandage, cohesive wrap, and finger-splint model; mannequin/dowel/paper-model route

docs.title: Non-Negotiable Safety Boundary
docs.text: This is career role-play, not first-aid certification or real treatment. Never practice on an injury. Do not straighten, pull, reduce, or force a body part. Offer three equal routes before grouping: model/mannequin, consenting uninjured partner, or observer/documenter. Stop for pain, numbness, tingling, color change, distress, or a request to stop. Route real injuries to the nurse/911 process.

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text: What makes a remote emergency different from one beside a hospital? Listen for distance, communication, weather, terrain, supplies, and time.

docs.title: Activity 1: Career Research (12 min)
docs.text: Students answer the three questions on the simulation record using the embedded workbook/deck and teacher-approved career sources. H&L may supplement but is not required.

docs.title: Activity 2: Materials and Boundaries (10 min)
docs.text: Use the Climber Notes supply table and image slide. Explain what each material represents. The slide's left image is the triangular-bandage example; the right image is the finger-splint example. Model permission, narration, loose placement, a comfort check, and an immediate stop.

docs.title: Activity 3: Two Short Rounds (18 min)
docs.text:
Round 1: one learner narrates and handles the model materials; the observer records. Pause for one safety or communication improvement. Round 2: switch roles when appropriate or repeat with the documented improvement. No learner is required to be touched.

Active monitoring: score permission, clear explanation, gentle/no-force handling, loose placement, comfort check, and response to feedback. Do not certify a medical technique.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Decision Tree / Branching Prompt) · Printable PDF:

A learner reports tingling after a wrap is placed. What happens next? Correct route: stop, remove or loosen the simulation material, check the learner, and notify the teacher; do not continue the practice round.

docs.title: Supports and Fallbacks
docs.text:
• Use a labeled picture card and read the boundary aloud before materials move.
  • A student may narrate, point, sketch, or document rather than handle materials.
  • No supplies: use a paper arm/finger model and describe placement. Absence: complete the record from the Canvas images.

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objective Write an accurate fictional Patient Care Report and choose a safety-first response to one wilderness complication TEKS d(1)(C), d(4)(F) Deliverable Fictional Patient Care Report and Safety Plan Scoring Patient Care Report Evidence Rubric Materials FYF pp. 53-54 and the locked Canvas trail images

docs.title: Before Class
docs.text: Post the report, rubric, and three complication choices. This is fictional documentation: students must not enter real names or medical information. Speaking is optional; each student submits written evidence.

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text: A receiving team gets a patient but no notes. What information is missing? Sort answers into scene, observations, actions, reasoning, and handoff.

docs.title: Activity 1: Patient Care Report (20 min)
docs.text: Students complete all five sections. Require observations instead of diagnoses. “The scenario shows a swollen, bent finger” is appropriate; inventing a specific fracture is not.

docs.title: Activity 2: Safety-First Complication (15 min)
docs.text:
Students choose thunderstorm, anxious patient, or fast-moving stream and plan a first action, communication, reassessment trigger, and alternative.

Answer guidance:

  • thunder: move toward a substantial enclosed building or hard-topped vehicle and stop outdoor activity; do not shelter under a tree or small open shelter;
  • fast/unknown water: do not enter; communicate, seek an alternate route or higher ground, and wait for trained help;
  • anxiety: use calm, honest communication, explain the plan, and offer reasonable choices without false promises.

docs.title: Activity 3: Review and Revise (7 min)
docs.text: Students use the four rubric criteria. Peer review may be replaced with a self-check or private teacher conference. A student revises one sentence for accuracy or safety.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Trade-off Dilemma) · Printable PDF:

Explain why entering fast water to save time creates a worse risk. Name the safer action and one fact dispatch needs.

docs.title: Supports and Fallbacks
docs.text:
• Provide sentence frames: “I observed ”; “Our team represented ”; “We would stop and reassess if ___.”
  • Permit speech-to-text or teacher scribing. Grade evidence, not English mechanics unless meaning is unclear.
  • An absent student completes the same report from the fictional scenario. No live simulation is required.

docs.title: Day 5: Career Decision and Integrity Reflection
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objective Complete the career comparison, synthesize week evidence, and explain how accurate reporting protects people TEKS d(1)(C), d(2)(A), d(4)(F) Deliverable First Responder Career and Integrity Reflection plus completed route guide Materials Day 1 route guide, Day 2 tracker, Day 4 report, FYF p. 58; optional Xello/H&L/Roadtrip Nation

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text: Interested, unsure, or not interested? Students choose privately and name one job-detail reason. “Not interested” is a valid informed outcome.

docs.title: Activity 1: Finish and Check Career Evidence (12 min)
docs.text: Students finish the three-route comparison and correct any claim that treats a national median as DFW starting pay. Detective is not a separate guaranteed time ladder: the BLS notes that detectives typically begin as police officers and gain experience.

docs.title: Activity 2: Integrity Across the Week (10 min)
docs.text: Build a class list of information people rely on: evidence files, scene observations, actions taken, handoff facts, and source labels. Students identify what could happen if one item were hidden, changed, or left undocumented.

docs.title: Activity 3: Individual Reflection (18 min)
docs.text:
Students complete all five prompts. Require one route fact, one work fact, one integrity moment, and one realistic next step. Do not require a particular career choice, public disclosure, or platform favorite.

Optional exploration after core evidence is complete: students may review the FYF App Exploration page, open H&L, or use Xello to investigate a local career figure. No required Grade 8 Xello completion standard is assigned in this week.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Concept Map / Connection Diagram) · Printable PDF:

Connect accurate information to one first-responder task, one person who depends on it, and one possible consequence of an inaccurate record.

docs.title: Teacher Check
docs.text: Collect the individual reflection and route guide. The Day 4 report is the week's durable 16-point evidence set; do not create another major grade from platform clicks or this reflection unless the six-weeks grade map needs it.

docs.title: Supports and Fallbacks
docs.text:
• Provide a vocabulary bank: route, responsibility, observation, handoff, integrity, reassess.
  • Let students rehearse with a partner but submit their own evidence.
  • The paper/Canvas reflection is the normal route. H&L, Xello, and a video may be omitted without losing the target.

docs.title: Week 2: First Responders — Evidence, Response, and Handoff
docs.text: 2nd Six Weeks | Law, Public Safety, Corrections & Security | 5 class periods (50 minutes each)

docs.title: Week at a Glance
docs.text:
Students compare five first-responder careers with a dated route guide, investigate the fictional Clinton Lake case, run a controlled trail-response simulation, and write a fictional Patient Care Report with a safety-first complication plan. The week ends with an individual career and integrity reflection.

Hats & Ladders and Xello may extend career exploration. Neither platform is required to complete the core evidence.

Learning target: I can compare first-responder routes, separate evidence from claims, document a fictional response accurately, and explain why integrity matters when other people rely on a professional's information.

Success criteria:

  • compare at least three careers using correctly labeled preparation and pay evidence;
  • use three Clinton Lake files and name an important uncertainty;
  • follow the trail simulation boundary or complete the equal observer/documenter route;
  • write all five sections of a fictional Patient Care Report; and
  • use week evidence to explain one career decision and one integrity risk.

docs.title: TEKS Alignment
docs.text:
• d(1)(B): Explore and describe a CTE career cluster (Day 1).
  • d(1)(C): Identify career opportunities within a cluster (Days 1, 3, 4, and 5).
  • d(2)(A): Research and describe academic, technical, certification, and training requirements (Days 1 and 5).
  • d(4)(F): Identify work ethic, integrity, dedication, and perseverance in professional decisions (Days 2, 4, and 5).

docs.title: Teacher-Ready Materials
docs.text:
• First Responder Route Guide
  • Clinton Lake Evidence Tracker
  • Injured on the Trail Simulation Record
  • Fictional Patient Care Report and Safety Plan
  • Patient Care Report Evidence Rubric
  • First Responder Career and Integrity Reflection
  • Find Your Future pp. 48-58 and Climber Notes decks “Clinton Lake Case” and “Injured on the Trail,” embedded only in authenticated Canvas

docs.title: Source-Control Notes
docs.text:
• Pay figures in the route guide are May 2024 U.S. medians, not starting salaries or DFW guarantees. Students may add a current Xello local figure only when they record geography, date, and salary type.
  • The current Irving ISD Singley Academy page lists Law Enforcement and Emergency Medical - EMT. Requirements and certifications must be rechecked before promising a specific credential.
  • The trail activity is a classroom simulation, not medical training or certification. Students never practice on an injury. A model, mannequin, or observer/documenter route earns the same credit.
  • The Clinton Lake packet does not prove one cause. Strong work distinguishes pollution evidence, possible-source evidence, source limits, and what investigators still need.

docs.title: Five-Day Sequence
docs.text: Day Focus Durable evidence 1 Career routes and Singley connections Three-route comparison 2 Clinton Lake evidence Six-file tracker and careful conclusion 3 Trail-response career simulation Research and simulation record 4 Patient report and complication Individual report and safety plan 5 Career and integrity synthesis Individual reflection

docs.title: Grading
docs.text: The Patient Care Report and complication plan form one 16-point durable evidence set. Score each student's writing with the district bands in the rubric. Do not grade platform access, willingness to be touched, physical technique, artistic presentation, or public speaking. The other artifacts are formative/minor candidates when the campus gradebook structure is confirmed.

docs.title: Access and Participation
docs.text:
• Keep all required directions visible; use Canvas accordions only for optional help.
  • Read case files aloud or provide their Canvas text descriptions. Students may annotate digitally or on paper.
  • Permit speech-to-text, oral rehearsal, labeled sketches, and teacher-scribed responses when documented.
  • Provide the observer/documenter role before students are asked to choose a simulation route.
  • An absent student uses the same embedded files and completes written evidence independently. No partner or vendor login is required.

docs.title: Day 1: Health Science Cluster + CNA / LVN
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Read the Health Science chapter opener and work the Be the Decision Maker prompt with a partner; explore the Health Science cluster in the H&L app; complete a career research worksheet for one nursing Hat; begin the Nursing Career Ladder worksheet (CNA + LVN rows) TEKS d(1)(B), d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up and Be the Decision Maker · Explain: Irving ISD programs of study walkthrough · Explore: App Exploration, Stop and Jot, and career research · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Career research worksheet (1 nursing career) + Nursing Career Ladder worksheet with CNA and LVN rows complete Materials Chromebooks, H&L accounts, Find Your Future workbook pp. 59, 84-86, printed career research worksheet, printed Nursing Career Ladder worksheet, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Name every type of healthcare worker you can think of in 60 seconds. How many did you get?

Take a quick whip-around and count the distinct careers students name. Most classes stop around 5-10, while Health Science contains more than 200. Today students begin sorting that larger field into pathways and job types.

docs.title: Activity 1: Exploring the World of Health Science (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 59: "Exploring the World of HEALTH SCIENCE")

Open the workbook to page 59. Read the chapter opener together: Health Science is about helping people stay healthy, recover from illness, and improve their quality of life, and the people who do it work in hospitals, laboratories, clinics, and community spaces. Some of them give direct patient care while others study diseases, develop treatments, or help people build healthier habits. Point to the three Hats printed on the opener page: MRI Technologist, Pediatrician, and Dentist, then ask the page's closing question: what strengths or values do you think people in these roles might need?

Tell students this is the start of a four-week run through Health Science (Wk 3 nursing, Wk 4 dental and medical billing, Wk 5 powerskills, Wk 6 biomedical).

The chapter does not print a pathway list. Walk through the five Health Science programs of study Irving ISD actually runs, from the district pages (FYF pp. 84-85: "What is Happening at My District?"):

  1. Patient Care Technician: direct patient care, monitoring vital signs, assisting with daily living activities, and supporting medical staff through clinical experiences. This is the nursing week's home.
  2. Medical Billing & Coding: health care administration, medical coding systems, insurance processes, documentation, and reimbursement.
  3. Dental Assistant: chairside assisting, sterilization techniques, and patient care in clinical settings.
  4. Emergency Medical Technician (EMT): emergency response, patient assessment, trauma care, and life-saving techniques.
  5. Biomedical Sciences: human body systems, disease, medical research and treatment, and laboratory procedures.

Point out that Health Science students at Singley Academy job-shadow at local hospitals and dental offices, and that the labs there use programmable patient simulators whose manikins display changing vital signs. That is the professional version of the monitor students build on Day 3.

Be the Decision Maker (FYF p. 59): Read the opener's boxed prompt aloud. Students are helping create a health fair for families in their community. What would they include to help people learn about healthy habits, exercise, nutrition, or mental wellness in a way that is fun and memorable?

Think-Pair-Share: 30 seconds of silent Think, then Partner A for 30 seconds, then Partner B for 30 seconds. Post two stems so every pair has a way in: "One booth I would set up is _ because " and "Families would remember __ better than a poster because _____." Call on two pairs to share, chosen from what you heard while circulating rather than from raised hands. Listen for pairs who name the health worker who would staff the booth, not just the activity.

Facilitation Tip

The health fair prompt is the bridge to Day 3's micro:bit project. When a pair proposes a blood pressure check or a temperature station, highlight that those tools are electronic and someone PROGRAMMED them to work. That is the connection to the vital signs monitor build.

docs.title: Activity 2: Health Science App Exploration + Career Research (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 86: "App Exploration") + CCE career research worksheet

Nursing is not one career. It is a ladder. A CNA certification takes 4 to 12 weeks, and the same field climbs all the way to Nurse Practitioner with a doctoral degree. Each step up means more education, more responsibility, and more money. Frame the app browse with that idea before students open their Chromebooks.

[H&L PLATFORM] The App Exploration page walks students through the cluster in order. Today they do the first half: open the Hats & Ladders app, go to Clusters, click the Health Science Cluster, watch the "Cluster Tour" video, play "Game Time" and write down one thing they learned, then open "Pathway Possibilities," answer its questions, and rate at least 1 pathway. Students record their answers on workbook page 86. The rest of the page, the fit and non-fit Hats and the 3 Hat ratings, finishes on Day 5.

Stop and Jot procedure: While watching the cluster tour video, students pause TWICE in their engineering notebook (dated entry, labeled "2SW Wk3 Health Science") to write (1) one healthcare career that surprised them and (2) one question they still have about the cluster.

Then students use the Hat Finder to look at the four nursing Hats specifically: CNA, LVN, RN, Nurse Practitioner, noting the education path and DFW salary for each. Each student picks ONE nursing career and completes the printed career research worksheet. This is the same six-field format students learned in Wk0, so name the connection rather than reteaching it:

  • Name of Career
  • What Interests You?
  • Brief Job Description
  • Education/Training Needed
  • Average Salary
  • What Tools, Equipment, or Skills are Needed for This Career?

Students pull each field from the Hat's profile in the app, then confirm the salary and training figures against at least one additional source, such as the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook.

docs.title: Activity 3: Begin the Nursing Career Ladder Worksheet (12 min)
docs.text:
Distribute the Nursing Career Ladder worksheet. The worksheet has 4 rows (one per level) and 5 columns:

Level Education Time to Complete DFW Salary One Daily Task

Walk students through the CNA row as a worked example on the projector:

  • Level: CNA (Certified Nursing Assistant)
  • Education: State-approved CNA certification program
  • Time to Complete: 4-12 weeks
  • DFW Salary: ~$30K-$35K (BLS)
  • One Daily Task: Help patients with bathing, feeding, mobility

Students then complete the LVN row independently using H&L Hat Finder data and BLS supplements.

DOK 2: How would you describe the difference between a CNA and an LVN in terms of what they do each day?

Facilitation Tip

Some students will get stuck on the difference between LVN and LPN. Tell them: "LVN = Licensed Vocational Nurse (Texas term). LPN = Licensed Practical Nurse (other states). Same job, different name." This is a Texas-specific vocabulary item.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Comparison Matrix) · Printable PDF:

Compare TWO nursing career ladder levels you explored today (CNA or LVN).

CNA LVN Training time DFW salary (rough) One daily task

Bottom line: A 19-year-old who needs to start earning money quickly should pick CNA or LVN? Circle one, then use one specific cell from the matrix to explain. Submit your career research worksheet with this ticket. (d(1)(B), d(1)(C))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a CNA-modeled career research worksheet so students see the level of detail expected. Allow voice-to-text for students who struggle with writing. Provide a Stop and Jot template with sentence stems: "One healthcare career I did not expect is _. One question I have is ___."
  • Extension: Students complete TWO career research worksheets and write a 1-sentence comparison: "Career A starts you working faster, but Career B has higher pay long-term."
  • ELL: Bilingual nursing career glossary (CNA = Asistente de Enfermería Certificado, LVN = Enfermera Vocacional Licenciada, RN = Enfermera Registrada). Pre-teach: Patient = Paciente, Care = Cuidado, Hospital = Hospital.

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Complete the RN and NP rows of the Nursing Career Ladder; analyze the relationship between education time and salary; compare three nursing salaries TEKS d(2)(A), d(2)(B), d(5)(E) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: RN and NP ladder rows from H&L and BLS data · Explain: Salary analysis and whole-class share · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed Nursing Career Ladder worksheet (all 4 rows) + 2-sentence salary analysis answer Materials Chromebooks, H&L accounts, BLS RN and NP pages, Find Your Future workbook pp. 84-85, Nursing Career Ladder worksheet from Day 1, calculator (optional)

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: If you could earn money faster with less school (CNA in 12 weeks) OR earn more money with more school (NP in 8 years), which would you choose? Why?

Take 3-4 responses. Some students will say "more money, more school," some will say "start working now." Bridge: there is no wrong answer, but today students get the actual data to make an informed choice.

docs.title: Activity 1: Complete the RN Row (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: Hats & Ladders app + BLS Registered Nurses page; program context from (FYF pp. 84-85: "What is Happening at My District?")

Students return to the Nursing Career Ladder worksheet from Day 1. They complete the RN row using H&L Hat Finder + BLS data.

The RN row has a complication: there are TWO entry paths to RN. Walk students through both options on the projector:

  • ADN Path: Associate Degree in Nursing, 2 years at a community college (Dallas College, Tarrant County College)
  • BSN Path: Bachelor of Science in Nursing, 4 years at a university (UT Arlington, Texas Woman's University)

Both paths lead to the same RN license (the NCLEX exam). The BSN often pays more long-term and is required for some hospital systems. Students should record BOTH paths in the Education column.

[H&L PLATFORM] In the H&L app, click the Registered Nurse Hat, scroll to the education section. The H&L data shows DFW-localized salary information. Students record the salary in their worksheet.

DFW RN Salary (BLS): ~$80K median.

Facilitation Tip

The two-path RN is a great teaching moment for d(2)(B). Most students think there is one "right" way to become an RN. The reality: both ADN and BSN graduates take the same NCLEX exam. The choice is about cost, time, and long-term plans.

docs.title: Activity 2: Complete the NP Row (12 min)
docs.text:
Students complete the NP row independently. Key data points:

  • Education: RN license + Master's degree in Nursing (MSN) or Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP)
  • Time to Complete: 6-8 years total after high school (4 years BSN + 2-4 years MSN/DNP)
  • DFW Salary: ~$120K median (BLS)
  • One Daily Task: Diagnose patients, prescribe medications, manage chronic conditions

Students then look at the FULL completed worksheet (CNA → LVN → RN → NP) and circle the salary differences between adjacent levels.

docs.title: Activity 3: Salary Analysis (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: Completed Nursing Career Ladder worksheet

Project the discussion question and let students work individually or in pairs to answer:

DOK 3: What conclusions can you draw about the relationship between education level and salary in nursing? Is more education ALWAYS worth the investment? Use specific salary numbers from your worksheet to support your answer.

Stop and Jot: Students write a 2-sentence answer below the worksheet. Give a 4 minute time box with the prompt on screen and offer two stems: "More education pays off when _" and "More education is NOT worth it when ___." Strong answers will:

  • Cite specific DFW salaries (CNA ~$32K, NP ~$120K)
  • Acknowledge that the answer depends on the student's life situation (family obligations, financial resources)
  • Identify the "biggest jump", typically LVN → RN, where ~1 year of additional education yields ~$30K salary increase

After 10 minutes, take 3-4 answers that recommend different routes. Record the education time and salary fact behind each choice so students can see why the same table produces different decisions.

Close the share by opening the district page's Career Exploration Connection on financial resources (FYF p. 84). Education and training programs cost money, but grants, scholarships, and loans help cover the expense. Grants and scholarships usually do not have to be repaid; loans are borrowed money that has to be paid back over time. Put the page's own discussion question to the class: why is it important to understand the costs of a big decision before making it?

DOK 3: Compare the salaries of three nursing careers (CNA, RN, NP) and explain which offers the BEST balance of education time and salary.

Facilitation Tip

Watch for students who say "More school = always better." Push back: "What if you have to work full-time to support your family while in school?" Real career decisions involve tradeoffs, not just the highest number. The grant-versus-loan distinction is the piece most students have never heard, so leave it on the board through the exit ticket.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Ranked Justification) · Printable PDF:

Rank all four nursing levels from BEST BALANCE of education time to salary (1) to WORST (4) FOR YOU personally. Use your completed Nursing Career Ladder worksheet.

  • CNA: rank ____
  • LVN: rank ____
  • RN: rank ____
  • NP: rank ____

For EACH rank, write ONE data point (time, cost, or salary) from your worksheet that backs up the rank.

  • Rank 1 (best balance for me): _____________

  • Rank 4 (worst balance for me): _____________

Bottom line: The factor that matters MOST in my rank is (circle one): years of training / cost of school / starting salary / long-term salary. In one sentence, why does this factor matter most to me? (d(2)(B), d(5)(E))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Pre-fill the LVN and RN rows; students complete only NP. Provide a "best balance" sentence stem: "I would pick _ because it takes years and pays __."
  • Extension: Students calculate the 5-year and 10-year earnings for a CNA vs. an RN, including 2 years of "lost income" while in nursing school. Where is the break-even point?
  • ELL: Bilingual worksheet column headers. Pre-teach: Salary = Salario, Education = Educación, Degree = Título, Bachelor's = Licenciatura, Master's = Maestría.

docs.title: Day 3: Vital Signs Monitor — Build Phase
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Complete "Vitals in Motion" Step 1 team research on the four vital signs tools; build a working vital signs monitor in MakeCode using the micro:bit; program Button A to display heart rate and Button B to display temperature with an LED animation TEKS d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Vitals in Motion Step 1 tool research · Explain: MakeCode demo · Explore: Student build time · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed "Vitals in Motion" Step 1 answers (FYF p. 60) + working MakeCode program with both buttons functional (saved as student.hex file or screenshot of finished code blocks) Materials Chromebooks, micro:bit devices (1 per team of 2-3), MakeCode website (makecode.microbit.org), USB cables, Find Your Future workbook p. 60, Climber Notes deck "Vitals in Motion" (slides 2-4), projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: What are vital signs? Name as many as you can. Hint: think about what a nurse checks at the start of every doctor's visit.

Take responses. Students should name: heart rate (pulse), temperature, blood pressure, respiration rate (breathing). If they miss respiration rate, name it for them.

docs.title: Activity 1: "Vitals in Motion" Team Research (8 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 60: "Vitals in Motion", Step 1), a Career Climb activity

Open the workbook to page 60. Read the scenario together: not all nurses work in the same place every day. Travel nurses move from city to city and step in wherever care is needed most, including community events. It is a bright Saturday morning at a community summer fun run, families and neighbors are walking and jogging, a medical tent is set up near the finish line, and the student is the travel nurse on duty. The job listed on the page is to collect and record vital signs, use medical tools correctly, communicate clearly and calmly, and rotate roles and document findings.

Step 1: Team Research and Share. Students pair up or join a small group and answer the page's five questions in the workbook. Project the Climber Notes deck while they work (Climber Notes: "Vitals in Motion", slides 2-4), which carries the tool reference table and the fever, blood pressure, and pulse oximeter charts:

  • What is blood pressure, and what can it indicate?
  • What is the correct way to use a blood pressure cuff?
  • What does a pulse oximeter measure? Why is it important?
  • What is the correct way to use a pulse oximeter?
  • What does body temperature tell you about a person's condition?

Students take these readings on each other on Day 4. Today the research is the preparation for that, and it is also the specification for the device they are about to build.

Project specifications (project on the board):

  • Press Button A → display a simulated heart rate (number between 60-100) + LED animation showing "pulse"
  • Press Button B → display a simulated temperature (number between 97.0-99.5) + LED animation showing "thermometer"
  • Bonus (Day 4): Add an alarm if the heart rate is above 100 or below 60

Name the local tie before students open MakeCode. Patient Care Technicians monitor vital signs every shift, and the Singley Academy labs run programmable patient simulators whose manikins display changing vital signs to replicate critical emergencies. The micro:bit build is the classroom-scale version of that machine.

docs.title: Activity 2: MakeCode Demo (10 min)
docs.text:
Open makecode.microbit.org on the projector. Walk students through:

  1. Create a new project named "Vital Signs Monitor"
  2. Drag in on button A pressed from the Input drawer
  3. Inside the button block, drag in show number from Basic
  4. Set the number to a variable called heartRate initialized to 75
  5. Test on the simulator: click Button A and watch the LED grid display "75"

Then add the LED animation:

  1. Show LEDs block from Basic, draw a simple heart pattern
  2. Pause 200ms
  3. Show LEDs with empty heart
  4. Loop 3 times for the pulse effect

Walk students through saving the project and downloading it to the micro:bit (drag the .hex file to the MICROBIT drive).

Facilitation Tip

Don't spend more than 10 minutes on the demo, the goal is to get students building, not watching. Demonstrate the heart rate (Button A) only, then let students build Button B independently using the same pattern. They learn faster by doing.

docs.title: Activity 3: Student Build Time (22 min)
docs.text:
Students work in teams of 2-3 with one micro:bit per team. They:

  1. Recreate the Button A heart rate display using the demo as reference
  2. Add Button B for temperature: on button B pressed → show number (temperature variable initialized to 98.6) → LED thermometer animation
  3. Test both buttons on the simulator first, then download to the physical micro:bit
  4. Show the teacher when both buttons work. This is the Day 3 checkpoint

Active Monitoring: Walk a fixed pathway with one target per lap rather than drifting toward raised hands, marking the 3-checkpoint rubric as you go:

  • Lap 1 target: Button A displays a heart rate number ✓
  • Lap 2 target: Button A shows an LED animation ✓
  • Lap 3 target: Button B displays a temperature number ✓

Pivot condition: if more than a handful of teams miss the lap 2 target, stop and reproject the pause block to the whole room instead of fixing it team by team.

Teams that finish early add a third button (touch logo) for a bonus vital sign or build the Day 4 alarm feature.

DOK 2: How would you describe the connection between the programming you are doing today and the technology that real nurses use in hospitals?

Facilitation Tip

The most common error is forgetting to set the variable. Tell students: "If your number doesn't show up, your variable is empty. Initialize it to a number first." Project the variable initialization as the troubleshooting reference.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Decision Tree / Branching Prompt) · Printable PDF:

My role today: Patient Care Technician (a nursing career in Health Science)

Scenario: During my shift, I press Button A on my vital signs monitor and see a heart rate of 130 (way above normal).

Step 1: What does my role do FIRST in the next 30 seconds?

Step 2: Which OTHER Health Science role do I need to tell, and why? (Pick one: CNA / LVN / RN / NP / doctor)

I need to tell: _____

Because: ________

Step 3: Branch on the patient response —

IF the patient is AWAKE and talking, what do I do next? _____________

IF the patient is NOT responding, what do I do next? _____________

(d(1)(C))

Show the teacher your working program before leaving.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a MakeCode starter file with the variable already initialized and the Button A block already in place. Students just complete Button B.
  • Extension: Add a third button (logo touch) for blood pressure (display two numbers, systolic and diastolic). Or add a randomization so the heart rate changes each press. Teams that finish both buttons well ahead of the checkpoint start the "Ultrasound Detectives" enrichment (FYF pp. 64-68) with a partner, working Step 1 (match the three ultrasound types to their purposes) and Step 2 (read a practice scan and say what clues led to the guess) while the teacher projects the scan images (Climber Notes: "Ultrasound Detectives", slides 2-4).
  • ELL: Visual MakeCode cheat sheet with screenshots of each block. Pair ESL students with bilingual peers as the "code reader" while they build. Pre-teach: Heart Rate = Frecuencia Cardíaca, Temperature = Temperatura, Button = Botón, Display = Mostrar.

docs.title: Day 4: Vital Signs Monitor — Test + Present
Lesson Overview
