docs.title: Formative Assessment
docs.text:
• Conflict plan + advertisement poster + Decision Tree exit ticket (new CNA + shift-partner conflict scenario, branch on response). Day 1, d(4)(B)
  • Detail sort + clarifying questions + role-play observation + Mini-Case exit ticket (sore-ankle triage account; essential vs. background detail + one clarifying question + one non-healthcare career that needs the skill). Day 2, d(4)(B)
  • SMART Goal worksheet + SCR exit ticket (goal + hardest component + this-week action). Day 3, d(4)(A), d(4)(B)
  • Little Library post + healthcare role-play + Trade-off Dilemma exit ticket (note-only vs. verbal+note handoff of refused medication). Day 4, d(4)(B)
  • Xello Time Management + CareerOneStop Skills Matcher + Concept Map exit ticket (skill + Matcher career + SMART goal fit + classmate skill compare). Day 5, d(1)(A), d(4)(A), d(4)(B)

docs.title: Summative Assessment
docs.text: SMART Goal + Communication Reflection (Day 5): Students submit (1) the polished SMART goal worksheet from Day 3 and (2) a 4-sentence reflection paragraph: "The transferable skill I improved most this week is _. It connects to the career of because __. I will practice this skill in [Wk 6 / outside class] by _____." Scored on: SMART goal quality (d(4)(A)), transferable skill identification (d(4)(B)), and whether the named career genuinely uses the named skill (d(4)(B)).

docs.title: Scaffolded Learning
docs.text:
• SMART goal examples and non-examples to clarify each component
  • Pre-built role-play scripts with dialogue suggestions
  • Sentence stems for the reflection paragraph
  • Pair work for all role-plays (no solo performance required)

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
• Create a Communication Skills Guide for one chosen career pathway listing the top 5 communication skills needed
  • Finish the workbook's advocacy project (FYF p. 135, Steps 2-4): a mobile farmers' market flyer with a mission statement, at least 10 nutritious offerings, and a reason to use it
  • Compare CareerOneStop Skills Matcher results to the core personality type recorded in Week 0 from the H&L "Discover Your Core" task, what is the overlap?
  • Lead a small-group review of one Powerskill lesson for peers who missed a day

docs.title: ELL Language Support
docs.text:
• Pre-teach: Conflict = Conflicto, Listen = Escuchar, Feedback = Retroalimentación, Advocacy = Defensa, Goal = Meta, Skill = Habilidad, Transferable = Transferible
  • Bilingual role-play cards with key phrases in both languages
  • Bilingual SMART goal worksheet
  • Pair ESL students with bilingual peers for role-plays
  • The workbook reads well above grade level. Read the scenario paragraphs aloud (FYF pp. 62, 134, 144, 147) and allow browser translation for any independent reading

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Explore the Biomedical Sciences pathway in the Hats & Ladders app; identify 3 biomedical careers; draft a cover letter using the 5-step format TEKS d(1)(C), d(7)(B) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Biomedical Hat browse and career research worksheet · Explain: NIH scientist profile and Stop and Jot · Extend: Cover letter draft and partner feedback · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Career research worksheet (1 biomedical career) + draft cover letter (all 5 sections) Materials Chromebooks, Find Your Future workbook pp. 84-86 and pp. 290-291, printed career research worksheet, printed cover letter worksheet, one real entry-level lab or clinic job posting, NIH STEM video link, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Name one medical technology that did not exist when your grandparents were young. How do you think it was invented?

Take 3-4 responses (MRI machines, mRNA vaccines, prosthetics, gene therapy). Bridge: every modern medical technology was invented by a biomedical scientist or engineer. Today the class meets the people who INVENT healthcare.

docs.title: Activity 1: H&L Biomedical Pathway Tour (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 86: "App Exploration") + (FYF p. 84: "What is Happening at My District?")

The workbook's district pages describe the Biomedical Sciences program of study as preparing students for careers in health care by focusing on the study of human body systems, disease, medical research and treatment, and laboratory procedures, while building skills in scientific investigation and critical thinking. Read that description aloud and put it next to the app.

Students then work the App Exploration steps for the Health Science cluster. This is the cluster's fourth and final week, so students go straight to the pathway work rather than repeating the cluster tour they took in Week 3.

[H&L PLATFORM] Open the Hats & Ladders app. Go to Clusters and click the Health Science Cluster. Click "Pathway Possibilities," answer the questions, then explore and rate at least 1 pathway. Rate at least 3 Hats before leaving the cluster.

Inside the cluster, students browse 5 specific biomedical Hats:

  1. Biomedical Engineer
  2. Lab Technician
  3. Research Scientist
  4. Pharmacist
  5. Genetic Counselor

For each Hat they note the education time and the DFW salary on scratch paper. Most of these careers require a master's or doctoral degree, and students will notice they carry the longest education paths in the Health Science cluster, commonly 6 to 10 years after high school.

Then students complete the career research worksheet for ONE biomedical career of their choice. This is the same worksheet format taught in Week 0 and used in every cluster week.

Facilitation Tip

Do not hide the long education path or reduce the decision to salary. Have students compare the years of school, likely debt, daily work, and reported pay so they can explain whether that route fits them.

docs.title: Activity 2: NIH STEM Video (5 min)
docs.text:
Project a short NIH STEM video clip from science.education.nih.gov featuring a real biomedical scientist or engineer. Students use Stop and Jot to capture (1) one technology shown and (2) one quality the scientist demonstrates.

If a video is unavailable, project an NIH career profile page and read it aloud. Students still record one technology and one quality shown by the person in the profile.

docs.title: Activity 3: Write a Cover Letter (22 min)
docs.text:
A cover letter is like a book introduction. It gives a sneak peek of who you are and makes the reader want to learn more. It is a short letter sent with a resume for a job application, personalized to one employer and one job.

Start with what the employer actually asked for (4 min). Project one real entry-level lab or clinic job posting and pull it apart the way the workbook's Capstone rung does (FYF pp. 290-291: "Rung 5: Local Connections"): what 2 or 3 responsibilities are listed, what skills and qualifications are required, and what level of education or experience the employer wants. Those four answers are exactly what the cover letter has to respond to. Students complete this rung for a career of their own in 6th Six Weeks, so today is the preview.

Then project the 5 sections of a cover letter:

  1. Begin with a Professional Greeting: "Dear Ms. Smith" or "Dear Hiring Manager"
  2. Opening Paragraph: Mention the job title, company name, and why you are excited to work there
  3. Body Paragraph (Show What You Can Do): Show off skills and experience with examples
  4. Closing Paragraph: Thank the employer, express enthusiasm, mention you would love an interview
  5. Sign Off Professionally: "Sincerely" or "Best Regards" + full name

Walk through a worked example on the projector. Use the biomedical career the class just explored:

Dear Hiring Manager,

I am writing to apply for the Lab Assistant position at UT Southwestern Medical Center. Biomedical research is exciting to me because it solves problems that affect millions of people, and your work on cancer research is particularly inspiring.

I have strong skills in math and science. In my 7th-grade Career and College Exploration course, I designed a vital signs monitor using a micro:bit microcontroller and led my team's emergency response project. I learn quickly and pay attention to detail.

Thank you for your time. I would love the opportunity to interview and learn more about the Lab Assistant role.

Sincerely, [Student Name]

Students then draft their own cover letter for a job they would love to have at a company they are interested in. The job can be biomedical, but it doesn't have to be, the goal is to practice the 5-section format against a real posting's requirements.

After drafting, students swap with a partner and give one piece of constructive feedback on the Body Paragraph, which is the section that decides whether an employer keeps reading.

DOK 2: How would you describe what makes a cover letter different from a resume? Why do employers want to read both?

Facilitation Tip

Tell students upfront: this is a DRAFT. Real cover letters get revised many times. The goal today is to learn the 5-section structure, not to write a perfect letter.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Mini-Case / Scenario Application) · Printable PDF:

Scenario: Imani is applying for a summer Lab Assistant position at UT Southwestern Medical Center. She is 17, has NO paid work experience, but she is on her school's Science Olympiad team and helped at a community health fair last summer.

  1. Which TWO cover letter sections (of the 5 from today: Greeting / Opening Paragraph / Body Paragraph / Closing Paragraph / Sign Off) are MOST important for Imani's case, and why?

Section A: _____. Why: _____________

Section B: _____. Why: _____________

  1. Write ONE sentence Imani could include in her Body Paragraph to "show what she can do" using her real experience (Science Olympiad OR the health fair):

(d(1)(C), d(7)(B))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a fill-in-the-blank cover letter template with each of the 5 sections labeled. Allow students to write the letter for a familiar job (cashier, babysitter) instead of a biomedical career.
  • Extension: Students write TWO cover letters, one for a Lab Tech position and one for a customer service position. How does the language change to match each audience?
  • ELL: Bilingual cover letter template. Pre-teach: Greeting = Saludo, Position = Puesto, Skills = Habilidades, Experience = Experiencia, Sincerely = Atentamente.

docs.title: Day 2: Mini Medics — Design a Medical Nanobot
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Complete the "Mini Medics" nanobot design activity: review the medical team's requirements, plan and size a nanobot, draw and label it on chart paper, map its journey through the body, and share the design with another team TEKS d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: Nanobot mission briefing · Explore: Plan, draw, label, and map the nanobot · Evaluate: Group design share and Exit Ticket Deliverable Labeled nanobot drawing on chart paper + completed plan (name, size comparison, guidance tools, 3 clot-breaking tools) + journey sketch Materials Find Your Future workbook pp. 79-81, chart paper or poster board, markers, rulers, plain paper, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: A doctor needs to reach a blood clot deep inside a patient's body. Name one way to get a tool or medicine to that exact spot without cutting the patient open.

Take 3-4 responses (a pill, an IV line, a catheter, a scope). Bridge: engineers are now building machines so small they travel inside the bloodstream. Today the class designs one.

docs.title: Activity 1: Mini Medics — Mission Briefing (8 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 79-80: "Mini Medics"), a Career Climb activity

Open the workbook to page 79 and read the scenario together. Nanobots are tiny machines scientists are testing that could one day carry medicine to the exact place it is needed, break apart dangerous blockages, or help repair damaged tissue. Students are nanobot engineers, and their team has been asked to design a tiny medical robot that travels through the bloodstream to break up a dangerous blood clot before it blocks blood flow to the brain or heart.

Project the four constraints the medical team gives in Step 1 (p. 79):

  • Blood is always moving and can push the robot in different directions
  • Blood vessels are very narrow, so the nanobot must be extremely small
  • The robot must break the clot apart without damaging the walls of the blood vessel
  • Doctors guide the nanobot with magnetic tools and imaging machines that track its movement

Then project the four things the nanobot has to do: travel safely through the bloodstream, reach the clot, break the clot into smaller pieces so blood can flow again, and send a signal back to the doctors when the mission is complete.

Name the careers standing behind this one device: biomedical engineers design it, medical researchers test whether it is safe, and imaging technologists run the machines that track it inside the patient. All three sit in the Health Science cluster students have been exploring for four weeks.

Facilitation Tip

Post the four mission requirements where students can see them all period. Teams that skip the "send a signal back" requirement produce a robot that works and then disappears, which is the most common miss on this activity.

docs.title: Activity 2: Plan, Draw, and Label Your Nanobot (32 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 80-81: "Mini Medics", Steps 2-4)

Students work in pairs or teams of three. Run the workbook's three steps one at a time and check each before releasing the next.

Step 2: Plan Your Nanobot (10 min). Teams fill in the workbook's plan on p. 80:

  • Name of your nanobot
  • How big is it? Compare its size to something familiar so other people can picture how small it is
  • How does your nanobot work with the tools doctors use to guide it?
  • What equipment helps doctors track or steer your robot?
  • What special tools does your nanobot have to break up the blood clot? Three tools, listed separately

Check before moving on: every team has a size comparison and three named tools.

Step 3: Draw and Label Your Nanobot (14 min). Teams draw their nanobot large on chart paper or poster board. Every important part and tool gets a label, and each label carries a short note saying what that part does and how it helps complete the mission.

Time, Voice, Body: Voice 1 for team drawing talk and Voice 0 for the last two minutes of labeling so teams can hear their own thinking. Markers stay capped on the table between uses, chart paper stays flat on the desk rather than on the floor, and a visible 14 minute countdown runs on the screen.

Check before moving on: every part on the drawing has a label, and every label has a purpose written next to it.

Step 4: Plan Your Nanobot's Journey (8 min). Teams write or sketch how the nanobot completes the mission inside the body, answering the workbook's four questions: how does the nanobot enter the patient's body, how does it travel through the bloodstream, what happens when it reaches the blood clot, and what happens after the mission is complete.

DOK 3: Two teams built nanobots the same size but chose different tools to break the clot. What evidence would a medical researcher need before deciding which design is safer for a real patient?

Facilitation Tip

Watch for size comparisons like "very tiny" or "super small." Those are not comparisons. Push for something a reader can picture: smaller than a grain of salt, about the width of a human hair, one tenth the size of a red blood cell. The comparison is what makes the rest of the design believable.

docs.title: Activity 3: Present Your Nanobot (3 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 81: "Mini Medics", Step 5)

Each team joins one other team. Both share their nanobot design and explain how it completes the mission, naming the tools and ideas each person contributed. The joined group then decides which of the two designs is the most creative, the most useful, or the most likely to work in the real world, and that design is the one nominated to present to the whole class.

If time allows, take the workbook's class discussion question (p. 81): if nanobots become common in medicine, what new jobs might exist to design, control, or repair them?

docs.title: Exit Ticket (2 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Comparison Matrix) · Printable PDF:

Compare YOUR nanobot to the other design in your group.

My nanobot: _______ Other nanobot: _______ Size compared to something familiar One tool it uses to break the clot How doctors track or steer it
  1. Which design is more likely to work inside a real blood vessel? Use ONE row from the chart to explain.
  1. Name ONE Health Science career that would help build, test, or run this nanobot. Say what that person would do.

Career: _____

What they do: ___________

(d(1)(C))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a pre-drawn nanobot outline students label rather than drawing from scratch. Provide a size-comparison word bank (grain of salt, human hair, grain of sand, red blood cell, dust speck) and a tool word bank (spinning blade, heat tip, medicine sprayer, tiny drill, magnet arm, suction tube).
  • Extension: Take the workbook's second class discussion question and design around it: what challenges might engineers face when building robots that travel through the human body? Add one safety feature to the drawing that answers a challenge you named, and label what it does.
  • ELL: Bilingual anatomy and design glossary (Blood clot = Coágulo, Blood vessel = Vaso sanguíneo, Bloodstream = Torrente sanguíneo, Tool = Herramienta, Signal = Señal, Label = Etiqueta). Allow labels to be written in Spanish. The drawing carries most of the meaning, so students can present the design visually and name parts in either language.

docs.title: Day 3: Outbreak Investigators — Examine the Clues
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Read the Fairview Edge case file and environmental clues; identify the likely source of a waterborne outbreak; complete the Investigation Report; analyze the pattern and severity of the illness TEKS d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: What environmental epidemiologists do · Explore: Fairview Edge clues, Investigation Report, and outbreak analysis · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed Investigation Report (outbreak description, 3+ pieces of evidence, possible source, symptoms, likely cause) + outbreak analysis (pattern, severity, risk check) Materials Find Your Future workbook pp. 74-77, projector for the case-file image clues

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Six people on your street get the same stomach bug in the same week. What would you check FIRST to find out why?

Take 3-4 responses: what they ate, where they swam, what they drank, and who they were around. Sort the answers by possible exposure. Environmental epidemiologists compare those exposures to find how an illness spread; students do the same with today's outbreak file.

docs.title: Activity 1: What Does an Environmental Epidemiologist Do? (5 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 74: "Outbreak Investigators"), a Career Climb activity

Read the workbook's opening description together. Environmental epidemiologists are scientists who study how and why people get sick, and how illnesses spread from person to person. They gather information, look for patterns, and figure out what might be causing a health problem. Their work keeps communities safe and keeps food, water, and the environment healthy.

Nursing and dental careers often treat one patient at a time. Epidemiologists compare cases across a community to find a shared source and prevent more illness. Both are Health Science work, and today's use of evidence and investigation also appears in Irving ISD's Biomedical Sciences program of study.

Set the case: a small town is suddenly seeing people fall ill, and the class has been called in to investigate a waterborne outbreak, identify the source, and plan how to stop it from spreading.

docs.title: Activity 2: Examine the Clues (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 74-75: "Outbreak Investigators", Step 1)

Think-Pair-Share: the workbook pairs students for this step. Hold a silent 30 second Think while students read the case file on their own, then Partner A talks for 30 seconds about the pattern they see, then Partner B for 30 seconds. Two pairs share with the whole class before anyone writes anything down. Post two stems at different levels: "Everyone who got sick _" and "The one thing the people who did NOT get sick have in common is ___."

Case File: Fairview Edge. A small town of about 2,000 residents. Most people drink water from a local well or from the town's water system. The town recently had heavy rainfall and minor flooding.

Resident Age Water source Recent activity Symptoms Symptoms started Alex 12 Tap water Soccer practice Stomach pain, vomiting Monday Maria 34 Tap water None Diarrhea, fever Monday Jamal 15 Tap water Basketball Nausea, stomach pain Tuesday Mrs. Lee 52 Tap water Gardening Diarrhea, vomiting Monday Ethan 10 Bottled water None None Never got sick Sofia 13 Tap water Swimming in the river Vomiting, fever Tuesday Mr. Cruz 41 Tap water None Diarrhea Monday Lilly 11 Bottled water Dance class None Never got sick

Environmental clues (p. 75):

  • The town's main water well is located near a river
  • After the heavy rain, the river overflowed its banks
  • Some residents reported that their tap water looked slightly cloudy for a short time
  • The town has not recently tested the water quality

The workbook also prints image clues on page 75. Project that page so the whole class studies the same images at the same time rather than crowding around one book.

Facilitation Tip

The two residents who stayed healthy are the strongest clue in the case, and most students skip right past them. If a pair is stuck, point at Ethan and Lilly and ask what those two did differently. Comparing who got sick with who did not is the move the workbook asks for again on Day 4.

docs.title: Activity 3: Complete the Investigation Report (10 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 75: "Outbreak Investigators", Step 2)

Pairs complete the workbook's Investigation Report. Every field gets filled:

  • Outbreak Description: what students notice about the illness, including symptoms, how many people are affected, and the timing
  • Evidence: at least 3 clues from the case file that students think matter
  • Possible Source: check all that apply from well water, river water, tap water, bottled water, food or drinks
  • Symptoms Observed: what symptoms people are showing
  • What do you think caused the outbreak? possible causes based on the clues

Hold pairs to the "at least 3" evidence requirement. A report that names one clue is a guess, not an investigation.

docs.title: Activity 4: Analyze the Outbreak (12 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 76: "Outbreak Investigators", Step 3)

Pairs move to the workbook's analysis page and answer three questions:

  • Pattern of Illness: who got sick first, and who got sick later?
  • Severity of Illness: how serious are the symptoms, mild, moderate, or severe? Why did you choose that level?
  • Risk Check: are more people at risk if the water is not treated? Yes or no, and explain the answer

The severity choice is the one that produces real argument. There is no single correct level, but the reasoning has to cite symptoms from the case file rather than a general feeling.

DOK 3: What patterns do you see in who got sick and when? What does the two-day gap between the Monday cases and the Tuesday cases tell you about how this illness spreads?

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Ranked Justification) · Printable PDF:

Rank these four clues from MOST useful (1) to LEAST useful (4) for proving the TAP WATER made people sick.

  • Ethan and Lilly drank bottled water and did not get sick: rank ____
  • The town's water well sits next to a river that overflowed: rank ____
  • Sofia swam in the river before she got sick: rank ____
  • The town has not tested its water quality recently: rank ____

For your #1 and your #4, write one sentence saying why.

  • Rank 1 (most useful): _____________

  • Rank 4 (least useful but still matters): _____________

Bottom line: Epidemiologists find the source of an outbreak. Name ONE other Health Science career that would help Fairview Edge after the source is found, and say what that person would do. (d(1)(C))

Career: _____

What they do: _________

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide the case-file table with the "water source" and "symptoms started" columns already highlighted so students compare the two variables that matter most. Provide a sentence stem for the outbreak description: "_ people got sick. They all . The first cases started on __."
  • Extension: Rebuild the case file for a food outbreak instead of a water outbreak. Which column in the table would you change, and what new clue would you have to add so an investigator could still find the source?
  • ELL: Bilingual investigation glossary (Outbreak = Brote, Source = Fuente, Evidence = Evidencia, Symptoms = Síntomas, Well = Pozo, Flooding = Inundación, Pattern = Patrón). The case-file table is mostly names and short symptom words, so it reads well with translation support. Pair ELL students with a bilingual partner for the Think-Pair-Share.

docs.title: Day 4: Outbreak Investigators — Build the Response Plan
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Choose the tests that confirm the outbreak source; estimate the impact of an uncontrolled outbreak; write immediate actions and a prevention plan; present the response plan to another team TEKS d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Confirming tests and estimated impact · Extend: Immediate actions and prevention plan · Explain: Response-plan presentations · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed Response Plan (investigation steps, estimated impact, immediate actions, prevention plan, each with written reasoning) + 3-minute pair presentation Materials Find Your Future workbook pp. 77-78, Investigation Report and outbreak analysis from Day 3, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: The city announces that your tap water may be unsafe. What is the FIRST thing your family should do TODAY? What should the city do so this never happens again?

Take 3-4 responses. Bridge: those are two different jobs. One keeps people safe right now, the other keeps the town safe next year. A response plan has to do both, and today the class writes one.

docs.title: Activity 1: Confirm the Source and Estimate the Impact (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 77: "Outbreak Investigators", Step 4)

Pairs return to yesterday's Investigation Report and open the workbook's response-plan page. Start with the workbook's Helpful Info for Investigators box and read the five facts aloud, because the whole plan is built on them:

  • Waterborne illnesses often spread through contaminated drinking water
  • Common symptoms include stomach pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and fever
  • Boiling water can kill many harmful germs
  • Scientists test water by collecting samples and checking for bacteria
  • Flooding can cause dirty water to mix with clean water sources

Investigation Steps. Pairs check every step they would take to confirm the source: test water from the well, test river water, ask people about their symptoms, compare who got sick and who did not, or write their own step in the Other line. Then they answer the workbook's follow-up in writing: why are these steps important?

Estimated Impact. Pairs choose how many people could be affected if the outbreak is not controlled, a few dozen, hundreds, or thousands, and explain the reasoning. The town has about 2,000 residents and nearly everyone drinks from the same system, so the estimate has to square with the population number from the Day 3 case file.

Active Monitoring: Walk one lap per part. Lap 1 target: does the pair's set of investigation steps include at least one test of a water source AND one comparison of sick to healthy residents? Lap 2 target: does the estimated-impact reasoning cite the 2,000-resident population or the shared water system rather than a feeling? Have the response ready before class for the two predictable misses: pairs who check every box without explaining any, and pairs who estimate thousands in a town of 2,000. If more than a handful miss the population check, pause the room and reproject the Fairview Edge background paragraph instead of correcting pair by pair.

docs.title: Activity 2: Immediate Actions and Prevention Plan (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 78: "Outbreak Investigators", Step 4)

Immediate Actions. Pairs check what people should do right away to stay safe: boil water before drinking, avoid drinking tap water, drink bottled water, close the water source, or their own action in the Other line. They then explain their choices in writing. Push on the trade-offs: closing the town's water source protects people but leaves 2,000 residents with no tap water at all, so the plan has to say what replaces it.

Prevention Plan. Pairs check how this outbreak could be prevented in the future: regularly test water quality, protect the water source from flooding, improve water treatment systems, educate the community about safe water, or their own idea. They explain those choices too.

Name the difference out loud, because it is the day's core idea. Immediate actions treat the emergency that already happened. Prevention steps change the system so the next flood does not become the next outbreak. Public health careers are built around the second one.

Facilitation Tip

Pairs that check all four prevention boxes with one shared sentence have not made a plan, they have made a list. Ask which single prevention step they would fund first if the town could only afford one, and make them defend it with a clue from the case file. That question turns the checklist back into reasoning.

docs.title: Activity 3: Present the Response Plan (12 min)
docs.text:
Each pair joins another pair and presents its plan in 3 minutes. Every presentation covers four things:

  1. The source we identified and the evidence that points to it
  2. The tests we would run to confirm it, and why those tests
  3. Two immediate actions and what each one protects people from
  4. One prevention step and why we would fund that one first

The listening pair responds with one strength they heard and one question they still have. Then the pairs switch roles. This is a check on reasoning, not a performance, so keep the feedback to those two items and move on.

Close with the workbook's class discussion questions (p. 78): what clues helped you figure out the source of the illness, what other ways could epidemiologists help the community, and why do epidemiologists need to know what activity people were doing before they got sick?

DOK 4: Fairview Edge can afford exactly one of these: a new water treatment system, yearly water testing for the whole town, or a flood barrier around the well. Which one would prevent the most future illness? Defend the choice with evidence from the case file.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Venn Diagram Comparison) · Printable PDF:

Compare the TWO halves of your Fairview Edge response plan.

Only in IMMEDIATE ACTIONS (2 things people do this week):

Only in the PREVENTION PLAN (2 things the town does for next year):

TRUE OF BOTH (2 things both halves need):

Bottom line: One of these two halves is the everyday work of a public health career. Name a Health Science career that does that work, and say in one sentence which half it lives in and why. (d(1)(C))

Career: _____

Which half and why: __________

Submit your completed Response Plan with this ticket.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide the response plan with the Helpful Info facts printed at the top of the page so students do not have to flip back. Provide sentence stems for the written explanations: "We would test _ first because " and "People should __ right away because _____."
  • Extension: Write the one-paragraph public notice the town would post at the grocery store and the school. It must say what happened, what people should do today, and when the town will test again. Keep it short enough for someone to read while walking past.
  • ELL: Bilingual response-plan glossary (Prevention = Prevención, Treatment = Tratamiento, Boil = Hervir, Safe = Seguro, Test = Analizar, Water source = Fuente de agua). The plan is built from checkboxes, so ELL students can complete the choices independently and use the stems for the written explanations. Pair ELL students with a bilingual partner as co-presenter.

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Research one emerging biomedical occupation; finalize Health Science cluster favorites in H&L; complete the Xello Save Careers activity; update the My Career Journey reflection for the 2nd Six Weeks TEKS d(1)(D), d(2)(A), d(5)(A) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Emerging biomedical career research · Extend: Xello Save Careers and Health Science cluster ratings · Evaluate: 2SW reflection and Exit Ticket Deliverable Emerging Biomedical Career Research template (1 emerging career, all fields) + updated H&L Climber Profile (5+ Health Science favorites) + Xello Save Careers completion + 2SW reflection Materials Chromebooks, H&L accounts, Xello accounts, Find Your Future workbook pp. 82-83 and p. 86, BLS Career Outlook page, NIH STEM site, printed Emerging Career Research template, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: COVID-19 vaccines were developed in record time. What types of scientists made that possible? Name as many as you can in 60 seconds.

Take responses and add any missing examples: virologists, immunologists, biomedical engineers, lab technicians, clinical trial coordinators, and manufacturing scientists. Ask which of these jobs depends on a tool or treatment that was uncommon or unavailable ten years ago.

docs.title: Activity 1: Emerging Biomedical Career Research (20 min)
docs.text:
Project a list of emerging biomedical careers on the board for students to choose from:

  • Genomic Counselor: helps families understand genetic test results
  • Bioinformatics Specialist: analyzes biological data with software
  • 3D Bioprinting Engineer: designs printable tissues and organs
  • mRNA Vaccine Specialist: develops messenger-RNA-based vaccines
  • AI Drug Discovery Specialist: uses machine learning to find new drugs
  • Telehealth Coordinator: manages remote patient care systems
  • Wearable Health Tech Designer: designs Fitbit/Apple Watch-style health devices
  • CRISPR Gene Editing Technician: works on gene therapy procedures
  • Robotic Surgery Technician: assists surgeons using robotic equipment

Each student picks ONE emerging career. They use BLS Career Outlook, H&L Hat Finder (if the career is listed), NIH STEM resources, and Google to complete the Emerging Career Research template:

Field Content Career name What it involves (2 sentences) Education needed Salary range Why it is "emerging" (what trend created this career?) One DFW employer that hires for this role Labor market trend (growing fast? slow? stable?)

[H&L PLATFORM] In the H&L app, search the Hat Finder for the chosen emerging career. Some emerging careers (like Bioinformatics Specialist) are listed; others students must research outside the app. The H&L app shows DFW-localized salary and demand data when available.

DOK 4: Based on your research, what argument would you make to convince a school district that biomedical science should be a required course for all high school students? Use labor market data and emerging career trends to support your argument.

Facilitation Tip

If a student writes "It's important" or "People need it," ask: "What problem does this career solve? Why didn't it exist 10 years ago?" Require the answer to name the technology, medical need, or job task involved.

docs.title: Activity 2: Xello Save Careers (8 min)
docs.text:
Open Xello and direct students to the required Grade 8 Save careers task. Students must explore and save at least 3 careers, then use those saved options in later Skills and Explore Career Matches lessons.

Students:

  1. Open their Xello profile
  2. Search for at least 3 careers they explored in 2SW (legal, nursing, dental, biomedical)
  3. Click "Save" on each career
  4. Add a brief note about why they saved each one

This creates a Xello-side record of the student's evolving career interests, complementing the H&L Climber Profile.

docs.title: Activity 3: H&L Health Science Cluster Wrap-Up (10 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 86: "App Exploration")

Students return to the H&L app and finalize ALL their Health Science favorites. They should now have 5 or more Health Science favorites spanning nursing, dental, medical billing, and biomedical. The App Exploration page closes the cluster with two questions worth answering out loud before students leave it: which Hat matches your personality or interests, and which Hat is clearly NOT a fit for you.

[H&L PLATFORM] Open the Hats & Ladders app. Go to Clusters and click the Health Science Cluster. Confirm at least 3 Hats and 1 pathway are rated, and that 5+ Health Science careers are favorited (heart icon). Then click "Climber Profile." Students should now see favorites from FOUR clusters: Manufacturing (1SW), IT (1SW), Law (2SW Wk 1-2), and Health Science (2SW Wk 3-6).

The teacher circulates and asks: "Which Health Science career is your TOP favorite, and why?" This is a quick formative check for the entire 4-week Health Science exploration.

docs.title: Activity 4: 2nd Six Weeks Reflection (5 min)
docs.text:
Students update their My Career Journey reflection document (originally created in Week 0 of 1SW). They add:

  • Clusters explored this six weeks: Law (Wks 1-2), Health Science (Wks 3-6)
  • New favorites added to the Climber Profile
  • SMART goal progress update (from Wk 5)
  • One Powerskill they improved this six weeks

This living document will be reviewed again at mid-year (4SW Wk 1: Career Planning Mid-Year Review).

DOK 4: Based on everything you have explored so far. Manufacturing, IT, Law, and Health Science, what pattern do you notice about the types of careers that attract you? What does that pattern tell you about what to explore next?

docs.title: Exit Ticket (2 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Concept Map / Connection Diagram) · Printable PDF:

My emerging biomedical career (from Day 5 research): _____

Connect this career to THREE things:

1. The BLS labor market trend I found today (growing fast, stable, or slow)

My trend: _____. In one sentence, what NEW technology or need created this emerging career in the last 10 years?

2. The Irving High Biomedical Science pathway (leads to BACE certification)

Does the Irving High pathway lead DIRECTLY to my emerging career, or is it a STEPPING STONE through further school? Circle: DIRECT / STEPPING STONE. One sentence why:

3. What I learned about MYSELF across 2SW (Law + Health Science clusters)

One sentence, what pattern do I notice about the careers that attract me after 6 weeks of Health Science + Law exploration?

(d(1)(D), d(2)(A), d(5)(A))

Submit the Emerging Career Research template + the updated 2SW reflection as the Week 6 + 2SW summative deliverable.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a list of 6 pre-approved emerging biomedical careers with starter research links. Provide a fill-in-the-blank reflection template.
  • Extension: "Patient Education" (FYF pp. 82-83). Partners pick one organ or bone from the workbook's list (heart, lungs, brain, stomach, femur, skull, spine), write an AI prompt for a labeled educational illustration a hospital could show patients, generate the image, record what went right and what needs improvement, revise the prompt, generate a second image, and choose the better mock-up to share. Confirm the campus has an approved AI image tool for student use before offering this; if it does not, students write and swap prompts and critique a teacher-generated image on the projector. Students who prefer research instead investigate a DFW biotech employer (UT Southwestern, McKesson, Kimberly-Clark Health) and add it to the research template.
  • ELL: Bilingual research template. Pre-teach: Emerging = Emergente, Trend = Tendencia, Employer = Empleador, Investigation = Investigación. Pair ESL students with bilingual peers for the Xello Save Careers step.

docs.title: Week 6: Science Meets Medicine — Biomedical Careers
docs.text: 2nd Six Weeks | Health Science Cluster | 5 class periods (50 min each)

docs.title: Lesson Objective
docs.text:
Students explore the Biomedical Sciences pathway through Hats & Ladders and the Find Your Future workbook, design and label a medical nanobot in "Mini Medics," investigate a waterborne outbreak and build a public health response plan in "Outbreak Investigators," write a cover letter against a real job posting, research one emerging biomedical occupation, and finalize their Health Science cluster favorites in the Climber Profile.

Learning Target: I can name at least three biomedical careers and the training each one needs, design a nanobot that meets the medical team's four requirements, find the source of a waterborne outbreak and plan how to stop it, and write a cover letter with all five sections.

Success Criteria: I will know I am successful when my career research worksheet lists the job, the training, and the pay for one biomedical career, when my nanobot drawing is labeled with a size comparison and three clot-breaking tools, when my Investigation Report names at least three clues and one likely source, when my response plan has two immediate actions and one prevention step, and when my cover letter has all five sections.

docs.title: Demonstration of Learning
docs.text: "I can describe at least three biomedical careers, design and label a medical nanobot that meets a mission spec, investigate a waterborne outbreak and write a response plan for the community, write a professional cover letter, research an emerging biomedical occupation, and finalize my Health Science cluster favorites."

docs.title: TEKS Alignment
docs.text:
• d(1)(C): Identify various career opportunities within the Health Science cluster (Days 1-5).
  • d(1)(D): Research and evaluate emerging occupations related to career interest areas (Day 5 Emerging Biomedical Career Research).
  • d(2)(A): Research and describe applicable academic, technical, certification, and training requirements (Day 5 template).
  • d(5)(A): Analyze labor market trends related to a career of interest (Day 5 BLS labor market row).
  • d(7)(B): Write business correspondence (Day 1 cover letter draft).

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Chromebooks with internet access (1 per student)
  • Hats & Ladders student accounts + Find Your Future workbook, Health Science chapter (printed pp. 74-86)
  • Chart paper or poster board, markers, and rulers for Day 2 (FYF pp. 79-81: "Mini Medics")
  • Projector for the Fairview Edge image clues (FYF p. 75) and for reading workbook pages as a class
  • One real entry-level lab or clinic job posting for Day 1, pulled from a job site or a hospital careers page (FYF pp. 290-291: "Rung 5: Local Connections")
  • Printed cover letter worksheet (5 sections; CCE artifact)
  • Printed career research worksheet (CCE artifact; the research format is taught in Wk0)
  • Printed Emerging Biomedical Career Research template
  • BLS, Biomedical Engineers: bls.gov/ooh/architecture-and-engineering/biomedical-engineers.htm
  • BLS, Pharmacists: bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/pharmacists.htm
  • NIH STEM Teaching Resources: science.education.nih.gov
  • Xello accounts (Save Careers activity)

docs.title: Career Connection
docs.text:
Biomedical engineers design artificial organs, prosthetics, and devices such as the nanobots students prototype on Day 2. Lab technicians help develop drugs and vaccines. Epidemiologists trace outbreaks to their source so public health teams can stop further illness. Many of these careers require a master's or doctoral degree. By the end of this cluster wrap-up, students identify which Health Science pathways fit their interests and update the Career Plan they have built across two six-week periods.

What is Happening at Irving ISD? Biomedical Sciences at Irving High School is the district program of study behind this week. The workbook's district pages describe it as preparing students for health care careers by studying human body systems, disease, medical research and treatment, and laboratory procedures while building scientific investigation and critical thinking skills (FYF pp. 84-85: "What is Happening at My District?"). Those pages also name the industry certifications Health Science students can earn, including the Biotechnology Aptitude and Competency Exam, Patient Care Technician, Certified Registered Dental Assistant, Phlebotomy, and Billing and Coding Specialist, and they name HOSA as the student organization. Health Science students at Singley Academy job-shadow at local hospitals and dental offices and practice on programmable patient simulators that display changing vital signs. The same pages run a Career Exploration Connection on financial resources worth five minutes of Day 1: grants and scholarships usually do not have to be repaid, while loans are borrowed money that does.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text:
• Biomedical Engineering: The application of engineering principles to medicine and biology, designing medical devices, prosthetics, and drug delivery systems.
  • Biotechnology: The use of living organisms and biological systems to develop products and technologies for healthcare, agriculture, and industry.
  • Nanobot: A machine small enough to travel inside the human body, designed to carry medicine, break up blockages, or repair damaged tissue.
  • Epidemiologist: A scientist who studies how and why people get sick and how illness spreads through a community.
  • Waterborne Illness: Sickness caused by germs in drinking water, often after flooding mixes dirty water into a clean water source.
  • Clinical Trial: A research study that tests new medical treatments or drugs on human volunteers to determine safety and effectiveness.
  • Research Scientist: A professional who conducts experiments to advance knowledge in a specific field like medicine, biology, or chemistry.
  • Emerging Occupation: A new or rapidly growing career that reflects current trends in technology, science, or society.
  • Cover Letter: A short personalized letter sent with a resume that introduces a job applicant to an employer.

docs.title: Bridge to Theory (Hats & Ladders)
docs.text:
The Find Your Future workbook gives Health Science printed pages 59-86, shared across the four weeks of this cluster. Weeks 3 and 4 work the front of the chapter. This week takes the back half, where the activities move from treating one patient to designing devices and protecting whole communities.

This week uses two chapter activities:

  • Mini Medics (Day 2): Career Climb activity. Students are nanobot engineers designing a robot small enough to travel through the bloodstream and break up a dangerous blood clot without damaging the vessel wall. They plan the robot, size it against something familiar, name three clot-breaking tools, draw and label it on chart paper, map its journey through the body, and pick the strongest design in their group (FYF pp. 79-81: "Mini Medics").
  • Outbreak Investigators (Days 3-4): Career Climb activity. Students are environmental epidemiologists investigating a waterborne outbreak in Fairview Edge, a town of 2,000 that recently flooded. They examine a case file of eight residents against a set of environmental clues, complete an Investigation Report, analyze the pattern and severity of the illness, and build a response plan covering confirming tests, estimated impact, immediate actions, and prevention (FYF pp. 74-78: "Outbreak Investigators").

Day 1's app work follows the cluster's own App Exploration page (FYF p. 86: "App Exploration"), which sends students to Pathway Possibilities, one rated pathway, and three rated Hats. Because this is the cluster's fourth week, students skip the cluster tour they already took in Week 3 and go straight to the pathway and rating steps, then finish the ratings on Day 5. The cover letter has no workbook activity behind it; it is a CCE artifact, and the "what employers are looking for" input comes from the Capstone rung students will complete for themselves in 6th Six Weeks (FYF pp. 290-291: "Rung 5: Local Connections").

A third chapter activity, Patient Education (FYF pp. 82-83), puts partners on a hospital patient-education team writing AI prompts for a labeled medical illustration, then judging what the AI got right and wrong. It runs as the Day 5 extension and needs a campus-approved AI image tool.

docs.title: IISD Instructional Strategies
docs.text:
• Think-Pair-Share: Day 3, Activity 2, the Fairview Edge case file, which the workbook itself pairs students for. Distinguished: hold a silent 30 second Think while students read the eight-resident table alone, then time Partner A for 30 seconds on the pattern they see and Partner B for 30 seconds, and post two stems at different levels: "Everyone who got sick _" and "The one thing the people who did NOT get sick have in common is ___." Two pairs share before anyone writes. Listen during pair talk for who names Ethan and Lilly, the two bottled-water residents who stayed healthy, and choose your share-out pairs from what you heard rather than from raised hands. If no pair reaches the healthy residents, point the whole room at those two rows before releasing the Investigation Report.
  • Stop and Jot: Day 1, Activity 2, the NIH scientist video. Distinguished: name both stop points before the clip starts, give 45 seconds per jot with the prompt on screen, and offer two stems: "One technology this scientist uses is _" and "One quality this scientist shows is , and I saw it when __." Read jots over shoulders during both pauses and track which qualities students name. If nearly every jot says "smart," push the cover letter Body Paragraph work in Activity 3 toward the qualities employers actually list in the posting, such as attention to detail and following a procedure exactly.
  • Active Monitoring: Day 4, Activities 1 and 2, the four parts of the Fairview Edge response plan. Distinguished: walk one lap per part with a single target each. Lap 1 target: does the pair's investigation-steps list include at least one water test AND the sick-to-healthy comparison? Lap 2 target: does the estimated-impact reasoning cite the 2,000-resident population or the shared water system? Lap 3 target: does each checked immediate action carry a written reason? Lap 4 target: does the prevention plan name one step the pair would fund first? Have feedback ready before class for the two predictable misses: pairs who check every box and explain none, and pairs who estimate "thousands" in a town of 2,000. If more than a handful miss the population check, pause and reproject the Fairview Edge background paragraph instead of correcting pair by pair.
  • Chunking: Day 2, Activity 2, the three Mini Medics steps. Distinguished: run plan, then draw and label, then journey, and state what each chunk is for before releasing it (the plan sets the specs, the drawing proves the specs, the journey proves the mission). Close each chunk with the check already written into the plan: every team has a size comparison and three named tools before drawing starts, and every label carries a purpose before the journey starts. Note which check holds teams up. If most teams stall on the size comparison, run a 2 minute whole-class round of comparisons before the drawing chunk, and release teams that already cleared it to start labeling early.
  • Time, Voice, Body (TVB): Day 2, Activity 2, the chart-paper nanobot drawing. Distinguished: post the three blocks before any marker comes off the table. Voice 1 for team drawing talk and Voice 0 for the last two minutes of labeling, markers capped between uses, chart paper flat on the desk rather than on the floor, and a visible 14 minute countdown on the screen. Narrate the teams meeting the expectation rather than correcting the ones who are not. If the room is losing drawing time to marker hunting, move a marker set to each table before the countdown starts and say why you moved it.
