docs.title: Formative Assessment
docs.text:
• Career research worksheet + draft cover letter + Mini-Case exit ticket (Imani's Lab Assistant application; 2 cover letter sections + body sentence). Day 1, d(1)(C), d(7)(B)
  • Labeled nanobot drawing + journey sketch + Comparison Matrix exit ticket (my nanobot vs. the group's other design on size, tool, and tracking). Day 2, d(1)(C)
  • Investigation Report + outbreak analysis + Ranked Justification exit ticket (4 clues ranked for proving the tap water source). Day 3, d(1)(C)
  • Response Plan + pair presentation + Venn Diagram exit ticket (immediate actions vs. prevention plan). Day 4, d(1)(C)
  • Emerging Career Research + Xello Save Careers + Concept Map exit ticket (emerging career + BLS trend + Irving High pathway + 6-week self-pattern). Day 5, d(1)(D), d(2)(A), d(5)(A)

docs.title: Summative Assessment
docs.text: 2nd Six Weeks Portfolio Update (Day 5): Students submit (1) the completed Emerging Biomedical Career Research template, (2) their updated My Career Journey reflection covering both 1SW and 2SW, and (3) their refined SMART goal from Week 5. The portfolio shows their growth across two complete six-week periods. Scored on: emerging career research quality (d(1)(D)), labor market analysis (d(5)(A)), education pathway knowledge (d(2)(A)), and self-reflection growth.

docs.title: Scaffolded Learning
docs.text:
• Cover letter sentence stems for each of the 5 sections
  • Pre-drawn nanobot outline students label rather than drawing from scratch, plus a size-comparison word bank and a clot-tool word bank
  • Fairview Edge case-file table with the water-source and symptoms-started columns pre-highlighted so students compare the two variables that matter
  • Response plan with the Helpful Info for Investigators facts reprinted at the top of the page
  • Pre-filled emerging career research template with one career modeled

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
• "Patient Education" (FYF pp. 82-83): partners write, test, and revise AI prompts for a labeled medical illustration, then judge accuracy against what a patient would actually need
  • Research a specific DFW biotech employer (McKesson, Kimberly-Clark Health, UT Southwestern Medical Center) and identify what careers they hire for
  • Calculate the total education cost for a Biomedical Engineer and find the salary break-even point
  • Build a 4-year plan for the Irving High Biomedical Sciences pathway including AP Biology and dual credit options
  • Write the one-paragraph public notice Fairview Edge would post at the grocery store and the school

docs.title: ELL Language Support
docs.text:
• Pre-teach: Biomedical = Biomédico, Research = Investigación, Laboratory = Laboratorio, Emerging = Emergente, Cover Letter = Carta de Presentación, Outbreak = Brote, Blood clot = Coágulo
  • Bilingual labels allowed on the nanobot drawing; the drawing carries most of the meaning, so students can present visually and name parts in either language
  • Bilingual Fairview Edge case-file table with the symptom words translated
  • Pair ELL students with bilingual peers for the Day 3 Think-Pair-Share and the Day 4 presentations
  • The workbook reads well above grade level, so read the scenario paragraphs aloud and encourage browser translation for any independent reading

docs.title: Day 1: Ag Cluster Tour + Animal Systems Hats
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Welcome the new six weeks and the new cluster; explore the Agriculture, Food & Natural Resources cluster in H&L; identify Animal Systems careers; complete a career research worksheet for one veterinary career TEKS d(1)(B), d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up and Be the Decision Maker · Explain: Check Out These Hats share-out · Explore: App cluster tour and career research worksheet · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed career research worksheet for one Animal Systems career Materials Chromebooks, H&L accounts, Find Your Future workbook pp. 87 and 102, printed career research worksheet, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: If your dog or cat got sick, who would you take them to? What does that person actually do all day?

Discuss 2-3 student responses, then add the work students may not have named: diagnostics, surgery, nutrition counseling, behavior, and research. This opens the 3rd Six Weeks and the Animal Systems pathway.

docs.title: Activity 1: H&L Agriculture Cluster Tour (20 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 87: "Exploring the World of AGRICULTURE, FOOD, AND NATURAL RESOURCES") + (FYF p. 102: "App Exploration")

Open the lesson by framing the move from Health Science (last six weeks) into a brand new cluster. Reassure students that even though the cluster name says "Agriculture," it is much broader than farming. It includes vets, food scientists, environmental engineers, and drone pilots.

Read the chapter opener together (FYF p. 87). The workbook frames the cluster as growing food, caring for animals, and managing the land and resources people depend on every day, plus the people who keep those systems running by testing soil and water and protecting natural spaces. The work happens on farms, in greenhouses, in labs, and outdoors. The page puts three Hats in front of students: Feedlot Manager, Agricultural Engineer, and Veterinarian.

Be the Decision Maker (FYF p. 87). The opener hands students a design problem: you are in charge of designing a "future farm" that has to feed a busy city. Would you build it underground, on rooftops, or in giant vertical towers? What would you grow or raise there, and how would it all work together? Think-Pair-Share: 30 seconds of silent Think, then Partner A for 30 seconds, then Partner B for 30 seconds. Two pairs share out.

Close the read with the opener's own reflection question about the three Hats: how do these careers impact our lives on a daily basis? Take three responses and push each one to name a specific object or moment from an ordinary day.

[H&L PLATFORM] Project the App Exploration steps (FYF p. 102) and release them one at a time. Students open the Hats & Ladders app, go to Clusters, and click the Agriculture, Food, and Natural Resources cluster. They watch the "Cluster Tour" video, then click "Game Time," play the game, and write down one thing they learned. Then they find 1 Hat that matches their personality or interests and 1 Hat that feels like it is NOT a fit, recording why for each. The "Pathway Possibilities" and Hat-rating steps on the same page are saved for Day 5.

Facilitation Tip

Many students assume agriculture means farming and feel like this cluster doesn't apply to them. The chapter opener does the work for you. Name the three Hats printed on the page (Feedlot Manager, Agricultural Engineer, Veterinarian), then add two more from the app browse that are nowhere near a field, such as a food scientist or a water conservation specialist. The pathway names live in the app under "Pathway Possibilities" and on the district pages, not in the chapter text, so hold that step for Day 5 instead of listing pathways from memory.

docs.title: Activity 2: Career Research — One Animal Systems Career (20 min)
docs.text:
Source: CCE career research worksheet (the research routine is taught in Wk0 from FYF pp. 4-5: "Perks and Quirks") + (FYF p. 102: "App Exploration")

Transition into the Animal Systems pathway. Project the Animal Systems pathway page in H&L and point out that this pathway includes careers from kennel assistants to wildlife biologists to veterinarians.

Each student picks ONE Animal Systems career that interests them. Veterinarian, Vet Technician, Animal Trainer, Wildlife Biologist, or Zookeeper, and completes the career research worksheet.

[H&L PLATFORM] Students click on the Hat Finder, filter to the "Agriculture, Food, and Natural Resources" cluster, and open their chosen Animal Systems career. They pull the education, salary, daily task, and tool details straight off the Hat profile onto the worksheet. This is the same research routine Wk0 taught on two Hats, run here on one.

The career research worksheet requires these fields:

  • Name of Career
  • What Interests You? (1-2 sentences)
  • Brief Job Description
  • Education/Training Needed
  • Average Salary
  • What Tools, Equipment, or Skills are Needed for This Career?

DOK 2: Compare the daily responsibilities of a Vet Technician versus a Wildlife Biologist. What overlap do you see, and where do they differ?

Facilitation Tip

If students struggle to find a career inside the H&L app, walk them through: Hat Finder → filter by cluster (Agriculture, Food, and Natural Resources) → scroll the career list. Have them pause and check education/salary fields specifically. Those are the data they need for tomorrow's comparison.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Mini-Case / Scenario Application) · Printable PDF:

Scenario: Sofia loves animals but is allergic to cats and dogs. She also loves being outside. Sofia is looking at the H&L Animal Systems pathway.

  1. Which Animal Systems career would you recommend to Sofia (examples: Wildlife Biologist, Zookeeper, Marine Biologist, Equine Trainer, Animal Shelter Manager)? Use your career research worksheet or today's Hat browse.

My pick: _____

  1. In one sentence, use ONE detail from your research (education, daily task, setting) that makes your pick BETTER than a general Veterinarian for Sofia specifically:
  1. Name ONE other Animal Systems career from today that would NOT fit Sofia, and why:

Bad-fit career: _____. Why not: _____________

(d(1)(B), d(1)(C))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a partially completed career research worksheet with the career name and one section pre-filled as a model.
  • Extension: Research a SECOND Animal Systems career and prepare a side-by-side mini-comparison for tomorrow's class.
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Veterinarian = Veterinario/a, Animal = Animal, Education = Educación. Provide a bilingual career research worksheet with Spanish field labels. The workbook opener reads above grade level, so read FYF p. 87 aloud rather than assigning it as silent reading.

docs.title: Day 2: Vet Tech vs. Veterinarian — Career Deep-Dive
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Research the differences between Vet Tech and Veterinarian careers; compare education, salary, and daily tasks; complete a side-by-side comparison worksheet TEKS d(2)(A), d(2)(B) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: BLS page walkthrough · Explore: Comparison worksheet and side-by-side analysis · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed Vet Career Comparison worksheet (Vet Tech vs. Veterinarian) Materials Chromebooks, BLS website tabs pre-loaded, printed Vet Career Comparison worksheet, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: A Vet Tech earns about $38,000 a year. A Veterinarian earns about $108,000 a year. The Veterinarian's school takes 8 years after high school. The Vet Tech's school takes 2 years. Which job sounds better to YOU, and why?

Take 3-4 quick responses without judgment. Put the trade-off on the board: more school may lead to more pay, but it also means more years in school and possibly more debt. Students will use today's research to check both sides against BLS data.

docs.title: Activity 1: BLS Career Research (20 min)
docs.text:
Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook

Project the BLS Veterinarians page. Walk students through the page sections:

  • What They Do (read aloud the first paragraph)
  • Pay (median annual wage)
  • How to Become One (education, license, hours)
  • Job Outlook (% growth over 10 years)

Then show the Vet Tech page and call out the same sections side by side.

Direct students to open both pages in tabs on their Chromebooks:

  • BLS Veterinarians: bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/veterinarians.htm
  • BLS Vet Technologists & Technicians: bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/veterinary-technologists-and-technicians.htm

Students complete the Vet Career Comparison worksheet using both pages. The worksheet has a 6-row table with columns for Vet Tech and Veterinarian:

Field Vet Tech Veterinarian Median Annual Pay Years of School After HS Required License/Cert Job Outlook (% growth) One Daily Task One Workplace Setting

Facilitation Tip

The BLS pages are dense. Project the Veterinarian page, point out the median pay number under the "Pay" tab, and have students find it on their own screens before they continue. Repeat the demo for the Vet Tech page.

docs.title: Activity 2: Side-by-Side Analysis (20 min)
docs.text:
After the worksheet is complete, students answer two analysis questions on the back of the worksheet. Stop and Jot: both answers are written, not discussed, and the stems stay on the screen while students write: "A Vet Tech earns $_ after years of school. A Veterinarian earns $ after _ years." and " fits me better right now because ."

  1. Math check: Calculate the difference in salary between the two careers. Then calculate how many extra YEARS of school it takes to become a Veterinarian vs. a Vet Tech. If a vet earns $70,000 more per year but goes to school 6 extra years, after how many years does the extra pay catch up to the extra school cost? (Assume vet school costs $50,000 per year.)

  2. Personal fit: Which career fits YOU better right now? Use at least two pieces of evidence from your worksheet to defend your answer.

DOK 3: What conclusions can you draw about why some students would choose Vet Tech over Veterinarian, even though Veterinarians earn more?

Connection to TEKS d(2)(B)

This activity covers d(2)(B) by having students use BLS to evaluate education and training options. Make sure every student cites BLS data in their personal-fit answer, not just opinion.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Comparison Matrix) · Printable PDF:

Use the BLS data from your worksheet to fill in the matrix.

Vet Tech Veterinarian Years of school AFTER high school Median annual pay (BLS) One daily task

Bottom line: After comparing both careers, I am more interested in becoming a _____.

In one sentence, use ONE SPECIFIC NUMBER from the matrix to explain why my choice fits me BETTER than the other: (d(2)(A), d(2)(B))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Pre-fill the worksheet with the median pay numbers already entered. Students focus on filling in the other rows and the analysis questions.
  • Extension: Research a third related career. Veterinary Specialist (e.g., Veterinary Surgeon, Veterinary Cardiologist). How does the salary and education differ from a general Veterinarian?
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Salary = Salario, Median = Mediana, Outlook = Perspectiva, Required = Requerido. Provide a bilingual comparison worksheet with Spanish column headers.

docs.title: Day 3: Powerskill: Critical Thinking — Veterinary Triage
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Work the triage desk at an emergency animal hospital; compare two patients' vitals against normal-range references; identify the critical information in each chart; decide who is seen first and defend the decision with evidence TEKS d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up and triage scenario · Explore: Patient charts and normal-range check · Explain: Share and compare decisions · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed triage notes for both patients (critical information for Leo and Barnaby) + a written decision naming who is seen first and the evidence behind it Materials Find Your Future workbook pp. 96-99; projector; optional printed copies of the two patient charts and the normal-range references for students who need them off-screen

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Two sick animals arrive at an animal hospital at the exact same second. Only one vet is free. How would you decide who gets seen first?

Take 3 fast responses and write the deciding factor from each one on the board (loudest, biggest, sickest, first through the door). Leave the list up. Today students find out that the real answer is none of those, and that the job of sorting patients by urgency has a name.

docs.title: Activity 1: The Triage Desk + Meet the Patients (10 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 96-97: "Powerskill: Critical Thinking"), Step 1

Introduce the Powerskill first. The workbook defines critical thinking as the ability to analyze information and make thoughtful decisions. Strong critical thinkers ask questions, look closely at details, and use evidence to guide their choices. Point at the warm-up list on the board and note which of those factors are guesses and which are evidence.

Set the scenario (FYF p. 96). Students are a veterinary technician working the triage desk at a busy emergency animal hospital. Triage is the critical first step when a sick or injured animal arrives. Today two very different patients arrive at the exact same time, and the technician has to decide who needs emergency care first.

Patient Chart #1: Leo (FYF p. 96). Leo is a 3-year-old ball python. The owner reports that Leo has not eaten recently, has been hiding, and hissed when handled, and notes dull skin and cloudy eyes. The family recently moved to a new apartment and added a new water bowl last week. Triage assessment: weight 2.64 pounds, behavior alert and defensive and coiled tightly, heart rate 34 bpm. Physical observations: eyes are opaque and milky blue with complete loss of clarity, skin across the whole body is dull and dry with slight wrinkling near the neck, inside of the mouth is normal color, no external parasites or wounds.

Patient Chart #2: Barnaby (FYF p. 97). Barnaby is a 4-year-old Golden Retriever. The owner reports that he began pacing and whining about an hour after eating, with abdominal swelling, and has been retching repeatedly with no productive vomit, producing only white foamy saliva. Triage assessment: weight 74.96 pounds, behavior highly anxious and pacing and unable to get comfortable, heart rate 150 bpm with a pulse that feels weak and rapid. Physical observations: abdomen visibly distended, firm, and painful on gentle touch.

Students read both charts and underline every number and every physical observation. No decision yet.

Facilitation Tip

Most students pick Leo on first read, because cloudy eyes and dull skin look alarming and a snake is unfamiliar. Do not correct that yet. The whole point of Step 2 is that a symptom cannot be judged until it is measured against what is normal for that animal, and the reversal lands harder if students commit to a first impression before they get the reference pages.

docs.title: Activity 2: Normal Ranges, Critical Information, Decision (25 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 98-99: "Powerskill: Critical Thinking"), Steps 2-4

Step 2: Check the Normal Ranges (8 min). Students turn to the reference page (FYF p. 98) and ask one question about every stat they underlined: is this normal or abnormal? The workbook supplies both reference sets.

Reference Ball python (adult) Canine, Golden Retriever (adult male) Weight 1,000 to 1,500 grams (2.2 to 3.3 lbs) 65 to 75 lbs Heart rate / pulse 25 to 40 bpm, steady 60 to 100 bpm, strong and steady Behavior Calm, slow-moving, tolerates gentle handling Alert, relaxed, able to settle comfortably Physical findings Eyes clear and glossy, skin smooth and vibrant Abdomen soft, flat, not painful when touched gently

Both reference boxes carry an "Important note" that decides the case, and students need to read both before they go on. The ball python note explains that a python preparing to shed will refuse food, hide, become irritable, and develop dull skin and cloudy eyes, a normal biological process called ecdysis. The canine note explains that in large, deep-chested breeds, bloating with unproductive retching after eating can point to a serious internal condition, and that unlike a regular stomach upset this kind of situation can become life-threatening quickly.

Step 3: Identify Critical Information (10 min). Students write the critical information for each patient in the two columns on FYF p. 99. Stop and Jot: 5 minutes per patient, silent, with two stems on the screen: "This finding is outside the normal range because _" and "This finding looks bad but the reference page says it is normal because ___." Every line students write has to name the reference number or the note it came from.

Step 4: Make a Decision (7 min). Each student answers the workbook question on p. 99: who needs to be seen first, and why? The justification has to cite at least two pieces of evidence from the charts or the reference page.

Facilitation Tip

Walk a fixed pathway three times, one target per lap. Lap 1, every student has compared Barnaby's 150 bpm against the 60 to 100 reference. Lap 2, every student has found the ecdysis note and marked Leo's cloudy eyes and dull skin as expected rather than alarming. Lap 3, every decision sentence carries two pieces of evidence. Two misconceptions are worth having an answer ready for before class: "the snake looks worse" (send them back to the reference line, not the photo) and "the dog is not bleeding so he can wait" (send them to the note about deep-chested breeds). If more than a handful of students miss the Lap 2 target, pause the room and reread the ecdysis note together instead of repeating it desk by desk.

DOK 3: What conclusions can you draw about why a triage technician has to know the normal range for every species that walks in, instead of trusting how sick a patient looks?

docs.title: Activity 3: Share and Compare (8 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 99: "Powerskill: Critical Thinking"), Step 5 and Class Discussion

Students join a small group and compare decisions using the workbook's own prompts: did every group member choose the same patient to be seen first, and did they use the same evidence to get there? Groups that agree on the patient but disagree on the evidence are the interesting ones, so ask those groups to report both routes.

Close with two of the workbook's class-discussion questions (FYF p. 99): why is critical thinking a Powerskill in a high-stress workplace like an emergency animal hospital, and what is the difference between a symptom that looks scary and a symptom that is actually dangerous? Then name the team: a real clinic runs this decision through a Veterinarian, a Vet Tech, an Animal Care Assistant, and a Practice Manager, and the triage technician's call sets the order everyone else works in.

What the Evidence Should Show

Barnaby is seen first. His heart rate of 150 bpm is well above the 60 to 100 canine range, his pulse is weak and rapid, and his abdomen is distended, firm, and painful, which the reference page ties to a condition that can turn life-threatening quickly. Every one of Leo's findings sits inside the ball python reference ranges (2.64 lbs, 34 bpm) or is explained by the shedding note. Leo still gets an appointment, just not the emergency slot.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (2 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Decision Tree / Branching Prompt) · Printable PDF:

My role: veterinary technician at the triage desk.

New patient: Daisy is an adult Golden Retriever. Her owner says she threw up once this morning and then ate her breakfast. Daisy is standing calmly and wagging her tail. Her heart rate is 80 bpm.

Step 1: What is your FIRST action at the triage desk? (One specific action.)

Step 2: A normal dog heart rate is 60 to 100 bpm. Daisy's is 80 bpm. Circle one: NORMAL / ABNORMAL

In one sentence, does Daisy need the emergency slot ahead of a dog like Barnaby? Why?

Step 3: Now change ONE thing. Daisy's belly is hard, swollen, and hurts when you touch it.

What do you do differently, and why? _____________

Step 4: Name ONE career on the vet clinic team you would tell first, and say what that person would do next:

Career: _____. What they do: _____________

(d(1)(C))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a triage note-catcher with the four reference rows pre-printed and a blank NORMAL / ABNORMAL box beside each finding, so students sort before they write. Sentence stems: "Barnaby's heart rate is _ and the normal range is , so it is __." and "Leo's cloudy eyes are _ because the reference page says ___."
  • Extension: Write Patient Chart #3 for a third animal arriving at the same time, with a full triage assessment and at least one finding that looks alarming but is normal for that species. Trade with a partner and see whether they can spot the fake alarm.
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Triage = Triaje, Symptom = Síntoma, Heart rate = Frecuencia cardíaca, Swollen = Hinchado, Normal range = Rango normal, Evidence = Evidencia. The two charts read well above grade level, so read them aloud while students underline, and let students write their critical-information notes in Spanish or bilingually.

docs.title: Day 4: Xello Life Experiences + Volunteer Hours
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Complete the Xello Life Experiences lesson; log existing volunteer hours; understand how informal experiences (chores, pet care, sports) build the skills colleges and employers look for TEKS d(1)(A), d(1)(C), d(4)(E) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Xello Life Experiences and Volunteer Hours · Extend: Connect experiences to vet careers · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed Xello Life Experiences lesson (screenshot of completion screen) + at least one Volunteer Hours entry (or planned entry) Materials Chromebooks, Xello student accounts, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: List one thing you do regularly that nobody pays you for, chores, walking a dog, watching a sibling, helping a neighbor, sports practice. Now: what skill does that activity teach you?

Take 4-5 fast responses. The point: students already have life experiences that will matter to colleges and employers. Today they learn how to log them in Xello so they don't get forgotten.

docs.title: Activity 1: Xello Life Experiences Lesson (25 min)
docs.text:
Source: Bowie Grade 8 Xello Completion Standard, "Life experiences"

Open Xello on the projector. Sign in with the school SSO and walk students through finding the Life Experiences lesson:

  1. From the Xello dashboard, click on the lessons tab
  2. Find "Life Experiences" in the 7th-grade lesson list
  3. Click "Start" or "Continue"

Students complete the Xello Life Experiences lesson on their own Chromebooks. The lesson typically includes:

  • A short video or slide deck explaining what counts as a life experience
  • Examples of life experiences (jobs, sports, hobbies, family responsibilities, volunteer work)
  • Reflection prompts about what each experience teaches

As students work, circulate and check that they are reading and reflecting, not just clicking through. Pause the class once at the midpoint to ask: "What is one experience you wrote down that you almost forgot was important?"

Facilitation Tip

Students often think "experience" means a paid job, so they leave the form blank. Reframe with examples: babysitting a younger sibling = experience with childcare and patience. Walking a neighbor's dog = experience with reliability and animal handling. Helping at family events = experience with hospitality. Every veterinary job application asks about animal handling experience, informal pet care counts.

docs.title: Activity 2: Xello Volunteer Hours Entry (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: Bowie Grade 8 Xello Completion Standard, "Volunteer hours"

After completing the Life Experiences lesson, students navigate to the Volunteer Hours section in their Xello profile (typically under "About Me" or "My Profile"). They add at least ONE volunteer hours entry. If they have never officially volunteered, they can:

  • Log a recurring family/community responsibility (helping at church, cleaning common areas, helping at family events)
  • Log a one-time school volunteer event (book fair, club setup, school cleanup)
  • Plan a future volunteer activity to log later

Each entry needs: organization name, role, hours, and a 1-2 sentence description of what they did and learned.

[VERIFY IN Xello] Confirm with your district that the Volunteer Hours field is enabled in your school's Xello configuration. If it is not, students complete the Life Experiences lesson only and log volunteer experiences in their notebook for later transfer.

DOK 2: How does logging volunteer hours in middle school help you when you apply to a vet science high school pathway like Nimitz HS in 8th grade?

docs.title: Activity 3: Connect to Vet Careers (3 min)
docs.text: Quick whole-class share: which life experience or volunteer activity from today would help on a vet clinic job application? (Examples: pet sitting, animal shelter volunteering, 4-H club, family farm chores, working at a pet store.) Write 2-3 student examples on the board.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (2 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Short Constructed Response) · Printable PDF:

  1. One life experience I logged in Xello today: _____

  2. ONE specific skill this experience teaches me (NOT "responsibility" — be specific: "handling a sick dog," "speaking clearly to customers," "showing up on time for practice"):

  1. ONE veterinary career (or Animal Systems career) that VALUES this exact skill, and why:

Career: _____. Why the skill matters: _____________

  1. One volunteer activity I could do in the NEXT 2 WEEKS to add another logged hour (animal shelter, 4-H, community garden, school cleanup, church event):

(d(1)(A), d(1)(C), d(4)(E))

Submit your Xello Life Experiences completion screenshot with this ticket.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a printed list of common middle-school life experiences students can choose from if they get stuck thinking of their own.
  • Extension: Plan a real volunteer opportunity in the next two weeks at a local animal shelter, vet clinic, or community garden. Bring back proof to log in Xello.
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Volunteer = Voluntario/a, Experience = Experiencia, Hours = Horas. Xello supports Spanish language toggle, show students how to switch the interface language if needed.

docs.title: Day 5: Nimitz Vet Pathway + H&L Favorites
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Research the Nimitz HS Veterinary Science pathway and Elanco certification; favorite vet careers in H&L Climber Profile; write a personal pathway brief TEKS d(2)(A), d(2)(B), d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: Nimitz pathway map · Explore: App Exploration and Climber Profile favorites · Extend: Veterinary Pathway Brief · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable One-page Veterinary Pathway Brief (career research worksheet + comparison + reflection paragraph + Climber Profile screenshot) Materials Chromebooks, H&L accounts, Find Your Future workbook pp. 100-102, Vet Career Comparison worksheet from Day 2, career research worksheet from Day 1, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: After this week, do you see yourself working with animals as a career? Why or why not? One sentence.

Take 4 student responses. Some students will say yes, some will say no, and some will be undecided. Ask each student to name the experience or information behind the answer; CCE does not require a student to choose the pathway.

docs.title: Activity 1: Nimitz Vet Science Pathway Research (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 100-101: "What is Happening at My District?") + Irving ISD Pathways reference (PATHWAYS.md): Nimitz HS Veterinary Science pathway leading to Elanco Veterinary Medical Applications certification

Project the workbook's district pages (FYF pp. 100-101). Nimitz High School's Agricultural Science program has a greenhouse, an orchard, more than 40 chickens, and a daily petcare program where students care for, handle, and train dogs. The pages name Plant Science and Animal Science as the programs of study, Elanco Veterinary Medical Applications as the industry certification, and Future Farmers of America (FFA) as the student organization. Before moving to the map, take two responses to the pages' question about what makes someone a good mentor.

Walk students through the pathway map:

  • Middle school (now): CCE course, explore Animal Systems, complete the career research worksheet
  • High school at Nimitz: Veterinary Science pathway → Elanco Veterinary Medical Applications certification
  • Post-high school options:
    • Direct to vet clinic employment as Veterinary Assistant or Kennel Tech (with high school cert)
    • Community college Vet Tech program (2 years) → state credential as Vet Tech
    • 4-year university pre-vet program → 4-year DVM at vet school → Veterinarian
    • Animal-related military career (Army Veterinary Corps)

Students take notes on which post-high school option appeals to them and why. They identify which middle school courses would help them prepare: science, math, English (for client communication), CTE electives.

Facilitation Tip

Some students will think "I have to decide right now." Reassure them: the goal of taking this pathway in high school is OPTIONS. A Nimitz Vet Science graduate can work in a clinic the day after graduation, or use it as a credential while going to community college. The pathway opens doors; it doesn't lock them in.

docs.title: Activity 2: H&L Favorites + Climber Profile Update (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 102: "App Exploration"), the Pathway Possibilities and Hat-rating steps held back from Day 1

Students return to Hats & Ladders and finish the App Exploration page. They click "Pathway Possibilities," answer the questions, and explore and rate at least 1 pathway, then rate at least 3 Hats in the cluster. This is where the Agriculture pathway names live now, so it is the first time students see the full pathway list.

[H&L PLATFORM] Direct students to the Hat Finder in the H&L app, filter by the Agriculture, Food, and Natural Resources cluster, browse Animal Systems careers, and click the heart/favorite icon on each Hat they want to save. The favorited Hats appear in their Climber Profile under "Favorites." Students favorite 2-3 Animal Systems careers.

After favoriting, students take a screenshot of their Climber Profile favorites screen and save it to their Google Drive (or print). This screenshot is part of today's deliverable.

docs.title: Activity 3: Veterinary Pathway Brief (12 min)
docs.text:
Students assemble their one-page summative brief. The brief is the synthesis of everything they did this week. Time, Voice, Body: post the three blocks before the assembly starts, Voice 0 for the reflection paragraph, Voice 1 for checking a missing piece with a neighbor, a visible countdown on the screen, and one stated place on each table where the Day 1 and Day 2 worksheets go so nobody loses a component while writing.

Brief includes:

  1. Career research worksheet from Day 1 (one Animal Systems career, fully filled in)
  2. Vet Career Comparison worksheet from Day 2 (Vet Tech vs. Veterinarian table + analysis)
  3. Reflection paragraph (4-6 sentences) answering: Does the Nimitz HS Vet Science pathway interest me? Why or why not? Use specific evidence from this week's research.
  4. Screenshot of H&L Climber Profile favorites from Activity 2

The reflection paragraph is the only new writing, the rest is assembly of work already completed. Students write the reflection in their notebook or in a Google Doc.

DOK 4: Looking back at all 5 days this week, what is one thing you now KNOW about veterinary careers that you did not know on Monday? How did you learn it (which activity)?

Sentence stems for the reflection

"After researching this week, I am [interested / not yet sure / not interested] in the Nimitz Vet Science pathway because _. The most surprising thing I learned was . If I do pursue this pathway, my next step would be __."

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Concept Map / Connection Diagram) · Printable PDF:

A veterinary career I favorited in H&L today: _____

Connect this career to THREE things:

1. The Nimitz HS Veterinary Science pathway (leads to Elanco Veterinary Medical Applications certification)

Does the Nimitz pathway lead DIRECTLY to my favorited career or is it a STEPPING STONE? Circle: DIRECT / STEPPING STONE. One sentence why:

2. ONE life experience I logged in Xello yesterday

My experience: _____. In one sentence, how does this experience prepare me for the favorited career?

3. My Wk0 core personality type (Doer, Analyzer, Creator, Helper, Persuader, or Organizer)

My core personality type: _____. In one sentence, does this career fit my type, and why?

(d(2)(A), d(2)(B), d(1)(C))

Submit your Veterinary Pathway Brief with this ticket.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a Brief Assembly Checklist with each component listed and a checkbox. Students check off each piece as they assemble it.
  • Extension: Add a fourth section to the brief: a 4-year high school course plan based on the Nimitz Vet Science pathway requirements. Use the Nimitz HS course catalog as a reference.
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Pathway = Carrera/Camino, Certification = Certificación, Brief = Resumen. The reflection paragraph may be written in English, Spanish, or bilingual. Provide Spanish sentence stems.

docs.title: Week 1: Animal Planet — Veterinary Science Careers
docs.text: 3rd Six Weeks | Agriculture, Food & Natural Resources Cluster | 5 class periods (50 min each)

docs.title: Lesson Objective
docs.text:
Students explore the Agriculture, Food & Natural Resources cluster through Hats & Ladders and the Find Your Future workbook, investigate veterinary careers from Vet Tech to Veterinarian, compare education pathways, and work the triage desk in the workbook's "Powerskill: Critical Thinking" activity, weighing two emergency patients against normal-range references to decide who is seen first.

Learning Target: I can name at least three veterinary careers, tell how much school a Vet Tech and a Veterinarian each need, compare a sick animal's vitals to the normal range for its species, and decide which patient the vet sees first.

Success Criteria: I will know I am successful when my career research worksheet lists the job, the training, the pay, and the tools for one Animal Systems career, when my comparison worksheet fills in all six rows for both the Vet Tech and the Veterinarian, when my triage notes name the critical information for both patients and my decision cites two pieces of evidence, and when my Veterinary Pathway Brief has all four parts.

docs.title: Demonstration of Learning
docs.text: "I can describe at least three veterinary careers, explain the difference between a Vet Tech and a Veterinarian's education pathway, use normal-range evidence to decide which emergency patient is seen first, and connect the Nimitz HS Veterinary Science pathway to a real career goal."

docs.title: TEKS Alignment
docs.text:
• d(1)(A): Analyze and discuss assessment results (Day 4 Xello Life Experiences reflection).
  • d(1)(B): Explore and describe the CTE career clusters (Day 1).
  • d(1)(C): Identify various career opportunities within the Ag, Food & Natural Resources cluster (Days 1-5).
  • d(2)(A): Research and describe applicable academic, technical, certification, and training requirements (Days 2, 5).
  • d(2)(B): Use available resources to research and evaluate educational and training options (Days 2, 5).
  • d(4)(E): Community service and volunteerism (Day 4 Xello Volunteer Hours).

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Chromebooks with internet access (1 per student)
  • Hats & Ladders student accounts + Find Your Future workbook, Agriculture, Food, and Natural Resources chapter (printed pp. 87-102)
  • BLS, Veterinarians: bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/veterinarians.htm
  • BLS, Vet Technologists & Technicians: bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/veterinary-technologists-and-technicians.htm
  • Xello student accounts (Life Experiences activity + Volunteer Hours)
  • Printed Vet Career Comparison worksheet (Vet Tech vs. Veterinarian)
  • Printed Animal Systems career research worksheet (CCE artifact; the research format is taught in Wk0)
  • Optional printed copies of the two patient charts and the normal-range references for Day 3 (FYF pp. 96-99: "Powerskill: Critical Thinking")
  • Projector

docs.title: Career Connection
docs.text:
Vet Techs assist with surgery, run lab tests, and may use 3D printing for prosthetics and surgical guides. Veterinarians diagnose illness, perform surgery, and make treatment decisions after about eight years of college and veterinary school. This week lets students compare the daily work, pay, and training instead of treating every animal-care job as the same career.

What is Happening at Irving ISD? Veterinary Science at Nimitz High School leads to the Elanco Veterinary Medical Applications certification. The workbook's district pages describe a greenhouse, an orchard, more than 40 chickens, and a daily petcare program where students care for, handle, and train dogs (FYF pp. 100-101: "What is Happening at My District?"). The pages name Plant Science and Animal Science as the programs of study, Elanco Veterinary Medical Applications as the industry certification, and Future Farmers of America (FFA) as the student organization. Day 5 uses the pages' mentorship prompt to discuss how students learn this work from someone with experience.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text:
• Veterinary Technician: A professional who provides support to veterinarians in medical and surgical procedures. Requires a 2-year associate degree and state credentialing.
  • Veterinarian: A doctor of veterinary medicine (DVM). Requires 4 years of undergraduate study + 4 years of veterinary school + state license.
  • Animal Systems: The CTE pathway focused on the care, management, and health of animals.
  • Diagnostic Testing: Medical tests used to identify diseases or conditions in animals.
  • Triage: Sorting patients by how urgently they need care. It is the first step when a sick or injured animal arrives at an emergency clinic.
  • Powerskill: In Hats & Ladders, a skill that carries across careers. This week's Powerskill is critical thinking: analyzing information and using evidence to make a decision.
  • Climber Profile: The H&L app feature where students save favorite Hats and track exploration.
  • Hat: In H&L, a "Hat" is a career profile with information about education, daily tasks, salary, and demand.

docs.title: Bridge to Theory (Hats & Ladders)
docs.text:
The Find Your Future workbook gives Agriculture, Food, and Natural Resources printed pages 87-102. The chapter opener (FYF p. 87: "Exploring the World of AGRICULTURE, FOOD, AND NATURAL RESOURCES") frames the cluster as growing food, caring for animals, and managing the land and resources people depend on, hands students a "Be the Decision Maker" future-farm design problem, and prints three Hats on the page: Feedlot Manager, Agricultural Engineer, and Veterinarian. The chapter does not print a pathway list. Students meet the Agriculture pathways in the Hats & Ladders app instead, through the Pathway Possibilities step on the App Exploration page (FYF p. 102: "App Exploration"), and they meet Irving ISD's own programs of study on the district pages (FYF pp. 100-101).

One chapter activity carries this week. Powerskill: Critical Thinking (Day 3) puts students at the triage desk of a busy emergency animal hospital (FYF pp. 96-99: "Powerskill: Critical Thinking"). Two patients arrive at the same second: Leo, a ball python whose owner reports cloudy eyes, dull skin, and refused food, and Barnaby, a Golden Retriever retching with a swollen abdomen an hour after eating. Students compare each chart against the workbook's printed normal-range references, identify the critical information, decide who is seen first, and compare their evidence in a small group. The reversal the activity is built around, that Leo's alarming symptoms are normal shedding while Barnaby's are not, is the same reasoning a Vet Tech runs at a real triage desk, and it replaces the old food-science teamwork activity with content that sits inside this week's own career field.

The chapter's three Career Climb activities belong to the other two weeks of this six weeks: Grow System Rescue (FYF pp. 88-90) and Farm to Table (FYF pp. 91-92) run in Week 2 Plant Science, and Ag-Tech Pest Patrol (FYF pp. 93-95) runs in Week 3 Sustainable Engineering. Leave them for those weeks.

docs.title: IISD Instructional Strategies
docs.text:
• Think-Pair-Share: Day 1, Activity 1, the "Be the Decision Maker" future-farm prompt on the chapter opener (FYF p. 87), where students design a farm that has to feed a busy city. Distinguished: pose it to the whole group, hold a silent 30 second Think, then time Partner A for 30 seconds and Partner B for 30 seconds, and post two stems at different levels: "I would build it _ because " and "A farm inside a city has to solve __, so I would _____." Ask two pairs to share, not one. Listen while pairs talk for who names a constraint (space, water, light, delivery) rather than just a location, and pick your share-out pairs from what you heard rather than from raised hands.
  • Stop and Jot: Day 2, Activity 2, the two analysis questions on the back of the Vet Career Comparison worksheet. Distinguished: give a stated time box, keep the BLS tabs open, and post two stems so the salary and training vocabulary is in front of every student: "A Vet Tech earns $_ after years of school. A Veterinarian earns $ after _ years." and " fits me better right now because ." Read jots over shoulders while students write and track who is answering the personal-fit question with opinion instead of a number. If most jots skip the data, stop the room and model one sentence that cites a BLS figure before students move to the exit ticket, since the ticket demands a specific number.
  • Active Monitoring: Day 3, Activity 2, the normal-range check and triage decision. Distinguished: walk a fixed pathway three times, one target per lap (lap 1, every student has compared Barnaby's 150 bpm against the 60 to 100 canine reference; lap 2, every student has found the shedding note and marked Leo's cloudy eyes as expected; lap 3, every decision sentence carries two pieces of evidence). Have the feedback ready before class for the two known misconceptions: "the snake looks worse" and "the dog is not bleeding so he can wait." If more than a handful of students miss the lap 2 target, pivot and reread the shedding note with the whole room instead of fixing it desk by desk.
  • Chunking: Day 1, Activity 1, the App Exploration sequence (FYF p. 102). Distinguished: project the page and release one step at a time rather than handing students the whole list (Cluster Tour video, then Game Time and the one-thing-I-learned line, then the fit Hat, then the non-fit Hat), say what each step is for before students run it, and check the room between steps before releasing the next one. Note which step stalls. If the non-fit Hat is the one students cannot finish, that becomes a 3 minute reteach at the top of Activity 2, because naming why a career does not fit is exactly what the Day 1 exit ticket asks for.
  • Time, Voice, Body (TVB): Day 5, Activities 2 and 3, the Climber Profile screenshot and the Veterinary Pathway Brief assembly. Distinguished: post the three blocks before the brief starts, Voice 0 for the reflection paragraph, Voice 1 for checking one missing component with a neighbor, a visible countdown on the screen, and one stated place on each table where the Day 1 and Day 2 worksheets go so no component gets lost mid-assembly. Narrate the students who are meeting the expectation rather than correcting the ones who are not. If several students are still hunting for a worksheet when the countdown starts, pause it and run a 60 second component check before the writing time begins.

docs.title: Summative Assessment
docs.text: Veterinary Pathway Brief (Day 5): Students submit a one-page brief that includes (1) the career research worksheet for one veterinary career, (2) the comparison worksheet showing Vet Tech vs. Veterinarian education and salary, (3) a paragraph explaining whether the Nimitz Vet Science pathway interests them and why, and (4) a screenshot of their updated H&L Climber Profile. Scored on accuracy of education/training data (d(2)(A)), depth of comparison (d(2)(B)), and connection to a personal career goal (d(1)(C)).

docs.title: Day 1: Plant Science + Environmental Pathway Hats
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Explore the Agriculture, Food, and Natural Resources cluster and its Plant Science and Environmental & Natural Resources pathways in the H&L app; research 2 careers on the career research worksheet; diagnose a failing hydroponic grow system and justify which problem to fix first TEKS d(1)(B), d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Cluster tour and Grow System Rescue diagnosis · Explain: Compare solutions and class discussion · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Career research worksheet rows for 2 plant science or environmental careers + completed "Grow System Rescue" pages (problem circled, reasoning written, first fix justified) Materials Chromebooks, H&L accounts, Find Your Future workbook pp. 88-90 and p. 102, printed career research worksheet, chart paper and markers for the extension, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Trace one meal you ate yesterday back to the farm. What plants were in it? Where did they grow? Who harvested them?

Take 3-4 student responses, then place Animal Systems and Plant Systems side by side on the board. Both are part of agriculture; today students work with plants and the conditions they need to grow.

docs.title: Activity 1: Ag Cluster Tour + Two Pathways (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 102: "App Exploration"), Agriculture, Food, and Natural Resources chapter

Students work the workbook's App Exploration page, which gives the exact app path for this cluster.

[H&L PLATFORM] Open the Hats & Ladders app. Go to Clusters and click the Agriculture, Food, and Natural Resources Cluster. Watch the "Cluster Tour" video, then click "Pathway Possibilities," answer the questions, and rate at least one pathway.

Name the two pathways this week lives inside while students browse:

  • Plant Science: advances crop growth, production, and agricultural research
  • Environmental and Natural Resources: conserves and manages natural resources like water and forests

Careers worth pointing out as students move through the cluster: Botanist (studies plants and how they grow), Horticulturist (grows and breeds plants for food, ornamental, and landscaping use), Soil Scientist (studies soil composition and what it can grow), Agricultural Engineer (designs farming equipment and systems), Park Ranger, Forester, and Environmental Scientist.

Stop and Jot: The App Exploration page asks two questions. Give 45 seconds for each. First, find one Hat that matches your personality or interests and write which Hat and why. Second, find one Hat that feels like it is NOT a fit and write which Hat and why.

Students then open both Hats and fill two rows of the career research worksheet:

Field Career 1 (fits me) Career 2 (not a fit) Career Name Education/Training Average Salary One Daily Task

[H&L PLATFORM] Each Hat profile carries Education, Salary, and Daily Tasks sections. Students copy those three fields plus the career name onto the worksheet.

Facilitation Tip

Many students assume "Park Ranger" is the only outdoor career. Surface 3-4 less obvious careers (Soil Scientist, Sustainability Consultant, Water Treatment Specialist) so they see how broad the field is.

docs.title: Activity 2: Grow System Rescue — Diagnose the Grow Zone (25 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 88-90: "Grow System Rescue"), a Career Climb activity

Open the workbook to page 88. Students are the hydroponics technician on duty at a large indoor farm. A section of lettuce is in trouble: leaves are yellowing, roots are weak, and some plants have stopped growing. If nobody acts quickly, part of the harvest is lost. Release the steps one at a time and check each before the next.

Step 1: Learn about Hydroponic Systems (3 min). Read the four parts of a hydroponic system together (p. 88). Water flow moves water and nutrients to the roots, nutrients help plants grow strong, lights replace sunlight indoors, and a clean system prevents blockages. A good system moves water evenly to all plants, delivers the right amount of nutrients, provides consistent light, and keeps plants healthy. Check: every student can name the four parts before Step 2 opens.

Step 2: Investigate the Grow Zone (6 min). Students read the four observations from the affected section (p. 89): several leaves are yellow, some roots look dry or thin, water is moving slowly in part of the system, and lights in one area are dim. They weigh each observation against the workbook's four diagnostic tips and write what the clues might mean.

Step 3: Identify the Problem (4 min). Students circle one or more causes from the workbook's list (p. 89): water flow problem, lighting problem, nutrient problem, or system cleanliness problem. They write the reasoning that got them there. More than one answer can be defended here, and the reasoning is what gets scored, not the circle.

Step 4: Decide What to Fix First (5 min). A technician cannot fix everything at once (p. 90). Students pick the one problem to solve first and write why it is the priority and how fixing it helps the lettuce.

Step 6: Compare Solutions (5 min). Partners trade books and compare two things: which problem each one is fixing first, and the reason behind it. Step 5, the chart paper system design, runs as today's extension, so pairs compare diagnoses rather than drawings.

Class Discussion (2 min). Use the workbook's own prompts (p. 90): what other roles would a hydroponics technician work with, and what Powerskills does a hydroponics technician need to be successful?

Facilitation Tip

Students who circle all four causes on Step 3 have not committed to anything. Push them back to the four diagnostic tips on page 89 and ask which single tip their strongest clue matches. Dim lights and yellow leaves both point at light; slow water and thin roots both point at flow. Either is defensible when the reasoning names the clue.

DOK 3: Two technicians look at the same grow zone. One says the pump is the problem and the other says the lights are. What evidence in the grow zone would settle the argument, and which one would you check first?

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Comparison Matrix) · Printable PDF:

Use your career research worksheet to fill in the matrix.

Career 1: ___ Career 2: ___ Pathway (Plant Science OR Environmental & Natural Resources) Training time (rough years) One daily task

Bottom line: Which pathway does EACH career belong to, and which career would be a better fit for someone who wants to work OUTDOORS most days? Use one cell from the matrix to back your pick. (d(1)(B), d(1)(C))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Pre-fill the career research worksheet with 2 specific careers (e.g., Botanist and Park Ranger) so students don't have to choose. For "Grow System Rescue," hand out a Step 2 with two of the four clues already matched to a diagnostic tip so students copy the pattern for the other two.
  • Extension: Complete the workbook's Step 5 (FYF p. 90): design an improved hydroponic system on chart paper and label how water flows to all plants, how nutrients are delivered, how lights reach every plant, and where the plants sit. Students with extra time in the app play "Game Time" and rate three Hats (FYF p. 102).
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Plant = Planta, Soil = Suelo, Forest = Bosque, Water = Agua, Roots = Raíces, Nutrients = Nutrientes. Bilingual career research worksheet with Spanish field labels.

docs.title: Day 2: Farm to Table — Brainstorm + Sketch
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Read the Farm to Table brief from Sunny Fields Farm; brainstorm an infographic about a chosen crop; sketch the infographic layout on paper before building in Canva tomorrow TEKS d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: Email from Sunny Fields Farm · Explore: Crop brainstorm and paper sketch · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed Farm to Table brainstorm sheet + paper sketch of infographic Materials Find Your Future workbook pp. 91-92, printed brainstorm sheet, sticky notes, plain paper for sketching, colored pencils or markers, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Imagine you bought a strawberry at the grocery store. List the steps that strawberry took to get from the field to your hand. How many steps can you name?

Take 4-5 student responses and write them on the board. The class should land on something like: planted → grown → harvested → packaged → trucked → distributed → stocked → bought. This primes the Farm to Table activity perfectly.

docs.title: Activity 1: Read the Farm to Table Scenario (10 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 91: "Farm to Table"), a Career Climb activity

Read the workbook background aloud (p. 91). The farm-to-table process is how fresh fruits and vegetables reach consumers, and small farms often teach people how their food is grown and delivered so customers trust them and see what makes the farm different. Students take the role of an Agricultural Communications Specialist, someone who combines expertise in agriculture with design skills to help small agricultural businesses. Sunny Fields Farm has hired them to build an infographic that shows how its strawberries, grapes, bell peppers, and cucumbers get from the fields to the table.

Step 1: Read the Email From Sunny Fields Farm. The workbook prints the client's email (p. 91). Read it as a class and have students underline the facts they could use:

  • The farm was started in 1998 by the Gordon family with a single acre of land.
  • It specializes in strawberries, grapes, bell peppers, and cucumbers.
  • It never uses harsh chemical pesticides.
  • Schools and families can tour the farm.
  • It uses miniature drones to monitor its crops.
  • Its fruits and vegetables are sold all over the United States.

The same email lists what the client expects: an engaging title, an exciting and colorful design, clear graphics and wording covering planting, growing, harvesting, and selling, and fun facts about the farm. That list is the spec students design against for the next two days.

[H&L PLATFORM] The scenario lives entirely in the workbook, so no app work is needed today. Students do refer back to the Plant Science pathway careers from Day 1 to think about which specialists are involved at each step of the journey.

Facilitation Tip

Show one example infographic on the projector before students brainstorm, such as the USDA "MyPlate" infographic or a farm-to-table graphic from the FDA or a state ag department. Students need to SEE what an infographic looks like before they can plan one. Caution: the model is for inspiration only, students should NOT copy it.

docs.title: Activity 2: Brainstorm — Choose Your Crop (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 92: "Step 2: Brainstorm Ideas")

The workbook asks students to grab sticky notes and brainstorm ideas for the infographic, thinking about what consumers should know about the farm and how visuals help them learn it. Sunny Fields Farm grows four crops: strawberries, grapes, bell peppers, cucumbers. Each student picks ONE crop, parks their sticky notes on the brainstorm sheet, and answers:

  • What crop will your infographic be about? (one of the four)
  • What information do you think consumers most want to see? (e.g., where it's grown, how long it takes to grow, what's healthy about it, how it's harvested)
  • How will this infographic help Sunny Fields Farm? (e.g., builds trust, shows freshness, makes the farm stand out from grocery store competitors)

Students write 1-2 sentences in each box on the brainstorm sheet (provided by the teacher).

Think-Pair-Share: 30 seconds of silent Think on what a customer most wants to know about this crop, then Partner A explains their crop and what information they will include for 30 seconds, then Partner B for 30 seconds. Each partner offers one suggestion to make the other's infographic stronger. Two pairs share with the whole class.

docs.title: Activity 3: Paper Sketch — Layout Plan (15 min)
docs.text:
Before opening Canva tomorrow, students plan their layout on paper. This step prevents students from wasting class time tomorrow scrolling through Canva templates without a plan.

The sketch must include:

  • Title (e.g., "From Sunny Fields to Your Table. Strawberries")
  • At least 4 numbered steps (planting → growing → harvesting → selling)
  • Space for one fun fact
  • One picture or icon spot per step (rough drawings, they'll add real images in Canva tomorrow)
  • A logo spot for Sunny Fields Farm

The sketch can be done in pencil or marker. It's a planning document, not a final product.

DOK 2: Why is a "Farm to Table" infographic more useful for a small farm than a giant grocery store like Kroger? What does a small farm get from showing the journey?

Connection to Career

An Agricultural Communications Specialist has to understand the crop and the customer before designing the message. Students will see this pairing again on Day 4, when each emerging agriculture career combines plant science with another skill set.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Mini-Case / Scenario Application) · Printable PDF:

Scenario: A new client calls Sunny Fields Farm: a DFW elementary school wants an infographic to show KINDERGARTENERS (age 5-6) where their lunch food comes from.

  1. Which crop from the workbook list (strawberries, grapes, bell peppers, cucumbers) fits kindergarteners BEST, and why?

My pick: _____

Why: ____________

  1. What is ONE design choice you would CHANGE from YOUR Day 2 sketch to make it kindergarten-friendly? (Shorter text? Bigger pictures? Fewer steps?)
  1. What is the MOST interesting fact about your crop that a 5-year-old would remember?

(d(1)(C))

Submit your brainstorm sheet and paper sketch with this ticket.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Pre-fill the brainstorm sheet with the crop selected (e.g., assign strawberries) and one info point already written as an example. Provide a pre-printed sketch grid with the title bar and 4 step boxes already drawn.
  • Extension: Sketch TWO infographics, one for the same crop targeting kids, and one targeting adult shoppers. How does the design change for each audience?
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Crop = Cultivo, Step = Paso, Harvest = Cosecha, Customer = Cliente. The infographic can be designed with bilingual labels in Canva tomorrow.

docs.title: Day 3: Farm to Table — Build in Canva
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Translate yesterday's paper sketch into a finished Canva infographic; use design tools (text, icons, color) to create a clear visual; export the final infographic as PNG TEKS d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: Canva setup walkthrough · Explore: Build the infographic · Extend: Interview the Sunny Fields Farm Team · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed Farm to Table infographic exported as PNG and submitted to Google Classroom + two interview questions for the farm team Materials Chromebooks, Canva for Education accounts, Find Your Future workbook p. 92, paper sketches from Day 2, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Look at your paper sketch from yesterday. What is ONE thing you want to make better when you build it in Canva today?

Take 2-3 student responses. The point: students should know their plan before they touch Canva so the design time is focused.

docs.title: Activity 1: Canva Account + Template Setup (10 min)
docs.text:
Walk students through opening Canva on the projector:

  1. Navigate to canva.com/education
  2. Sign in with school Google account (Canva for Education is free for students)
  3. From the home page, click "Create a design" → search "Infographic"
  4. Choose a blank infographic template OR a template that matches the layout from your paper sketch

Common Issue

Some students will pick an over-designed template with 12 sections when they only have 4 steps. Push them toward a SIMPLE template with 4-6 sections that matches their sketch. The template should serve their plan, not the other way around.

Verify all students have a blank or simple infographic open before continuing.

docs.title: Activity 2: Build the Infographic (30 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 92: "Step 3: Create Your Infographic")

The workbook lets students build with a digital tool or on chart paper. This week the tool is Canva. Students follow their paper sketch from Day 2, and the client's email from p. 91 stays open beside them as the spec. Each infographic must include:

  • Title at the top: "From Sunny Fields to Your Table, [Crop Name]"
  • Sunny Fields Farm logo spot (use Canva's "Elements" → Shapes to create a simple text logo, or use a sun icon)
  • At least 4 numbered steps with:
    • A short heading (e.g., "1. Planting")
    • A 1-sentence description
    • An icon or image (search Canva's free icon library)
  • One fun fact box (e.g., "Strawberries are not actually berries, they're aggregate fruit!")
  • Color scheme that matches the crop (red/green for strawberries, purple/green for grapes, etc.)

Walk a fixed pathway through the room three times, one target per lap: at minute 8 every student has all four step headings typed, at minute 15 every step box carries its sentence of text, and at minute 20 every step carries an icon or image. Feedback on each lap is specific to that lap's target, and if a whole table misses the minute 20 target, pause and project the Elements icon search instead of fixing screens one at a time.

Facilitation Tip

The biggest time-waster in Canva is changing fonts and colors over and over. Set a 5-minute soft deadline: by the 15-minute mark, all 4 step boxes should be filled in with text, even if the design isn't polished. Polish comes after the content is in place.

After 25 minutes of building, give students a 5-minute "polish + export" warning. Students export the final design:

  • Click Share → Download → PNG in Canva
  • Save the PNG to their Google Drive
  • Submit the PNG to Google Classroom (or print to share with the class)

DOK 2: Look at your final infographic. If a 6-year-old saw it, would they understand how the strawberry got from the farm to their table? What detail makes it clear (or unclear)?

docs.title: Activity 3: Interview the Farm Team + Quick Show and Tell (3 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 92: "Step 4: Interview the Sunny Fields Farm Team")

The workbook closes the activity by asking students what else they would want to know. In the first 90 seconds, every student writes two interview questions they would ask the Sunny Fields Farm Team to add detail to the project. The questions go on the workbook page or the back of the Day 2 sketch.

In the time left, 1-2 volunteers display their infographic on the projector and read one of their interview questions. Use the workbook's own discussion prompts (p. 92) if the share runs quick: why does it matter that farms teach consumers where food comes from, and what questions might a customer still have after reading the infographic?

docs.title: Exit Ticket (2 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Venn Diagram Comparison) · Printable PDF:

My Farm to Table infographic is designed for adult grocery shoppers. A classmate's infographic is designed for the same crop. Trade infographics in the last 3 minutes of class with a peer who picked the SAME crop you did.

My crop: _____

Unique to MY infographic (2 design choices that are different from my classmate's):

Unique to CLASSMATE's infographic (2 design choices my classmate made that I did NOT):

SHARED by both (2 things we BOTH did, like a similar step or fun fact):

Bottom line: Which infographic is more effective for ADULT SHOPPERS, mine or my classmate's? Use ONE specific design choice to back the pick. (d(1)(C))

Submit your PNG to Google Classroom with this ticket.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a pre-built Canva template (shared via Canva for Education classroom feature) with all 4 step boxes already laid out. Students fill in the text and icons rather than designing from scratch.
  • Extension: Add a fifth step that shows what happens to the food after the customer takes it home (e.g., washed, eaten, composted). This connects to the sustainability theme in Week 3.
  • ELL: Bilingual infographic, design with both English and Spanish labels for each step. Canva supports both languages in the same design.

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Research one emerging agriculture career using BLS and USDA resources; identify the technology and societal trend driving the career's growth; complete a research template TEKS d(1)(D) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: What is an emerging career · Explore: BLS and USDA research · Explain: Paired template trade · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed Emerging Ag Career Research template (one career, fully filled in) Materials Chromebooks, BLS Career Outlook tabs, USDA Careers page, printed Emerging Career Research template, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Drones can now fly over a 50-acre farm and find pest damage in 30 minutes, work that used to take a farmer 2 days. Who flies the drone? Did that job exist 20 years ago?

Take 3 student responses. Define an emerging career as a job created or substantially changed by newer technology or a newer social need. Students will choose one to research today.

docs.title: Activity 1: What Is an Emerging Career? (10 min)
docs.text:
Source: TEKS d(1)(D): Research and evaluate emerging occupations related to career interest areas

Project the definition of "emerging occupation" on the board: a career that has grown rapidly because of new technology, new social needs, or new economic conditions.

Walk through 4 examples in agriculture that didn't exist (or were tiny) in the year 2000:

  • Agricultural Drone Operator: flies drones over fields to detect pests, monitor crop health, and apply targeted spray
  • Precision Agriculture Technician: uses GPS, soil sensors, and data software to help farmers maximize yields with minimum waste
  • Vertical Farming Manager: runs urban indoor farms that grow leafy greens in stacked trays under LED lights
  • Hydroponic Specialist: grows plants in nutrient-rich water without soil, used in cities and even on the International Space Station. Students already worked a day in this job on Day 1, diagnosing the failing lettuce section in "Grow System Rescue"

Each of these is part of a real H&L Hat or BLS career profile. Students will pick ONE for today's research.

Facilitation Tip

Some students will say, "I don't care about farming." Show the work before asking again: Precision Ag Technicians earn $50,000-$80,000 and use drones, GPS, and Python data scripts. These are technology careers applied to agriculture.

docs.title: Activity 2: BLS + USDA Research (25 min)
docs.text:
Source: BLS OOH + USDA Careers page

Students choose ONE emerging ag career and complete the research template using two sources:

  • BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook: bls.gov/ooh/: search for the career or its parent category (e.g., Agricultural Technicians, Agricultural Engineers)
  • USDA Careers: usda.gov/our-agency/careers: find federal ag jobs and read the descriptions

The research template has these fields:

  • Career Name:
  • One-Sentence Description (in your own words):
  • Education/Training Required:
  • Average Salary Range:
  • Job Outlook (% growth or "fast/slow growing"):
  • Technology Used: (drones, GPS, sensors, software, etc.)
  • What Societal/Tech Trend Drives This Career?: (e.g., climate change, urban food deserts, labor shortages on farms)
  • One Real Employer Hiring This Role: (find from a job board search)

Time, Voice, Body: Post the three blocks before anyone opens a browser tab. Voice 0 for the research block, a visible countdown on screen, and finished templates go face up on the corner of the desk so the trade in Activity 3 starts without a hunt.

Walk around and help students who get lost on the BLS site. The most helpful trick: search "Agricultural" in the BLS search bar and pick the closest matching career.

DOK 4: Based on labor market data and the technology driving this career's growth, what argument would you make for why schools should teach this career topic alongside traditional farming?

docs.title: Activity 3: Quick Pair Share (8 min)
docs.text:
In the last 8 minutes, students pair up and trade research templates. Each partner reads the other's template silently for 2 minutes, then asks 2 questions about it. The questions can be:

  • Why did you pick this career?
  • What surprised you most in your research?
  • Would you actually want this job? Why or why not?

This gives every student exposure to a second emerging ag career without doing double the research.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (2 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Ranked Justification) · Printable PDF:

Rank the four emerging ag careers from today by WHICH YOU WOULD PURSUE FIRST (1) to LAST (4), based on what I learned today.

  • Agricultural Drone Operator: rank ____
  • Precision Agriculture Technician: rank ____
  • Vertical Farming Manager: rank ____
  • Hydroponic Specialist: rank ____

For EACH rank, write ONE reason (technology, salary, daily task, growth) from today's research.

  • Rank 1 (most likely for me): _____________

  • Rank 4 (least likely for me): _____________

Bottom line: The emerging ag career I researched is _____ and it is growing because _____________. (d(1)(D))

Submit the research template with this ticket.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Pre-fill the template with the career name (e.g., "Agricultural Drone Operator") and the BLS link. Students focus on filling in the data fields.
  • Extension: Compare your emerging career to its 20-year-old version. (e.g., "Agricultural Drone Operator" vs. "Crop Scout 20 years ago.") What changed?
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Emerging = Emergente, Career = Carrera, Outlook = Perspectiva, Technology = Tecnología. Bilingual research template with Spanish field labels.

docs.title: Day 5: Xello Work Experiences + Nimitz Plant Science Pathway
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Complete the Xello Work Experiences lesson; research the Plant Science program of study at Nimitz HS and explain what a CTE completer is; favorite plant science careers in H&L TEKS d(1)(A), d(1)(C), d(2)(B) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Xello Work Experiences · Explain: Plant Science program of study · Extend: H&L favorites and the 3SW pattern · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Logged Xello Work Experiences entry + Plant Science program of study notes + screenshot of H&L Climber Profile Materials Chromebooks, Xello accounts, H&L accounts, Find Your Future workbook pp. 100-102, Nimitz Plant Science pathway info sheet, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: This week we explored plants, the environment, and emerging ag tech. What career from this week could you actually see yourself doing? Why?

Take 4-5 student responses. Validate ALL answers, including "none of them." Career exploration is about clarity, not commitment.

docs.title: Activity 1: Xello Work Experiences Lesson (20 min)
docs.text:
Source: Bowie Grade 8 Xello Completion Standard, "Work experiences"

Open Xello on the projector and walk students through finding the Work Experiences lesson:

  1. From the Xello dashboard, click Lessons
  2. Find "Work Experiences" in the 7th-grade lesson list
  3. Click Start or Continue

Students complete the Xello Work Experiences lesson on their own Chromebooks. The lesson typically includes:

  • A definition of "work experience" (paid or unpaid work, including informal jobs)
  • Examples: babysitting, dog walking, helping at a family business, summer jobs, working at a school event
  • Reflection prompts about what each experience teaches and what skills it builds

After completing the lesson, students log at least ONE Work Experience entry in their Xello profile (typically under "About Me" or "My Profile"). Each entry needs:

  • Job title or role
  • Employer / who they worked for
  • Dates / how long
  • 1-2 sentences on what they did and what they learned

If a student has truly never worked in any capacity, they can log a future plan: "Plan to work at the school book fair in October, will gain customer service and cash handling experience."

[VERIFY IN Xello] Confirm with your district that the Work Experiences field is enabled in your school's Xello configuration. If not, students complete the lesson and write entries in their notebook.

Facilitation Tip

Students often feel embarrassed that they don't have "real" jobs. Reframe: at age 12-13, the "real" experiences are babysitting, helping family, lemonade stands, and school activities. These all count. Future-you will be glad past-you wrote them down.

docs.title: Activity 2: Plant Science Program of Study at Nimitz (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 100-101: "What is Happening at My District?") + the Irving ISD CTE listing for Nimitz High School

Project the workbook's district pages. They print two Irving ISD Agriculture programs of study, and the one this week points at is Plant Science: it prepares students for careers in agriculture and horticulture, with coursework in plant growth, soil science, greenhouse management, and floral design (p. 100). The Agricultural Science program at Nimitz High School runs a greenhouse and an orchard on campus (p. 101), and Future Farmers of America (FFA) is its student organization. The pathway's industry certification is BASF Plant Science.

The same pages introduce the CTE completer, a student who finishes a full sequence of CTE courses and requirements in one career field instead of taking a single class. Put the workbook's own question to the room (p. 101): why might completing a sequence of courses be worth more than taking just one class?

Walk students through the pathway map:

  • Middle school (now): CCE course, explore Plant Science, complete the career research worksheet
  • High school at Nimitz: Plant Science program of study in the School of Agriculture Science → BASF Plant Science certification
  • Post-high school options:
    • Direct employment with a landscape, nursery, or greenhouse company (with certification in hand)
    • Texas A&M Horticulture or Plant Science degree
    • Community college Sustainable Agriculture program
    • USDA federal employment

Also note: Nimitz HS offers the Sustainable Engineering pathway (AutoDesk CAD and Inventor certifications), which connects to the Week 3 sustainable engineering content.

Students take 5 minutes of notes on the pathway map: which post-high school option appeals to them and why?

docs.title: Activity 3: H&L Favorites + Climber Profile Screenshot (8 min)
docs.text:
Source: H&L Climber Profile favorites. The app path for this cluster is printed on the workbook's App Exploration page (FYF p. 102).

[H&L PLATFORM] Direct students to the Hat Finder in the H&L app, filter by Plant Science and Environmental & Natural Resources, and click the heart/favorite icon on 2-3 careers from this week. The favorited Hats appear in their Climber Profile under "Favorites."
