docs.title: Day 1: Business Cluster Tour + Defining Entrepreneurship
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Read the Business, Marketing, and Finance chapter opener and work the Be the Decision Maker prompt; tour the cluster in the H&L app; define entrepreneurship in your own words; identify entrepreneurial opportunities in 5 different career clusters TEKS d(3)(I) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up and Be the Decision Maker · Explain: Chapter opener and Irving ISD programs · Explore: Cluster app exploration and Stop and Jot · Extend: Cross-cluster entrepreneurship list · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Cross-cluster entrepreneurship list (5 examples) + 1-sentence personal definition of entrepreneurship Materials Find Your Future workbook pp. 221 and 252-254, Chromebooks, H&L accounts, notebook, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: If you could start any business tomorrow with $0, what would it be? Be specific, name it, describe what it sells, and who buys it.

Take 4-5 student responses and sort them on the board into food, art, technology, services, or products. Each category can become a business. Point students to entrepreneur, one of the four roles on the workbook's cluster opener.

docs.title: Activity 1: Exploring the World of Business, Marketing, and Finance (12 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 221: "Exploring the World of BUSINESS, MARKETING, AND FINANCE")

Open the workbook to page 221. Read the chapter opener together: this cluster is about helping organizations grow, connect with customers, and make smart financial decisions. Some roles focus on understanding what customers want; others manage money, build brands, or create new opportunities. Point to the three Hats printed on the page: Business Analyst, Financial Examiner, and E-Commerce Specialist. Ask the page's closing question: what skills do these roles need to make important decisions about money, customers, and business growth?

Be the Decision Maker (FYF p. 221): Read the boxed prompt aloud. A local business has enough money to do only one thing this year: launch a major advertising campaign, hire more employees, or invest in new equipment. Which option would you choose? How would you decide what gives the business the best chance to grow, and what information would you need before making the final call?

Think-Pair-Share: 30 seconds of silent Think, then Partner A for 30 seconds, then Partner B for 30 seconds. Post two stems so every pair has a way in: "I would pick _ because " and "Hiring more people helps the business __, but new equipment helps it _____." Call on two pairs to share, chosen from what you heard while circulating rather than from raised hands.

The chapter does not print a pathway list. Students meet the cluster's pathways in the Hats & Ladders app in Activity 2. Irving ISD's own programs of study sit on the workbook's district pages (FYF pp. 252-253: "What is Happening at My District?"): Business Management, Administrative Management, Retail Management, Real Estate, Entrepreneurship, and Marketing & Sales. Name the Entrepreneurship program of study specifically, since it is this week's topic, along with its Entrepreneurship and Small Business certification and the two student organizations behind it, DECA and Business Professionals of America.

docs.title: Activity 2: Cluster App Exploration + Defining Entrepreneurship (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 254: "App Exploration") and (FYF p. 252: "What is Happening at My District?")

[H&L PLATFORM] The App Exploration page walks students through the cluster in order: open the Hats & Ladders app, go to Clusters, click the Business, Marketing, and Finance Cluster, watch the "Cluster Tour" video, play "Game Time," then find 1 Hat that matches their personality or interests and 1 Hat that does not fit them. Students record their answers on page 254. They finish the rest of the page, Pathway Possibilities and rating 3 Hats, on Day 5.

Stop and Jot: while the cluster tour video plays, students pause TWICE in their notebook (dated entry, labeled "3SW Wk6 Business") for 45 seconds each, with the prompt on screen:

  • Stop 1: One business career you did not know existed
  • Stop 2: One question you still have about starting a business

The district page describes Irving ISD's Entrepreneurship program of study as preparing students to start and manage businesses through innovation, business planning, financial management, and marketing strategies, while building critical thinking and leadership skills. Put that list on the board. Ask students which of those five words does the most work in a real business.

After the app exploration, each student writes their OWN definition of entrepreneurship in 1 sentence in their notebook. Examples:

  • "An entrepreneur is someone who turns an idea into a real business that customers pay for."
  • "Entrepreneurship is taking the risk of running your own company in exchange for the chance to build something you love."

Take 3-4 student definitions and write them on the board. Discuss: which definition is strongest? Why?

Facilitation Tip

Some students will define entrepreneurship as "rich people who own companies." Push back: entrepreneurs include lawn-mowing teenagers, food truck owners, Etsy sellers, and freelance graphic designers. Most are not rich. Most are people who saw a problem and built a solution.

docs.title: Activity 3: Cross-Cluster Entrepreneurship List (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: Connecting all 8 clusters explored this year

Students create a list of 5 entrepreneurial opportunities, one in each of FIVE different clusters they've explored this year. The clusters covered so far:

  • Manufacturing (1SW)
  • IT (1SW)
  • Law & Public Service (2SW)
  • Health Science (2SW)
  • Agriculture (3SW Wks 1-3)
  • Hospitality & Tourism (3SW Wk 4)
  • Human Services (3SW Wk 5)
  • Business (3SW Wk 6, current)

Each entry needs:

  • Cluster name
  • Entrepreneurial opportunity (specific business idea, not vague)
  • One business skill needed (not a technical skill, a BUSINESS skill like marketing, accounting, customer service)

Example list:

Cluster Opportunity Business Skill Needed Health Science Mobile dental hygienist serving rural areas Scheduling and billing Agriculture Drone-based crop scouting service Sales prospecting Hospitality Food truck for office workers downtown Daily revenue tracking Human Services Mobile barber for elderly clients in care facilities Insurance and licensing Business Marketing agency for local Irving small businesses Client communication

DOK 4: Look at your list. Which entrepreneurial opportunity is the EASIEST to start with little money? Which is the HARDEST? Defend your answer with at least one specific reason.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Mini-Case / Scenario Application) · Printable PDF:

Scenario: My older cousin has $3,000 saved up and wants to start a small business in one of the clusters we've explored (Manufacturing, IT, Law, Health Science, Agriculture, Hospitality, Human Services, or Business).

  1. Which cluster would I recommend for a low-budget ($3,000) startup, and why?

My pick: _____

Why: ____________

  1. What is ONE specific entrepreneurial business my cousin could start in that cluster?

Business idea: _____

  1. What is ONE business skill (NOT technical skill) my cousin needs to succeed?

Business skill: _____

My 1-sentence definition of entrepreneurship: "Entrepreneurship is _____________."

(d(3)(I))

Submit your cross-cluster list with this ticket.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a partial list with 3 cluster names and 1 opportunity already filled in. Students fill in the remaining 2 clusters.
  • Extension: Add a 6th cluster to your list and explain why it's the BEST cluster for entrepreneurship in Texas right now.
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Entrepreneur = Emprendedor/a, Opportunity = Oportunidad, Skill = Habilidad. Bilingual cross-cluster list template.

docs.title: Day 2: Million Dollar Idea — Spot the Problem and Generate Ideas
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Name a problem worth solving at school, in your community, in your country, or in the world; generate at least 10 business ideas in a timed five-minute sprint; screen the list down to your two strongest ideas and defend each pick TEKS d(3)(I) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Spot the Problem and the rapid idea sprint · Explain: Idea Swap partner screen · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable "Million Dollar Idea" Steps 1-3 completed: written problem statement + 10 or more ideas + top 2 ideas with reasons Materials Find Your Future workbook pp. 234-235, visible countdown timer on the projector, notebook, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Name one thing at school, in your neighborhood, or online that does not work the way it should. What exactly goes wrong?

Take 5-6 responses quickly and list them without judging them. Ask which annoyance someone might pay to remove. Students will use that test on a problem of their own.

docs.title: Activity 1: Step 1 — Spot the Problem (10 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 234: "Million Dollar Idea", Step 1)

Open the workbook to page 234 and read the opener together. Most people think entrepreneurs land one perfect idea right away, and that is not how it works. Entrepreneurs come up with lots of ideas, quickly and without overthinking. Some are strong, some are strange, and some do not work at all. Entrepreneurs test their ideas, learn from them, and decide which ones are worth their time.

Students then work Step 1. The workbook asks them to think of a problem they care about and gives four places to look:

  • A problem at school
  • A problem in your community
  • A problem in your country
  • A problem in the world

Each student writes the problem clearly on page 234, then answers the second prompt: what is happening, and why is it a problem?

Facilitation Tip

Students who write "world hunger" or "climate change" stall in the next step because the problem is too large to attack with one idea. Ask them for the version they can see with their own eyes: not hunger, but the lunch line running out of food before sixth period. A problem a seventh grader has personally watched happen produces far better ideas than an abstract one.

docs.title: Activity 2: Steps 2-3 — Rapid Idea Generation and Choose Your Best Ideas (20 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 235: "Million Dollar Idea", Steps 2-3)

Step 2: Rapid Idea Generation (8 min). The workbook gives students five minutes to write as many business ideas as they can that could solve their problem, aiming for at least 10 to 12. Post the workbook's four rules where the whole room can see them:

  • Do not judge your ideas
  • Do not stop to fix anything
  • Keep writing even if ideas seem wild or unrealistic
  • The more ideas, the better

Run a visible five-minute countdown. Pens stay down until the timer starts, nothing gets crossed out while it runs, and when it ends students count their ideas and write the number at the top of the page.

Step 3: Choose Your Best Ideas (12 min). Students read back through their list and choose the top 2 with the most potential, using the workbook's three screening questions:

  • Which ideas actually solve the problem?
  • Which ideas feel realistic to create?
  • Which ideas would people actually use?

For each of the two, they write why they chose it.

Active Monitoring: walk two laps with one target each. Lap 1 at minute 3 of the sprint checks that every page has at least six ideas on it and nobody is erasing. Lap 2 during Step 3 checks that each "why this works" sentence answers one of the three screening questions instead of just repeating the idea. Have the response ready for the two predictable misconceptions: a student who stops at four ideas because they want good ones, and a student who picks the first idea on the list instead of screening. If more than a handful of pages stall under six ideas, pause the room, put three of your own throwaway ideas on the board to show how low the bar is, and restart the clock for the remaining time.

docs.title: Activity 3: Idea Swap (10 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 235: "Million Dollar Idea", Step 3 screening questions)

Pairs trade workbooks. Each partner reads the other's problem statement and top 2 ideas, then answers the same three screening questions as an outsider who has never seen the idea before. Partners mark which of the two ideas they would actually use.

Think-Pair-Share: 30 seconds of silent Think on the prompt "which of my partner's two ideas would I actually use, and why," then Partner A for 30 seconds and Partner B for 30 seconds. Post two stems: "I would use idea _ because " and "Idea __ solves the problem better, but idea _ is easier to build because ___." Two pairs share with the class, chosen from what you heard while circulating.

Students note in their own workbook where their partner disagreed with them. That disagreement is the first piece of real customer feedback they have received, and it feeds tomorrow's stress test.

DOK 3: Why do entrepreneurs write 10 or 12 ideas before picking one instead of starting with the best idea they already have? What would they miss if they stopped at the first idea?

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Short Constructed Response) · Printable PDF:

  1. The problem I chose to solve: _____________

  2. How many ideas did I write during the five-minute sprint? _____

  3. My strongest idea: _____. In one sentence, how does it solve the problem?

  1. One idea I did NOT pick. Why did I leave it behind? (Use one of these three reasons: it does not really solve the problem / it is not realistic to build / people would not use it.)

Idea I dropped: _____

Reason: __________

  1. My partner said they would use idea _. The HARDEST part of the five-minute sprint was ___________.

(d(3)(I))

Submit your workbook pages 234-235 with this ticket.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Give a problem menu with six school-sized problems already written (lunch line, lost water bottles, phone charging, bus wait, homework tracking, recycling) so no student loses the sprint choosing a problem. Provide an idea sheet with 10 numbered blanks so the target is visible.
  • Extension: Take your third-best idea, the one you did not pick, and rewrite it so it beats your top idea on one of the three screening questions. What did you have to change?
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Problem = Problema, Idea = Idea, Solve = Resolver, Realistic = Realista, Customer = Cliente. Ideas may be written in Spanish, English, or both during the sprint; speed matters more than language during Step 2.

docs.title: Day 3: Million Dollar Idea — Stress Test and Make the Call
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Test your two strongest ideas against the workbook's three entrepreneur questions; decide Move Forward, Needs Work, or Abandon It for your best idea and defend the call in writing; pitch your problem, idea, and decision to a small group and choose the group's strongest venture TEKS d(3)(I) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Stress-testing the two ideas · Explain: Make the Call and the small-group pitch · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable "Million Dollar Idea" Steps 4, 5, and 7 completed: stress-test notes on both ideas + written call with strength and risk + the group's chosen venture Materials Find Your Future workbook pp. 236-237, workbook pages 234-235 from Day 2, timer, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Think of a project you gave up on: a game plan, a science fair build, a drawing. Was giving up the right call? What told you it was time to stop?

Take 4 responses. Listen for evidence rather than mood: "it kept falling over" gives the class something to test; "I got bored" does not. Students will need that kind of reason when they decide what to do with their own idea.

docs.title: Activity 1: Step 4 — Think Like a Real Entrepreneur (10 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 236: "Million Dollar Idea", Step 4)

In Step 4, students test the two ideas they chose on Day 2. They answer three questions for EACH idea on page 236:

  • How well does this solve the problem?
  • Why would someone choose this over other options?
  • What challenges might come up if you tried to create it?

Chunking: teach the three questions one at a time rather than releasing all three at once. Say what each question is for before students write (question 1 tests the fit, question 2 tests the competition, question 3 tests the build), give roughly two minutes per question for both ideas, and take a thumbs check between questions before releasing the next one. Note which question draws the most thumbs down, because that is the question the whole class needs re-taught before Step 5.

Facilitation Tip

Question 2 is the one students skip or answer with "because mine is better." Push on what "other options" actually means: a competitor already selling something similar, a free workaround people already use, and doing nothing at all. If a student cannot name what their idea is competing against, they have not tested it yet.

docs.title: Activity 2: Step 5 — Make the Call (10 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 237: "Million Dollar Idea", Step 5)

Students choose their strongest idea and mark one of the three calls the workbook offers:

  • Move Forward: this idea is worth continuing
  • Needs Work: it has potential but is not ready yet
  • Abandon It: it is not worth pursuing right now

Then they explain the decision in writing on page 237: why is this idea worth your time or not, what is its biggest strength, and what is its biggest risk.

Make clear before students write that Abandon It is a full-credit answer. An entrepreneur who can explain why an idea should die has learned more than one who keeps a weak idea alive. What earns the credit is the reasoning, not the verdict.

Facilitation Tip

Watch the printed step numbers on page 237. The workbook jumps from Step 5 straight to Step 7 and there is no Step 6. Nothing is missing from the activity; the numbering is a printing error. Tell students up front to work straight through from Make the Call to Pitch and Decide so nobody stops to hunt for a missing page.

docs.title: Activity 3: Step 7 — Pitch and Decide (22 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 237: "Million Dollar Idea", Step 7 and Class Discussion)

Put students in groups of 4. Each student takes a turn sharing three things, about 2 minutes each:

  • Their problem
  • Their best idea
  • Their final decision (Move Forward, Needs Work, or Abandon It)

After all four have shared, the group discusses the workbook's questions: what kinds of problems did people choose, which ideas seemed the strongest and why, and did anyone abandon an idea the rest of the group thought was good?

The group then agrees on ONE idea with the most potential overall and writes it on page 237. That idea becomes the group's venture for tomorrow's pitch day, so the group also writes down which member's workbook holds the Step 1 through Step 5 work behind it.

Class Discussion (5 min). Use the workbook's own closing prompts (FYF p. 237): why do you think entrepreneurs generate so many ideas instead of focusing on just one, what made an idea feel worth it to continue, and what can be learned from abandoning an idea?

DOK 4: Your group picked one idea out of four. What made the winning idea stronger: the problem it solved, how realistic it was to build, or how many people would use it? Defend your answer with a specific comparison to one idea the group passed over.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Comparison Matrix) · Printable PDF:

Fill in the matrix for the two ideas you stress-tested today.

Idea 1: ___ Idea 2: ___ How well it solves my problem (one phrase) Why someone picks it over other options Biggest challenge to build it

My call on my strongest idea (circle one): Move Forward / Needs Work / Abandon It

Bottom line: which ROW above made the decision for me, and why did that row matter more than the other two? (d(3)(I))

Submit your workbook pages 236-237 with this ticket.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a stress-test grid with the three questions already written across the top and the two ideas down the side, plus stems: "This solves the problem because _," "Someone would pick this instead of because __," "The hardest part to build would be _____."
  • Extension: Take the idea your group did NOT choose and write the one change that would have made it the group's pick. Then say what that change would cost in money, time, or difficulty.
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Test = Probar, Challenge = Desafío, Risk = Riesgo, Strength = Fortaleza, Decision = Decisión. The three call options may be recorded in Spanish (Seguir Adelante / Necesita Trabajo / Abandonarla) with the English term written next to it.

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Build a one-page venture brief for your group's chosen idea using the work already in your workbook; deliver a 2-minute pitch to a classmate investor panel; give and receive star and wish feedback; name the work ethic quality you brought to the pitch TEKS d(3)(I), d(4)(F) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Venture brief build and practice · Extend: Pitches to the investor panel · Explain: Work ethic reflection · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable One-page venture brief + 2-minute pitch delivered + star and wish feedback from at least 2 other groups Materials Workbook pages 234-237 from Days 2-3, printed venture brief template, printed "Star + Wish" peer feedback forms, timer, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: When you watch Shark Tank or a real business pitch, what makes some pitches work and others flop? List ONE thing each.

Take 4 student responses. Capture the patterns: confidence, clear numbers, knowing the customer, having a real answer to "how do you make money," practiced delivery. These are the same things an investor panel listens for.

docs.title: Activity 1: Build the Venture Brief (12 min)
docs.text:
The idea each group chose at the end of Day 3 is the venture they pitch today. Every line of the brief comes from work already sitting in somebody's workbook, so no group starts on a blank page.

Brief section Where it comes from The problem Step 1 problem statement (FYF p. 234) The idea Step 3 chosen idea (FYF p. 235) Why us and not the other options Step 4, question 2 (FYF p. 236) Our biggest challenge Step 4, question 3 (FYF p. 236) Our call and why Step 5 (FYF p. 237) What we need to start One new line the group writes: the people, money, or tools it would take to build the first version

Groups fill the six sections on one page, assign one section to each member so everyone speaks, then practice the pitch once out loud against a timer. Pitches are 2 minutes maximum.

Facilitation Tip

Some groups will spend all 12 minutes decorating the brief instead of rehearsing. Set a hard rule: by the 6-minute mark the brief is done and the rest of the time is practice out loud. A plain brief delivered well beats a colorful brief read off the page.

Facilitation Tip

Groups who ask for a script are asking for the wrong tool today. The formal 30-second sales pitch structure, with its hook, benefits, and call to action, gets taught later in the year in the Sales and Presentations week (FYF pp. 241-243: "30 Seconds to Sell"). Today the target is a clear 2-minute explanation of a real problem and a real idea.

docs.title: Activity 2: Pitches to the Investor Panel (25 min)
docs.text:
Groups pitch in a random order, drawn from a hat so no group gains an advantage from going last. Each pitch is 2 minutes maximum. Three or four students sit as the investor panel and rotate between pitches so that most of the class serves on the panel at least once.

After each pitch the panel asks ONE question and the group gets 30 seconds to answer. Keep a short bank of questions on the board so panelists are never stuck:

  • Who exactly has this problem?
  • What stops someone else from copying this?
  • What is the first thing you would build?

Time, Voice, Body: post the three blocks before the first group stands up. Voice 0 while a group sets up, Voice 3 for whoever is speaking, and Voice 1 for the star and wish writing between pitches. Run a visible 2-minute countdown for every pitch, and name one spot on the front desk where finished star and wish slips go so the handoff does not eat the next group's clock.

After all groups have pitched, hold a class vote on the most convincing venture by show of hands or sticky notes.

The peer feedback form ("Star + Wish") goes to each group after the vote:

  • Star: What did you do well? (1 specific thing)
  • Wish: What would I change to make the pitch stronger? (1 specific thing)

Each group should receive feedback from at least 2 other groups.

DOK 3: Looking at the pitches you heard today, what are 2 things that separated the strongest pitches from the weakest ones? Use specific examples.

docs.title: Activity 3: Work Ethic Reflection (5 min)
docs.text:
Source: TEKS d(4)(F): work ethic, integrity, dedication, perseverance

Connect the pitch experience to work ethic. The pitches that landed were the ones where the group was prepared, on time, and focused. The pitches that struggled often had a member who had not read the brief, had not practiced their section, or was not listening when the panel asked its question.

Quick whole-class discussion (3 minutes):

  • What did you do to PREPARE for today's pitch?
  • What does work ethic mean for an entrepreneur specifically?
  • Why does perseverance matter MORE for entrepreneurs than for employees?

Then each student writes one sentence in their notebook:

  • "The work ethic quality I demonstrated today was _____." (Examples: dedication, preparation, teamwork, perseverance, integrity)

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Trade-off / Dilemma Analysis) · Printable PDF:

Your group has 12 minutes before pitching. You see TWO problems:

  • (A) The venture brief looks plain (no title, no color, no sketch). Could polish for 8 minutes.
  • (B) One group member has not practiced their section out loud. Could rehearse them for 8 minutes.

Pros of picking A (polish the brief): _____________

Pros of picking B (practice the group member): _____________

My group's choice (A or B): __

Quality list: preparation / dedication / teamwork / perseverance / responsibility / reliability.

Which work-ethic quality matters MOST in this decision, and why is it the right one over the others? (d(3)(I), d(4)(F))

My quality: _____

Why: ____________

Submit your group's venture brief + at least 2 peer feedback forms with this ticket.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a venture brief template with the six section headers pre-printed and a sentence stem under each: "The problem is _. Our idea is . People pick us over because _. Our biggest challenge is . Our call is because _. To start we need ___."
  • Extension: Rewrite your group's brief as a 30-second version. Which two sections did you have to cut, and what did the pitch lose when you cut them?
  • ELL: The pitch can be delivered in English, Spanish, or bilingual. Many real Texas business pitches are delivered bilingually. Pair with bilingual peers if needed for translation support, and allow the panel question to be answered in either language.

docs.title: Day 5: Personal Budget + Xello Save Careers
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Finish the Business cluster App Exploration page and pick the career whose salary drives your budget; build a personal budget on DFW cost-of-living data; use Xello to save favorite careers from this six weeks; reflect on the entire 3rd Six Weeks TEKS d(3)(I), d(5)(D) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Pathway Possibilities and the salary number · Extend: Personal budget build · Explain: Xello save and 3SW reflection · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed personal budget worksheet + Xello Save Careers entries + 3SW capstone reflection paragraph Materials Chromebooks, H&L accounts, Xello accounts, Find Your Future workbook p. 254, printed Personal Budget worksheet with DFW cost-of-living data, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: If you earned $4,000 a month, would that be enough to live the lifestyle you want? List the 3 biggest things you'd spend it on.

Take 4-5 student responses and group them as rent, transportation, food, phone, savings, or entertainment. Students will put amounts beside those categories using a career salary they researched this six weeks.

docs.title: Activity 1: Pathway Possibilities and Your Salary Number (10 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 254: "App Exploration")

Four lifestyle questions frame the budget, and they sit at the top of the CCE budget worksheet: what kind of lifestyle do I want as an adult, where do I want to live and work, what will I want to buy, and what savings goals will I have? Put them on the board while students finish the App Exploration page they started on Day 1.

[H&L PLATFORM] Open the Hats & Ladders app, go to Clusters, click the Business, Marketing, and Finance Cluster, click "Pathway Possibilities" and answer the questions, then rate at least 1 pathway and at least 3 Hats. Students record their answers on page 254.

Each student then picks ONE career to budget on. It can be a Hat they rated today or any career they favorited during this six weeks, and they pull its DFW salary from the app. That number runs the whole budget.

Project the conversion once so every student uses the same method: a $50,000 salary is about $4,166 a month before taxes, and roughly $3,200 a month after taxes in Texas, where there is no state income tax.

Facilitation Tip

Students always overestimate how much they'll have left after rent. Show them: in Irving, a 1-bedroom apartment is $1,200-$1,600/month. That's 30-40% of a $50K salary. The first lesson of budgeting is that rent eats more than you expect.

docs.title: Activity 2: Build Your Personal Budget (20 min)
docs.text:
Distribute the Personal Budget worksheet with DFW cost-of-living data already loaded. Each student builds the budget on the salary they pulled in Activity 1.

The budget worksheet has these categories:

Category Estimated DFW Cost (per month) Your Allocation Rent / Housing $1,200-$1,800 Utilities (electric, water, internet) $150-$250 Groceries $300-$500 Phone $40-$80 Transportation (car payment, gas, insurance) $400-$700 Entertainment / Eating Out $100-$300 Savings (emergency + long-term) At least 10% Clothes & Personal Care $50-$150 Other (subscriptions, gym, etc.) $50-$200 TOTAL

Students fill in their allocations and total them up. The total must NOT exceed their monthly take-home pay.

After filling in the budget, students answer these analysis questions:

  • What percentage of your monthly income goes to rent? (Calculate: rent ÷ income × 100)
  • Is the salary from your chosen career enough to live the lifestyle you want? Yes / No / Almost
  • If "no," what would you change, your career, your lifestyle, or both?

DOK 3: What conclusions can you draw about how your career choice directly affects the lifestyle you can afford? Use specific numbers from your budget.

docs.title: Activity 3: Xello Save Careers + 3SW Capstone Reflection (12 min)
docs.text:
Source: Bowie Grade 8 Xello Completion Standard, "Save careers"

Direct students to open Xello and save 2-3 careers from this six weeks to their Xello profile. The Save Careers task lives under "Career Match" or "Saved Careers" depending on the Xello version.

[VERIFY IN Xello] Confirm with your district that the Save Careers task is enabled. If not, students log saved careers in their notebook for later transfer.

Tell students where the saved career goes next: at mid-year they run a Career Deep Dive on their top career goal (FYF pp. 285-286: "Rung 3: Career Deep Dive"), researching the education and training it requires, its starting salary, the national average pay, and whether the field is growing. Today's saved list is the short list they will choose that goal from.

After saving careers in Xello, students write a 3SW capstone reflection paragraph (5-7 sentences) in their notebook. The reflection covers:

  • The clusters explored this six weeks (Agriculture, Hospitality, Human Services, Business)
  • One new favorite career and why
  • One thing they learned about entrepreneurship
  • Whether they see themselves as an entrepreneur and why or why not (this is the BIG d(3)(I) reflection)

Sentence stems available for students who need them:

  • "This six weeks I explored _, , __, and _____ clusters."
  • "My favorite new career is _ because ___."
  • "The most important thing I learned about entrepreneurship is _____."
  • "I [do / do not] see myself as an entrepreneur because _____."

DOK 4: Looking at all the career clusters you've explored so far this year, what patterns do you see in the careers that attract you? What does this tell you about who you are as a future professional?

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Concept Map / Connection Diagram) · Printable PDF:

My favorited career from this 3SW + the salary I used in today's budget: ___ ($___/month take-home)

Connect this career to THREE things:

1. The biggest line item in my budget today (usually rent, transportation, or food)

Line item: ___ = $___ (_____% of my monthly income). In one sentence, does this career's salary comfortably cover this line item?

2. Whether this career has an ENTREPRENEURIAL version (small business, solo practice, freelance, food truck, salon ownership, etc.)

The entrepreneurial version: _____. In one sentence, would starting my own version of this work CHANGE my monthly budget?

3. ME as an entrepreneur (or not)

"I DO / DO NOT see myself as an entrepreneur because _____________."

(d(3)(I), d(5)(D))

Submit your personal budget + 3SW capstone reflection paragraph with this ticket.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a pre-filled budget worksheet with the salary already entered, taxes already calculated, and rent already chosen. Students fill in only the discretionary categories.
  • Extension: Build TWO budgets, one for an entry-level job in your favorite cluster, and one for a senior job in the same cluster. How does the lifestyle change?
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Budget = Presupuesto, Income = Ingreso, Rent = Renta, Savings = Ahorros. Bilingual budget worksheet with Spanish category labels. The reflection paragraph may be written in English, Spanish, or bilingual.

docs.title: Week 6: Be Your Own Boss — Entrepreneurship
docs.text: 3rd Six Weeks | Business, Marketing & Finance Cluster | 5 class periods (50 min each)

docs.title: Lesson Objective
docs.text:
Students explore the Business, Marketing, and Finance cluster through the Hats & Ladders app and the Find Your Future workbook, define entrepreneurship in their own words, and work the full "Million Dollar Idea" entrepreneurial process (FYF pp. 234-237): spot a problem worth solving, generate at least 10 business ideas in a timed sprint, screen the list to two, stress-test both, and make the call to move the strongest idea forward, keep working on it, or abandon it. Groups then pitch their chosen venture to a classmate investor panel, and students close the six weeks by building a personal budget on a real DFW career salary. This is the strongest d(3)(I) week of the entire year.

Learning Target: I can find a problem worth solving, turn it into business ideas, test my two best ideas, decide which one is worth my time, pitch it to a group, and build a budget on a real career salary.

Success Criteria: I will know I am successful when my cross-cluster list names a business and one business skill for five different clusters, when my idea sprint page holds at least 10 ideas and my top 2 each have a reason, when my strongest idea carries a written call of Move Forward, Needs Work, or Abandon It with its biggest strength and biggest risk, when my group's venture brief fills all six sections and I speak one of them in the 2-minute pitch, and when my personal budget totals no more than my monthly take-home pay.

docs.title: Demonstration of Learning
docs.text: "I can define entrepreneurship in my own words, find a problem worth solving and generate at least 10 business ideas from it, test my two strongest ideas and decide whether to move one forward, pitch my group's venture to a class investor panel, build a personal budget that reflects a future career salary, and identify entrepreneurial opportunities across at least 3 career clusters."

docs.title: TEKS Alignment
docs.text:
• d(3)(I): Define entrepreneurship and identify entrepreneurial opportunities within a field of personal interest (Days 1-5). (PRIMARY, strongest d(3)(I) week of the year)
  • d(4)(F): Define and identify examples of work ethic, integrity, dedication, and perseverance (Day 4, the pitch preparation reflection).
  • d(5)(D): Prepare a personal budget reflecting the student's desired lifestyle (Day 5).

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Chromebooks with internet access (1 per student)
  • Hats & Ladders student accounts + Find Your Future workbook, Business, Marketing, and Finance chapter (printed pp. 221, 234-237, 252-254)
  • Xello student accounts (Save Careers task)
  • Visible countdown timer for the Day 2 idea sprint and the Day 4 pitches
  • Printed venture brief template (CCE artifact; its six sections are drawn from FYF pp. 234-237)
  • Printed "Star + Wish" peer feedback forms
  • Printed Personal Budget worksheet with DFW cost-of-living data (CCE artifact)
  • Printed problem menu and 10-blank idea sheet for the Day 2 sprint scaffold
  • BizKids: bizkids.com
  • JA (Junior Achievement): jausa.ja.org
  • Projector

docs.title: Career Connection
docs.text:
Students have already encountered business ownership in every cluster: technology startups, food trucks, solo law practices, salons, urban farms, and freelance design. This week they use one process across those fields: identify a problem, generate possible solutions, test two ideas, choose one, pitch it, and check whether the numbers work in a personal budget.

What is Happening at Irving ISD? Business, Retail Management and Entrepreneurship is offered at MacArthur High School; Cardwell Career Preparatory Center offers Business Management; and Irving High School and Nimitz High School offer Business Management and Marketing. The workbook names six programs of study, including Entrepreneurship, with work in innovation, business planning, financial management, and marketing (FYF pp. 252-253: "What is Happening at My District?"). It also describes students producing content and pitching social media campaigns for the district, as well as school stores selling student-designed products. The industry certification is Entrepreneurship and Small Business, and the student organizations are DECA and Business Professionals of America (BPA).

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text:
• Entrepreneur: A person who creates, organizes, and manages a business, taking on financial risk in hopes of making a profit.
  • Problem Statement: One or two sentences naming what is going wrong and why it matters. Every idea this week starts from one.
  • Rapid Idea Generation: Writing as many ideas as possible in a short, timed burst without stopping to judge, fix, or erase any of them.
  • Validation: Testing an idea before building it. Does it solve the problem, would someone choose it over other options, and what would make it hard to build?
  • Investor: A person or company that puts money into a business with the hope of earning more money in return.
  • Pitch: A short, persuasive presentation that explains a business idea and asks the listener to back it.
  • Profit: Revenue minus expenses. The money a business owner keeps after paying all costs.
  • Personal Budget: A plan for managing income and expenses over a specific time period (usually monthly).
  • Work Ethic: A set of values centered on the importance of hard work, reliability, and dedication.

docs.title: Bridge to Theory (Hats & Ladders)
docs.text:
The Find Your Future workbook gives Business, Marketing, and Finance printed pages 221 to 254. The chapter opener (FYF p. 221: "Exploring the World of BUSINESS, MARKETING, AND FINANCE") frames the cluster as helping organizations grow, connect with customers, and make smart financial decisions, puts a "Be the Decision Maker" spending dilemma in front of students, and introduces three Hats on the page: Business Analyst, Financial Examiner, and E-Commerce Specialist. The chapter does not print a pathway list. Students meet the cluster's pathways in the Hats & Ladders app through Pathway Possibilities on the App Exploration page (FYF p. 254), and they meet Irving ISD's own programs of study on the district pages (FYF pp. 252-253).

One chapter activity carries this week:

  • Million Dollar Idea (Days 2-3): Career Climb activity, and the workbook's longest, with 55 lines of student writing across four pages. Students spot a problem they care about, generate at least 10 to 12 ideas in a five-minute sprint without judging any of them, screen the list to their top 2, stress-test both against three entrepreneur questions, and then make the call: Move Forward, Needs Work, or Abandon It. The activity closes with a small-group pitch where each group picks the one idea with the most potential (FYF pp. 234-237: "Million Dollar Idea").

Printing Error on Page 237

The printed steps in "Million Dollar Idea" jump from Step 5 to Step 7. There is no Step 6 and nothing is missing from the activity. Walk students straight through from Make the Call to Pitch and Decide so nobody stops to hunt for a missing page.

The rest of this chapter is taught in later weeks and is referenced here, not adopted: real-estate investing and property marketing sit in 5SW Wk6, consulting and advertising sit in 6SW Wk3, and the 30-second sales pitch (FYF pp. 241-243) sits in 6SW Wk4. Day 4's investor panel is a CCE-authored structure, not a workbook activity; every line of the venture brief students pitch traces back to their own Million Dollar Idea pages.

docs.title: IISD Instructional Strategies
docs.text:
• Think-Pair-Share: Day 1, Activity 1, the "Be the Decision Maker" prompt on the chapter opener (FYF p. 221), where a local business can afford exactly one of three moves this year: an advertising campaign, more employees, or new equipment. Distinguished: pose it to the whole group, hold a silent 30 second Think, then time Partner A for 30 seconds and Partner B for 30 seconds, and post two stems at different levels: "I would pick _ because " and "Hiring more people helps the business __, but new equipment helps it _____." Ask two pairs to share, not one. Listen while pairs talk for who names what information they would need before deciding, and pick your share-out pairs from what you heard rather than from raised hands.
  • Stop and Jot: Day 1, Activity 2, the two pauses during the Business cluster tour video on the App Exploration page (FYF p. 254). Distinguished: name both stop points before the video starts, give 45 seconds per jot with the prompt on screen, and post two stems: "One business career I did not know existed is _" and "One question I still have about starting a business is ." Keep a third stem on the board for the cross-cluster list in Activity 3: "An entrepreneurial opportunity in is _, and it needs work ethic because ." Read jots over shoulders during both pauses. If the jots name only store owners and YouTubers, steer the Hat browse toward Business Analyst, Financial Examiner, and E-Commerce Specialist so Activity 3's list is not five versions of the same business.
  • Active Monitoring: Day 2, Activity 2, the five-minute idea sprint and the top-2 screen that follows. Distinguished: walk two laps with one target each, lap 1 at minute 3 of the sprint checking that every page carries at least six ideas and nobody is erasing, lap 2 during Step 3 checking that each "why this works" sentence answers one of the workbook's three screening questions instead of restating the idea. Have the response ready before class for the two predictable misconceptions: the student who stops at four ideas because they only want good ones, and the student who picks the first idea on the list without screening it. If more than a handful of pages stall under six ideas, pause the room, model the low bar by putting three of your own throwaway ideas on the board, and restart the clock for the time that remains.
  • Chunking: Day 3, Activity 1, the three stress-test questions in Step 4 (FYF p. 236). Distinguished: release one question at a time rather than all three, say what each one is for before students write (question 1 tests the fit, question 2 tests the competition, question 3 tests the build), give roughly two minutes per question across both ideas, and take the thumbs check between questions before releasing the next. Note which question draws the most thumbs down. That question becomes a 3 minute re-teach before Step 5, and students who cleared all three start drafting their Make the Call reasoning early instead of waiting.
  • Time, Voice, Body (TVB): Day 4, Activity 2, the venture pitches to the investor panel. Distinguished: post the three blocks before the first group stands, Voice 0 while a group sets up, Voice 3 for whoever is speaking, and Voice 1 for the star and wish writing between pitches, with a visible 2 minute countdown on every pitch. Name the one spot on the front desk where finished feedback slips go, and hold the rule that every group member speaks one section of the brief. Narrate the groups that are meeting the expectation rather than correcting the ones that are not. If the rotation is running long by the third group, cut the panel question to a single panelist and announce the change before the next group begins.

docs.text: Day Focus Key Activities Deliverable 5E 1 Business Cluster + Defining Entrepreneurship Chapter opener and Be the Decision Maker pair talk + cluster app exploration + cross-cluster entrepreneurship list Cross-cluster entrepreneurship list (5 examples) + personal definition Engage · Explain · Explore · Extend · Evaluate 2 Million Dollar Idea. Problem and Ideas "Million Dollar Idea" Steps 1-3 (FYF pp. 234-235): problem statement, five-minute idea sprint, top 2 screened, partner idea swap Problem statement + 10 or more ideas + top 2 with reasons Engage · Explore · Explain · Evaluate 3 Million Dollar Idea. Stress Test and Decide "Million Dollar Idea" Steps 4, 5, and 7 (FYF pp. 236-237): stress-test both ideas, make the call, small-group pitch and venture pick Stress-test notes + written call + group's chosen venture Engage · Explore · Explain · Evaluate 4 Venture Pitch Day Venture brief build + 2-minute pitches to a classmate investor panel + star and wish feedback + work ethic reflection Venture brief + pitch delivered + 2 peer feedback forms Engage · Explore · Extend · Explain · Evaluate 5 Personal Budget + Xello Save Careers Finish App Exploration (FYF p. 254), pick a salary, build the DFW budget, Xello Save Careers, 3SW reflection Completed personal budget + saved careers in Xello Engage · Explore · Extend · Explain · Evaluate

docs.title: Formative Assessment
docs.text:
• Cross-cluster entrepreneurship list + Mini-Case exit ticket (cousin with $3,000 picks a cluster, a business, and a business skill). Day 1, d(3)(I)
  • Problem statement, sprint idea count, and top 2 with reasons + Short Constructed Response exit ticket (strongest idea, one dropped idea and the screening reason it failed). Day 2, d(3)(I)
  • Stress-test notes on both ideas + written call + Comparison Matrix exit ticket (two ideas across the three tests, then the row that decided it). Day 3, d(3)(I)
  • Venture brief + 2-minute pitch + peer feedback + Trade-off Dilemma exit ticket (polish the brief vs. rehearse the group member; work-ethic quality pick). Day 4, d(3)(I), d(4)(F)
  • Personal budget + Xello saves + Concept Map exit ticket (career + biggest budget line item + entrepreneurial version + self-as-entrepreneur). Day 5, d(3)(I), d(5)(D)

docs.title: Summative Assessment
docs.text: Entrepreneurship Portfolio (3rd Six Weeks Capstone): Students submit (1) their completed "Million Dollar Idea" pages from Days 2-3 (FYF pp. 234-237: problem statement, idea list, top 2 with reasons, stress-test notes, and the written call), (2) the group venture brief and the peer feedback forms from Day 4, (3) the completed personal budget from Day 5, and (4) a one-paragraph reflection answering: "Do I see myself as an entrepreneur? Why or why not?" Scored on entrepreneurship definition and application across clusters (d(3)(I)), budget accuracy (d(5)(D)), work ethic reflection (d(4)(F)), and personal career self-awareness. A written call of Abandon It earns full credit when the reasoning names a real strength and a real risk; the verdict is not what is being scored.

docs.title: Scaffolded Learning
docs.text:
• Problem menu with six school-sized problems already written (lunch line, lost water bottles, phone charging, bus wait, homework tracking, recycling) so no student loses the Day 2 sprint choosing a problem
  • Idea sheet with 10 numbered blanks so the sprint target is visible on the page
  • Stress-test grid with the three Step 4 questions across the top and the two ideas down the side
  • Venture brief template with the six section headers and a sentence stem under each
  • Personal budget worksheet with DFW cost-of-living data already entered

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
• Take the idea your group did NOT choose and name the one change that would have made it the pick, then price that change in money, time, or difficulty
  • Rewrite your group's venture brief as a 30-second version. Which two sections did you cut, and what did the pitch lose?
  • Research a real young entrepreneur (BizKids profile or local Irving small business owner) and present findings
  • Build a full year-1 plan for the group's venture: projected costs, projected income, and the month it would break even

docs.title: ELL Language Support
docs.text:
• Pre-teach: Entrepreneur = Emprendedor/a, Business = Negocio, Problem = Problema, Risk = Riesgo, Investor = Inversor/a, Budget = Presupuesto, Profit = Ganancia, Pitch = Presentación
  • Bilingual venture brief and budget templates with Spanish section labels
  • Ideas may be written in Spanish, English, or both during the Day 2 sprint; speed matters more than language while the timer runs
  • The venture pitch can be delivered in English, Spanish, or bilingual, many real Texas business pitches are bilingual
  • Pair with bilingual peers during pitch prep

docs.title: Day 1: Rung 1 — Who You Are + Favorites Audit
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Compare Week 0 core personality type results to current career interests; complete Rung 1 of the Capstone ladder using the Hats & Ladders profile; audit all favorited careers from the first 18 weeks TEKS d(1)(A) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Rung 1 profile review and favorites audit · Explain: Growth discussion and share-out · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed Core Types vs. Favorites worksheet listing top 3 clusters by favorite count plus a one-sentence growth statement, and a filled Rung 1 page Materials Chromebooks, H&L accounts, Find Your Future workbook pp. 281-282, Climber Notes deck "Learning Your Core Personality Types" (slides 3-4), printed Core Types vs. Favorites worksheet, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
Before the Warm-Up. Return Week 0 Reflections

Have students pull out their Week 0 My Career Journey reflection from the class folder you saved them in per the 1SW Wk0 Day 5 Persistent Portfolio admonition. If a student was absent during Week 0 or is new to the class this semester, have them run the H&L Discover Your Core task today as their personal baseline, treat this week as their Wk0 equivalent. Also have every student open their Climber Profile in H&L now (before the warm-up prompt) to surface any login or data-access issues before the activity begins.

WARM-UP: Look back at your Week 0 My Career Journey sheet (or pull up your Climber Profile in H&L). Do you think you would get the same core personality type if you took Discover Your Core again today? Why or why not?

Collect 2-3 student responses. If students have gone hazy on the six types, reproject the type table from the Climber Notes deck (Climber Notes: "Learning Your Core Personality Types", slide 3) for 30 seconds rather than re-teaching it. Bridge to the idea that career exploration is supposed to change you. The point of the first 18 weeks was not to lock students into a career, it was to give them enough data to make a real choice.

docs.title: Activity 1: Rung 1 — Who You Are (12 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 281-282: "Rung 1: Who You Are"), the first rung of the Capstone ladder

Open the workbook to page 281 and read the framing together. Rung 1 is the foundation of the eight-rung career ladder students will finish and present at the end of the year, and it is entirely about the student.

[H&L PLATFORM] The rung's own instruction is to open the Hats & Ladders app and review the profile: top Hats, Pathway Possibilities, Building Blocks, Powerskills, and favorite pathways and clusters. Students have been feeding that profile since Week 0, so this is a review pass, not a new assessment.

Students then write or sketch on page 282, reflecting on the six inputs the rung names: interests, Building Blocks, personality types, work values, strengths, and skills. The workbook supplies four starter questions:

  1. What do I like to do in my free time?
  2. What school subjects do I enjoy most?
  3. What are some things I feel confident doing?
  4. What do people say I am good at?

The rung also models the specificity bar with its own example: "I like video games" is too thin, while "I like playing strategy video games because I enjoy challenges, solving problems, and thinking ahead" names the skill underneath the interest. Project that pair before students start writing. It is the difference between a Rung 1 that carries the rest of the ladder and one that has to be redone in 6SW.

Partner Activity (p. 282): In the last 3 minutes, students share their page with a partner and the partner adds one strength or skill the writer did not think of. The addition goes on the writer's page, in the partner's handwriting, so it stays visible as outside evidence.

Facilitation Tip

Watch for students who write nothing because "I'm not good at anything." That is usually self-doubt rather than reality. Point them at one thing they did well earlier this year, name the skill it took, and have them write that line first. The Partner Activity is the second safety net; make sure those students get a partner who will actually name something.

docs.title: Activity 2: Favorites Audit (20 min)
docs.text:
Source: H&L Climber Profile + scope-and-sequence Ch 1-13 history

Students open the H&L app and navigate to their Climber Profile. They scroll to the favorited Hats section and count how many careers they have favorited in each of the eight clusters explored so far:

  1. Manufacturing (1SW Wk1)
  2. IT (1SW Wk2-5)
  3. Law & Public Service (2SW Wk1-2)
  4. Health Science (2SW Wk3-4, Wk6)
  5. Agriculture (3SW Wk1-3)
  6. Hospitality (3SW Wk4)
  7. Human Services (3SW Wk5)
  8. Business (3SW Wk6)

[H&L PLATFORM] In H&L, students go to Climber Profile → Favorited Hats to see every career they have liked across all clusters. If the app sorts by date rather than cluster, students will need to manually tally. That tally itself is the activity. The core personality type they are comparing against comes from the Discover Your Core task in the Profile section, which students completed in Week 0.

Stop and Jot: Name the stop points before students start tallying. Every three minutes, pause the room for a 45 second jot using one of two stems: "The cluster with the most hearts is _, which surprises me because " or "A cluster I expected to like more is __."

On the printed Core Types vs. Favorites worksheet, students fill in: - Column A, core personality type from Week 0 (Doer, Analyzer, Creator, Helper, Persuader, or Organizer) - Column B, Number of favorites in each cluster (8 rows) - Column C, The 3 clusters with the most favorites, ranked - Column D, Does my Week 0 core type match my current top cluster? (Yes / No / Sort of)

Students who have not favorited many careers spend the first 5 minutes browsing their Climber Profile history and adding 3-5 favorites they remember liking but never tagged.

Facilitation Tip

Some students will have zero favorites, usually because they forgot to tap the heart icon during earlier weeks. Let them go back through clusters now and add favorites based on memory. The point of the audit is the reflection, not the historical accuracy of when the favorite was added.

docs.title: Activity 3: Think-Pair-Share — Growth Discussion (10 min)
docs.text:
In pairs, students share:

  1. Their core personality type from Week 0
  2. Their top cluster by favorite count today
  3. Whether the two match, and if not, what explains the gap

Hold a silent 30 second Think on question 3 first, then time Partner A and Partner B for 30 seconds each before opening the rest of the pair talk. After 4 minutes of partner talk, collect 3 responses from across the room. Look for both "my type matches perfectly" and "my favorites went a totally different direction" stories, both are valid mid-year outcomes, and make sure at least one of the three is a student whose data did not match.

DOK 2: How would you explain the difference between "interests" and "favorites" using your data from today? Which one do you trust more, and why?

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Comparison Matrix) · Printable PDF:

Use your Day 1 worksheet to fill in the matrix.

Week 0 (start of year) Mid-Year (today) My core personality type My top cluster by favorites (N/A — no favorites yet in Wk 0) # of favorited careers 0

Bottom line: Does my Week 0 core personality type MATCH my current top cluster? Circle: YES / NO / SORT OF.

In one sentence, if my interests shifted, what CAUSED the shift? (Example activity, teacher, classmate, surprise career fact.) (d(1)(A))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: For students who cannot find their Week 0 results, project the H&L Profile → Discover Your Core navigation steps. If they still cannot find it, give them the option to run the task today and treat that as their baseline. For Rung 1, give the four starter questions on a half sheet so students answer one box at a time instead of facing a blank page.
  • Extension: Compare core personality type to favorited Hats by counting how many of the favorites match the recommended Hats for that type in H&L. Calculate a "match percentage."
  • ELL: Bilingual core personality type card (Doer = Hacedor, Analyzer = Analizador, Creator = Creador, Helper = Ayudante, Persuader = Persuasor, Organizer = Organizador). Rung 1 accepts sketches as well as writing, so students can draw their answers. Allow students to write the growth statement in Spanish.

docs.title: Day 2: The Career Iceberg + Rung 2 — Career Goal
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Complete "The Career Iceberg" activity and build a personal iceberg for a career goal; complete Rung 2 of the Capstone ladder using the H&L Career Plan tool; cross-reference the app's pathway recommendations with available Irving ISD pathways TEKS d(1)(A), d(8)(A) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: Trophy iceberg example · Explore: Nurse frame and personal iceberg · Extend: Rung 2 Career Snapshot and Irving ISD pathway cross-reference · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed personal iceberg (≥3 items on top, ≥10 items underneath) + Rung 2 Career Snapshot naming a career goal + screenshot of H&L Career Plan showing top recommended pathway Materials Chromebooks, H&L accounts + Find Your Future workbook pp. 6-8 and pp. 283-284, blank iceberg template, Irving ISD CTE Pathways poster, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Think of someone who is great at something, an athlete, a musician, a YouTuber, a family member at their job. What do most people see them doing? What do most people NOT see?

Take 2-3 quick responses. Draw a waterline through one answer: place the visible career result above it and the training, practice, setbacks, and help below it. Students will build their own version today.

docs.title: Activity 1: The Career Iceberg (20 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 6-8: "The Career Iceberg"), a Chapter 1 activity

This activity lives in Chapter 1, not at the end of the book

The workbook opens with the iceberg because first impressions of a job form before any research does. CCE runs it here, at mid-year, when students have 18 weeks of favorites to test it against, and 6SW Wk6 returns to the same pages when the ladder is assembled. Nothing about the activity is a year-end wrap-up.

Step 1: Look at an example (4 min). Project page 6 and read the framing: job titles make careers look simple, but underneath the surface workers solve problems, communicate, make decisions, and handle challenges nobody sees from the outside. The book's worked example is an iceberg about winning a trophy in a sports competition. Partners compare what sits on top against what sits underneath and answer the book's question: what does that tell you about winning first place?

Step 2: Build the career frames (5 min). Pages 7 and 8 print two career icebergs, an Electrician and a Nurse, with the drawing frames already there. Do the Nurse frame with the whole class so the research move is modeled once. Above the waterline students write what they think the job does. Below it they research and add the deeper parts: skills, responsibilities, tools, training, and challenges. Push past "helps people" to items like anatomy coursework, 12-hour shifts, drawing blood under pressure, and explaining bad news to a stranger's family. The Electrician frame on page 7 is the extension for students who finish early.

Class Discussion (p. 8), 2 min: How did your thinking change after researching the career? Which responsibility underneath the iceberg was most surprising? Why is it important to learn more about careers before making decisions about the future?

Step 3: Build your own iceberg (9 min). Page 8 closes with an Extra Time prompt to choose a career and build a personal iceberg. That prompt is this week's artifact. Students pick a career from their Day 1 audit, ideally one of their top favorites, and draw it on the blank template (or in a digital canvas if they prefer):

  • Title at the top of the iceberg
  • At least 3 words or images on the top (visible) section, what people will see when they reach this career
  • At least 10 words or images underneath the iceberg, the hidden work, skills, training, and small steps

Students who get stuck should browse the H&L app or flip back through their own workbook pages rather than inventing items. The underwater list should be things they have actually seen, read, or practiced this year.

Facilitation Tip

Students may put only vague, positive ideas underwater, such as "hard work" or "studying." Ask what the work cost: "missed friend's birthday," "got a bad grade and had to retake," or "had to ask for help when I didn't want to." The iceberg should show a specific cost students could not see above the waterline.

docs.title: Activity 2: Rung 2 — Career Goal (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 283-284: "Rung 2: Career Goal"), the second rung of the Capstone ladder

Facilitation Tip. Verify Before Class

Before class, open H&L in a test or teacher account and confirm the Career Plan tool loads, shows pathway recommendations, and matches your district's configuration. If the tool is unavailable at your district, skip directly to Activity 3 (Pathway Cross-Reference) and use the printed Irving ISD CTE Pathways poster as your single source of truth, with the Rung 2 pages as the student artifact.

Now shift from the personal reflection to the rung. Rung 2 opens by telling students this is a starting point, not a forever decision, which is worth reading aloud to the room.

Students look at their top Hats and choose one Hat as their career goal, write the name on page 283, then answer Why This Career? in their own words, specifically, not "it pays well."

[H&L PLATFORM] The rung's Career Snapshot instruction is to open the Hats & Ladders app, click Career Plan, and complete the steps before answering the workbook questions. If the Career Plan tool is not yet active for your district, students research the same questions from the Hat pages and BLS and answer them on pages 283-284 on paper.

The Career Snapshot questions on pages 283-284:

  1. What does someone in this career do? (a short, plain summary)
  2. Where might they work? (office, outdoors, hospital, school, and so on)
  3. Do they work mostly with people, ideas, data, or tools?
  4. What are the perks (things you are excited about) and quirks (things you are hesitant about)?
  5. Connection to Me: how does this career connect to your interests, Powerskills, Building Blocks, and personality types from Rung 1?

Then students take a screenshot of their Career Plan home screen showing recommended pathways and save it to their student drive folder under "4SW Wk1 Career Plan."

Active Monitoring: Walk a fixed pathway three times, one target per lap. Lap 1: every student has located the Career Plan. Lap 2: every student has a named Hat on the career goal line. Lap 3: the people-ideas-data-tools question is answered. Have feedback ready for the two predictable stalls, an app that opened on the Profile tab instead of Career Plan, and a named career goal with Why This Career left blank. If more than a handful stall on the same lap, reproject that step to the whole room instead of fixing it screen by screen.

Facilitation Tip

If the H&L Career Plan tool is not configured for Irving ISD or shows no recommendations, have students manually compare their top 3 favorited Hats to the Irving ISD CTE Pathways poster on the wall. The cross-referencing, not the tool, is the actual learning.

Rung 3 is tomorrow, and Rungs 6 and 7 (FYF pp. 292-296) are next week's course-mapping work.

docs.title: Activity 3: Pathway Cross-Reference (7 min)
docs.text:
Students look at the H&L recommended pathways and the Irving ISD CTE Pathways poster side by side. They write on the back of their iceberg sheet:

  • H&L recommended pathway #1: _____
  • Closest Irving ISD pathway available: _____
  • Campus where it is offered: _____ (Irving High, MacArthur, Nimitz, Singley Academy, Cardwell Career Prep, Ratteree Career Development Center, or multi-campus)

If H&L recommends something not offered locally (e.g., Marine Biology), students pick the closest analogue (Veterinary Science at Nimitz).

DOK 3: What conclusions can you draw about the overlap between H&L's recommended pathways and the actual pathways available at Irving ISD high schools? What would you do if your top recommendation is not offered locally?

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Concept Map / Connection Diagram) · Printable PDF:

My Rung 2 career goal: _____

Connect this career to THREE things:

1. One item from UNDERNEATH my iceberg I had NOT thought about before today

My hidden item: _____. In one sentence, why is this item the thing I had not seen before?

2. An H&L recommended pathway from my Career Plan tool

H&L recommendation: _____. Does it match my Rung 2 career goal? Circle: YES / NO. One sentence why:

3. An Irving ISD pathway + campus (Singley / MacArthur / Irving High / Nimitz / Cardwell / Ratteree)

My pathway: ___ at ___. In one sentence, why is this the closest local match for my career goal?

(d(1)(A), d(8)(A))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Pre-built iceberg template with the underwater section divided into 4 labeled zones. Skills, Tools, Training, Challenges, the same four the workbook names, so students know what to put where. Students who finish the basic 10 items can keep going. For Rung 2, give the five Career Snapshot questions on separate lines with the first one answered as a model.
  • Extension: Fill the Electrician frame on page 7 as a second iceberg, then compare. What is different underwater between the Electrician and the student's own career? Which iceberg has more overlap with the student's current strengths?
  • ELL: Visual iceberg template with image search permission. Students can paste images instead of writing words. Pre-teach: Iceberg = Iceberg, Hidden = Oculto, Visible = Visible, Pathway = Trayectoria, Perks = Ventajas, Quirks = Inconvenientes.

docs.title: Day 3: Xello Quick Sims — The Real Game
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Complete the Xello "Quick Sims: The Real Game" simulation; track financial decisions made during the simulation; complete Rung 3 of the Capstone ladder for the Day 2 career goal; compare lifestyle desires to career salary realities TEKS d(5)(D), d(8)(A) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Real Game simulation and decision log · Extend: Rung 3 Career Deep Dive for the student's own career goal · Explain: Career vs. lifestyle debrief · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed Real Game decision log showing all major lifestyle choices and the running budget impact + completed Rung 3 pages Materials Chromebooks, Xello student accounts, Find Your Future workbook pp. 285-286, printed Real Game decision log (1 per student), projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: If you earned $40,000 per year (about $2,500/month after taxes), how would you spend that money? List your top 5 monthly expenses and rough amounts.

Collect 2-3 student responses on the board without correcting the numbers. Keep them visible so students can compare their guesses with the housing, transportation, food, and entertainment costs in Xello.

docs.title: Activity 1: Xello "Quick Sims: The Real Game" (35 min)
docs.text:
Source: Xello supplemental activity, "Quick Sims: The Real Game." This activity is not a Bowie Grade 8 completion standard.

Direct students to log into Xello and navigate to Quick Sims. The Real Game simulation puts students into a young adult scenario where they make decisions about housing, transportation, food, entertainment, and savings based on a realistic salary tied to a career.

[XELLO SUPPLEMENTAL] Quick Sims is available in Xello but is not a Bowie Grade 8 completion standard. Use it only when it supports the day's learning target; do not count it toward required completion.

Students work through the simulation independently. As they make each decision, they log it on the printed decision log:

Decision Category What I Chose Monthly Cost Running Budget Remaining Career & Salary Housing Transportation Food / Groceries Phone / Internet Entertainment Savings Insurance / Healthcare

The decision log is critical. Without it, the simulation becomes a video game students click through. With it, students see the math piling up against their early choices.

Facilitation Tip

Circulate aggressively for the first 10 minutes. Students who skip the decision log lose the entire point of the activity. If a student finishes the Sim in under 5 minutes, they clicked through without thinking, make them restart and log every decision.

Common Misstep

Students may pick the cheapest option for everything to "win" the simulation. Stop the room at minute 15 and ask whether those choices match the life they described in the warm-up. Their budget should test a realistic lifestyle, even when that lifestyle does not balance.

Rung 3 as students finish. The Sim hands students a salary. Rung 3 asks them to find their own (FYF pp. 285-286: "Rung 3: Career Deep Dive"). As each student finishes the simulation, they open pages 285-286 and complete the deep dive for the career goal they named on Rung 2 yesterday:

  • Education or Training Required: check one of high school diploma, trade or technical school, associate's degree, bachelor's degree, master's degree or higher, or other
  • Special certifications, licenses, or training needed
  • About how long it takes to prepare for this career
  • Salary and Outlook: estimated starting salary, national average, average in your area, and whether the field is growing, stable, or declining

Numbers come from the Hats & Ladders Hat page, BLS, and the app's Career Plan. The Skills Check on page 286 is Activity 2.

Facilitation Tip

Rung 3 is one of the three rungs this week has to protect if a testing day eats a period. If the simulation is running long, cut the decision log to the three categories named in Support rather than cutting Rung 3. The salary numbers on page 286 are the ones 5SW's budget week builds a full monthly budget from, and 6SW pulls into the finished ladder.

docs.title: Activity 2: Debrief — Career vs. Lifestyle (8 min)
docs.text:
After students complete the Sim, run a quick whole-class debrief. Ask:

  1. Who ran out of money? Why?
  2. Who had to give up something they really wanted?
  3. Who picked an expensive lifestyle and could afford it? What career did you have?
  4. Who picked a cheap lifestyle on purpose? Why?
  5. How does the Sim's salary compare to the starting salary you just wrote on Rung 3 for your own career goal?

Compare the choices that balanced with the ones that did not. Ask what changed when students adjusted the career, housing, transportation, or entertainment line. Do not rank the careers; keep the discussion on the tradeoff each budget made visible.

Stop and Jot: Close the debrief with the Skills Check on page 286. Give students 3 minutes and the three lines the workbook prints: skills this career might need, skills I already have, and skills I will need to build. Post a stem for the third line, "A skill I will need to build is _, and I can start by ___." Read the third line over shoulders. Whichever skill shows up most across the room is the one to name again on Day 5 when students write their mid-year update.

DOK 3: What conclusions can you draw about the relationship between the career you want and the lifestyle you can afford? Did the simulation change your thinking about your top career from yesterday?

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Trade-off / Dilemma Analysis) · Printable PDF:

You finished The Real Game. You got ONE career and ONE monthly budget. Now imagine your SAME career, but you have to pick between two lifestyles:

  • (A) Cheaper lifestyle (smaller apartment, used car, eat-at-home): you save $400/month extra.
  • (B) More-expensive lifestyle (nicer apartment, newer car, eat out weekly): you save nothing extra but enjoy more now.

Pros of picking A: _____________

Pros of picking B: _____________

My choice (A or B): __

Quality list: patience / discipline / flexibility / dedication / self-awareness / confidence.

Which QUALITY does my choice require MOST, and why is it the right quality for this specific tradeoff? (d(5)(D), d(8)(A))

My quality: _____

Why: ____________

Submit your Real Game decision log and your Rung 3 pages with this ticket.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Pre-print the decision log with the categories already filled in. Students only have to add their choices and the dollar amounts. For students who struggle with budgeting math, pair them with a partner who tracks the running total while they make choices.
  • Extension: After completing the Sim once, restart it with a different career (one that pays significantly less or more). Compare the two budget outcomes side by side. Which lifestyle was more sustainable? Then check the Rung 3 outlook box against BLS. Is the field growing, stable, or declining, and does that change the comparison?
  • ELL: Xello includes Spanish-language interface options, confirm with your district admin and direct ESL students to the language toggle if available. Pre-teach: Budget = Presupuesto, Salary = Salario, Expense = Gasto, Savings = Ahorros, Rent = Alquiler, Training = Capacitación. Rung 3's education box is a checkbox list, so students can complete it before writing anything in prose.

docs.title: Day 4: eDynamic 8.1 — Choosing a Career Path
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Work through eDynamic Learning Unit 8.1: Your Turn! Choosing a Career Path; rank top 3 Irving ISD pathways with rationale; identify professional organizations connected to chosen pathways and name one specific benefit of joining in 9th grade TEKS d(3)(F), d(8)(A), d(8)(B) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: eDynamic Unit 8.1 self-paced work · Explain: Pathway Ranking Sheet rationale and organization match · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable eDynamic 8.1 progress + completed Pathway Ranking Sheet (top 3 with rationale and one professional organization per pathway) Materials Chromebooks, eDynamic Learning Unit 8.1 access, printed Pathway Ranking Sheet, Irving ISD CTE Pathways poster, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: What is the difference between a career and a job? Write your answer in one sentence, no looking it up.

Take 3-4 student definitions and project all of them. Then offer the working definition: a job is something you do for money right now; a career is work built over time, often across multiple jobs in the same field. Ask students to keep that difference in mind as they make choices in eDynamic.

docs.title: Activity 1: eDynamic Unit 8.1 — Choosing a Career Path (30 min)
docs.text:
Source: eDynamic Learning Unit 8.1, Your Turn! Choosing a Career Path

[VERIFY IN eDynamic] Confirm with your district admin that Unit 8.1 is the correct unit for "Choosing a Career Path." If the unit numbering has shifted in your eDynamic license, locate the equivalent unit on personal assessment review and career path selection.

Students log into eDynamic and open Unit 8.1. Teacher orients students to the unit structure on the projector, most eDynamic units have an introduction, content sections, an interactive activity, and a check-for-understanding quiz.

The unit walks students through: 1. Reviewing personal assessment results (core personality types, Work Values) 2. Strategies for matching assessments to career choices 3. Introduction to job search basics 4. Identifying professional organizations connected to a career interest

Students work at their own pace. As they work, they note three things on their Pathway Ranking Sheet: - One key strategy from the unit for matching assessment results to careers - One professional organization the unit mentions that connects to their chosen pathway - One question they still have about choosing a career path

Active Monitoring: Walk the room twice during the self-paced block. Lap 1 at minute 8, target: every student is past the introduction and into the assessment-review section. Lap 2 at minute 15, target: every student has reached the professional organizations section. Students still on the introduction get a private nudge, not a whole-class announcement. If more than a handful miss the minute 15 target, pivot and project the organizations section to the room so the Pathway Ranking Sheet still has the data it needs. The unit is self-paced but the class period is not.

Facilitation Tip
