docs.text: TinkerCAD Building Presentation (Day 5): Students present their 3D building design and explain: (1) design decisions and how they connect to real architecture, (2) one A&C career involved in building it, (3) one idea from their firm's novelty landmark that plain bricks and wood could not build. Scored on design quality, career knowledge (d(1)(B), d(1)(C)), education/training accuracy (d(2)(A)), and salary comparison data (d(5)(E)).

docs.title: Scaffolded Learning
docs.text:
• TinkerCAD starter template with a basic floor plan pre-built for students who need extra support
  • Simplified salary worksheet with one career row pre-filled as an example
  • Pair work option for TinkerCAD, one student designs, the other navigates/coaches
  • Pre-printed safety poster layout with three labeled boxes (top 5 rules, essential equipment, safety map) so students who need support spend the Day 1 window on content rather than on layout

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
• Research the MacArthur HS Revit certification pathway and create a 4-year course plan
  • Powerskill: Tolerance for Ambiguity (FYF pp. 180-181), the Day 3 extension: partners are the site foreman on a 3D-printed home with a half-finished client brief, sort what they know from what they do not, draw a rough floor plan on chart paper anyway, and log each assumption they had to make and why
  • 60-second self-pitch (CCE-original): students who finish early on Day 5 write and deliver a 60-second pitch about themselves, using their Building Blocks as evidence. There is no workbook page for this pitch, so the delivery standard comes from the checklist at (FYF p. 299: "Prepare & Present"): speak clearly at a steady pace, look up and engage the audience, show confidence even when nervous, and use notes to guide rather than reading word for word. The district page supplies the framing question (FYF p. 196): what makes a strong first impression?
  • Compare Architect vs. Civil Engineer career trajectories using BLS data from both weeks

docs.title: ELL Language Support
docs.text:
• Pre-teach: Architecture = Arquitectura, Blueprint = Plano, Design = Diseño, Scale = Escala
  • TinkerCAD is highly visual and accessible for all language levels. Provide bilingual command reference card (Drag = Arrastrar, Resize = Cambiar tamaño, Group = Agrupar, Hole = Agujero)
  • Bilingual salary comparison worksheet with Spanish category labels
  • Pair ESL students with bilingual peers during presentations

docs.title: Day 1: Engineering Cluster Tour + Systems Thinking
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Explore the Engineering cluster in the workbook and the Hats & Ladders app; research one engineering career on the career research worksheet; plan a kitchen cabinet layout where every placement affects the rest of the room TEKS d(1)(B), d(1)(C), d(2)(A) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up and Be the Decision Maker · Explore: Cluster tour, career research, and cabinet layout · Explain: Layout review with another pair · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed Engineering career research worksheet (1 career) + cabinet layout drawn on the workbook floor plan (pp. 174-175) Materials Chromebooks, H&L accounts, Find Your Future workbook pp. 103, 110, and 174-175, printed Engineering career research worksheet, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Name a bridge, highway, or water system in Irving that you use regularly. Someone ENGINEERED that, designed it, calculated how much weight it could hold, figured out where to put it, and made sure it would last 50+ years. What kind of education do you think that takes?

Collect 2-3 responses. Last week students designed buildings; this week they test what happens when a design has to carry weight, move water, or hold up a road.

docs.title: Activity 1: Engineering Cluster Tour + Be the Decision Maker (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 103: "Exploring the World of ENGINEERING") + (FYF p. 110: "App Exploration")

Open the workbook to the chapter opener and read it together. Engineering is about designing, building, and improving the world around us, and engineers, technicians, and systems designers work together to solve problems and develop new ideas, whether that is a stronger bridge, an advanced aircraft, or a more powerful machine. Three Hats sit on the page: Aerospace Engineer, Biomedical Engineer, and CAD Technician. The chapter prints no pathway list, so the pathways come from the app.

Think-Pair-Share: Read the page's "Be the Decision Maker" prompt: a company has asked students to help design the airplane of the future, and they have to say which features they would include and why their design would improve the trip. Hold a silent 30 second Think, then time Partner A for 30 seconds and Partner B for 30 seconds. Two pairs share with the whole class.

[H&L PLATFORM] Open the Hats & Ladders app, go to Clusters, and click the Engineering Cluster, which is the path the App Exploration page uses (FYF p. 110). Students watch the "Cluster Tour" video, play "Game Time," and write one thing they learned in the box on page 110. They then use the Hat Finder to browse engineering Hats, prioritizing Civil Engineer, Structural Engineer, and Environmental Engineer this week because those are the Architecture and Construction overlap careers.

Facilitation Tip

Engineering appears in both the Architecture & Construction cluster (Construction Management and Inspection) and the Engineering cluster (Civil, Structural, Environmental). Show students that careers overlap across clusters. This is how the real world works.

docs.title: Activity 2: Engineering Career Research (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: CCE career research worksheet (the research format is taught in Wk0); app steps follow (FYF p. 110: "App Exploration")

Students select one engineering career (Civil Engineer, Structural Engineer, or Environmental Engineer is recommended this week) and complete every field on the research worksheet:

  • Name of Career
  • What Interests You?: why this career caught their attention
  • Brief Job Description: what this professional does daily
  • Education/Training Needed: degrees, certifications, licensing (PE license)
  • Average Salary: DFW data from the Hat profile, confirmed against BLS
  • Tools, Equipment, or Skills Needed: AutoCAD, Revit, math, physics, problem-solving

[H&L PLATFORM] Students pull each worksheet field from the Hat profile in the app, then confirm the salary and training figures against at least one additional source, such as the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook page for civil engineers. Before they close the app, they finish two steps from the App Exploration page (FYF p. 110): find 1 Hat that matches their personality or interests and 1 Hat that does not feel like a fit, and write why for each.

Facilitation Tip

Civil engineers need a Bachelor's degree plus a Professional Engineer (PE) license, which takes 4 more years of experience plus two exams. This is a long pathway, point it out as a contrast to trade careers students saw in 4SW.

docs.title: Activity 3: Powerskill: Systems Thinking — Kitchen Layout (10 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 174-175: "Powerskill: Systems Thinking")

Introduce the idea the rest of the week runs on. Systems thinking means seeing how all the pieces of a project fit together, thinking ahead, and noticing how a change in one area affects other areas. Civil engineers live in that problem: widen a road and the water has somewhere new to go; raise a bridge and the approach ramps have to move with it.

The workbook puts students in a smaller version of the same problem. Students and a partner are the lead carpenters hired to design cabinets for a client's new kitchen. The floor plan already has a sink, a stove, a refrigerator, and counters.

Step 1: Explore the Kitchen Layout (4 min). Partners study the floor plan and answer the workbook's three questions: where could cabinets go without blocking plumbing or appliances, how will people move through the room if cabinets go in certain spots, and could placing a cabinet in one area cause a problem somewhere else.

Step 2: Plan the Cabinets (4 min). Partners draw their cabinet layout on the workbook floor plan, adjusting placements to keep the room functional and easy to use.

Step 3: Review with Another Group (2 min). Pairs swap plans with another pair and answer one question out loud: which choice had the biggest effect on how the room works. Each pair marks one placement they would move after seeing the other plan.

DOK 2: Name one choice in your kitchen layout that forced you to change something else. What was the second change, and why was it necessary?

Facilitation Tip

Pairs that finish Step 2 in two minutes usually placed cabinets on empty wall space and never tested the walking path. Ask them to trace with a finger how someone carries a hot pan from the stove to the sink. That one question sends most pairs back to the plan.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Mini-Case / Scenario Application) · Printable PDF:

Scenario: Irving had 3 inches of rain last night. Parts of Trinity River flooded, a major highway is closed, and a bridge over the creek is showing cracks.

  1. Which TYPE of engineer would LEAD the investigation of each issue? Match:

  2. Flooding: Civil Engineer / Structural Engineer / Environmental Engineer

  3. Highway closure: Civil Engineer / Structural Engineer / Environmental Engineer

  4. Bridge cracks: Civil Engineer / Structural Engineer / Environmental Engineer

  5. In the kitchen activity, moving one cabinet changed something else in the room. Name ONE thing in Irving that would change if the city closed that bridge for six months of repairs:

  1. Name ONE education requirement a civil engineer needs (degree, license, or certification):

(d(1)(B), d(1)(C), d(2)(A))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a pre-marked kitchen floor plan with the sink, stove, and refrigerator circled and the walking path drawn as a dotted line, so partners spend their time on placement instead of plan-reading. Give the research worksheet with one row filled in as an example.
  • Extension: Research one real DFW infrastructure project (the High Five interchange, DART Silver Line, or the Trinity River Flood Control) on the TxDOT projects and studies page. What problem did civil engineers solve, and what else in the city had to change because of it?
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Infrastructure = Infraestructura, Flooding = Inundación, Cabinet = Gabinete, Layout = Distribución. The kitchen floor plan is a visual task, so ELL students can plan the layout before they need the vocabulary. Pair ELL students with bilingual peers for the Step 3 review.

docs.title: Day 2: PSAT/SAT/ACT — Why They Matter + Emerging Engineering Careers
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Compare postsecondary options; compare PSAT, SAT, ACT, ASVAB, and TSI tests; explain how scores affect engineering college admissions; research 1-2 emerging engineering occupations TEKS d(3)(E), d(1)(D) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: Post-secondary options and the six tests · Explore: Test comparison Gallery Walk · Extend: Emerging engineering careers research · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed PSAT/SAT/ACT Impact worksheet + Emerging Engineering Careers research template Materials Chromebooks, projector, Find Your Future workbook pp. 108-109, College Board website, printed test comparison cards (PSAT 8/9, PSAT/NMSQT, SAT, ACT, ASVAB, TSI), printed Impact worksheet, printed Emerging Careers template

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Have you heard of the SAT? When do students take it? Does it affect YOU as a 7th grader?

Quick show of hands, most students will assume it is a high school problem. Bridge: decisions students make in 7th and 8th grade (course selection, study habits, math placement) directly affect PSAT 8/9 scores in 9th grade. Engineering programs look at these scores closely.

docs.title: Activity 1: Standardized Test Overview (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 108-109: "What is Happening at My District?") + College Board PSAT/SAT resources

Start where the workbook's Engineering district pages start. Their Career Exploration Connection is Post-Secondary Options: there is no single path to success after high school, and four-year colleges, community colleges, technical and trade schools, apprenticeships, military service, training programs, and going straight to work are all real options. Read the page's Discuss question and take two answers: how can someone decide which postsecondary option is the best fit? Point out that the tests below are gates for some of those options and irrelevant to others, which is why students need to know which ones apply to them.

Then teach each test with a short, concrete description and one key reason it matters. Keep it to 2-3 sentences per test. Students do deeper comparison in Activity 2.

  • PSAT 8/9: Taken in 9th grade. Practice run. Does NOT count for college admission, but scores identify strengths and weaknesses early.
  • PSAT/NMSQT: Taken in 10th or 11th grade. This is the National Merit qualifying test, top 1% earn National Merit scholarships worth $2,500+.
  • SAT: The primary college admissions test. Measures reading, writing, and math. Most four-year universities use SAT scores as one factor in admissions.
  • ACT: Alternative to the SAT. Includes science reasoning (SAT does not). Many students take both and submit the higher score.
  • ASVAB: Military aptitude test. Required if entering ANY branch of the U.S. military. Used to determine which military jobs a recruit qualifies for.
  • TSI (Texas Success Initiative): Required by Texas community colleges and universities before enrolling in college-level courses. Measures reading, writing, and math readiness.

Facilitation Tip

Include scholarships when explaining how colleges use SAT or ACT scores. Use a current Texas university scholarship table if you want to attach dollar amounts; award thresholds change and should not be estimated from memory.

docs.title: Activity 2: Gallery Walk — Test Comparison (15 min)
docs.text:
Before class, post 6 index cards around the room, one for each test (PSAT 8/9, PSAT/NMSQT, SAT, ACT, ASVAB, TSI). Each card shows: when it is taken, what it measures, what it is used for, and who should take it.

Time, Voice, Body: Set the three blocks before the first rotation. A visible 2 minute countdown per station, Voice 1 for partner talk at a card and Voice 0 while walking between cards, one rotation direction so pairs do not cross the room, and the Impact worksheet stays in hand rather than on a desk.

Students rotate through the stations in pairs, taking notes on their PSAT/SAT/ACT Impact worksheet. In 15 min, pairs will not hit all six stations, aim for the four most relevant to a 7th grader's pathway (PSAT 8/9, SAT, ACT, TSI) and skim the remaining two only if time allows. They answer:

  1. Which tests apply to MY pathway? (If engineering → SAT/ACT. If military → ASVAB. If community college → TSI. All students → PSAT 8/9.)
  2. What is the earliest test I will take? (PSAT 8/9 in 9th grade, just 1-2 years away.)
  3. What skills does it measure? (Reading, writing, math, science reasoning.)
  4. How does this test affect scholarships? (National Merit is PSAT/NMSQT; merit scholarships use SAT/ACT.)

DOK 3: How could your 7th-grade choices (course selection, math class, reading habits) affect your PSAT 8/9 score in two years? Name two specific things you could start doing now.

docs.title: Activity 3: Emerging Engineering Careers Research (12 min)
docs.text:
Source: Scope and sequence d(1)(D) + BLS OOH Engineering section

Introduce "emerging occupations", careers that did not exist 10 years ago or are rapidly growing due to new technology or environmental needs. In engineering, the top emerging categories are Green Building / LEED Engineering, Smart Infrastructure, and Sustainability/Environmental Engineering. Ground these categories in BLS OOH: Environmental Engineers (bls.gov/ooh/architecture-and-engineering/environmental-engineers.htm) lists sustainability, green building, and environmental compliance as growth areas through 2032.

Students pick one emerging engineering career and complete the Emerging Engineering Careers research template:

  • Career Name (e.g., Green Building Engineer, Smart Traffic Systems Engineer, Sustainability Consultant)
  • Why is it "emerging"?: what changed in the last 10 years that created this career?
  • Education required: bachelor's in traditional engineering + specialty certification (LEED AP, PE)
  • Estimated DFW salary from BLS
  • Why DFW needs it: population growth, climate, aging infrastructure

Stop and Jot: Box the "Why is it emerging?" line at 90 seconds with the stem on the board: "A Smart Infrastructure Specialist is an EMERGING career because _. The technology or need that made it grow is ___."

Students begin research in class and finish as homework if needed.

Facilitation Tip

Point out that "emerging" does not always mean new companies, it often means traditional engineers who added a specialty certification. A civil engineer who earns a LEED AP credential can charge higher rates.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Comparison Matrix) · Printable PDF:

Compare 3 standardized tests on how they matter to MY pathway.

Test When I'd take it What it's used for Relevant to my pathway? (YES/NO) PSAT 8/9 9th grade SAT or ACT 11-12th grade TSI / ASVAB (pick one) post-HS

Bottom line: ONE test most relevant to my pathway: _____. In one sentence, why it matters for MY chosen field:

ONE emerging engineering career I researched today: _____. (d(3)(E), d(1)(D))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Simplified PSAT/SAT worksheet with pre-filled rows for PSAT 8/9 and SAT. Students fill in only the tests relevant to their pathway.
  • Extension: Research the average SAT math score required for admission to Texas engineering programs (UT Austin, Texas A&M, UT Dallas). What would you need to score?
  • ELL: Bilingual test comparison cards (College Board publishes SAT prep materials in Spanish). Pre-teach: Standardized Test = Examen estandarizado, Admission = Admisión, Score = Puntuación.

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Apply the Engineering Design Process (EDP) phases 1-2: Define the problem and research/sketch 2 bridge design options before building TEKS d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: Design challenge and Engineering Design Process · Explore: Bridge type research and two design sketches · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Approved bridge sketch showing two design options with labeled structural elements (truss, arch, or beam) Materials Chromebooks, printed Bridge Design sketch page, projector, PBS Design Squad videos, bridge materials for display only (not yet built)

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Think about the strongest bridge you have ever seen. What made it strong, the shape, the materials, or the size? Write down your best guess.

Collect 2-3 guesses, then test the shapes. A triangle holds its shape under load, while a square can fold into a parallelogram.

docs.title: Activity 1: The Challenge + Engineering Design Process (10 min)
docs.text:
Source: CCE-original challenge. The Find Your Future workbook prints no civil engineering activity, so the problem below is grounded on the TxDOT Dallas district project listings and the BLS civil engineers page rather than on a workbook scenario.

Name the real version of the problem first, in one minute. TxDOT's Dallas district is rebuilding interchanges and frontage roads across the metroplex, the Trinity River flood control system keeps water out of neighborhoods that flooded before it existed, and the DART Silver Line runs a rail corridor through Irving that had to cross roads already in use. Every one of those projects is somebody deciding how much load a structure has to carry and what happens to everything around it. Today students take the same decision at desk scale.

Announce the challenge clearly so students understand the constraints:

The Challenge: In teams of 2-3, design and build a bridge that spans a 12-inch gap between two desks. The bridge must hold as much weight as possible without collapsing. The winning bridge holds the most weight per gram of materials used (strength-to-weight ratio).

Material limits per team:

  • 40 plastic drinking straws
  • 3 feet of masking tape
  • 5 index cards
  • Scissors

Introduce the Engineering Design Process. Civil engineers follow this same process in real projects.

  1. Define the Problem: What exactly are we solving? (Span 12 inches, hold maximum weight.)
  2. Research & Ideate: How have others solved this problem? What designs work?
  3. Prototype: Build it.
  4. Test: Measure performance.
  5. Redesign: Fix what failed.

Today's goal: Complete Phases 1 and 2.

Facilitation Tip

Do not distribute materials today. Students who get materials immediately start building without thinking. The point of Day 3 is forcing them to plan first, just like a real civil engineer does before pouring a single cubic yard of concrete.

docs.title: Activity 2: Bridge Type Research (15 min)
docs.text:
Chunking: Project one bridge type at a time and say what each one is for before showing it. Close each type with the three research questions below before moving to the next, and demonstrate the triangle-versus-square load test on the projector inside the truss chunk.

Project a quick 3-minute visual tour of bridge types on the screen, use PBS Design Squad or a static comparison slide:

  • Beam Bridge: simplest. A flat deck with supports on each end. Weak unless the beam is thick.
  • Truss Bridge: triangular framework. Distributes load across many small pieces. Common in railroads.
  • Arch Bridge: curved. The weight pushes outward into the ground. Very strong but hard to build.

After the tour, teams research bridge types online (PBS Design Squad, BLS civil engineering page, or a teacher-curated image set). They identify:

  • Which type fits a 12-inch span with straws?
  • What is the key structural element of each?
  • Which uses triangles and why are triangles strong?

Why Triangles?

A triangle is the only shape that does not deform under load without breaking a connection. Push on a square and it becomes a parallelogram. Push on a triangle and nothing moves unless one of the sides breaks. This is why trusses are made of triangles.

docs.title: Activity 3: Design Two Options + Peer Critique (17 min)
docs.text:
Each team sketches two different bridge designs on the provided sketch page. The sketches must include:

  • Top-down view of the bridge
  • Side view showing the structural shape
  • Labels for each structural element (truss, arch, beam, support column)
  • Predicted weak points: where do they think it will break first?

After sketching, teams swap sketches with another team for a 2-minute peer critique. The critiquing team answers: "Where do you think this design will fail first, and why?"

Teams then pick one design to build on Day 4 based on the peer feedback.

DOK 2: Why is a truss stronger than a simple beam bridge? Use your sketch to explain.

Facilitation Tip

Approve each team's final design before they leave class. If a team picked a flat beam bridge with no triangular reinforcement, prompt them with: "What shape holds its form under load?" and send them back to revise. Avoid saying "That won't work", let them engineer their own realization.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Short Constructed Response) · Printable PDF:

  1. My team's bridge type (circle one): Truss / Arch / Beam / Other: _____

  2. Space below, sketch the chosen design (top view OR side view) with at least 3 structural elements labeled:

  1. ONE design feature I picked specifically to MAKE IT STRONGER:

Feature: _____. Why it makes it stronger in one sentence:

  1. The WEAK POINT I expect to fail first: _____. Why I expect that in one sentence:

(d(1)(C))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide truss and arch bridge templates with basic geometry already drawn. Students adapt the template for the 12-inch span rather than designing from scratch.
  • Extension: Research cable-stayed and suspension bridges, why are these used for very long spans? How do they differ from truss bridges?
  • ELL: Visual bridge type poster with Spanish labels: Truss = Armadura, Arch = Arco, Beam = Viga, Support = Soporte, Load = Carga. Bridge-building is highly visual and accessible across language levels.

docs.title: Day 4: Bridge Challenge — Build and Test
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Apply EDP phases 3-4: Build the bridge prototype from the approved Day 3 design; test weight capacity incrementally; record max weight held TEKS d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Prototype build and weight testing · Explain: Redesign reflection · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed bridge prototype + test results sheet (max weight held) Materials Bridge-building materials (40 straws, 3 ft tape, 5 index cards, scissors per team), 12-inch gap test station, weights (pennies in cups, washers, or a digital kitchen scale with textbooks), stopwatch, test results sheet

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: What is one thing that could go wrong while you build your bridge? How will you know if it is happening?

Take a quick share, then name the habit as quality control: checking measurements and connections during the build, before a weak joint is buried under more material.

docs.title: Activity 1: Build Phase with Checkpoints (22 min)
docs.text:
Distribute materials to each team. Emphasize: follow your approved sketch from Day 3. This is the "Prototype" phase of the EDP.

Use three visual checkpoints to keep teams on pace. Walk with a clipboard and mark each team's progress.

Active Monitoring: Walk the same pathway three times, one lap per checkpoint, with a single target per lap. If more than a handful of teams miss the minute 15 target, pivot and reproject the truss geometry to the whole room instead of repeating it team by team.

docs.title: Checkpoint 1 — by minute 8
docs.text: Base structure complete. Two long support rails (straws taped together) should span roughly 12 inches. Most teams are still shaky here, that is fine.

docs.title: Checkpoint 2 — by minute 15
docs.text: Triangular reinforcement added. Diagonal members (making truss triangles) should be visible connecting the two support rails. Teams with no triangles need a reminder, point to their Day 3 sketch.

docs.title: Checkpoint 3 — by minute 22
docs.text:
Deck surface complete. Index cards or taped straws form a flat deck where weight can be placed. The bridge should stand on its own without being held.

Facilitation Tip

The most common build failure is students taping straws end-to-end (flimsy) instead of bundling 3-4 straws together with tape (strong). Walk by each team in the first 5 minutes and prompt them: "Are those straws bundled or just connected in a line?" One nudge early saves a collapse at testing.

docs.title: Activity 2: Weight Testing Phase (15 min)
docs.text:
Set up the test station at the front of the room: two desks (or stacks of books) 12 inches apart with the bridge spanning the gap.

Each team brings their bridge forward for testing. Use one of these methods:

  • Method 1 (simple): Add pennies to a cup sitting in the center of the bridge, one at a time. Define "failure" before testing starts so teams cannot argue in the moment: STOP at the first visible sag OR the first taped joint that separates, teacher's call is final. Record the penny count at the stop.
  • Method 2 (precise): Use a digital kitchen scale placed on the bridge, and stack textbooks until failure. Record weight in grams.

Testing protocol:

  1. Team places bridge on the test station
  2. Weight is added slowly (one unit every 2 seconds)
  3. Teacher calls "STOP" at first visible failure (buckling, collapse, or deck breaking)
  4. Teacher records max weight on a class-visible whiteboard

Each team records their own result on their test results sheet along with notes on where the bridge failed first (usually the deck, a support rail, or a taped joint). Teams waiting their turn at the test station should start Activity 3 (redesign reflection) at their desks instead of sitting idle. This keeps the test queue moving and distributes the 15-min activity time across testing and writing.

DOK 4: What design features correlated with the strongest bridges in our class? Use evidence from at least two teams' results.

docs.title: Activity 3: Redesign Reflection (5 min)
docs.text:
Before clean-up, each team writes a quick redesign statement on their test results sheet:

  • What failed? Name the specific element that broke first.
  • Why did it fail? Was it the material, the shape, or the connection method?
  • What would you change? Describe one specific change that would make the bridge stronger.

This reflection is the "Redesign" phase of the EDP. Real civil engineers rarely get it perfect on the first try. They iterate.

Connection to Real Infrastructure

Remind students that this bridge challenge is a desk-scale version of the TxDOT and Trinity River work named on Day 3. Real civil engineers work at a much bigger scale and with much longer test cycles, and they carry the Day 1 systems-thinking problem with them: a change at one end of a structure shows up somewhere else. The process is the same.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Ranked Justification) · Printable PDF:

Rank these 4 design factors from MOST important (1) to LEAST (4) based on what made class bridges STRONG or WEAK today.

  • Triangular reinforcement (trusses): rank ____
  • Bundled straws (3+ straws taped together): rank ____
  • Deck thickness (index cards doubled up): rank ____
  • Tape placement (joints reinforced): rank ____

My bridge's MAX WEIGHT HELD: ____

First element that failed: _____

For EACH rank, write ONE piece of evidence (from my bridge OR another team's):

  • Rank 1 (most important): _____________

  • Rank 4 (least important): _____________

Bottom line: ONE change I would make in a redesign:

(d(1)(C))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide pre-bundled support rails (3 straws taped together) for teams who need a head start. Their challenge becomes the truss design rather than the material prep.
  • Extension: Teams who finish early get a second set of materials (or use materials from other teams who finished) and build a stronger V2 based on their redesign statement. Test and compare.
  • ELL: Testing is visual and universally accessible. Pair ELL students with bilingual peers during the reflection writing. Provide sentence stems: "My bridge failed at the _ (En la ). I would change __ (Cambiaría _____)."

docs.title: Day 5: Bridge Results + Mission to Mars
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Present bridge results with design rationale; design and label a Mars Rover prototype for an environment nobody in the room has built for; rate engineering pathways and Hats and favorite the week's careers TEKS d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: Bridge results presentations · Extend: Mission to Mars rover design · Explore: App Exploration pathways and favorites · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Bridge results presentation + labeled Mars Rover sketch (p. 107) + rated pathway and 3 rated Hats + submitted Emerging Engineering Careers research template Materials Chromebooks, H&L accounts, Find Your Future workbook pp. 106-107 and p. 110, chart paper or sticky notes, whiteboard with Day 4 results, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: When engineers investigate why a structure failed, what kinds of questions do they ask? (Example: a section of highway settles unevenly after a few years, who figures out why?)

Discuss briefly. The answer is forensic structural engineers: civil engineers who study why structures fail. Connect that work to yesterday's test results. A bridge that held less weight still gives the team a failed joint, buckled member, or weak shape to study before redesigning.

docs.title: Activity 1: Results Share-Out + Team Presentations (15 min)
docs.text:
Post the Day 4 results and the weight each bridge held, but do not rank teams from highest to lowest. Ask students to find patterns. Name the best strength-to-weight ratio (the lightest bridge that held substantial weight), the most unusual structural approach, and the highest-weight result.

Each team gives a 60-second rapid presentation covering:

  1. Our design: What bridge type did we use? (Truss, arch, beam)
  2. Our result: Max weight held.
  3. What broke first: The element that failed.
  4. Our redesign: What we would change.

Facilitation Tip

Use a 60-second timer on the projector. Keep presentations fast and consistent. Students watching should note which designs held the most, it informs class discussion about triangles vs. beams.

After presentations, lead a 3-minute class discussion: What pattern do you see in the top-performing bridges? (Expect: trusses, triangular reinforcement, and bundled straws rather than single straws.)

DOK 3: Based on your team's results AND everyone else's results, what conclusions can you draw about what makes a structure strong?

docs.title: Activity 2: Mission to Mars — Design the Next Rover (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 106-107: "Mission to Mars"), a Career Climb activity

Turn the week's engineering thinking loose on a place none of it was built for. Students are an aerospace engineer at NASA. The current Mars Rover has been exploring for years and it is time for it to retire, so NASA wants ideas for a replacement that can cross rocky terrain, collect important samples, and send data back to Earth.

Step 1: Brainstorm Ideas (4 min). Read the conditions NASA supplied on page 106: temperatures from 70 to -225 degrees F, a rocky surface with canyons and volcanoes, and high winds that cause large dust storms. The rover has to collect rock samples, send pictures and data back to Earth, and move quickly enough to cover a lot of ground. Students use chart paper or sticky notes to list the key components the rover needs.

Step 2: Design Your Rover (6 min). Students sketch a prototype on page 107 and label the key components. Every label should answer one of the three conditions or one of the three requirements.

Step 3: Discuss with a Group (5 min). Students get into groups of 3 or 4, present their sketch, and discuss the workbook's two questions: which conditions on Mars were the hardest to design around, and what tests would you need to run before the rover could be used on a real mission.

Facilitation Tip

Yesterday's weight test is the hook for Step 3's second question. Students already know what it feels like to find out a design fails under load, so push past "we would test it" to what specifically gets tested and in what order. Cold chamber before dust chamber, or the other way around, and why.

docs.title: Activity 3: App Exploration — Pathways, Favorites, and Submissions (7 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 110: "App Exploration"), the Pathway Possibilities and Hat rating steps

[H&L PLATFORM] Students return to the Engineering Cluster in the Hats & Ladders app and click "Pathway Possibilities." They answer the questions there, then explore and rate at least 1 pathway. These are the steps of the App Exploration page held back from Day 1, because a pathway rating means more after a week of career research, design, and testing. Students then rate at least 3 Hats and use the Hat Finder to favorite 2-3 engineering careers. Civil Engineer, Structural Engineer, and Environmental Engineer are the natural fits from this week, and students may also favorite Aerospace Engineer or Drone Engineer if those interest them. Favorites are saved to the Climber Profile and accumulate across the year.

Name where this goes next. At mid-year, students choose one top Hat as a career goal and write why (FYF p. 283: "Rung 2: Career Goal"), then run a Career Deep Dive on it that asks for the education or training it requires, the starting salary, and whether the field is growing (FYF pp. 285-286: "Rung 3: Career Deep Dive"). The favorites saved today are the short list that choice comes from, and the research worksheet from Day 1 is the first draft of that deep dive.

Before logging off, students submit the Emerging Engineering Careers research template they began on Day 2. It is part of the summative and it should carry the career name, why it is emerging, the education required, a DFW salary estimate, and why DFW needs it.

docs.title: Activity 4: Reflection and Preview (5 min)
docs.text:
Short whole-class reflection. Ask:

  • Who is considering engineering as a career path after this week? (Show of hands.)
  • Who now knows what PSAT 8/9 is and when they will take it? (Most should raise hands.)
  • What is the most surprising thing you learned this week?

Preview next week: Construction trades. Students will explore the people who actually BUILD what civil engineers design, carpenters, masons, heavy equipment operators, and construction managers.

DOK 3: Is engineering a good fit for you based on your core personality type, this week's bridge challenge performance, and the education requirements you researched? Write two sentences explaining your position.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Concept Map / Connection Diagram) · Printable PDF:

The engineering career I favorited this week: _____

Connect this career to THREE things:

1. Day 2 emerging-career research (what makes this career "emerging" OR relevant to modern DFW needs)

What makes it emerging: ___________

2. One standardized test from Day 2 (PSAT 8/9 / SAT / ACT / TSI / ASVAB)

My test: _____. In one sentence, how does my test score affect my path to this career?

3. The MacArthur ACE Engineering pathway

Does this pathway lead DIRECTLY to my career or is it a STEPPING STONE? Circle: DIRECT / STEPPING STONE. One sentence why:

(d(1)(C))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Allow students uncomfortable presenting to submit a written 60-second script instead of speaking. It still counts toward d(4)(C) practice. For the rover sketch, provide a component checklist (power, wheels or tracks, sample tool, camera, antenna, weather shielding) so students label rather than invent from a blank page.
  • Extension: Answer the workbook's Class Discussion question on page 107: what other professionals could an aerospace engineer collaborate with to design a rover, and what would each one contribute? Or pick one real DFW infrastructure project from the TxDOT projects and studies page and write what it would cost the city to leave the problem unsolved.
  • ELL: Provide bilingual sentence starters for presentations: "Our bridge design was a _ (Nuestro diseño fue un/una ). It held __ pennies/grams before failing (Aguantó _____ antes de fallar)." The rover sketch is a labeling task, so ELL students can show what they know before they need the sentence. Pre-teach: Rover = Vehículo explorador, Dust storm = Tormenta de polvo, Sample = Muestra.

docs.title: Week 2: Building Strong — Civil Engineering Careers
docs.text: 5th Six Weeks | Architecture & Construction / STEM Cluster | 5 class periods (50 min each)

docs.title: Lesson Objective
docs.text:
Students explore civil and structural engineering careers through the Hats & Ladders app and the Find Your Future workbook, practice systems thinking on a kitchen layout where one choice changes the whole room, investigate emerging occupations in green building and smart infrastructure, research the impact of standardized tests (PSAT/SAT/ACT) on engineering college admissions, and apply the Engineering Design Process to a weight-bearing bridge challenge and to a Mars Rover design brief.

Learning Target: I can name at least three civil engineering careers and the training each one needs, explain how PSAT, SAT, and ACT scores affect getting into an engineering program, and design, build, and test a bridge that holds weight across a 12-inch gap.

Success Criteria: I will know I am successful when my research worksheet lists the job, the training, the pay, and the tools for one engineering career, when my cabinet layout shows one placement I changed because it affected something else in the room, when my test worksheet names the one test that matters most for my pathway and why, when my bridge sketch labels at least three structural elements, and when my bridge holds weight in the class test and my redesign statement names what failed first.

docs.title: Demonstration of Learning
docs.text: "I can describe at least three civil engineering careers, explain how PSAT/SAT/ACT scores affect college admission for engineering programs, and apply engineering design principles to build a weight-bearing bridge."

docs.title: TEKS Alignment
docs.text:
• d(1)(B): Explore and describe the CTE career clusters (Day 1).
  • d(1)(C): Identify career opportunities within the Engineering pathway (Days 1, 3, 4, 5).
  • d(1)(D): Research and evaluate emerging occupations (green building, smart infrastructure) (Day 2).
  • d(2)(A): Research and describe academic and training requirements for engineering careers (Day 1 career research worksheet).
  • d(3)(E): Explain the impact of standardized testing (PSAT/SAT/ACT/ASVAB/TSI) on postsecondary opportunities (Day 2).

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Chromebooks with internet access (1 per student)
  • Hats & Ladders student accounts + Find Your Future workbook, Engineering chapter (printed pp. 103-110) and the Powerskill: Systems Thinking pages (printed pp. 174-175)
  • Bridge-building materials: plastic drinking straws (40 per team), masking tape, index cards, scissors, small weights (pennies, washers, or a digital scale and textbooks)
  • 12-inch gap station (two desks or books spaced apart)
  • Chart paper or sticky notes for the Day 5 rover brainstorm (FYF p. 106: "Mission to Mars")
  • PBS Design Squad: pbskids.org/designsquad
  • BLS, Civil Engineers: bls.gov/ooh/architecture-and-engineering/civil-engineers.htm
  • TxDOT projects and studies, Dallas district: txdot.gov/projects/projects-studies.html
  • College Board PSAT/SAT: collegeboard.org
  • Printed Engineering career research worksheet (CCE artifact; the research format is taught in Wk0)
  • Printed PSAT/SAT/ACT Impact worksheet
  • Printed Emerging Engineering Careers research template
  • Printed Bridge Design sketch page

docs.title: Career Connection
docs.text:
Civil engineers design and maintain roads, bridges, water systems, airports, and buildings. DFW population growth keeps that work visible: students can look at TxDOT's interchange and frontage-road projects, the Trinity River flood-control system, and the DART Silver Line corridor through Irving. Because the workbook prints no civil engineering activity, this week is CCE-original and uses the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook and TxDOT's Dallas district project and study listings.

This week also introduces standardized testing. Four-year engineering programs may use PSAT/SAT/ACT scores for admission and scholarships, and current 7th graders will take the PSAT 8/9 in 9th grade. The workbook's Engineering district pages place that planning inside Post-Secondary Options: four-year colleges, community colleges, technical and trade schools, apprenticeships, military service, training programs, and going straight to work (FYF pp. 108-109: "What is Happening at My District?").

What is Happening at Irving ISD? The same district pages name Autodesk Fusion 360, Autodesk CAD Inventor, and FAA Part 107 as the cluster's industry-based certifications, and SkillsUSA, VEX Robotics, and the Technology Student Association as its student organizations. They also carry a Work-Based Learning box and one Irving story worth reading aloud: Irving ISD Engineering students have designed and built prosthetic limbs so classmates could play in middle school band and orchestra. The Irving ISD CTE offerings page lists Engineering as one of four pathways in MacArthur High School's School of Architecture, Construction and Civil Engineering (ACE), alongside Architecture, Construction, and Welding.

[VERIFY with CTE coordinator] Irving ISD's program certifications poster labels the MacArthur ACE engineering pathway Civil Engineering and pairs it with Autodesk Fusion 360, while the MacArthur CTE page lists the pathway as Engineering and names no certification. The workbook lists Fusion 360 for the cluster but attaches it to no campus. Confirm the current pathway name and the certification it leads to before telling a student where to enroll.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text:
• Civil Engineer: An engineer who designs, builds, and maintains infrastructure like roads, bridges, and water systems.
  • Structural Engineer: A civil engineer who specializes in the load-bearing elements of buildings and bridges.
  • Systems Thinking: Seeing how the pieces of a project fit together, so you can tell how a change in one place will affect everything else.
  • PSAT/SAT: College Board standardized tests used for college admissions and National Merit Scholarship qualification.
  • ACT: Alternative college admissions test measuring English, math, reading, and science reasoning.
  • Smart Infrastructure: Modern infrastructure that uses sensors and data to manage systems efficiently (e.g., adaptive traffic lights, smart water grids).
  • Green Building: Construction practices that reduce environmental impact. LEED is the industry certification standard.
  • Truss: A structural framework of triangles used to support bridges and roofs because triangles distribute load efficiently.

docs.title: Bridge to Theory (Hats & Ladders)
docs.text:
The Find Your Future workbook gives Engineering printed pages 103-110, the thinnest cluster chapter in the book, and it prints no civil engineering activity anywhere. The chapter opener (FYF p. 103: "Exploring the World of ENGINEERING") frames the cluster as designing, building, and improving the world around us, puts a "Be the Decision Maker" prompt in front of students about designing the airplane of the future, and introduces three Hats on the page: Aerospace Engineer, Biomedical Engineer, and CAD Technician. The chapter prints no pathway list. Students meet the engineering pathways in the app instead, through the Pathway Possibilities step on the App Exploration page (FYF p. 110: "App Exploration"), and they meet Irving ISD's programs of study, certifications, and student organizations on the district pages (FYF pp. 108-109).

Two workbook activities anchor the week, and only one of them comes from the Engineering chapter:

  • Powerskill: Systems Thinking (Day 1): Students are the lead carpenters designing cabinets for a client's new kitchen. They read the floor plan, talk through with a partner where a cabinet can go without blocking plumbing, an appliance, or the path people walk, plan the layout, then review it with another pair and name which choices changed the room the most (FYF pp. 174-175: "Powerskill: Systems Thinking"). The lesson is borrowed from the Architecture and Construction chapter because it is the book's clearest statement of the idea this week runs on: one decision changes everything else.
  • Mission to Mars (Day 5): Career Climb activity. Students are an aerospace engineer at NASA designing the rover that replaces the one now retiring. They read the conditions on Mars (70 to -225 degrees F, rocky canyons and volcanoes, high winds and dust storms), brainstorm components on chart paper or sticky notes, sketch and label a prototype, then present it to a group of 3 or 4 and discuss which Martian condition was hardest to design around and what tests the rover would need before launch (FYF pp. 106-107: "Mission to Mars").

The chapter's other activity, Protecting Wildlife (FYF pp. 104-105), is a robot blueprint brief for a wildlife conservationist. It belongs to the 4SW drone engineering week and this week does not run it.

Everything else here is CCE-original by necessity. The workbook prints no bridge, no highway, no water system, and no civil engineering career, so the straw bridge challenge, the DFW infrastructure framing, and the emerging-careers research run on BLS, TxDOT, and the Hats & Ladders app rather than on a workbook page. That gap is named here so no one goes looking for a page that does not exist.

docs.title: IISD Instructional Strategies
docs.text:
• Think-Pair-Share: Day 1, Activity 1, the "Be the Decision Maker" prompt on the chapter opener (FYF p. 103), where a company asks students to design the airplane of the future. Distinguished: pose it to the whole group, hold a silent 30 second Think, then time Partner A for 30 seconds and Partner B for 30 seconds, and post two stems at different levels: "One feature I would add is _ because " and "That feature would improve the trip for __, but it would cost the airline _____." Ask two pairs to share, not one. Listen while pairs talk for who names a tradeoff rather than a wish list, and pick your share-out pairs from what you heard rather than from raised hands.
  • Stop and Jot: Day 2, Activity 3, the "Why is it emerging?" line on the Emerging Engineering Careers template. Distinguished: box it at 90 seconds with the prompt on screen and post two stems at different levels: "A Smart Infrastructure Specialist is an EMERGING career because _. The technology or need that made it grow is " and "This career did not exist 10 years ago because __." Read the lines over shoulders while students write. If most jots say only "new technology," pull the class back for 60 seconds and name the three drivers on the board (aging infrastructure, climate and water, population growth) before students finish the rest of the template.
  • Active Monitoring: Day 4, Activity 1, the three timed build checkpoints. Distinguished: walk a fixed pathway three times, one lap per checkpoint, each lap with a single target (minute 8 base rails spanning 12 inches, minute 15 diagonal members forming visible triangles, minute 22 deck complete and the bridge standing on its own), marking the three-phase clipboard as you go. Have feedback ready before class for the two known build failures: straws taped end to end instead of bundled three or four together, and a deck laid across rails that were never triangulated. If more than a handful of teams miss the minute 15 target, pivot and reproject the truss geometry to the whole room, a triangle holding its shape under load and a square folding into a rhombus, instead of repeating it team by team.
  • Chunking: Day 3, Activity 2, the three bridge types. Distinguished: project one type at a time, say what each one is for before showing it (a beam spans, a truss spreads the load across many small pieces, an arch pushes the weight into the ground), demonstrate the triangle-versus-square load test on the projector inside the truss chunk, and close each type with the same three questions the plan already gives teams: does it fit a 12-inch straw span, what is its key structural element, and where are its triangles. Note which type draws the blankest answers. That type becomes a 2 minute re-teach before Activity 3 sketching starts, and teams who cleared all three chunks start their second sketch early instead of waiting.
  • Time, Voice, Body (TVB): Day 2, Activity 2, the six-station test comparison Gallery Walk. Distinguished: post the three blocks before the first rotation, a visible 2 minute countdown per station, Voice 1 for partner talk at a card and Voice 0 while walking between cards, and a stated rotation direction so pairs do not cross the room. Say where the Impact worksheet travels (in hand, not left on a desk) and which four cards are the priority if time runs short. Narrate the pairs who are meeting the expectation rather than correcting the ones who are not. If the rotation is running long by the third station, announce the cut to four stations before the next rotation rather than after it.
