On sticky notes, students answer the five questions on page 217: what the activity is called, what children do step by step, how they practice balancing, how they practice cutting, and what classroom materials the activity uses.

Step 4: Create Your Activity (12 min)

Students build the activity on chart paper or poster board using the art supplies. The instructions have to be written for a young child, in the order a child would do them.

Step 5: Partner Practice (8 min)

Partners test each other's activity. They take turns acting as the "child" and the "teacher", practice the gross motor balancing movement, and practice the fine motor cutting task. While testing, they check three things from the page: does this actually build the skill, is it fun and easy to follow, and could a young child really do it? Each student then writes at least two ways they would change or improve their activity to make it better for young children.

Time, Voice, Body (TVB): Post the three blocks before any scissors come out. Voice 1 for build talk in Step 4 and Voice 2 in Step 5, where one partner has to give a young child instructions out loud. Run a visible countdown for the build and another for the partner test. Name where scissors, tape, and scrap paper go when a pair finishes, and mark the floor space each pair uses for the balancing test so nobody is balancing next to a table corner. Narrate the pairs meeting the expectation instead of correcting the ones who are not.

Facilitation Tip

The workbook prints no rubric for this activity, so carry a three-checkpoint clipboard instead: both target skills are actually practiced, the steps are written so a young child could follow them, and the materials are things a real classroom has. Checking all three during Step 4 is faster than a written score and it catches the most common miss, an activity that is fun to play but never gets to the cutting task.

DOK 3: A 3-year-old and a 5-year-old both try your activity. Name TWO things you would change for the younger child, and say which target skill each change protects.

docs.title: Activity 2: Community Service Reflection (12 min)
docs.text:
Source: Scope-and-sequence d(4)(E) + the Education and Training cluster's service framing

Connect the activity to community service. Teaching work can happen before someone has the job title: helping a younger sibling with homework, tutoring a friend, mentoring at camp, or volunteering at school all ask someone to spend time on another person's learning.

Distribute the Community Service Reflection handout. Students complete:

  1. List 2-3 community service or volunteer experiences: Include school-based activities (TSA, peer mentoring, helping a teacher), formal volunteering (food bank, church, community event), or informal helping (tutoring a neighbor, helping a younger sibling with reading)
  2. For each experience, identify the SKILL it built:
    • Tutoring → patience + communication
    • Food bank → teamwork + organization
    • Helping at a school event → leadership + planning
    • Helping a younger sibling → empathy + clear explanation
  3. Write 3 sentences: "My community service connects to a career in _ because I built the skill of . This is important to that career because __."

DOK 4: Why might colleges and employers value community service experience as much as grades when evaluating applications? Use one specific skill from your reflection to support your answer.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Ranked Justification) · Printable PDF:

Rank these 4 community service experiences from BUILDS MOST career-relevant skills (1) to BUILDS FEWEST (4) based on today's reflection:

  • Tutoring a younger student: rank ____
  • Volunteering at a food bank: rank ____
  • Helping at a school event (book fair, science night): rank ____
  • Helping a younger sibling with reading: rank ____

For EACH rank, write ONE specific skill that experience builds:

  • Rank 1: Skill = _____

  • Rank 4: Skill = _____

Bottom line: ONE community service experience I HAVE HAD (or plan to do) + ONE specific career skill it built + TODAY'S Teach Through Play theme + the ONE change I would make for a younger child: (d(1)(C), d(4)(E))

My service: ___. Skill: ___

My theme: ___. My change: ___

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide an activity template with a sample structure ("First, children _. Then, . Finally, __.") so students write child-facing steps rather than a description. For the community service reflection, accept hypothetical service if students have limited real experience: "If I volunteered at _, I would build the skill of ___."
  • Extension: Students answer the workbook's Class Discussion questions (p. 217) in writing: how can teachers make learning feel like play, and how do movement skills connect to what children do later in sports, writing, and daily tasks. Then they build a second version of the activity for a child who is not ready to use scissors independently, and name the fine motor task they used instead.
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Activity = Actividad, Balance = Equilibrio, To Cut = Cortar, Volunteer = Voluntario, Community = Comunidad. Gross motor and fine motor are best taught by demonstration: balance on one foot, then cut a line, then name each one. Allow the activity to be designed and explained in Spanish. Bilingual community service reflection template with Spanish sentence stems.

docs.title: Day 5: Irving ISD Pathways + eDynamic 7.2 + Education Favorites
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Read the Irving ISD Education and Training programs of study and map them to campuses and credentials; begin eDynamic Unit 7.2 (Getting the Training You Need); finish the App Exploration page and favorite Education careers in H&L TEKS d(1)(C), d(2)(A), d(2)(B) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: Irving ISD programs of study · Explore: eDynamic 7.2 · Extend: App Exploration wrap-up and Career Plan update · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Irving ISD pathway reflection + eDynamic 7.2 progress + completed App Exploration page with 2-3 Education career favorites Materials Chromebooks, H&L accounts, Find Your Future workbook printed pp. 218-220, Irving ISD CTE Pathways handout, eDynamic Learning access, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Could you see yourself as a teacher? A school counselor? A principal? An instructional designer? Why or why not? Be honest.

Take 4-5 student responses. Some students will say "no way", push them to explain WHY. Others will say "maybe", ask which Education career fits best. This sets up the favorites activity.

docs.title: Activity 1: Irving ISD Education Pathways (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 218-219: "What is Happening at My District?") + Irving ISD CTE Pathways handout

Open the workbook's district pages and the printed pathways handout together. The Program Spotlight is the Irving ISD "I Am Next" pinning ceremony, which celebrates students who are committing to a career in teaching. The same pages carry a student's own line about the program, which is worth projecting: coming to class every day and working with younger students to help them learn something new. Two programs of study serve this cluster.

Education and Training (Irving High School, MacArthur High School, Nimitz High School)

  • Prepares students for careers in teaching and educational leadership by building skills in instruction, communication, and classroom management through coursework and hands-on child development experiences
  • During their junior and senior years, students visit elementary schools daily to work with and support younger students (FYF p. 219)
  • Industry certification named on the district pages: Educational Aide I
  • Student organization: Texas Association of Future Educators (TAFE)
  • Educational Aides work as paid paraprofessionals in classrooms, supporting teachers, working with small groups, and gaining real classroom experience. The credential is a launchpad for a university Education program or for direct employment in a district after high school

Early Childhood Education (Cardwell Career Preparatory Center)

  • A travel-to career center pathway: students split their day between their home campus and Cardwell
  • Prepares students for careers working with young children by building skills in child development, learning activities, health and safety, and classroom support
  • Focuses on Pre-K through age 5, which is exactly the age band students designed for in the Teach Through Play activity
  • Irving ISD's program certifications reference lists the Child Development Associate (CDA) credential for this pathway

[VERIFY with CTE coordinator] The workbook's district pages name Educational Aide I as this cluster's industry certification and name no credential for Early Childhood Education. The Irving ISD program certifications reference lists Child Development Associate for the Cardwell pathway. Confirm the current credential for each program, and confirm which campuses host them, before telling a student where to enroll.

What are endorsements? The district pages close with the question (FYF p. 219). Endorsements are groups of related courses that focus on one area such as business, arts, technology, or public service, and choosing one is how a student goes deeper in a field in high school. Put the page's own discussion question to the class: is it better to choose an endorsement based on current interests, future goals, or both? Students write the full version of that plan in the Capstone, where they name their courses, clubs, and student organizations (FYF pp. 294-296: "Rung 7: High School Plan").

Connection to today's work: Both programs start in 9th grade, so the courses a student picks when registering for high school next year decide whether either one is open to them.

Students complete a brief reflection on the back of the handout: "The Irving ISD education pathway that interests me MORE is _ because . (Or: Neither education pathway interests me because __.)"

docs.title: Activity 2: eDynamic Unit 7.2 — Getting the Training You Need (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: eDynamic Learning Unit 7.2 (scope-and-sequence column 9)

Direct students to log into eDynamic Learning and open Unit 7.2: Getting the Training You Need. This unit covers the different training and education options after high school, university, community college, trade school, military, apprenticeship, and helps students think about which path matches their career goals.

The unit is a great complement to today's Irving ISD pathway discussion because it zooms out from "Irving ISD specifically" to "what are ALL the ways to get teacher training in America."

Students work at their own pace through the eDynamic module. They will likely not finish today, that is fine. The unit continues into the next class.

[VERIFY IN eDynamic] Confirm which specific activities and quizzes are in Unit 7.2 and how teachers can monitor student progress through the eDynamic dashboard.

Facilitation Tip

Use the eDynamic dashboard to spot students who blow through the unit without engaging. They should not finish in 5 minutes. If a student claims to be done, ask them to summarize one training option from the unit before logging it as complete.

docs.title: Activity 3: Education Favorites + App Exploration Wrap-Up (12 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 220: "App Exploration")

Students finish the App Exploration page they started on Day 1 and close out the cluster in the app. Three tasks:

  1. Finish the App Exploration page: the Pathway Possibilities step and the cluster jot. The page ends with a space for their thoughts on the cluster in emojis, pictures, or words.
  2. Favorite at least 2-3 Education & Training careers using the Hat Finder. These save to the Climber Profile.
  3. Update Building Blocks: Add tutoring, mentoring, peer help, or any community service. The H&L app uses Building Blocks to refine career recommendations. If a student has tutored a younger sibling, that is a Building Block.

[H&L PLATFORM] Students return to the Education and Training Cluster in the Hats & Ladders app and finish the App Exploration page (FYF p. 220): click "Pathway Possibilities," answer the questions there, then explore and rate at least 1 pathway, and jot their thoughts on the cluster in the space the page provides. In the Hat Finder they click the heart icon on 2-3 Education and Training Hats and open "Climber Profile" to confirm the favorites appear there. Last, they open the Career and Course Plan in the app and add the Education cluster next to the clusters they explored earlier in the year. The plan is cumulative, so they add to it rather than starting over.

Name where this goes next. The Hats favorited today join the set students review in the Capstone, where they read back their own profile of top Hats, pathways, Building Blocks, and Powerskills before choosing a career goal (FYF pp. 281-282: "Rung 1: Who You Are").

Students should now have favorites spanning every cluster explored this year (Manufacturing, IT, Law, Health Science, Ag, Hospitality, Human Services, Business, A&C, Engineering, Transportation, and now Education).

DOK 2: Look at your Career Plan as it stands today. Is Education one of your top 3 clusters? Why or why not?

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Concept Map / Connection Diagram) · Printable PDF:

The Education career I favorited this week: _____

Connect this career to THREE things:

1. An Irving ISD pathway (Education and Training at Irving High / MacArthur / Nimitz → Educational Aide I, OR Early Childhood Education at Cardwell → Child Development Associate)

My pathway: _____. Does it lead DIRECTLY to my career or is it a STEPPING STONE? Circle: DIRECT / STEPPING STONE. One sentence why:

2. My Day 4 Community Service reflection — a real experience I have had

My experience: _____. In one sentence, how does this experience prepare me for my favorited education career?

3. My Day 2 leader strength (calm under pressure / quick decision maker / extremely organized / creative thinker)

My strength: _____. In one sentence, how would this strength show up in my favorited career DAILY?

(d(1)(C), d(2)(A))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Pair students who struggle with Career Plan navigation. Provide a printed "Education Hat" cheat sheet listing 6 education careers and their typical salaries so students can pick favorites without getting lost in the app.
  • Extension: Students research the Educational Aide I certification process specifically, what is the pay, what are the duties, can you stay an Educational Aide forever, or is it usually a stepping stone? They write a 1-paragraph career profile.
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Pathway = Camino, Certification = Certificación, Aide = Asistente, Early Childhood = Primera infancia, Endorsement = Especialización. Pair with bilingual peers for the Career Plan navigation. The Cardwell early childhood pathway is especially relevant for bilingual ESL students because Texas has a major shortage of bilingual early childhood teachers.

docs.title: Week 1: Teaching Tomorrow — Education & Training Careers
docs.text: 6th Six Weeks | Education & Training Cluster | 5 class periods (50 min each)

docs.title: Lesson Objective
docs.text:
Students explore the Education and Training career cluster through the Hats & Ladders app and the Find Your Future workbook, design a learning space and a persuasive poster in the "Community Classroom" activity, compare traditional and alternative certification pathways for Texas teachers, rank four leaders against workplace situations in the "Powerskill: Leadership" lesson, read real local job postings to see what employers ask for, and design an early childhood play activity that builds gross and fine motor skills in "Teach Through Play." Students connect the cluster to Irving ISD's Education and Training and Early Childhood Education programs of study.

Learning Target: I can name at least three Education and Training careers, tell what training each one needs, design a learning space and a play activity that meet stated goals, and read a real job posting to say what an employer wants.

Success Criteria: I will know I am successful when my Community Classroom poster explains the space, persuades a teacher to book it, and names the learning goals it meets, when my Pathway Comparison worksheet has every cell filled for both certification routes, when my two job posting records list the responsibilities and the education each employer asks for, and when my Teach Through Play activity gets a partner to balance on one foot for 5 seconds and cut along a straight line.

docs.title: Demonstration of Learning
docs.text: "I can describe at least three Education & Training careers, explain the difference between a traditional teaching degree and alternative certification, design a learning space and an early childhood play activity, and name two leader strengths that would make me a great educator."

docs.title: TEKS Alignment
docs.text:
• d(1)(B): Explore and describe the CTE career clusters (Day 1).
  • d(1)(C): Identify various career opportunities within the Education & Training cluster (Days 1-5).
  • d(2)(A): Research and describe applicable academic, certification, and training requirements (Days 2, 3, 5).
  • d(2)(B): Use available resources to evaluate educational and training options (Days 2, 5).
  • d(4)(E): Explain the value of community service and volunteerism (Day 4).

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Chromebooks with internet access (1 per student)
  • Hats & Ladders accounts + Find Your Future workbook, Education and Training chapter (printed pp. 213-220)
  • Find Your Future workbook, Powerskill: Leadership (printed pp. 17-20) for Day 2
  • Find Your Future workbook, Rung 5: Local Connections (printed pp. 290-291) for Day 3, read but not filled in
  • Sticky notes for Day 1 and Day 4 brainstorming (FYF p. 215, FYF p. 217)
  • Chart paper or poster board plus art supplies (paper, markers, scissors, tape) for Day 4 (FYF p. 217: "Teach Through Play")
  • Printed Community Classroom poster template
  • Printed Education Pathway Comparison worksheet
  • Printed career research worksheet (CCE artifact; the research format is taught in Wk0)
  • Printed practice Job Posting handout, 2 per student, for Day 3
  • Printed Community Service Reflection handout
  • Teach.org: teach.org
  • TEA Educator Certification: tea.texas.gov/texas-educators/certification
  • BLS, High School Teachers: bls.gov/ooh/education-training-and-library/high-school-teachers.htm
  • Irving ISD careers page and one job search site for the Day 3 postings
  • eDynamic Learning Unit 7.2: Getting the Training You Need
  • Xello student accounts (Discover Learning Pathways lesson)
  • Projector for modeling

docs.title: Career Connection
docs.text:
Texas has two main pathways into teaching: a four-year Education degree with student teaching, or a bachelor's degree in another subject followed by an alternative-certification program such as iTeach or Texas Teachers. Both lead to the same TEA teaching certificate. Students compare the time and cost of those routes, then connect teaching to d(4)(E) through tutoring, mentoring, and other community-service work they may already have done.

What is Happening at Irving ISD? The workbook's district pages (FYF pp. 218-219: "What is Happening at My District?") open with the "I Am Next" pinning ceremony, which celebrates students committing to a career in teaching, and they name two programs of study. Education and Training builds foundational skills in instruction, communication, and classroom management, and during their junior and senior years its students visit elementary schools daily to work with and support younger students. It is offered at Irving High School, MacArthur High School, and Nimitz High School, a multi-campus pathway students can pursue regardless of their home school. Early Childhood Education builds skills in child development, learning activities, health and safety, and classroom support, and it is offered at Cardwell Career Preparatory Center as a travel-to career center pathway. The same pages name Educational Aide I as the cluster's industry certification and the Texas Association of Future Educators (TAFE) as its student organization, and they close by asking students whether an endorsement should be chosen for current interests, future goals, or both. Day 5 carries a [VERIFY with CTE coordinator] note on the Early Childhood credential, which the workbook's district pages do not name.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text:
• Alternative Certification: A pathway to becoming a teacher without a traditional Education degree. Requires a bachelor's degree in any field plus completion of an approved certification program.
  • Student Teaching: A semester-long supervised classroom experience required as part of a traditional Education degree.
  • Community Service: Unpaid work done to benefit the community. Community service builds career skills like leadership, communication, and empathy.
  • Educational Aide: A paraprofessional who assists teachers in the classroom. Irving ISD's Education and Training program of study names Educational Aide I as its industry certification.
  • TEA: Texas Education Agency, the state organization that oversees public education and teacher certification in Texas.
  • Instructional Designer: A professional who designs curriculum, courses, and learning experiences (often for online or corporate training).
  • Gross Motor Skills: Big movements like balancing, jumping, and running. They build strength and coordination, and early childhood teachers plan play that practices them.
  • Fine Motor Skills: Small hand and finger movements like cutting and drawing. They build the control a child needs for writing.
  • Endorsement: A group of related high school courses focused on one area such as business, arts, technology, or public service.

docs.title: Bridge to Theory (Hats & Ladders)
docs.text:
The Find Your Future workbook gives Education and Training printed pages 213-220, the thinnest cluster chapter in the book. The opener (FYF p. 213: "Exploring the World of EDUCATION AND TRAINING") frames the cluster as helping people learn, grow, and build skills for the future, in classrooms and workplaces both. It puts a "Be the Decision Maker" prompt in front of students, who are in charge of curriculum at a school and must invent a brand new class every middle schooler has to take, and it prints three Hats on the page: Curator, Early Childhood Teacher, and Middle School Teacher. The chapter prints no pathway list. Students meet the cluster's pathways in the Hats & Ladders app instead, through the Pathway Possibilities step on the App Exploration page (FYF p. 220), and they meet Irving ISD's own programs of study on the district pages (FYF pp. 218-219).

Two chapter activities carry this week:

  • Community Classroom (Day 1): Career Climb activity. Students are in charge of curriculum at a school and design an exciting new learning space for third-grade science. They learn the requirements, brainstorm with a partner on sticky notes, build a poster that explains the concept and persuades teachers to book the space, and present it to a second pair playing third-grade teachers (FYF pp. 214-215: "Community Classroom").
  • Teach Through Play (Day 4): Career Climb activity. Students step into an early childhood teacher's role and design a themed play activity that gets young children to balance on one foot for 5 seconds and cut along a straight line. They build it on chart paper, test it with a partner taking turns as child and teacher, and write two improvements (FYF pp. 216-217: "Teach Through Play").

Two activities cannot carry five days, so the week borrows from two other chapters. Powerskill: Leadership (FYF pp. 17-20) sits in the World of Work chapter. Students meet four leaders with named strengths and challenges, rank them best fit to worst fit against workplace situations, and defend each ranking with evidence from the profiles. It runs on Day 2. Rung 5: Local Connections (FYF pp. 290-291) belongs to the Capstone. Students search real local job postings and record the responsibilities, skills, qualifications, and education each employer asks for. They practice it on Day 3 inside the Education cluster on a practice handout, and the graded rung pages are completed later this six weeks in the job-skills week, so the workbook pages stay blank. The rest of the week runs on the Hats & Ladders app, Xello, eDynamic, and CCE-authored worksheets.

docs.title: IISD Instructional Strategies
docs.text:
• Think-Pair-Share: Day 1, Activity 1, the "Be the Decision Maker" prompt on the chapter opener (FYF p. 213), where students invent a brand new class every middle schooler must take. Distinguished: pose it to the whole group, hold a silent 30 second Think, then time Partner A for 30 seconds and Partner B for 30 seconds, and post two stems at different levels: "My class is called _ and students would learn " and "Middle schoolers need this class because __, so the teacher would have to be good at _____." Ask two pairs to share, not one. While pairs talk, listen for who gets past naming the class to naming what its teacher would have to be able to do, and pick your share-out pairs from what you heard rather than from raised hands.
  • Stop and Jot: Day 1, Activity 1, the two pauses during the Education and Training cluster tour video. Distinguished: name both stop points before the video starts, give 45 seconds per jot with the prompt on screen, and offer two stems: "One education career I did not know existed is _" and "One thing I still want to know about is __." Read jots over shoulders during both pauses and track which careers students name. If nearly every jot says Teacher, steer the Hat browse that follows toward Curator, Instructional Designer, School Counselor, and Corporate Trainer so Day 2's career research worksheets are not all the same career.
  • Active Monitoring: Day 3, Activity 2, the search for two local job postings. Distinguished: walk a fixed pathway three times with one target per lap, lap 1 that a real current local posting is open rather than a career article, lap 2 that the responsibilities are copied from the posting's own list, lap 3 that the education and experience fields are filled in even when the posting buries them. Have the feedback ready before class for the two known errors: a job board career profile recorded instead of an actual opening, and "college degree" written where the posting says a diploma plus 48 college credit hours. If more than a handful of students miss the lap 1 target, pivot and reproject the search string and the district careers page to the whole room instead of fixing it screen by screen.
  • Chunking: Day 2, Activity 1, the two certification pathways, and Day 3, Activity 1, the four job posting field groups. Distinguished: teach one pathway and one field group at a time, say what each chunk is for before walking it, and close each chunk with a check a student can visibly fail, restating what the traditional route costs in time on Day 2 and pointing to the answer on the projected posting on Day 3. Whichever chunk students cannot restate is the one to reproject before independent work starts, and students who clear all four posting chunks early begin their first search instead of waiting.
  • Time, Voice, Body (TVB): Day 4, Activity 1, the Teach Through Play build and partner test. Distinguished: post the three blocks before any scissors come out, Voice 1 for build talk in Step 4 and Voice 2 in Step 5 where one partner gives a young child instructions out loud, a visible countdown for the build and another for the partner test, a named place where scissors, tape, and scrap paper go when a pair finishes, and a marked floor space for each pair's balancing test. Narrate the pairs meeting the expectation rather than correcting the ones who are not. If a pair is losing test time to hunting for supplies, move that pair's materials to the table before the next countdown starts.

docs.title: Week at a Glance
docs.text: Day Focus Key Activities Deliverable 5E 1 Education Cluster + Community Classroom Chapter opener and Be the Decision Maker + App Exploration + Community Classroom space and poster Learning space design + persuasive poster Engage · Explore · Explain · Evaluate 2 Certification Pathways + Leadership Traditional vs. alt-cert comparison + career research worksheet + Powerskill: Leadership rankings Pathway Comparison worksheet + career research worksheet + leader rankings Engage · Explain · Explore · Extend · Evaluate 3 Local Connections Reading one posting together + search for two local education job postings + Xello Discover Learning Pathways Two practice Job Posting records Engage · Explain · Explore · Extend · Evaluate 4 Teach Through Play + Community Service Early childhood play activity design and partner test + community service reflection Teach Through Play activity + service reflection Engage · Explore · Explain · Extend · Evaluate 5 Irving ISD Pathways + eDynamic 7.2 Irving ISD programs of study + eDynamic Unit 7.2 + App Exploration wrap-up and favorites Pathway reflection + eDynamic progress + 2-3 favorites Engage · Explain · Explore · Extend · Evaluate

docs.title: Formative Assessment
docs.text:
• Day 1: Community Classroom design and poster, presented to a second pair, + Mini-Case exit ticket. d(1)(B), d(1)(C)
  • Day 2: Pathway Comparison worksheet + career research worksheet + leader rankings with written defenses + Comparison Matrix exit ticket. d(2)(A), d(2)(B)
  • Day 3: Two practice Job Posting records + Short Constructed Response exit ticket. d(1)(C), d(2)(A)
  • Day 4: Teach Through Play activity, partner test, and two written improvements + community service reflection + Ranked Justification exit ticket. d(1)(C), d(4)(E)
  • Day 5: Completed App Exploration page + Irving ISD pathway reflection + Concept Map exit ticket. d(1)(C), d(2)(A), d(2)(B)

docs.title: Summative Assessment
docs.text: Education Career Portfolio (Day 5): Students submit (1) Community Classroom design + poster, (2) Pathway Comparison worksheet + career research worksheet, (3) two Job Posting records, (4) Teach Through Play activity with its two written improvements, and (5) one-paragraph reflection on whether teaching fits their career interests. Scored on education career knowledge (d(1)(B), d(1)(C)), pathway and posting research accuracy (d(2)(A), d(2)(B)), and community service connection (d(4)(E)).

docs.title: Scaffolded Learning
docs.text:
• Provide sentence starters for the Community Classroom poster: "My space is a _. Teachers should sign up because . Students will get to __."
  • Offer a simplified Pathway Comparison with one row pre-filled as an example.
  • Provide a printed list of Education hats so students who struggle to navigate the app still get exposure.
  • Provide one completed Job Posting record as a model before students search on Day 3.
  • Allow students to describe hypothetical community service if they have limited real experience.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
• Students research the Texas teacher shortage in a specific subject (math, science, special ed, bilingual) and propose how alternative certification could help.
  • Interview a teacher at your school about their pathway and present findings.
  • Compare Texas teacher salaries to three other states and analyze whether pay affects teacher supply.
  • Run the workbook's Leadership Twist (FYF p. 20): write a new challenge situation, trade it with another group, and rank the leaders for the situation you receive.

docs.title: ELL Language Support
docs.text:
• Pre-teach: Education = Educación, Certification = Certificación, Community Service = Servicio comunitario, Volunteer = Voluntario, Learning Space = Espacio de aprendizaje, Balance = Equilibrio
  • Bilingual Community Classroom poster template with Spanish sentence stems
  • Pair ESL students with bilingual peers during pathway comparison research
  • Education careers have strong visual context for ESL students, they interact with teachers daily. The workbook reads well above grade level, so read the scenario paragraphs aloud and encourage browser translation for any independent reading.

docs.title: Day 1: Arts/AV Cluster + Behind the Microphone
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Explore the Arts, Audio/Visual Technology and Communications cluster in the Hats & Ladders app; identify careers and pathways inside the cluster; plan and outline a podcast episode in "Behind the Microphone" TEKS d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up and Be the Decision Maker · Explore: Cluster app exploration and podcast planning · Explain: Episode outline pitch · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Podcast episode outline on chart paper (group of 3-4 students) Materials Chromebooks, H&L accounts, Find Your Future workbook pp. 255, 270-271, 276, chart paper, sticky notes, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Open your phone's camera roll (or just think about it). Who took most of the photos and videos on there? You are already creating visual content. Could that become a career?

Take 3-4 responses. Most students will say "me." Ask who made the images they were looking at. Movies, ads, social posts, and video games all depend on people whose job is visual communication.

docs.title: Activity 1: H&L Arts, A/V Technology, and Communications Cluster Tour (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 255: "Exploring the World of ARTS, AUDIO/VISUAL TECHNOLOGY AND COMMUNICATIONS") + (FYF p. 276: "App Exploration")

Open by framing this as the second-to-last six weeks block, but the FIRST week of intense job-readiness work (resumes start on Day 2). Today is the creative-careers warm-up.

Read the chapter opener together. This cluster is about creating the things people watch, hear, and share every day, and the work splits three ways: some careers shape how something sounds, some shape how it looks, and some shape how it makes people feel. The opener page puts three Hats in front of students right away: Photographer, Audio Engineer, and AV Technician.

Think-Pair-Share: Pose the opener's "Be the Decision Maker" scenario (FYF p. 255): "You are creating all the sound design for a major animated movie using only everyday household objects. Do you try to make things sound realistic or go completely weird and unexpected? Do you start with the biggest most important scenes or work through it beginning to end?" Hold a silent 30 second Think, then Partner A for 30 seconds and Partner B for 30 seconds. Two pairs share out.

Then direct students into the app.

[H&L PLATFORM] (FYF p. 276: "App Exploration") Open the Hats & Ladders app and go to Clusters. Click on the Arts, Audio/Visual Technology and Communications Cluster. Watch the "Cluster Tour" video, click "Game Time" and play the game, find 1 Hat that matches your interests and 1 Hat that does not, open "Pathway Possibilities" and rate at least 1 pathway, then rate at least 3 Hats.

Hats worth steering students toward while they browse: Graphic Designer, Animator, Video Editor, UX Designer, Photographer, Social Media Manager, Sound Engineer, Art Director. Irving ISD's own programs in this cluster, Digital Communications and Graphic Design & Illustration, appear on the district pages students meet on Day 5 (FYF pp. 274-275).

Stop and Jot: Pause the cluster tour twice, 45 seconds each. Prompt 1: one Arts/AV career that surprised you. Prompt 2: one question you still have about this cluster.

Facilitation Tip

Students often think "art = poor career." Push back with concrete data: UX Designer median salary is $85K+ in DFW. Animation lead at game studios can clear $100K. Show them the BLS page for Graphic Designers ($57K median nationally, higher in DFW) to anchor expectations.

docs.title: Activity 2: Behind the Microphone (25 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 270-271: "Behind the Microphone"), a Career Climb activity

Introduce the activity using the workbook framing: "Did you know that podcasting can mean huge business in today's world? There are some people who make podcasts just for fun while there are others who make podcasts as their full-time job and get paid to do it! Popular podcasts can make thousands, even millions, of dollars through ads, sponsorships, and subscriptions."

Today students plan their own podcast in groups of 3-4. They will not record, that is an extension. Today is about the creative planning process that podcast producers use.

Step 1: Brainstorm Ideas (4 min)

Groups of 3-4 brainstorm on sticky notes and settle the workbook's three questions (p. 270):

  • What is your podcast going to be about? (Sports, music, gaming, movies, true crime, school life, etc.)
  • Who is your target audience? (Kids, teens, adults, gamers, parents, etc.)
  • What makes your podcast stand out? Why would people want to listen?

Step 2: Plan an Episode (6 min)

Using the workbook table (p. 270), the group settles the key details of ONE specific episode:

  • Podcast Name: A catchy name for the show
  • Episode Title: What is this episode about?
  • Episode Length: How long will the episode run?
  • Hosts & Guests: Who is talking? One host, two, a group, a special guest?
  • Key Topics: Three main points, stories, or questions the episode will cover
  • Promotion Plan: How will people find out about the podcast? Social media, ads, something else?

Step 3: Create an Episode Outline (12 min)

Groups write their outline on chart paper and work the workbook checklist (p. 271) item by item:

  • Introduction: Welcome listeners, introduce host and guest
  • Main Topic: Provide an overview of what this episode is focused on
  • Engaging Material: Background information so listeners can follow along + interesting details that keep them engaged
  • Interview Questions: At least 3 engaging questions to ask the guest
  • Closing: Tie the episode together, thank listeners and guests, give a sneak peek of a new episode coming soon

Step 4: Podcast Pitch (3 min)

Each group pairs with another group and pitches: what the podcast is, how the episode is laid out, who the hosts are, and why someone would listen to this show instead of the thousands of others available. The listening group owes the presenters one thing they loved and one thing they would like to see improved.

Facilitation Tip

The workbook checklist IS the rubric. Walk around during work time with the checklist visible. Ask each group "Show me your three interview questions." If they only have one, redirect them. The checklist makes accountability visible.

DOK 2: How would you compare the work a podcast host does to the work a graphic designer does? Both are Arts/AV careers, what skills do they share? What skills are different?

DELIVERABLE: Podcast episode outline on chart paper (one per group of 3-4), photographed and submitted to Google Classroom or kept in the class binder.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Mini-Case / Scenario Application) · Printable PDF:

Scenario: A new DFW middle school wants to launch a podcast for 7th graders to learn about local careers. They have budget for ONE creative hire.

  1. Which Arts/AV career (Podcast Host / Sound Engineer / Social Media Manager / Video Editor / Graphic Designer / Writer) is the MOST CRITICAL first hire, and why?

My pick: _____

Why: ____________

  1. Classify TWO Arts/AV careers I explored today as (circle one per): solo work / team work / client-facing

Career 1: _____. Work style: solo / team / client-facing

Career 2: _____. Work style: solo / team / client-facing

  1. My core personality type from Wk0: _____. Which work style above fits that type best, and why?
  1. My team's podcast TITLE: ___. Target AUDIENCE: ___

(d(1)(C))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a podcast outline template with sample interview questions ("What inspired you to _?", "What is your favorite ?", "What advice would you give __?"). Allow students to use a podcast they already love as the basis for their planning rather than inventing from scratch.
  • Extension (from workbook): The workbook's own "Extra Time?" box (FYF p. 271) sends early finishers to RECORD their podcast episode, using a Chromebook microphone and free recording software (Audacity, Vocaroo, or Google Recorder).
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Podcast = Pódcast, Episode = Episodio, Audience = Audiencia, Host = Anfitrión, Interview = Entrevista. Students may plan the podcast in Spanish or make it bilingual, matching formats they can find in DFW media.

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Understand resume sections and purpose; complete a first-draft resume in Xello including header, career objective, education, skills, activities, and community service TEKS d(7)(A) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: Teacher resume modeling · Explore: Xello Resume Builder draft · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Draft resume (v1) saved in Xello Resume Builder Materials Chromebooks, Xello accounts, printed Resume Template (backup), CareerOneStop Resume Guide, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: If someone asked you to list every skill, every activity, every accomplishment, every responsibility, and every community service you have ever done, how long would the list be? Try it. Just write the list.

Give students 3 minutes to write. Most students will think they have nothing, then surprise themselves at how long the list gets when they actually try. This is the opening hook for "you have more resume content than you think."

docs.title: Activity 1: Teacher Resume Modeling (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: Xello Resume Builder + CareerOneStop Resume Guide

Open Xello and project the Resume Builder on the board. Walk through a sample middle school resume LIVE, building it as students watch. Use a fictional student: "Alex Martinez, 8th Grade, Oakview Middle School" (or substitute your own school name).

Chunking: Build one section at a time, say what the section is for before you fill it, and take a thumbs check after each one before moving to the next. Whichever section draws the most thumbs down is the section you revisit first while circulating in Activity 2.

Walk through each section:

Header (1 min): Name, address (city + state OK, no street for safety), phone, email, school. Make it look professional. No emojis. No nicknames.

Career Objective (3 min): One or two sentences about what the student wants. Show several samples:

  • "To explore a career in graphic design and contribute creative skills to a school yearbook or design club."
  • "To gain experience working with younger children through a tutoring or summer camp role."
  • "Seeking a part-time role using my customer service and communication skills."

Education (2 min): Current school, grade, expected graduation year. Honor roll, GPA (if strong), perfect attendance, anything that shows academic engagement.

Skills (3 min): Push students hard here. Skills include:

  • Technology: Google Workspace, Canva, basic coding (Scratch, Python intro), TinkerCAD, Adobe Express, Microsoft Office
  • Languages: English, Spanish, ASL, etc. (Bilingual = HUGE on a resume)
  • Soft skills: Communication, teamwork, time management, problem-solving, leadership

Activities & Awards (2 min): TSA, athletics, band, choir, theater, robotics, student council, honor roll, perfect attendance, science fair winner, art show, math team

Community Service (2 min): Tutoring, peer mentoring, food bank, church/temple/mosque service, family caregiver responsibilities, helping at school events

References (2 min): Skip this section on a middle school resume OR write "Available upon request"

The key teaching moment is to keep showing students that their lives ARE resume material. Tutoring a younger sibling = childcare experience. Helping at a church festival = event setup + customer service. Babysitting = responsibility + time management.

Facilitation Tip

During modeling, deliberately add something a student would think doesn't count ("helping my grandma with her phone"), then label it: "This shows patience, communication, and tech skills." Repeating this 3-4 times unlocks students' thinking about their own experiences.

docs.title: Activity 2: Xello Resume Builder (28 min)
docs.text:
Source: Xello Resume Builder, used as supplemental Grade 8 instruction. Resume is not a Bowie Grade 8 completion standard.

Direct students to log into Xello and open the Resume Builder feature. Xello walks them through each section step-by-step with prompts for what to include.

Students work independently. Active Monitoring: walk the room three times, one target per lap, and carry the three jobs below as the lap targets. If a lap turns up more than a handful of blank Skills sections, pivot and reproject the Skills list to the whole room instead of prompting student by student.

  1. Help students who claim they have nothing: Pull out their actual life: babysitting, tutoring, sports, helping family, school clubs. Push them to write SOMETHING in every section.
  2. Check skills sections: Most students undersell their tech skills. Ask "Have you used Canva? Google Slides? TinkerCAD? Scratch? Photoshop?" If yes, it goes on the resume.
  3. Check career objective quality: Vague objectives ("I want a job") get sent back. Specific objectives ("I want a part-time job working with animals or in a daycare") stay.

Goal for Day 2: Every student leaves with a complete first-draft resume saved in Xello, even if it is rough. Day 3 is for revision and refinement.

Facilitation Tip

Set a visible 5-minute warning before the end of class. Students MUST save their draft in Xello before logging off. The system saves automatically but only if they have entered something in each section.

DOK 2: How would you describe the purpose of a resume? Who reads it and what are they looking for in 10 seconds of skimming?

DELIVERABLE: Resume draft v1 saved in Xello Resume Builder. Visible on the Xello dashboard for the teacher to confirm completion.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (2 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Comparison Matrix) · Printable PDF:

For each of the 6 resume sections, mark whether I filled it in with SPECIFIC content (1 SPECIFIC item) or if it needs more work.

Section Filled with SPECIFIC content (check YES / NO) One SPECIFIC item I added (or note "still blank") Header (name/school/contact) Career Objective Education Skills Activities & Awards Community Service

Bottom line: The section that was HARDEST to fill in: _____. In one sentence, why was it hardest?

(d(7)(A))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide the printed Resume Template as a fallback for students struggling with Xello. Allow them to fill it out by hand and type it into Xello later. Provide a list of 20 sample skills (technology, language, soft skills) so students can pick from a menu instead of generating from scratch.
  • Extension: Students who finish early use CareerOneStop Resume Guide to learn about action verbs ("organized," "led," "created," "designed") and rewrite their bullet points using stronger language.
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Resume = Currículum, Education = Educación, Skills = Habilidades, Experience = Experiencia, Activities = Actividades, References = Referencias. Bilingual middle schoolers should ALWAYS list Spanish (or other home language) as a skill, bilingual is one of the most marketable skills in DFW. Pair ESL students with bilingual peers if needed.

docs.title: Day 3: Attention to Detail + Resume Revision
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Practice attention to detail by rewriting an incomplete audio cue script; refine resume through peer review using Two Stars and a Wish TEKS d(7)(A), d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Audio cue script fix · Explain: Resume peer review · Extend: Resume revision · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Revised resume v2 in Xello + rewritten audio cue script with the missing details added Materials Chromebooks, Xello accounts, Find Your Future workbook pp. 272-273, printed peer review form

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: If you were hiring someone for your dream job, what TWO things would you look for first when you read their resume?

Take 4-5 responses. Then put the same problems into a resume: a typo in the phone number, a missing activity, or a claim so vague it tells the employer nothing. Today's Powerskill activity is practice finding those gaps before the resume is sent.

docs.title: Activity 1: Powerskill — Attention to Detail (20 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 272-273: "Powerskill: Attention to Detail")

Introduce the activity using the workbook framing: "Attention to detail means noticing small things, making sure everything is correct, and including important details from the start. It helps you catch mistakes before they happen and ensures your work is complete and accurate."

The workbook scenario: students are the lead sound designer for a short movie called "Kitchen Mess!" The video is finished and it is time to add the sound effects, but the Audio Cue Script, the list that tells the sound team what to find or record, is missing most of what the team needs.

Step 1: Review the Audio Cue Script (5 min)

Students read the script on p. 272. Chef Tony runs into a kitchen carrying a large mixing bowl [AUDIO CUE: Running sound]. He trips and drops the bowl on the floor [AUDIO CUE: Drop sound]. Flour goes flying. A cat jumps onto the counter and knocks over the sugar [AUDIO CUE: Animal noise]. Tony yells at the cat, and the scene closes [AUDIO CUE: Background music starts].

Four cues, and not one of them tells the sound team what to actually record.

Step 2: Identify the Missing Details (5 min)

Students list what is missing, using the workbook's three prompts (p. 273):

  • Materials: what are things made of? A heavy metal object sounds nothing like a feather when it hits the ground.
  • Environment: what are the surfaces? What kind of floor is Tony running on?
  • Mood: how should the background music make the audience feel?

Students work individually or in pairs and write 4-6 missing details.

Step 3: Rewrite the Audio Cues (10 min)

Students rewrite all four cues so the sound team knows exactly what to record. Each rewritten cue names the material, the surface, and the feeling it should create, and it is specific enough that another person could produce the sound without asking a follow-up question.

Facilitation Tip

Rewrite the first cue live on the board before students start. "[AUDIO CUE: Running sound]" becomes "[AUDIO CUE: fast footsteps in rubber kitchen clogs on wet tile, about six steps, getting closer and slightly panicked]". The shift from vague to specific is the whole skill, and students will copy the format once they see it once.

DOK 2: What could happen to the movie if the sound team just guessed at the sounds instead of asking for details? How would that change the movie for the audience?

Connection to resumes: This same skill applies to the resume work students are doing this week. A resume that says "good with computers" is the cue that says "Drop sound." A resume that says "Used Canva and Adobe Express to design 5 school posters" is the cue that names the bowl, the tile, and the flour. Specific = stronger.

docs.title: Activity 2: Resume Peer Review (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: Xello Resume Builder + Two Stars and a Wish strategy

Pair students up. They trade Chromebooks (or pull each other's resume up on Xello). Each student reads their partner's resume like an employer would and writes feedback using the Two Stars and a Wish format:

Two Stars (specific strengths):

  • "Your skills section is strong because you listed specific software (Canva, Google Slides) instead of just 'computers.'"
  • "Your career objective is clear and specific."

One Wish (specific improvement):

  • "Your activities section is empty. I know you do TSA. Add it!"
  • "Your career objective says 'I want a job.' Make it specific to a type of job."

The teacher distributes a printed peer review form OR students write feedback directly on a sticky note. Specific feedback only, vague comments ("looks good") are sent back.

Facilitation Tip

Walk around with one question: "Show me ONE specific change your partner suggested that you actually made." Hold students accountable to acting on the feedback, not just receiving it.

docs.title: Activity 3: Resume Revision (8 min)
docs.text:
Students apply the peer feedback to their Xello resume. They strengthen weak sections, add missing items, and fix any vague language.

Goal: Every student leaves Day 3 with a noticeably stronger resume than when they walked in.

DOK 3: What is the connection between the audio cue rewrite and your resume revision today? Both required you to look for what was MISSING and add specifics. Why does this skill matter for any job?

DELIVERABLE: Revised resume v2 saved in Xello + rewritten audio cue script (in the workbook or digital).

docs.title: Exit Ticket (2 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Short Constructed Response) · Printable PDF:

  1. ONE specific change I made to my resume based on PEER FEEDBACK:

Change: ___________

  1. ONE missing detail I added to the AUDIO CUE SCRIPT:

Missing detail: _____________

  1. In one sentence, what do the resume revision AND the audio cue rewrite have IN COMMON as skills?
  1. ONE specific action verb (organized / led / created / designed / managed) I now use on my resume where I previously used vague language:

(d(7)(A))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a "Resume Revision Checklist", 5 yes/no questions ("Is your career objective specific? Did you list at least 3 skills? Did you list at least 2 activities? Did you list any community service? Did you spell-check?"). Students self-check before peer review.
  • Extension (from workbook): The workbook's "Extra Time?" box (FYF p. 273) pairs early finishers up. One partner reads the revised audio cue script aloud and the other tries to produce each sound effect using only their voice or objects in the room. Cues that cannot be reproduced still need more detail.
  • ELL: The audio cue rewrite is strong ELL practice, it explicitly trains students to add concrete nouns and adjectives. Pair ESL students with bilingual peers for the resume peer review. Allow the rewritten cues to be in Spanish or bilingual.

docs.title: Day 4: Game On! + Job Search Steps
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Create a Game Design Document (GDD) in a studio team with named roles; pitch the game to another team; identify the steps of an effective job search; begin eDynamic Unit 8.2 TEKS d(1)(C), d(6)(A) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Game Design Document build · Explain: Team pitches and feedback · Extend: Job search steps and eDynamic 8.2 · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Group Game Design Document + team pitch + 4-step job search notes Materials Chromebooks, Find Your Future workbook pp. 268-269, eDynamic Learning Unit 8.2 access, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Name your favorite video game. Now name FOUR different careers it took to make that game (think beyond "the programmer").

Take 3-4 responses. Most students will name only "designer" or "coder." List the roles they missed, then explain that today's studio team divides the work among specific jobs.

docs.title: Activity 1: Game On! (25 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 268-269: "Game On!"), a Career Climb activity

Introduce the activity using the workbook framing: "What do you think it takes to create a video game? The video game industry includes some of the fastest-growing careers in the world! In this career field, you can create new worlds, tell fantastic stories, and design otherworldly experiences. From game designers and programmers to artists, writers, and marketers, there are many different roles to choose from."

Today students work in teams of 3-5 to create a Game Design Document (GDD). A GDD is a detailed guide that game studios use to keep track of the theme, style, and core features of a game, and its whole purpose is to communicate the project to someone who was not in the room.

Step 1: Build Your Team (3 min)

Form groups of 3-5 and create a team name. Each student picks ONE role from the workbook list (p. 268) and writes their initials next to it. If the group is small, some students carry two roles:

  • Game Designer: Plans how the game will work and creates the rules
  • Artist: Designs the characters, environments, and objects in the game
  • Writer: Creates the story, dialogue, and quests
  • Sound Designer: Develops the music and sound effects

The workbook's opening paragraph also names programmers and marketers as game-industry careers, but the role list students choose from is these four. Teams that want a fifth role can add Programmer and give that student the job of keeping the team honest about what is actually buildable.

Step 2: Design Your Video Game (12 min)

Using a Google Doc (or the workbook space on p. 269), the team fills out the complete GDD:

  • Video Game Title
  • Intended Audience: Who is the game for?
  • Game Genre: Action, adventure, puzzle, racing, sports, RPG, etc.
  • Main Character(s): Who do players control? Describe them.
  • Setting: Where does the game take place? (city, planet, fantasy world, era)
  • Player's Main Goal/Objective: What is the player trying to do?
  • What is the game ABOUT?: One paragraph describing the game's story or premise
  • Visual Design Elements: What does the world look like? Color palette? Art style?
  • Music & Audio: Genre of music, sound effects style

Each role leads the section that fits their job. The Designer leads game mechanics, the Writer leads the story and characters, the Artist leads the visual section, and the Sound Designer leads the music section.

Step 3: Create a Pitch (4 min)

Teams build a pitch that explains the game and argues why the company should build it. The pitch names the genre, gives a short story summary, says what makes the game unique, and says why players would enjoy it. Teams practice it at least twice before they present.

Step 4: Share and Discuss (6 min)

Pair each team with another team. Take turns pitching, then trade one piece of positive feedback and one piece of constructive criticism per pitch.

Facilitation Tip

The workbook asks for a 3-5 minute pitch, which does not fit two teams inside a 6 minute share. Cap each pitch at 90 seconds and announce the cap before Step 3 so teams build to it. The full-length version is available as the extension. Separately, walk around during Step 2 with one question: "Tell me what your character's main goal is in 10 seconds." If the group can't, they have not converged on a concept yet. Push them to commit to a single clear sentence.

Extra Time?

Groups that finish early design a video game cover (digital or paper) including title, main character, background, and a short slogan.

DOK 3: Why does a real game studio require a GDD before any code is written? What problem does it prevent?

DELIVERABLE: Completed Game Design Document (one per group of 3-5) saved in Google Docs and submitted to Google Classroom, plus the pitch delivered to a partner team.

docs.title: Activity 2: Steps of an Effective Job Search + eDynamic 8.2 (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: CCE-original job-search framework + eDynamic Unit 8.2 (scope-and-sequence column 9)

Walk the four steps of an effective job search and have students copy them into their notes:

  1. Know Yourself: Use what you have learned about your interests, your core personality type, and your Building Blocks
  2. Get Your Materials Ready: Resume (this week!), cover letter, interview practice
  3. Search Smart & Connect: Use specific keywords on job boards, network, attend job fairs
  4. Ask for Help: School counselors, career coaches, family in the field

Step 3 is the one students already have a workbook page for. Rung 5 of the capstone (FYF pp. 290-291: "Rung 5: Local Connections") has them search actual postings in their community with a query like "[career name] jobs near me" and record the title, location, responsibilities, required skills, and education each employer is asking for. Students practice that search earlier in this six weeks and complete the graded Rung 5 pages later in it. Today's job is to see where the resume they just built fits in the sequence.

Then direct students to log into eDynamic Learning and open Unit 8.2 (Job Search). Students work through the eDynamic content for the rest of the period. They will not finish today, that is fine.

[VERIFY IN eDynamic] Confirm which sections of eDynamic Unit 8.2 specifically address job search steps. Students should focus on job search content this week, not personality assessment content.

Connection to the resume work: The resume students built this week is the deliverable for Step 2 ("Get Your Materials Ready"). They are already further along than they realize.

DOK 2: Of the 4 job search steps, which one are you most prepared for right now and which one are you least prepared for? Why?

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Ranked Justification) · Printable PDF:

Rank the 4 job search steps from MOST PREPARED for RIGHT NOW (1) to LEAST PREPARED (4).

  • Know Yourself: rank ____
  • Get Your Materials Ready: rank ____
  • Search Smart & Connect: rank ____
  • Ask for Help: rank ____

For EACH rank, write ONE piece of evidence:

  • Rank 1 (most prepared): _____________

  • Rank 4 (least prepared): _____________

Bottom line: My team's video game TITLE and MY role on the team:

Game title: _____

My role: _____

(d(1)(C), d(6)(A))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a printed GDD template with section headers and sentence starters ("This game is about a _ who must ___."). Allow students to draw their character on paper if they cannot articulate the visual style in writing.
  • Extension: Groups create the video game cover AND write a 1-paragraph "back of the box" description that markets the game to buyers. Teams that want the workbook's full-length pitch (FYF p. 269, Step 3 asks for 3-5 minutes) build and rehearse it for a lunch or advisory slot.
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Game Design = Diseño de juegos, Character = Personaje, Setting = Escenario, Genre = Género. Game design is highly visual and accessible across language levels. Pair ESL students into mixed-language teams so they can contribute through art and concept design.

docs.title: Day 5: Merch Mode Band T-Shirt Design
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Design a touring band's t-shirt in the "Merch Mode" activity; apply five graphic-design principles to the design choices; finalize the Xello resume; rate and favorite Arts/AV Hats in the app TEKS d(1)(C), d(7)(A) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Band style and design sketch · Explain: Design principles and share-out · Extend: Resume finalize and Hat rating · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Band t-shirt design (Canva or paper) + completed design-principle plan + finalized Xello resume Materials Chromebooks, Find Your Future workbook pp. 256-258 and 274-276, Canva accounts, Xello accounts, sticky notes, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Name a brand whose logo you would recognize anywhere, even without the name on it. What makes the brand stick in your memory?

Take 4-5 responses. Apple, Nike, McDonald's, and Target usually come up immediately. A designer made each mark recognizable in a few seconds. Today students have the same problem for a band about to start its first tour.

docs.title: Activity 1: Merch Mode (30 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 256-258: "Merch Mode"), an Arts chapter activity

Introduce the activity using the workbook framing: "Graphic designers are the creative minds behind the visuals you see every day like posters, logos, ads, and even the packaging on your favorite products. Their job is to make ideas look eye-catching... But graphic design isn't just about making things 'look cool', it's about solving problems and figuring out how to grab people's attention."

The scenario: a brand-new band is going on their first major music tour and needs a t-shirt that defines their look and gets their fans excited. Each student is the graphic designer on that job.

Time, Voice, Body: Post the three blocks before students open Canva. Voice 1 for the brainstorm and the sketch, Voice 3 for the presenter in Step 5, and a visible countdown for each step. Sticky notes go on the table edge, not in laptop keyboards, and finished sketches go face-up in the middle of the table so partners can see them during the share.

Step 1: Define Your Band's Style (5 min)

Students fill in the workbook page (p. 256): Band Name, Music Style or Genre, Visual Style (what people see when they think of the band, colors, mood, vibe), Stage Look (what the band wears or has on stage), Audience (what kind of fans connect with this band and what they wear), and Overall Band Identity (the feeling or message of the band in a few words).

Step 2: Review Design Principles (7 min)

The workbook's design-principles table (p. 257) is the teaching asset of this activity. Walk the five principles, then have students write their own plan in the third column:

Design Principle What It Means Your Plan The 3-Second Rule People only glance at a shirt for a few seconds. It has to be understood quickly. What is the ONE main idea your shirt should communicate instantly? Visual Hierarchy (Make It Pop!) The most important part should stand out the most: biggest, boldest, or brightest. What will people notice first on your design? Font Choice Matters Fonts affect readability and style. Bold and simple fonts usually work best on shirts. What kind of lettering fits your band's vibe? Memorable Design Strong designs often repeat or highlight a key symbol, shape, or style. What repeating element or symbol could you use? Does It Fit the Vibe? Everything should feel like it belongs together as one design. What feeling or style do you want your shirt to give off?

Step 3: Brainstorm Ideas (5 min)

Students jot phrases, list colors, and try out fonts on sticky notes. Every choice has to trace back to one of the five principles.

Step 4: Sketch Your Design (9 min)

Students sketch the shirt in Canva or on paper. One design, front of the shirt, with the type and the key symbol both visible.

Step 5: Share Your Ideas (4 min)

Students present to a partner, a small group, or the class, and explain what the band is like and how the design shows that style, why they chose those colors, fonts, and images, and how the design would help promote the band. Close with the workbook's discussion question (p. 258): what are the top 2 Powerskills that would matter in a graphic design career?

Facilitation Tip

Run the 3-Second Rule on the class before Step 3. Project one well-known band or team shirt for exactly three seconds, hide it, then ask what students remember. Whatever they name is the visual hierarchy working. Whatever nobody remembers is the part that would have to be cut from their own design.

DOK 4: Two bands could pick the same colors and the same font and still end up with shirts that say completely different things. Using at least two of the five design principles, explain what actually makes a design belong to one band and not the other.

DELIVERABLE: Band t-shirt design (Canva or paper) + the completed "Your Plan" column of the design-principles table.

docs.title: Activity 2: Finalize Xello Resume + H&L Hat Rating (10 min)
docs.text:
Source: Xello Resume Builder + (FYF p. 276: "App Exploration")

Direct students to open Xello and make ANY final changes to their resume based on the week's work. The resume is the official deliverable for d(7)(A) and should be in good shape by the end of today.

Then direct students to open H&L and complete two tasks:

  1. Rate at least 3 Arts/AV Hats and favorite the ones that fit (Graphic Designer, Animator, UX Designer, Video Editor, Photographer, Sound Engineer, Social Media Manager, Art Director).
  2. Update Building Blocks with the design work from this week: the podcast episode outline, the rewritten audio cues, the Game Design Document, the band t-shirt design, and the Xello resume itself.

[H&L PLATFORM] (FYF p. 276: "App Exploration") In the Hats & Ladders app, go to Clusters, open the Arts, Audio/Visual Technology and Communications Cluster, rate at least 3 Hats, and click the heart icon on the ones worth keeping. Ratings and favorites save to the Climber Profile.

Everything students record here comes back at the end of the year, when they check every rung of the career ladder before presenting it (FYF p. 299: "Prepare & Present").

While students work, project the workbook's district pages (FYF pp. 274-275: "What is Happening at My District?"). They name Irving ISD's two programs of study in this cluster, Digital Communications and Graphic Design & Illustration, the Adobe Certified Professional certification, TSA and SkillsUSA as the student organizations, the daily school-wide news program Digital Communications students produce and broadcast, and the annual Irving ISD Film Festival, a red carpet event that screens student work. Students need this page in front of them for the exit ticket.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Concept Map / Connection Diagram) · Printable PDF:

MY band t-shirt design in ONE sentence: _____________

Connect this design to THREE things:

1. The Arts/AV career that WOULD do this work professionally (Graphic Designer / Art Director / UX Designer / Social Media Manager / etc.)

My career: _____. Would I WANT this career? Circle: YES / NO / MAYBE. One sentence why:

2. An Irving ISD program in this cluster (Digital Communications OR Graphic Design & Illustration, at Irving High / MacArthur / Nimitz, Adobe Certified Professional certification)

Does this program lead DIRECTLY to my career or is it a STEPPING STONE? Circle: DIRECT / STEPPING STONE. One sentence why:

3. ONE specific Building Block I added this week (Canva / design principles / Game Design Document / podcast outline / Xello resume)

My Building Block: _____. In one sentence, how will this BB show up on my resume AND in a real design job?

(d(1)(C), d(7)(A))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide pre-made Canva t-shirt templates students can customize. Hand out the design-principles table with the first row already filled in as a model. Allow students to design only the key symbol instead of the full shirt.
  • Extension: Students who finish the sketch early take the TrailSip logo brief (FYF pp. 262-263: "Powerskill: Time Management"), a company that sells eco-friendly reusable water bottles to hikers and bikers, and use the workbook's 10 minute timeboxing plan to redesign its logo under a hard clock.
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Brand = Marca, Logo = Logotipo, Slogan = Eslogan, Font = Tipografía, Color Palette = Paleta de colores, Sketch = Bosquejo. The design work is HIGHLY visual and accessible across language levels. Allow the Step 5 share and the design-principle plan to be written or spoken in Spanish or bilingual format.

docs.title: Week 2: Design Your Brand — Graphic Design + First Resume
docs.text: 6th Six Weeks | Arts, A/V Technology & Communications Cluster | 5 class periods (50 min each)

docs.title: Lesson Objective
docs.text:
Students explore the Arts, Audio/Visual Technology and Communications career cluster through the Hats & Ladders app and the Find Your Future workbook, plan and outline a podcast episode in "Behind the Microphone," write their first professional resume in Xello, practice attention to detail by rewriting an incomplete audio cue script, build and pitch a Game Design Document in a studio team in "Game On!", design a touring band's t-shirt in "Merch Mode," and identify the steps of an effective job search to bridge into the job-readiness weeks ahead.

Learning Target: I can name at least three Arts/AV careers and say what each one does, write a complete resume in Xello, name the steps of an effective job search, and design a band t-shirt that follows the five design principles.

Success Criteria: I will know I am successful when my podcast outline has all five checklist parts, when my Xello resume has specific content in the header, career objective, education, skills, activities, and community service, when my rewritten audio cues name the material, the surface, and the mood, when my team's Game Design Document is complete and pitched, and when my band t-shirt design has one main idea, one repeating symbol, and a font that fits the band.

docs.title: Demonstration of Learning
