docs.title: Career Connection
docs.text:
Websites, apps, advertisements, social posts, and logos all need someone to make the visual decisions. DFW employers hire graphic designers, animators, video editors, UX designers, and social media managers for that work. Students also write their first professional resume in Xello this week and revise the same document through the rest of the six weeks.

What is Happening at Irving ISD? The district runs two programs of study in this cluster, Digital Communications and Graphic Design & Illustration, offered at Irving High School, MacArthur High School, and Nimitz High School, a multi-campus pathway students can pursue regardless of their home school. The workbook's district pages add the local detail students respond to most (FYF pp. 274-275: "What is Happening at My District?"): Digital Communications students produce and broadcast a daily school-wide news program on professional equipment, Graphic Design & Illustration builds visual communication, branding, layout, and creative problem solving, the industry certification is Adobe Certified Professional, TSA and SkillsUSA are the student organizations, and the annual Irving ISD Film Festival is a red carpet event that screens student-produced work with an awards ceremony. The page frames the whole cluster around Transitioning to High School, which is the right frame for a week that ends with students holding a resume.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text:
• Graphic Designer: A professional who creates visual content for print, digital, and social media using tools like Adobe Photoshop, Illustrator, and InDesign.
  • Resume: A one-page document summarizing your education, skills, activities, and career objective. Used when applying for jobs, internships, or college programs.
  • Portfolio: A collection of work samples that demonstrates a designer's skills and style. Essential for creative careers, often more important than the resume.
  • UX Designer: A User Experience Designer who focuses on how people interact with websites, apps, and digital products. One of the fastest-growing design careers.
  • Branding: How a business shows who they are through logos, colors, fonts, and messaging to make people remember them.
  • Visual Hierarchy: Making the most important part of a design stand out the most, through size, boldness, or brightness. One of the five design principles students apply in "Merch Mode."
  • Career Objective: A 1-2 sentence statement at the top of a resume that summarizes the kind of role you are seeking.

docs.title: Bridge to Theory (Hats & Ladders)
docs.text:
The Find Your Future workbook gives Arts, Audio/Visual Technology and Communications printed pages 255-276. The chapter opener (FYF p. 255: "Exploring the World of ARTS, AUDIO/VISUAL TECHNOLOGY AND COMMUNICATIONS") frames the cluster as creating the things people watch, hear, and share every day, splits the work into how something sounds, how it looks, and how it makes people feel, and puts three Hats on the page: Photographer, Audio Engineer, and AV Technician. Its "Be the Decision Maker" scenario hands students the sound design for an animated movie built entirely from household objects. The chapter prints no pathway list. Students meet the cluster's pathways in the app through the Pathway Possibilities step (FYF p. 276: "App Exploration") and meet Irving ISD's own programs on the district pages (FYF pp. 274-275).

Four chapter sections carry this week:

  • Behind the Microphone (Day 1): Career Climb activity. Groups of 3-4 brainstorm a podcast, settle the name, episode title, length, hosts and guests, three key topics, and a promotion plan, then write a full episode outline on chart paper against a five-part checklist and pitch it to another group (FYF pp. 270-271).
  • Powerskill: Attention to Detail (Day 3): Students are the lead sound designer on a short movie called "Kitchen Mess!" whose Audio Cue Script is missing the material, surface, and mood information the sound team needs. They name what is missing and rewrite all four cues (FYF pp. 272-273).
  • Game On! (Day 4): Career Climb activity. Teams of 3-5 name a studio, take one of four roles (Game Designer, Artist, Writer, Sound Designer), build a Game Design Document, and pitch the game to another team for feedback (FYF pp. 268-269).
  • Merch Mode (Day 5): Students design a touring band's t-shirt from the chapter's five-principle design table (The 3-Second Rule, Visual Hierarchy, Font Choice Matters, Memorable Design, Does It Fit the Vibe?) and present the choices they made (FYF pp. 256-258).

The Arts chapter has four more sections than this week can hold: The Visual Hook (FYF pp. 259-261), product packaging design with a target market, sales channels, and structured peer feedback; Powerskill: Time Management (FYF pp. 262-263), a logo redesign for an outdoor water-bottle company under a 10 minute timeboxing plan; Safety on the Set (FYF pp. 264-265), stunt coordination where partners each research one film safety method and teach the other; and Setting the Stage (FYF pp. 266-267), set design with labeled set elements, a blueprint, and a 3D prototype. Use any of the four as enrichment.

The resume half of this week is CCE-original. The Find Your Future workbook carries no resume, cover letter, or job-application activity anywhere in its 300 printed pages. Days 2 and 3 use the Xello Resume Builder as supplemental Grade 8 instruction plus the CareerOneStop Resume Guide, and the four job-search steps on Day 4 are a CCE framework paired with eDynamic Unit 8.2. The workbook's nearest relative is Rung 5 of the capstone (FYF pp. 290-291: "Rung 5: Local Connections"), where students search real local job postings and record what employers ask for.

docs.title: IISD Instructional Strategies
docs.text:
• Think-Pair-Share: Day 1, Activity 1, the chapter opener's "Be the Decision Maker" sound-design scenario (FYF p. 255). Distinguished: pose it to the whole group, hold a silent 30 second Think, then time Partner A for 30 seconds and Partner B for 30 seconds, and post two stems at different levels: "I would make it sound _ because " and "A realistic sound tells the audience __, but an unexpected sound tells them _____." Ask two pairs to share, not one. Listen while pairs talk for who names what the audience feels rather than what the object is, and pick your share-out pairs from what you heard rather than from raised hands.
  • Stop and Jot: Day 1, Activity 1, the two pauses during the Arts/AV cluster tour video. Distinguished: name both stop points before the video starts, give 45 seconds per jot with the prompt on screen, and offer two stems: "One Arts/AV career I did not expect is _" and "One thing I still want to know about is __." Read jots over shoulders during both pauses and track which careers get named. If most jots say Graphic Designer only, steer the Hat browse toward Sound Engineer, UX Designer, and Art Director so Day 5's exit tickets are not thirty copies of the same career.
  • Active Monitoring: Day 2, Activity 2, the Xello Resume Builder work time, and Day 3, Activity 2, the Two Stars and a Wish peer review. Distinguished: on Day 2, walk three laps with one target each (lap 1 header and career objective filled in, lap 2 at least three specific skills, lap 3 activities and community service not blank), carrying the Resume Revision Checklist as the clipboard, with feedback ready before class for the two predictable misconceptions, "I have nothing to put down" and a career objective that reads "I want a job." On Day 3 the lap target is the feedback itself: post the two star stems ("Your skills section is strong because _", "Your career objective is clear because ") and the one wish stem ("Your __ section would be stronger if you added _____"), and ask each pair to show you one specific change they actually made. If a lap turns up more than a handful of blank Skills sections, reproject the skills list to the whole room instead of prompting student by student.
  • Chunking: Day 2, Activity 1, the six resume sections modeled live in Xello. Distinguished: build one section at a time, say what each section proves before you fill it (Skills proves you can do something, Community Service proves you show up), and close each section with the thumbs check already written into the plan before starting the next. Note which section drew the most thumbs down; that section becomes lap 1's target in Activity 2, and students who cleared every chunk start on CareerOneStop action verbs instead of waiting. The same live-build move runs on Day 3, where the first audio cue gets rewritten on the board before students touch the other three.
  • Time, Voice, Body (TVB): Day 5, Activity 1, the Merch Mode sketch and share. Distinguished: post the three blocks before Canva opens, Voice 1 for the brainstorm and the sketch, Voice 3 for the presenter in Step 5, and a visible countdown on every one of the five steps. State where sticky notes go and where finished sketches sit so the share does not eat sketch time. Narrate the tables that are meeting the expectation rather than correcting the ones that are not. If the room is still sketching when the Step 4 countdown ends, cut the share to partners only and announce the change before the timer runs out.

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Explore the Business, Marketing, and Finance cluster in the Hats & Ladders app; write two contrasting calls to action for each of four products and build an ad mock-up using the "Click Factor" workbook activity TEKS d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Cluster tour and Click Factor ad analysis · Explain: Group CTA choice and ad mock-up · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Eight calls to action across the four workbook products + an ad mock-up with a headline, a short description, and the chosen CTA Materials Chromebooks, H&L accounts, Find Your Future workbook pp. 221, 225-227, 230, and 254, Canva accounts, printed blank ad mock-up sheets, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Name an online ad you actually clicked, or almost clicked. What did it ask you to DO? Someone's JOB was to write that line.

Take 4-5 responses. Push past "it looked cool" to the action the ad asked for: buy, sign up, download, watch, or swipe. Name that line as the call to action. The workbook asks students to write one as a digital marketing specialist.

docs.title: Activity 1: H&L Marketing Cluster Tour (10 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 221: "Exploring the World of BUSINESS, MARKETING, AND FINANCE") and (FYF p. 254: "App Exploration")

Open by clarifying a key point: Hats & Ladders does not have a separate "Marketing" cluster. Marketing careers live inside the Business, Marketing, and Finance cluster. This week students work the Marketing and Sales side of it.

Read the chapter opener together. The cluster is about helping organizations grow, connect with customers, and make smart financial decisions. The opener puts three Hats on the page: Business Analyst, Financial Examiner, and E-Commerce Specialist.

[H&L PLATFORM] Students follow the App Exploration page (FYF p. 254): open the Hats & Ladders app, go to Clusters, click the Business, Marketing, and Finance Cluster, watch the "Cluster Tour" video, then play "Game Time." Afterward they find 1 Hat that matches their interests and 1 Hat that does not, and answer why for each.

Stop and Jot: Pause the cluster tour video twice. Each pause gets 45 seconds and one of the workbook's own prompts from the App Exploration page: "One marketing career I did not know existed is _" and "One question I still have about how companies choose their ads is ___."

The chapter prints no pathway list. Students meet the cluster's pathways in the app through Pathway Possibilities, which they rate later in the week, and they meet Irving ISD's own Marketing & Sales program of study on the district pages (FYF pp. 252-253).

Use the Hat Finder to browse 2-3 marketing-specific Hats: Marketing Manager, Brand Manager, Market Research Analyst, Social Media Manager, Advertising Account Executive.

Facilitation Tip

Students often miss "Marketing" because it is nested under "Business, Marketing, and Finance" in the app. Walk the room for the first 2 minutes and confirm every student has clicked into the right cluster. The App Exploration page names the exact path, so project page 254 while students navigate.

docs.title: Activity 2: "Click Factor" Call to Action Lab (30 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 225-227 and 230: "Click Factor"), a Career Climb activity

The last page of this activity is printed out of order

"Click Factor" runs pages 225, 226, 227, and then jumps to page 230 for Step 4. Pages 228 and 230 were transposed at the printer. Tell students the jump before they start.

Use the workbook's setup: students are digital marketing specialists promoting new products. People decide in seconds whether to click, so the ad has to tell them what to do next. That line is the call to action. It may be short ("Buy Now!") or longer ("Sign up today for exclusive access"), but it needs to be clear, direct, and written for the product's audience.

Step 1: Analyze Two Ads (4 min)

Students open to page 225 and work with a partner to find the CTA in Ad #1 and Ad #2. Think-Pair-Share: 30 seconds of silent Think on which CTA feels stronger, then Partner A for 30 seconds, then Partner B for 30 seconds, using the workbook's four questions:

  • How are the two CTAs different?
  • Which one feels stronger?
  • Which one fits its product better, and why?
  • What is the audience being asked to do?

Two pairs share out, not one.

Step 2: Create Different Types of CTAs (12 min)

Project the workbook's CTA reference table (p. 226) and walk the five types with the workbook's own examples:

CTA Type What It Does Example Benefit Shows what the audience gains "Get better grades today" Urgency Pushes quick action "Buy now before it's gone!" Curiosity Sparks interest "See what everyone's talking about" Direct Command Clearly tells what to do "Download the app" Incentive Offers a reward "Sign up and get 20% off"

Students then write two different CTAs for each of the four products and label the type of each one. The products and their details are printed on pages 226 and 227:

  • Product A, Local Car Wash: fast service in five minutes or less, affordable prices, located near a busy road
  • Product B, Cooking Class: meets weekly, students make five different desserts, uses unusual ingredients
  • Product C, After-School Snack Box: delivered weekly, mix of sweet and salty, designed for busy students
  • Product D, Fishing Gear: monthly subscription of hooks, bobbers, worms, and line, designed for families

The point of writing two per product is contrast. If both CTAs for the car wash are Direct Commands, the student has written the same ad twice.

Facilitation Tip

The most common miss is a CTA that describes the product instead of asking for an action. "Our snack box has chips and cookies" is a description. "Grab your first box before Friday" is a CTA. If a student's line has no verb aimed at the reader, send them back to the type table and ask which of the five they were trying to write.

Step 3: Choose and Discuss (4 min)

Pairs join another pair. As a group of four they read all their CTAs and choose the ONE CTA per product that would most likely make them click or buy. Group members must be ready to say which CTA grabbed attention, which one made them want to act right away, and why it beat the others.

Step 4: Design the Ad (10 min)

Students turn to page 230 and build a mock-up of an ad for one product. A mock-up is a rough draft that shows what the finished ad will look like. The mock-up must include a headline, a short description, and the chosen CTA. Two design decisions get written down next to the sketch: where the CTA sits (top, middle, bottom) and how it is made to stand out (color, size, bold type).

Students use the printed mock-up sheet, Canva, or Google Drawings.

DOK 3: Product C targets busy students and Product D targets families. Take the same CTA type, Urgency, and write it for both audiences. What had to change in the wording, and what does that tell you about writing for an audience you are not part of?

DELIVERABLE: Eight CTAs (two per product) labeled by type, plus one ad mock-up with a headline, a short description, and a chosen CTA. Submitted to Google Classroom.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Mini-Case / Scenario Application) · Printable PDF:

Scenario: A DFW pet store is launching a dog-walking service. Their online ad reads: "We are a pet store. We have dog walkers. Thank you." Almost nobody clicks it.

  1. Write a stronger call to action for this ad (one short line):

  1. Which type is your CTA? (Circle one) Benefit · Urgency · Curiosity · Direct Command · Incentive

  2. Who is the audience for this ad, and why does your CTA fit THEM?

  1. Name ONE Marketing and Sales career from the H&L cluster whose job it is to write lines like this:

Career: _____

(d(1)(C))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Give three pre-written CTAs per product, already labeled by type, so students revise and re-label rather than starting from a blank line. Provide a mock-up sheet with the headline box, description box, and CTA box already drawn and labeled.
  • Extension: Students write two CTAs for a fifth product of their own invention and label the types, or build a second mock-up for the same product aimed at a different audience and write one sentence on what changed.
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Advertisement = Anuncio, Call to Action = Llamada a la acción, Headline = Titular, Audience = Audiencia, Reward = Recompensa. The five-type table carries the vocabulary visually, so keep it projected during Step 2. Spanish-language CTAs are a strong creative choice for DFW marketing, encourage them.

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Practice written communication by writing one Little Library social media post with a clear status, a call to action, and hashtags; analyze how economic conditions affect marketing employment TEKS d(1)(C), d(5)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Little Library post · Explain: Economic conditions chart and pair-share · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Little Library social media post + economic conditions analysis chart Materials Chromebooks, Find Your Future workbook pp. 147-148, sticky notes, printed Economic Conditions Analysis chart, BLS labor data, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: When the economy is doing well, do companies spend MORE or LESS on advertising? What about during a recession? Why?

Take 2-3 responses. Most students will guess that companies spend more when business is good. Connect that answer to d(5)(C): marketing jobs rise and fall with company budgets, so economic conditions can change hiring quickly in this field.

docs.title: Activity 1: H&L Powerskill — Written Communication (20 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 147-148: "Powerskill: Written Communication")

This lesson is not in the Business chapter

Written Communication sits in the Powerskills in Action chapter at pages 147-148, so students page backward from the Business chapter to reach it. Give the page number before they open the book.

Frame the skill from the workbook: communicating well means sharing your thoughts clearly and understanding other people, and at work that happens through emails, letters, reports, and social media. When it goes well, people avoid confusion and everyone is working from the same information.

Post the workbook's four tips for effective written communication (FYF p. 148) where students can see them while they draft:

  1. Put yourself in your reader's shoes: what information do they need?
  2. Be clear and concise
  3. Stay on topic: avoid irrelevant information
  4. Proofread to catch typos and confusing sentences

The workbook scenario: A town has several Little Libraries, small spaces where people can take, trade, or leave books for free. The community needs to know when a library needs more books, has too many, or has specific books available. The student has been given the job of running a social media account that keeps the community informed.

Step 1: Brainstorm Ideas (3 min)

Students imagine they are responsible for a Little Library in their neighborhood and brainstorm on sticky notes (FYF p. 147), then answer in writing:

  • Is your Little Library full, empty, or in need of specific types of books?
  • What do you want people to do (donate, take books, check out the selection)?
  • Where is your Little Library located?

Step 2: Create a Social Media Post (15 min)

Using a digital tool (Canva, Google Drawings) or paper, students create one social media post. The workbook (FYF p. 148) requires the post to:

  • Clearly explain the status of the Little Library
  • Include a call to action (ask people to donate, visit, or take books)
  • Include at least 2 hashtags that help people find the post

The post should look like a real Instagram or TikTok post, not just a paragraph. Students can include a photo, an emoji, a strong headline, and the hashtags at the bottom.

After designing, lead a quick partner discussion using the workbook's Class Discussion questions (FYF p. 148):

  • How did you make sure your message was clear?
  • Why is it important to be specific when asking for help or giving information?
  • How can social media be used effectively to communicate with others?

Facilitation Tip

The most common mistake is making the post too long. Show a real Instagram caption on the projector, most are under 50 words. The post is a marketing tool, not an essay. If a student writes a paragraph, push them to cut it in half.

Connection to marketing: This is exactly the work a Social Media Manager does daily, write short, clear, persuasive posts that drive action. It is one of the fastest-growing marketing careers.

docs.title: Activity 2: Economic Conditions and Marketing Jobs (20 min)
docs.text:
Source: BLS labor market data + scope-and-sequence d(5)(C)

Distribute the printed Economic Conditions Analysis chart. Students complete a side-by-side analysis:

Factor Strong Economy Weak Economy / Recession Marketing job availability Marketing budgets at companies Which marketing roles get cut first? Which marketing roles are recession-proof? What does this mean for a marketing professional?

Walk students through the key concepts (5 min):

  • When the economy is strong, businesses grow → more revenue → more marketing budget → MORE marketing jobs
  • When the economy slows down, marketing budgets are often the FIRST thing cut because it feels "optional"
  • BUT, even in recessions, some marketing roles stay strong:
    • Digital marketing (SEO, social media) tends to survive cuts because it has measurable ROI
    • Discount/value marketing grows because companies need to convince budget-conscious shoppers
    • In-house marketing teams survive better than agencies and freelancers

Students complete the chart (10 min) using BLS data and what they just learned. They search "marketing manager outlook" on bls.gov to find the projected growth rate (typically 6-8% over 10 years).

Pair-Share (5 min): Students share one row of their chart with a partner. The partner gives one suggestion to strengthen the answer.

DOK 3: What conclusions can you draw about why a marketing professional with BOTH traditional skills (TV, billboards, print) AND digital skills (social media, SEO, email) is more job-secure than someone with only one type of skill?

DELIVERABLE: Completed Little Library social media post + completed Economic Conditions Analysis chart.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Comparison Matrix) · Printable PDF:

Fill in each cell using today's Economic Conditions Analysis chart.

Strong Economy Weak Economy / Recession Marketing job availability (more / same / fewer) Which marketing role gets cut FIRST Which marketing role stays STRONG

Bottom line: ONE digital marketing skill that is "recession-proof" and the reason it survives cuts:

Skill: _____

Why it survives: ____________

(d(5)(C), d(1)(C))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a fill-in-the-blank social media post template ("Our Little Library at _ needs . Please bring __. #LittleLibrary #_____"). For the economic chart, fill in the "strong economy" column as an example so students only complete the "weak economy" column.
  • Extension: Students research a real recession (2008 or 2020) and find a specific marketing role that grew DURING the recession. They write one paragraph explaining why.
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Recession = Recesión, Budget = Presupuesto, Hashtag = Etiqueta. The social media post is highly visual. Allow it to be written in Spanish or bilingual, many DFW Little Libraries actually use bilingual posts because of the diverse community.

docs.title: Day 3: Expert Edge — Build Your Consulting Business
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Define entrepreneurship; turn one personal skill into a consulting service with a name, an offer, a mission statement, and a price; design a logo and pitch the service to a partner TEKS d(3)(I), d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Expert Edge skill brainstorm and service build · Explain: Logo and partner pitch with feedback · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed consulting service page (name, offer, mission statement, price, extra add-on) + logo + partner feedback form Materials Chromebooks, Find Your Future workbook pp. 222-224, sticky notes, Canva accounts, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: What are you the person your friends come to for help with? Gaming, homework, art, a sport, fixing something? Name it out loud.

Take 4-5 responses. Most students will name something they would not pay for themselves. Ask who might pay, and why. Consultants make a business out of skills their clients need but do not have; today students build that business around one skill of their own.

docs.title: Activity 1: "Expert Edge" Consulting Business (35 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 222-224: "Expert Edge"), a Career Climb activity

Frame the career from the workbook: a consultant sells skill and knowledge instead of a product. Consultants work in business, technology, sports, and plenty of other fields. They listen to a client, figure out what that client actually needs, and deliver a solution through advice, coaching, or a written plan. Today students step into the shoes of an entrepreneur opening a consulting business, and clients are looking for help. The job is to make a client feel confident choosing them.

This activity is the week's strongest entrepreneurship work. The offer, the price, and the mission statement are the three pieces every real small business has to write before it can sell anything.

Step 1: Discover Your Skill (7 min)

Students brainstorm on sticky notes, then write down three skills they are good at or enjoy (FYF p. 222). The workbook's own examples are coaching a friend in a video game, helping someone with homework or studying, giving tips on art, music, or sports, and sharing ideas for coding, building, or creating projects.

For each of the three skills, students describe: who might need help with it, why someone would want their help, and how they could use it to help others.

Step 2: Design Your Consulting Service (13 min)

Students choose ONE skill to build the business around and complete the service page (FYF p. 223):

  • Name Your Service
  • Describe Your Offer: what exactly will you do for your client? Clear and specific.
  • Create a Mission Statement: the purpose or game plan for the business.
  • Set Your Price: think about how much time and effort the service takes, then assign a price. It can be a one-time payment, an hourly rate, or a monthly subscription.
  • Extra Add On: one extra thing offered to make the service special.

Facilitation Tip

The most common miss is an offer written as a topic instead of a service. "I help with math" is a topic. "I build a two-week study plan for one class and check your work twice a week" is a service, because the client can picture what they receive. When you see a topic, ask "what does the client actually get, and when?" The second most common miss is a price with no unit: $20 for what, once or every week?

Step 3: Create a Logo (7 min)

Students design a logo that represents the service and the brand (FYF p. 224). Keep it simple but memorable, and make deliberate choices about colors, shapes, and images. Students sketch on the workbook page or build it in Canva.

Active Monitoring: Walk a fixed pathway through the room four times, one lap per step. Lap 1 target: three skills written, each with a named person who needs it. Lap 2 target: the offer names something the client receives. Lap 3 target: the logo is readable at arm's length. Lap 4 target: the pitch lands under two minutes. Carry the workbook's own feedback categories on the clipboard, Clarity, Creativity, and Persuasiveness, and mark them as you pass. If more than a handful of students miss the lap 2 target, pause and rewrite one volunteer's offer on the projector instead of fixing it desk by desk.

Step 4: Pitch Your Service (8 min)

Students present the consulting service to a partner in about 1 to 2 minutes. The listening partner fills in the workbook's feedback form (FYF p. 224): a rating, What They Did Well, and What They Could Improve On, judged against three questions the workbook supplies:

  • Clarity: did you understand their service?
  • Creativity: is the idea fun or interesting?
  • Persuasiveness: would you want to hire this consultant?

Then partners switch. Close with the workbook's Class Discussion (FYF p. 224): what makes a consulting service valuable to someone, how did you decide on your price, and which Powerskills would help someone succeed as a consultant?

DOK 4: Your price is set and a client says it is too high. Would you lower the price, cut part of the offer, or throw in the extra add-on to justify the price? Defend the call, and say what your choice costs you.

DELIVERABLE: Completed consulting service page (name, offer, mission statement, price, extra add-on), a logo, and a partner feedback form filled in for the classmate you listened to.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (10 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Short Constructed Response) · Printable PDF:

  1. Entrepreneurship in my own words (one sentence, no dictionary language):
  1. My consulting service in one sentence (name + what the client gets):
  1. Who needs my service (specific, not "everyone" or "kids"):
  1. My price, and ONE reason a client would pay it:

Price: _____

Why they would pay it: ______

(d(3)(I), d(1)(C))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a list of eight starter consulting skills (gaming coach, homework tutor, sneaker cleaning, phone photography, art commissions, party DJ, pet sitting, bike repair) so students choose rather than invent. Provide a sentence frame for the offer: "I will _ for you, times a week, and you will get __."
  • Extension: Students add a referral offer to their service and write what it costs them and what it earns them, or write a second version of the service priced for a different client (a classmate versus an adult) and explain what changed.
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Consultant = Consultor, Service = Servicio, Offer = Oferta, Mission Statement = Declaración de misión, Logo = Logotipo, Price = Precio. Allow the service page and the pitch in Spanish or bilingual format. The logo step carries meaning visually, so ELL students can show the brand before they have to explain it.

docs.title: Day 4: Marketing Career Research + Data-Informed Decision Making
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Research one Marketing career on the career research worksheet using the Hats & Ladders app; read three marketing data sets and choose a campaign strategy using the "Powerskill: Data-Informed Decision Making" workbook activity; connect school subjects to marketing careers in Xello TEKS d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Marketing career research and Family Fun Pass data · Explain: Strategy pitch and cross-group share · Extend: Xello School Subjects at Work · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Completed marketing career research worksheet + data-backed Family Fun Pass strategy pitch Materials Chromebooks, H&L accounts, Find Your Future workbook pp. 229, 228, and 254, printed marketing career research worksheet, Xello accounts, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Name ONE digital marketing skill you could learn TODAY that would make you more employable in 5 years.

Take 4-5 student responses. Most students will guess "social media", push them to be specific. "Editing TikToks" or "writing Instagram captions" or "designing Canva graphics" are all real, learnable skills that pay.

docs.title: Activity 1: Marketing Career Research (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: Career research worksheet (CCE artifact; the research format is taught in Wk0) + (FYF p. 254: "App Exploration")

[H&L PLATFORM] Students open the Hats & Ladders app, go to Clusters, then the Business, Marketing, and Finance Cluster, and use the Hat Finder to open one marketing Hat and read its full profile.

Students choose ONE Marketing-specific Hat and complete the career research worksheet on it. Suggested Hats:

  • Marketing Manager
  • Brand Manager
  • Market Research Analyst
  • Social Media Manager (often called Digital Marketing Specialist)
  • Advertising Account Executive
  • Public Relations Specialist
  • Content Creator / Content Strategist
  • SEO Specialist

The worksheet asks for:

  • Name of Career
  • What Interests You? (1-2 sentences)
  • Brief Job Description (3-4 sentences from the H&L Hat profile)
  • Education/Training Needed (degree, certifications)
  • Average Salary (DFW data from H&L or BLS)
  • Tools, Equipment, or Skills Needed (software, soft skills, etc.)

Students fill the worksheet from the Hat profile. They should not copy. They should summarize in their own words.

Any student who has not finished the App Exploration page from Day 1 (FYF p. 254) closes it out here: rate at least 1 pathway under Pathway Possibilities and rate at least 3 Hats.

Facilitation Tip

For Marketing Manager, BLS shows one of the highest-paying business roles ($140K+ median nationally). Walk by students who chose Marketing Manager and confirm they wrote the salary down correctly, they often think they misread it.

DOK 2: Compare the salary of your chosen Marketing career to a Graphic Designer from the graphic design and resume week. Which earns more, and why might that be?

docs.title: Activity 2: Powerskill — Data-Informed Decision Making (25 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 229 and 228: "Powerskill: Data-Informed Decision Making")

The steps of this activity are printed out of order

The activity opens on page 229 with Step 1, then continues on page 228 for Steps 2, 3, and 4. Pages 228 and 230 were transposed at the printer. Say the page jump out loud before students open the book.

Frame the skill from the workbook: good decisions are not guesses, they are backed by data. Data-informed decision making means using real information to guide a choice, spotting patterns, and using evidence to support what you decide.

Students work in pairs or small groups as a marketing team launching a Family Fun Pass, a monthly subscription that gives families access to local activities like mini golf, movie nights, and trampoline parks. The team has to decide the best marketing strategy to get families to sign up.

Step 1: Analyze the Data (10 min)

The workbook gives three data sets on page 229. Chunking: release them one at a time and say what each one answers before students read it. Take a thumbs check between sets before releasing the next.

Data set The question it answers Audience Preference by Age Which channel does each age group prefer? (Social Media Ads, Influencers, In-Store, Email, Video Ads across 25-34, 35-49, and 50+) Past Campaign Performance What actually sold? (clicks, sales, and engagement for each of the five campaign types) Focus Group Feedback Why did people respond that way? (five customer quotes)

Facilitation Tip

The data conflicts on purpose, and the conflict is the lesson. The Influencer Campaign drew fewer clicks than Social Media Ads but produced the most sales and the highest engagement, and one focus group quote explains why: people trust recommendations more than ads. Meanwhile In-Store wins with the 50+ group, which is not the family audience this product is for. Let groups find the conflict themselves before you name it.

Step 2: Choose Your Marketing Strategy (5 min)

Teams pick ONE strategy from the workbook's list (FYF p. 228): Social Media Ads, Influencer Partnership, In-Store Promotion, Email Campaign, Video Ads, or a strategy of their own under Other.

Step 3: Build Your Pitch (5 min)

Teams write a short pitch that names three things: the strategy they chose, the key data that supports the decision, and why families in particular would respond to it. A strategy with no number attached to it is not finished.

Step 4: Share and Discuss (5 min)

Teams present to another group. Listeners judge three things the workbook names: did the presenters use the data clearly, did the strategy match what families actually want, and what are the strengths and weaknesses of the plan? Close with the workbook's Class Discussion (FYF p. 228): how did you decide which data mattered most, and what should you do when two data points conflict?

DOK 3: The Influencer Campaign got fewer clicks than Social Media Ads but more sales. Which of those two numbers matters more for the Family Fun Pass, and what does your answer say about what this business is actually trying to buy?

docs.title: Activity 3: Xello School Subjects at Work (5 min)
docs.text:
Source: Xello supplemental lesson, "School subjects at work." This lesson is not a Bowie Grade 8 completion standard.

Direct students to log into Xello and open the School Subjects at Work lesson. This Xello activity connects middle school subjects to careers. Students see how Math connects to Market Research Analyst, English connects to Content Creator, Art connects to Graphic Designer, and so on.

Students complete the activity at their own pace. Most will need 5-10 minutes. Those who don't finish complete it as homework or during catch-up time.

Connection to today: The research worksheet shows students what one marketing career does all day. The Family Fun Pass data work shows them the thinking that career runs on. The Xello lesson shows them which school subjects feed both.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Ranked Justification) · Printable PDF:

Rank these 4 marketing careers from MOST interesting to you (1) to LEAST (4) based on TODAY's research and the Family Fun Pass data work.

  • Marketing Manager: rank ____
  • Social Media Manager / Digital Marketing Specialist: rank ____
  • Market Research Analyst: rank ____
  • Content Creator / Content Strategist: rank ____

Career I researched today: _____

Salary I found: $____

Strategy my team picked for the Family Fun Pass: _____

For EACH rank below, give ONE reason from today's work (the Hat profile OR the data sets):

  • Rank 1 (most interesting): ________

  • Rank 4 (least interesting): _______

(d(1)(C))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Pre-fill the research worksheet with the career name and one section so students only complete the rest. Highlight the two largest numbers in each column of the Audience Preference and Past Campaign Performance tables so students start from the pattern instead of hunting for it. Give a pitch frame: "We picked _ because the data shows , and families would respond because __."
  • Extension: Students open a Google Applied Digital Skills lesson at applieddigitalskills.withgoogle.com and start it. "Plan and Create a Website" builds a small business site, "Design a Presentation to Pitch Your Idea" builds a pitch deck that feeds the 30-second sales pitch in the Sales and Presentations week (FYF pp. 241-243: "30 Seconds to Sell"), and "Plan an Event" connects to event marketing. Or students complete a second research worksheet for a different marketing career and compare the salary, education, and daily work.
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Marketing Manager = Gerente de mercadotecnia, Salary = Salario, Data = Datos, Strategy = Estrategia, Survey = Encuesta. The three data sets are tables and quotes, so the numbers carry meaning without heavy reading. Google Applied Digital Skills offers Spanish-language lessons for the extension; show ESL students how to switch the interface.

docs.title: Day 5: Marketing Plan Pitches + eDynamic 4.1 + H&L Favorites
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Pitch a 1-minute Mini Marketing Plan combining the week's work; begin eDynamic Unit 4.1; favorite Marketing careers in H&L TEKS d(1)(C), d(3)(I), d(5)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: Mini Marketing Plan pitches and peer feedback · Extend: eDynamic 4.1 and H&L favorites · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable 1-minute Marketing Plan pitch + Marketing favorites in H&L + eDynamic 4.1 progress Materials Chromebooks, H&L accounts, Find Your Future workbook p. 254, eDynamic Learning Unit 4.1, projector, timer

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: If you could work at any company's marketing department in DFW, which company would you choose and why? AT&T, Toyota, Mary Kay, American Airlines, Frito-Lay, Topgolf, the Cowboys?

Take 4-5 student responses. This builds personal connection to the local marketing industry. DFW has one of the largest concentrations of corporate marketing teams in the country. Students should know they can have this career at home.

docs.title: Activity 1: Mini Marketing Plan Pitches (25 min)
docs.text:
Source: Compilation of the week's work ("Click Factor" + "Expert Edge" + the Family Fun Pass data work + the career research worksheet)

Today students pull together everything from this week into a 1-minute Mini Marketing Plan pitch. Most will pitch the consulting service they built in "Expert Edge" on Day 3, and any student who would rather pitch a different product or service may.

Pitch structure (1 minute, no more):

  1. Hook (10 seconds): One sentence that grabs attention. Example: "You have three days to learn a song for the talent show, and I am the person who gets you there."
  2. Product/Service (15 seconds): Name + what it is + what the client gets
  3. Target Audience (10 seconds): Who buys it and why
  4. One Marketing Channel (15 seconds): How will you reach that audience? Use the same six options the Family Fun Pass teams worked from on Day 4: social media ads, an influencer partnership, in-store promotion, an email campaign, video ads, or one of your own.
  5. Why it will sell (10 seconds): One sentence connecting to economic conditions: "This will sell because even in a tough economy, people still pay for something that saves them time."

Student work time (10 min): Students draft their 1-minute pitch on a notecard or in a Google Doc. They practice silently or with a partner.

Pitches (15 min): Students take turns presenting to a small group of 4-5 (NOT the whole class, there isn't time). Each student presents in 1 minute. Group members give Two Stars and a Wish feedback.

For larger classes, run pitches in parallel groups simultaneously. Each group selects ONE "best pitch" to present to the whole class at the end.

Facilitation Tip

Time, Voice, Body: post the three blocks before the first pitch. Project a 60 second visible timer for every pitch, hold Voice 0 while a group member is presenting, Voice 2 for the Two Stars and a Wish feedback, and say where presenters stand and where notecards go. Because pitches run in parallel small groups, not whole-class, students get a low-stakes first try at a timed delivery. Announce the 60 second limit before pitches start. If a student is still wrapping at 60 seconds, let them finish the sentence and move on.

DOK 4: What makes a pitch convincing? Is it the product, the target audience research, or the way the person delivers it? Which matters MORE in real marketing, and why?

DELIVERABLE: 1-minute Marketing Plan pitch (delivered orally to small group with feedback).

docs.title: Activity 2: eDynamic Unit 4.1 — Enterprise and Money Matters (12 min)
docs.text:
Source: eDynamic Learning Unit 4.1 (scope-and-sequence column 9)

Direct students to log into eDynamic Learning and open Unit 4.1: Enterprise and Money Matters. This unit covers Business Management & Administration, Finance, and Marketing/Sales/Service clusters together. Students focus specifically on the Marketing content.

[VERIFY IN eDynamic] Confirm which specific activities within eDynamic Unit 4.1 cover Marketing careers vs. Business Management vs. Finance. Direct students to marketing-specific content.

Students work at their own pace. They will not finish today, that is fine. The unit continues into next week's Sales/Presentations week.

docs.title: Activity 3: H&L Marketing Favorites + Career Plan Update (5 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 254: "App Exploration")

Direct students to open H&L and complete two tasks:

  1. Favorite at least 2 Marketing careers using the Hat Finder. Save them to the Climber Profile.
  2. Update Building Blocks: Add any marketing or design experiences from this week (built an ad mock-up, opened a consulting business, designed a logo, chose a campaign strategy from data, gave a pitch).

[H&L PLATFORM] Students click the heart icon on Hats they want to save. Favorites feed into the H&L Career Plan and the District Course Planner. Anyone still missing an App Exploration step from earlier in the week finishes it now: rate at least 1 pathway and at least 3 Hats.

The Career Plan is cumulative. Students should NOT start over. It now reflects every cluster they've explored this year.

Tell students where this week's saved careers go next. They already wrote a career goal and ran a deep dive on it at mid-year (FYF pp. 283-286: "Rung 2: Career Goal" and "Rung 3: Career Deep Dive"). A marketing career favorited this week that beats the one written on those pages is a reason to revise the goal before the Capstone presentation at the end of the six weeks (FYF p. 299: "Prepare & Present").

docs.title: Exit Ticket (3 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Concept Map) · Printable PDF:

Draw a quick concept map (bubbles + lines). Place MARKETING in the center and connect it to each of the FOUR items below. On each line, write ONE word or phrase that shows the link.

  1. My top Marketing career after this week: _____

  2. One Irving ISD campus where you could start toward this career (Irving High, Nimitz, MacArthur, Cardwell): _____

  3. ONE creative skill marketing needs (design, writing, video, etc.): _____

  4. ONE analytical skill marketing needs (data, research, ROI, etc.): _____

Bottom line (one sentence): Why marketing careers need BOTH creative AND analytical skills to survive a weak economy.

(d(1)(C), d(3)(I), d(5)(C))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Allow students to read their pitch from a notecard (not memorized). Provide a fill-in-the-blank pitch template ("Our product is _. It's for . We will reach them through __. People will buy it because _____.").
  • Extension: Students who finish their pitch early write a 2-paragraph "marketing resume" describing themselves as a marketing freelancer (skills, experience, services offered, target clients).
  • ELL: Allow pitch in Spanish or bilingual format. DFW has a huge Spanish-language marketing industry, bilingual marketers are highly paid. Pre-teach: Pitch = Presentación corta, Audience = Audiencia, Channel = Canal.

docs.title: Week 3: Sell It — Business Marketing Careers
docs.text: 6th Six Weeks | Marketing Cluster | 5 class periods (50 min each)

docs.title: Lesson Objective
docs.text:
Students explore Marketing careers within the Business, Marketing, and Finance cluster through the Hats & Ladders app and the Find Your Future workbook, write call-to-action ad copy for four products and build an ad mock-up in "Click Factor," draft a Little Library social media post in "Powerskill: Written Communication," analyze how economic conditions affect marketing employment, turn one personal skill into a consulting business in "Expert Edge," and read three marketing data sets to choose and defend a campaign strategy in "Powerskill: Data-Informed Decision Making."

Learning Target: I can name at least three marketing careers, write a call to action that fits a product and its audience, build a consulting service I could really offer, and use data to pick a marketing strategy.

Success Criteria: I will know I am successful when my ad mock-up has a headline, a short description, and my chosen call to action, when my consulting page names the service, the offer, the price, and carries a logo, when my Family Fun Pass pitch names the strategy I picked and the numbers behind it, and when my economic conditions chart is filled in for both a strong and a weak economy.

docs.title: Demonstration of Learning
docs.text: "I can describe at least three marketing careers, explain how economic changes affect marketing job availability, write a call to action that matches a product and its audience, and design a consulting service with a name, an offer, a price, and a logo."

docs.title: TEKS Alignment
docs.text:
• d(1)(C): Identify various career opportunities within the Marketing cluster (Days 1-5; researched on Day 4).
  • d(3)(I): Define entrepreneurship and identify entrepreneurial opportunities in marketing (Day 3 consulting business, Day 5 pitch).
  • d(5)(C): Analyze effects of changing societal needs and economic conditions on employment trends and career choices (Day 2 economic conditions chart).

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Chromebooks with internet access (1 per student)
  • Hats & Ladders student accounts + Find Your Future workbook, Business, Marketing, and Finance chapter (printed pp. 221-254)
  • Find Your Future workbook pp. 147-148, "Powerskill: Written Communication" (Powerskills in Action chapter, not the Business chapter)
  • BLS, Market Research Analysts: bls.gov/ooh/business-and-financial/market-research-analysts.htm
  • Google Applied Digital Skills: applieddigitalskills.withgoogle.com (Day 4 extension)
  • eDynamic Learning Unit 4.1: Enterprise and Money Matters
  • Xello School Subjects at Work lesson (supplemental; not a Bowie Grade 8 completion standard)
  • Printed blank ad mock-up sheets (1 per student) for "Click Factor" Step 4 (FYF p. 230)
  • Sticky notes for the "Expert Edge" skill brainstorm (FYF p. 222) and the Little Library brainstorm (FYF p. 147)
  • Printed marketing career research worksheet (CCE artifact; the research format is taught in Wk0)
  • Printed Economic Conditions Analysis chart (CCE artifact)
  • Canva for Education (ad mock-ups, logos, social posts)

docs.title: Career Connection
docs.text:
Marketing is the work of finding an audience and giving that audience a reason to act. In DFW, that work happens inside corporations such as AT&T, American Airlines, Toyota, Mary Kay, and Frito-Lay, at marketing and advertising agencies, and through freelance work. Students compare Marketing Manager and Brand Manager with digital roles such as Social Media Manager, Content Creator, and SEO Specialist.

What is Happening at Irving ISD? Business, Marketing and Finance (Business Management plus Marketing and Sales) is offered at Irving High School and Nimitz High School, with Entrepreneurship & Small Business as its industry certification. MacArthur High School runs its own School of Business and Entrepreneurship, holding Administrative Management, Entrepreneurship, Real Estate Marketing, and Sales Management. Cardwell Career Preparatory Center offers Business Management and Entrepreneurship through its School of Workforce Readiness. Marketing is not offered at Singley Academy. The workbook's district pages describe a Marketing & Sales program of study built on market research, advertising, branding, product promotion, and data-driven decision making; students who have produced content, photography, and social media pitches for Irving ISD events; student-operated school stores; and two student organizations, DECA and Business Professionals of America (BPA) (FYF pp. 252-253: "What is Happening at My District?"). Those pages also name a Retail Management program of study that no campus page lists, so treat that one as [VERIFY with CTE coordinator] before telling students where to take it.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text:
• Marketing: The process of promoting, selling, and distributing a product or service. Includes advertising, market research, branding, and social media.
  • Market Research: The process of gathering information about consumers' needs and preferences to guide business decisions.
  • Target Audience: The specific group of people a marketing campaign is designed to reach.
  • Call to Action (CTA): The part of an ad that tells the audience what to do next, like "Buy Now" or "Sign up today." The five types students use this week are Benefit, Urgency, Curiosity, Direct Command, and Incentive.
  • Mock-Up: A rough draft or sketch of an ad that shows the headline, the description, and where the call to action sits before the real ad is built.
  • Consultant: Someone who sells skill and knowledge instead of a product. Consultants listen to a client, figure out what the client needs, and deliver advice, coaching, or a plan.
  • Mission Statement: One or two sentences naming the purpose of a business and who it serves.
  • Data-Informed Decision Making: Using real information, not guesses, to choose what to do. Marketers use it to pick which campaign to run.
  • Economic Conditions: The state of the economy at a given time, including factors like employment rates, consumer spending, and business growth.

docs.title: Bridge to Theory (Hats & Ladders)
docs.text:
The Find Your Future workbook gives Business, Marketing, and Finance printed pages 221 to 254. The chapter opener (FYF p. 221: "Exploring the World of BUSINESS, MARKETING, AND FINANCE") frames the cluster as helping organizations grow, connect with customers, and make smart financial decisions, puts a "Be the Decision Maker" spending dilemma in front of students, and introduces three Hats on the page: Business Analyst, Financial Examiner, and E-Commerce Specialist. The chapter prints no pathway list. Students meet the cluster's pathways in the Hats & Ladders app through the Pathway Possibilities step on the App Exploration page (FYF p. 254: "App Exploration"), and they meet Irving ISD's own programs of study on the district pages (FYF pp. 252-253: "What is Happening at My District?").

Four workbook activities carry this week:

  • Click Factor (Day 1): Career Climb activity. Students are digital marketing specialists whose team needs ads that make people act, not just look. They find and compare the call to action in two printed ads, then write two contrasting CTAs for each of four products (Local Car Wash, Cooking Class, After-School Snack Box, Fishing Gear) using a five-type reference table, pair up with another group to pick the strongest CTA per product, and build an ad mock-up with a headline, a short description, and their chosen CTA (FYF pp. 225-227 and 230: "Click Factor").
  • Powerskill: Written Communication (Day 2): Students run the social media account for a neighborhood Little Library. They brainstorm the library's status on sticky notes, then write one post that states the status clearly, carries a call to action, and uses at least two hashtags, against the workbook's four tips for effective written communication (FYF pp. 147-148: "Powerskill: Written Communication"). This lesson sits in the Powerskills in Action chapter, so the page jump is backward from the Business chapter.
  • Expert Edge (Day 3): Career Climb activity. Students open a consulting business built on a skill they already have. They brainstorm three skills on sticky notes and name who needs each one, choose one to build on, then write the service name, the offer, a mission statement, a price, and one extra add-on, design a logo, and pitch the service to a partner who rates it for clarity, creativity, and persuasiveness (FYF pp. 222-224: "Expert Edge").
  • Powerskill: Data-Informed Decision Making (Day 4): Teams launching a "Family Fun Pass" family subscription read three data sets, an audience preference table by age, a past campaign performance table, and five focus group quotes, choose one marketing strategy from six, and build a short pitch naming the strategy, the data behind it, and why families would respond (FYF pp. 229 and 228: "Powerskill: Data-Informed Decision Making").

Two workbook pages are printed out of order

Pages 228 and 230 were transposed at the printer. "Click Factor" runs 225, 226, 227, and then 230 for Step 4. "Powerskill: Data-Informed Decision Making" opens on 229 and continues on 228 for Steps 2, 3, and 4. Tell students the page jump before they open the book so nobody loses activity time hunting for the next step.

The rest of this chapter is taught in other weeks and referenced here, not adopted: Million Dollar Idea (FYF pp. 234-237) ran in 3SW Wk6, Flip This House (FYF pp. 238-240) and Powerskill: Visual Storytelling (FYF pp. 231-233) ran in 5SW Wk6, and the 30-second sales pitch (FYF pp. 241-243), Powerskill: Problem Solving (FYF pp. 244-247), and Make the Call: CEO Edition (FYF pp. 248-251) sit in the Sales and Presentations week that follows this one. Day 5's Mini Marketing Plan pitch is a CCE-authored structure, not a workbook activity, and every line of it traces back to the student's own Click Factor, Expert Edge, and Family Fun Pass pages.

docs.title: IISD Instructional Strategies
docs.text:
• Think-Pair-Share: Day 1, Activity 2, Step 1 of "Click Factor" (FYF p. 225), where partners hunt the call to action in the two printed ads. Distinguished: release the workbook's four questions one at a time, hold a silent 30 second Think on which CTA feels stronger, then time Partner A for 30 seconds and Partner B for 30 seconds, and post two stems at different levels: "Ad ___ has the stronger call to action because _" and "Ad ___ fits its product better because its audience is and it asks them to __." Ask two pairs to share, not one. Listen while pairs talk for who argues from the audience rather than from the artwork, and pick your share-out pairs from what you heard rather than from raised hands.
  • Stop and Jot: Day 1, Activity 1, the two pauses in the Business, Marketing, and Finance cluster tour video and the workbook's own "What is one thing that you learned?" line on the App Exploration page (FYF p. 254). Distinguished: name both stop points before the video starts, give 45 seconds per jot with the prompt on screen, and offer two stems: "One marketing career I did not know existed is _" and "One question I still have about how companies choose their ads is ___." Read jots over shoulders during both pauses and track which careers get named. If most jots say Social Media Manager only, steer the Hat Finder browse toward Market Research Analyst, Business Analyst, and E-Commerce Specialist so Day 4's research worksheets are not five copies of the same career.
  • Active Monitoring: Day 3, Activity 1, the four steps of "Expert Edge" (FYF pp. 222-224). Distinguished: walk a fixed pathway four times, one lap per step, each lap carrying a single target (lap 1 three skills written with a named person who needs each one, lap 2 an offer that names something the client receives, lap 3 a logo readable at arm's length, lap 4 a pitch that lands under two minutes). Carry the workbook's own partner feedback categories on the clipboard, Clarity, Creativity, and Persuasiveness, and mark them as you pass. Have the feedback ready before class for the two predictable misses: an offer written as a topic ("I help with math") instead of a service, and a price with no unit attached. If more than a handful of students miss the lap 2 target, pause the room and rewrite one volunteer's offer on the projector instead of fixing it desk by desk.
  • Chunking: Day 4, Activity 2, the three data sets in Step 1 of "Powerskill: Data-Informed Decision Making" (FYF p. 229). Distinguished: release one data set at a time, say what each one answers before students read it (the age table says who prefers which channel, the campaign table says what actually sold, the focus group quotes say why), and take the thumbs check between sets before releasing the next. Note which set draws the most thumbs down. If it is the campaign table, spend the re-teach on the gap between clicks and sales before Step 2 opens, and let the groups who cleared all three sets start drafting their pitch early instead of waiting.
  • Time, Voice, Body (TVB): Day 5, Activity 1, the one-minute Mini Marketing Plan pitches. Distinguished: post the three blocks before the first pitch, Voice 1 for drafting and partner practice, Voice 0 while a group member is pitching, Voice 2 for the Two Stars and a Wish feedback, and run the visible 60 second countdown already written into the plan for every pitch. State where presenters stand and where notecards go so the rotation does not eat pitch time. Narrate the groups that are meeting the expectation rather than correcting the ones that are not. If the third pitch in a group is running long, cut feedback to one star and announce the change before the next presenter starts.

docs.title: Summative Assessment
docs.text: Marketing Plan Pitch (Day 5): Students present a 1-minute Mini Marketing Plan summary that includes: product or service name, target audience, marketing channel, key message, and economic justification ("This will sell because..."). Most students pitch the consulting service they built in "Expert Edge" on Day 3; the marketing channel comes from the same six-option list they worked in the Family Fun Pass activity on Day 4. Scored on marketing career knowledge (d(1)(C)), entrepreneurship application (d(3)(I)), and economic awareness (d(5)(C)).

docs.title: Scaffolded Learning
docs.text:
• Provide three sample CTAs per product for "Click Factor" Step 2, already labeled by type, so students revise instead of starting from a blank line
  • Provide an "Expert Edge" starter list of eight consulting skills (gaming coach, homework tutor, sneaker cleaning, phone photography, art commissions, party DJ, pet sitting, bike repair) so students choose rather than invent
  • Highlight the two largest numbers in each column of the Family Fun Pass data tables so students start from the pattern instead of hunting for it
  • Allow students to present their Mini Marketing Plan in written format if oral presentation is too challenging

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
• Students write CTAs for a fifth product of their own choosing and label which of the five types each one uses
  • Research a real DFW marketing agency (Tracy Locke, The Richards Group) and present what services it offers
  • Students who finish "Expert Edge" early add a referral offer to their service and explain what it costs them and what it earns them
  • Design TWO ad mock-ups for the same product targeting two different audiences and explain what changed and why

docs.title: ELL Language Support
docs.text:
• Pre-teach: Marketing = Mercadotecnia, Brand = Marca, Target Audience = Audiencia objetivo, Call to Action = Llamada a la acción, Consultant = Consultor, Data = Datos
  • Bilingual ad mock-up and social post templates with Spanish CTA options
  • Students may write the campaign in Spanish or make it bilingual; DFW audiences encounter marketing in both languages
  • The workbook reads well above grade level, so read the scenario paragraphs aloud and encourage browser translation for any independent reading
  • Pair ESL students with bilingual peers during pitch presentations

docs.title: Day 1: Sales Pathway + What Makes a Sales Pitch Work
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Explore Sales and Marketing careers in the Hats & Ladders app; learn the four parts of a sales pitch; choose a product or service and profile the audience for it TEKS d(1)(C), d(4)(B) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Sales pathway tour and salary check · Explain: The four parts of a pitch · Explore: Product choice and audience profile · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Product or service chosen + written audience profile Materials Chromebooks, H&L accounts, Find Your Future workbook pp. 241-242, 252-254, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Have you ever tried to convince someone to give you something, buy you something, lend you something, agree to a plan? What strategy did you use?

Take 4-5 responses. Pull out the words students use to convince someone: a reason, a benefit, or a direct request. Sales turns those same moves into a planned message for a buyer.

docs.title: Activity 1: H&L Sales Pathway Tour (10 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 254: "App Exploration") + (FYF pp. 252-253: "What is Happening at My District?")

Direct students into the Business, Marketing, and Finance cluster in the app and let them browse the Hats inside it. The workbook's district pages describe the Marketing and Sales program of study as preparation for careers in market research, advertising, branding, product promotion, and data-driven decision making, which is a wider job than the word "sales" suggests to most students.

[H&L PLATFORM] Open the Hats & Ladders app, go to Clusters, and click the Business, Marketing, and Finance cluster. Students browse Sales-specific Hats: Sales Manager, Account Executive, Retail Manager, Sales Representative, Inside Sales Specialist. Open "Pathway Possibilities" and rate at least one pathway.

Quick salary check (5 min): Students look up Sales Manager on bls.gov/ooh/management/sales-managers.htm. The median pay nationally is around $135K, with the top 10% over $200K. Sales is one of the highest-paying business careers WITHOUT requiring a graduate degree.

The big idea: many people think sales is "annoying phone calls." Real sales is more like consulting, understanding what customers need and helping them solve a problem. The best salespeople are great listeners.

Facilitation Tip

Students often write off sales as a career because of the stereotype. Counter it directly: "Real sales is helping people solve problems they have. The 'annoying salesperson' stereotype is bad sales, and bad salespeople don't last. Good salespeople build long-term relationships." Repeat this until at least one student rethinks their assumption.

docs.title: Activity 2: 30 Seconds to Sell — Steps 1-3 (30 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 241-242: "30 Seconds to Sell", Steps 1-3)

Open the workbook to page 241 and set the frame the activity uses: students are an entrepreneur who has started their own business, and one of their main jobs is selling what they built. In sales you rarely get a long explanation. Sometimes you get a few seconds. That is why sales professionals build a 30-second pitch, a message short enough to deliver in about half a minute and strong enough to make someone act.

Step 1: What Is a Sales Pitch? (10 min)

Walk the four parts of a strong pitch on the projector, one at a time, and say what each part is doing before moving to the next:

Part What it does Hook Grabs attention right away What it is Explains clearly what you are selling Benefits Says how it helps the customer Call to action Tells the customer what to do next

Then read the workbook's SparkClean Toothbrush example on p. 241 aloud once at normal speed, and a second time stopping after each sentence so students can name which of the four parts they just heard. The point the workbook makes with that example: a good pitch skips the detail list and keeps only what matters most.

Step 2: Choose What You're Selling (5 min)

Each student picks ONE and writes it in the workbook:

  • A product (game, app, snack, clothing item)
  • A service (landscaping, tutoring, pet care, cleaning)
  • Their own idea

Step 3: Know Your Audience (15 min)

Students choose the audience they are trying to convince from the workbook's list, students, parents, gamers, pet owners, busy families, or their own, and then answer the workbook's question: what does that audience care about most?

Stop and Jot: Give 90 seconds on the workbook prompt "What does your audience care about most?" The expectation is three lines, not three words. Post two stems: "My audience cares most about _ because " and "If I said __, my audience would stop listening because _____." Read jots over shoulders while students write. If most of the room names price and nothing else, put time, effort, and how the product makes the buyer look on the board before students move on.

With the remaining minutes, pairs trade audience profiles and each partner names one benefit that would land with the OTHER person's audience. Students write it in the margin of their own page. This is raw material for the pitch they write tomorrow.

Facilitation Tip

Walk around with one prompt: "Who is this for, and what do they want?" Students who cannot answer the second half will write a pitch that lists features instead of benefits. Push them to finish the sentence "This matters to my audience because _____" before they leave.

DOK 3: Two students are selling the exact same product but to different audiences. Why would the benefits they name be different? Use your own audience to explain.

DELIVERABLE: Product or service chosen + written audience profile naming what that audience cares about most.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Mini-Case / Scenario Application) · Printable PDF:

Scenario: Marcus is selling a $40 study headset that blocks noise. He wrote ONE pitch and used the same words with two very different audiences. To parents he said, "It blocks noise so homework gets done faster." To gamers he said the exact same sentence.

  1. Did that same sentence fit BOTH audiences? YES / NO

  2. ONE reason:

  1. What I am selling: _____

  2. My audience: _____

  3. ONE thing my audience cares about most:

  1. Circle ONE sales job you saw in the app today that you would want to try:

Sales Manager · Account Executive · Retail Manager · Sales Representative · Inside Sales Specialist

  1. Knowing what your audience cares about is a skill. Name ONE job that is NOT a sales job but still needs that same skill, and say why:

Job: _____

Why it needs that skill: ______

(d(1)(C), d(4)(B))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Give students a shortlist of three products and three audiences to choose from instead of an open choice. Provide the SparkClean example with the four parts already labeled in the margin so students can match their own pitch against a model. Allow the audience profile to be two lines instead of three.
  • Extension: Students write a second audience profile for the SAME product aimed at a different group, then list the two benefits that would have to change.
  • ELL: Pair ESL students with bilingual peers for the audience trade. Allow the audience profile to be written in Spanish and translated later. Pre-teach: Pitch = Presentación de venta, Audience = Audiencia, Benefit = Beneficio, Customer = Cliente.

docs.title: Day 2: Write and Practice Your 30-Second Pitch
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Plan the four parts of a sales pitch; write it in 4-6 sentences; practice it against a 30-second check; deliver it to a partner and record two pieces of feedback TEKS d(4)(B) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Pitch plan and draft · Explain: Partner delivery and feedback · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Written 4-6 sentence pitch + two recorded pieces of partner feedback Materials Chromebooks, Find Your Future workbook pp. 242-243, timer, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Think of a time someone gave you feedback that helped you improve. What made it useful, was it the words they used, the timing, the way they said it, or what?

Take 3-4 responses. Sort them into feedback a speaker can act on and feedback that gives no next step. Students will write and rehearse a pitch, trade it with a partner, and use one specific suggestion in the second version.

docs.title: Activity 1: 30 Seconds to Sell — Plan and Write the Pitch (25 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 242-243: "30 Seconds to Sell", Steps 4-5)

Step 4: Plan Your Pitch (10 min)

Students return to the product or service and the audience profile they wrote yesterday and use the workbook's planning space to sketch one line for each of the four parts:

  • Hook: How will you grab attention in the first few seconds?
  • What it is: What are you selling? Clear and simple.
  • Benefits: How does it help the customer, and why does that matter?
  • Call to action: What should the customer do next?

The audience profile decides the benefits line. A student selling the same snack to gamers and to busy parents writes two different benefit lines, and this is the step where that shows up.

Step 5: Write Your 30-Second Sales Pitch (15 min)

Students write the full pitch, about 4 to 6 sentences, in the workbook. The workbook sets three requirements for the draft:

  • Keep it clear and easy to understand
  • Focus on benefits, not just features
  • Make it exciting, engaging, and confident

Active Monitoring: Walk a fixed pathway twice while students draft. Lap 1 target: every pitch has a call to action, because that is the part students drop most often. Lap 2 target: at least one line names a benefit and not a feature. Have the feedback ready for the two predictable problems before class starts, a pitch that ends with "so yeah, that's it" and a pitch that is a specification list with no person in it. If more than a handful of drafts miss the lap 2 target, stop the room and reproject the SparkClean example from p. 241 with the benefit sentence underlined rather than fixing it desk by desk.

Facilitation Tip

Read one anonymous draft aloud at 30 seconds and one at 55 seconds without saying which is which, then ask students which one they stayed with. Length is easier to feel than to explain, and students trim their own drafts faster after hearing the difference.

docs.title: Activity 2: 30 Seconds to Sell — Practice, Deliver, and Give Feedback (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 243: "30 Seconds to Sell", Steps 6-7)

Step 6: Practice and Deliver (5 min)

Students practice the pitch out loud, quietly and at their own desk, and run the workbook's three self-checks:

  • Can you say it in about 30 seconds?
  • Are you speaking clearly, confidently, and with energy?
  • Does your pitch sound natural and engaging?

Before pairs form, remind the class of the feedback sandwich from the communication week: name something the person did well, name one thing to improve using specific language rather than "it was confusing," then close on a strength. This structure is CCE scaffolding used all year, not a workbook page, so students will not find it in the book.

Step 7: Partner Up (10 min)

Think-Pair-Share: 30 seconds of silent Think while each student reads their own pitch through once, then Partner A delivers for 30 seconds and Partner B responds with a feedback sandwich, then the pair switches. Post two feedback stems at different levels: "Your hook worked because _" and "I would change so the benefit is clearer, because right now it sounds like __." Each student records two pieces of feedback in the workbook space on p. 243. Ask two pairs, not one, to deliver again for the whole class, and choose them from what you heard while circulating rather than from raised hands.

Close with the workbook's own discussion question: why is it important to make a strong first impression in sales? Hold student answers. Day 4 turns that same question toward interviews.

DOK 2: What is the difference between a feature and a benefit? Quote one line from your own pitch and say which one it is.

DELIVERABLE: Written 4-6 sentence pitch + two recorded pieces of partner feedback.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Diagnostic MCQ with Misconception Distractors) · Printable PDF:

Circle the BEST answer for each question.

  1. Which line is a BENEFIT and not just a feature?

a) "It has a 5,000 mAh battery."

b) "It charges in 20 minutes, so you never get stuck at school with a dead phone."

c) "It comes in four colors."

d) "It was released this year."

  1. Which is the STRONGEST feedback on a partner's pitch?

a) "Good job!"

b) "I didn't really get it."

c) "Your hook made me look up, but you never said what I should do next. Add a call to action."

d) "You should change everything."

  1. A partner gives you a "wish" (something to improve). The BEST response is:

a) Defend your pitch out loud

b) Say thank you, write it down, decide later what to use

c) Change it on the spot even if you disagree

d) Ignore it, it is your product

  1. Circle EVERY job below where a person has to give feedback that is specific enough to act on:

coach · nurse · game tester · cashier · film director

  1. Pick ONE job you circled. What are they giving feedback ON?

Job: _____

They give feedback on: _______

  1. ONE change I made to MY pitch after partner feedback today:

(d(4)(B))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a pitch planner with the four parts pre-labeled and the SparkClean example written in a second column as a model. Allow a 3-sentence pitch instead of 4 to 6. Provide feedback sentence stems ("Your _ was strong because " / "I would change __ because _____").
  • Extension: Students write a second version of the same pitch for a different audience and mark the one sentence that had to change the most.
  • ELL: Allow the pitch to be drafted in Spanish and delivered bilingually. Pair ESL students with bilingual peers for Step 7. The feedback sandwich works in any language. Pre-teach: Feature = Característica, Benefit = Beneficio, Call to action = Llamado a la acción.

docs.title: Day 3: Campaign Rescue + Career Presentation Outline
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Analyze a marketing campaign that reached the right audience and still underperformed; brainstorm and choose fixes; build a mini campaign plan and present it; outline the individual 3-minute career presentation for Day 5 TEKS d(4)(C), d(1)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Campaign analysis and brainstorm · Explain: Redesign share-out · Extend: Career presentation outline · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Team problem statement, three chosen solutions, and mini campaign plan + individual career presentation outline Materials Chromebooks, Find Your Future workbook pp. 244-247, sticky notes, printed Career Presentation Outline template, printed Career Presentation Rubric, projector, timer

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Think of an ad you have seen recently that did NOT work on you. What made you scroll past it, skip it, or ignore it?

Take 3 responses. Then give students the day's problem: the campaign reached its intended audience and still failed. Their job is to find the break between reaching people and persuading them.

docs.title: Activity 1: Powerskill Problem Solving — BrainBoost Bars Campaign Rescue (25 min)
docs.text:
