Students complete the full job-seeking skill set: identify the steps of an effective job search and record what employers actually ask for in two real local job postings, write a cover letter and thank-you letter, complete a sample job application, learn the protocol for selecting and using references, and participate in a mock interview demonstrating professional appearance and communication.

Learning Target: I can name the steps of a job search, read what an employer asks for in a real job posting, write a cover letter and a thank-you letter, fill out a job application, pick three references and ask one for permission, and interview for a job.

Success Criteria: I will know I am successful when both of my job posting pages list the job title, the skills, and the education the employer wants, when my cover letter has a header, a greeting, three paragraphs, and a closing, when every line of my practice application is filled in and easy to read, when my reference list names three people and says why each one, when I have drafted a permission email to one of them, and when my mock interview is scored on the rubric and my thank-you letter is written.

docs.title: Demonstration of Learning
docs.text: "I can complete a job application, write a cover letter and thank-you letter, select appropriate references, and participate in a mock interview with professional appearance and communication."

docs.title: TEKS Alignment
docs.text:
• d(6)(A): Identify the steps of an effective job search (Day 1).
  • d(6)(B): Describe appropriate appearance for an interview (Days 4, 5).
  • d(6)(C): Participate in a mock interview (Day 4 fishbowl, Day 5 all students).
  • d(7)(B): Write business correspondence including a cover letter and thank-you letter (Days 2, 5).
  • d(7)(C): Complete sample job applications (Day 3).
  • d(7)(D): Describe the protocol for selecting and using references (Day 3).

docs.title: Career Connection
docs.text:
Students assemble the full professional-document set (cover letter, application, references, thank-you letter) and practice a mock interview with peer feedback. These are the documents and the interview format used in any job application across every Irving ISD pathway.

What is Happening at Irving ISD? This week's content is universal across all Irving ISD CTE pathways, every pathway eventually requires students to interview, apply, and provide references when they enter the workforce. The week still closes the Business, Marketing, and Finance cluster, and the workbook's district pages (FYF pp. 252-253: "What is Happening at My District?") name the six programs of study inside it: Business Management, Administrative Management, Retail Management, Real Estate, Entrepreneurship, and Marketing and Sales. Business Management focuses on leadership, organizational operations, and decision making. Administrative Management focuses on administrative procedures, professional communication, and organizational skills, which is the exact skill set this week assesses. Students in the Business and Marketing programs run student-operated school stores on their campuses and sell products they designed themselves. The district pages list Entrepreneurship and Small Business as the industry certification and DECA and Business Professionals of America (BPA) as the student organizations. Programs of study are offered at different campuses, so confirm which campus carries which one before naming a school to students. [VERIFY with CTE coordinator]

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text:
• Job Posting: An employer's public listing for an open job. It names the title, the duties, the skills required, and the education or experience wanted.
  • Cover Letter: A one-page letter sent with a resume introducing yourself and explaining why you want a specific position.
  • Job Application: A formal document providing an employer with your personal information, work history, education, and references.
  • References: People who can speak positively about your character, skills, and work ethic to a potential employer.
  • Mock Interview: A practice interview that simulates a real job interview, used for rehearsal and feedback.
  • Thank-You Letter: A brief letter sent within 24 hours of an interview thanking the interviewer and reaffirming your interest.
  • Greeting / Salutation: The opening line of a business letter, usually "Dear [Name]:", addressed to a specific person if possible.

docs.title: Bridge to Theory (Hats & Ladders)
docs.text:
The Find Your Future workbook has no job interview activity, interview question set, dress-code page, application form, cover letter, or thank-you letter. Those parts of this week are CCE-authored and carry no workbook citation. Use the printed templates as the source; there is no workbook page for students to find.

The workbook supplies three pieces that feed the CCE templates:

  • Rung 5: Local Connections (FYF pp. 290-291): students search actual job postings in their community for the career they chose on Rung 2, using searches like "[career name] jobs near me," then record for each of two postings the job title, the location, where they found it, two or three listed responsibilities, the required skills and qualifications, and the education and experience the employer wants. Students practiced this form earlier in the six weeks. This week is where Rung 5 is completed for credit, and it becomes the employer-expectation input for the cover letter on Days 1-2 and the practice application on Day 3.
  • Rung 4: Strengths Interview (FYF pp. 287-289): the out-of-class interview students were assigned earlier in the six weeks and carry into this week. Part 1 has them name a trusted adult to interview, plan questions from a provided list, and add at least two questions of their own. Part 2 is interview notes, and "Make Meaning of What You Heard" is the reflection. It is an informational interview with a trusted adult, not a job interview, so this week uses it for interview conduct only: what a prepared interviewer does, and what the asking side of the table feels like. The Rung 4 pages themselves are debriefed in the capstone week.
  • Make the Call: CEO Edition (FYF pp. 248-251): the Business chapter's Career Climb activity and the closest match in the book to this week's Office Manager, Executive Assistant, and Human Resources Specialist Hats. Partners run Summit Gear, review a six-situation Situation Board, sort each situation into Act Today, Plan This Week, or Monitor and Decide Later on a CEO Priority Map, justify one placement from each category, align with another pair, then absorb a CEO Curveball that cuts the budget 20 percent and removes a department leader. It runs as the Day 1 extension because every minute of the five days is already carrying a job-skills standard.
  • What is Happening at My District? (FYF pp. 252-253) and App Exploration (FYF p. 254) carry the Business, Marketing, and Finance cluster's district content and the app path used on Day 1.

docs.title: IISD Instructional Strategies
docs.text:
• Think-Pair-Share: Day 4, Activity 1, the partner read of the Interview Readiness Guide and the one-tip share-out. Distinguished: assign the read as partner work, hold a silent 30 second Think on "which of these would I forget on the day," then time Partner A for 30 seconds and Partner B for 30 seconds, and post two stems at different levels: "The tip I would most likely forget is _ because " and "Arriving 15 minutes early tells an employer __ before I say a word." Ask two pairs to share, not one. Listen while pairs talk for who names appearance and who names timing, then pick your two share-out pairs so both show up before Day 5 rather than taking raised hands.
  • Stop and Jot: Day 1, Activity 1, the notes students take as the seven steps go up on the board. Distinguished: name the jot before the first step goes up, give 45 seconds after Step 3 and again after Step 7 with the prompt on screen, and offer two stems: "Step _ is one I have already done this year, because " and "The step I would most likely skip is __, and skipping it would cost me _____." Read jots over shoulders during both pauses. If most students name Step 4 as the one they would skip, use the live posting search that follows to show that a posting tells you exactly what an application is going to ask for.
  • Active Monitoring: Day 5, Activity 1, the two paired mock interview rounds. Distinguished: walk a fixed pathway three times, one target per lap (lap 1 both partners have their question sheet out and the timer running, lap 2 the interviewee is holding eye contact and answering in more than one sentence, lap 3 the interviewer is scoring the rubric instead of watching), and score two or three students directly on the same rubric the students are using. Have feedback ready before class for the two known failures: a "tell me about yourself" answer that turns into a life story, and an interviewer who reads all eight questions without waiting for the answers. If more than a handful of pairs stall on the problem-solving question, pause the room, model one 30 second problem story, and restart the round.
  • Chunking: Day 3, Activity 1, the practice application walked section by section. Distinguished: project one section at a time (Personal Information, Education, Employment History, Skills, Availability, References, Signature), say what the employer is checking in that section before students write anything in it, and close each section with a check that every line in it is filled and legible before releasing the next. Note which section produces the most blanks. Employment History is the usual one, and if it stalls the room, stop and reteach that babysitting, lawn care, and family business help all count before students move on to Skills.
  • Time, Voice, Body (TVB): Day 5, Activity 1, the two interview rounds. Distinguished: post the three blocks before the first round, Voice 0 while partners read their prepared answers, Voice 2 for the interviews so two pairs can work side by side without shouting, and a visible countdown for every round with a short feedback window between. Define where the interviewer sits, where the interviewee sits, and where phones go for the whole period. Narrate the pairs who start on time rather than correcting the ones who do not. If the first round runs past the countdown, cut the feedback window to one star and one wish and announce the change before the switch.

docs.text:
• Sentence-by-sentence cover letter template with blanks for students to fill in

docs.title: Day 1: The Career Iceberg + Rung 4 Strengths Interview Debrief
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Compare what sits on top of a career iceberg with what sits underneath it; build a personal career-exploration iceberg; make meaning of the Rung 4 Strengths Interview and connect what a trusted adult said back to the Rung 2 career goal TEKS d(8)(A) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: Trophy iceberg example · Explore: Personal iceberg and Rung 4 debrief · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Personal career iceberg + the five Make Meaning answers on FYF p. 289 Materials Find Your Future workbook pp. 6-8 and pp. 287-289, students' completed Rung 4 interview notes, Week 0 My Career Journey reflections from the class folder, printed iceberg template, Chromebooks, H&L accounts, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Find your Week 0 My Career Journey sheet and read the one career you wrote down in September. Then open your H&L Climber Profile and count your favorited careers. What changed?

Take 4-5 student responses. This forces students to confront how much data they have already gathered. Most have 15+ favorites across 8+ clusters, and many will find that their September career is not the one they are about to present. Both outcomes are growth, and both are evidence they can use later in the week.

docs.title: Activity 1: The Career Iceberg (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 6-8: "The Career Iceberg"), a Career Climb activity in the World of Work chapter

Read the page 6 framing together. Some careers seem simple at first, because a job title is easy to guess at. Underneath the surface, careers are more complex than they appear: workers solve problems, communicate, make decisions, and handle challenges people do not notice right away. Careers are like an iceberg. On top is what you think the job does. Underneath are the deeper skills, responsibilities, and challenges that are also part of the job.

The iceberg opens the workbook, it does not close it

The Career Iceberg is printed in the World of Work chapter at the front of the book, not in the Capstone chapter. Students met it in the fall. Do not introduce it as a final-chapter activity. Introduce it as the first thing the book taught them, brought back on the last week so they can see how much is now under their own water line.

Step 1: Look at the example (3 min): The workbook's printed example is an iceberg about winning a trophy in a sports competition (FYF p. 6). Think-Pair-Share: 30 seconds of silent Think while partners read the page, then Partner A for 30 seconds and Partner B for 30 seconds comparing what is printed on top with what is printed underneath, then two pairs share with the whole class. The book's own question is the prompt: what does this tell you about winning first place?

Step 2: Create your own iceberg (10 min): Students build a personal Career Exploration Iceberg on the printed template, in Google Drawings, or in Canva. The specs below are CCE's, not the workbook's. Pages 7 and 8 print two blank iceberg frames, labeled Electrician and Nurse, for students to research and fill in, and they set no required number of items.

  • A title
  • At least 3 words or images on TOP of the iceberg: what people see (your career goal, your favorite cluster, your dream job)
  • At least 10 words or images UNDERNEATH the iceberg: what people do not see (your Discover Your Core result, every career research worksheet, the mock interview, the resume, the cover letter, the thank-you email, the personal budget, every Career Climb activity you finished)

The visible items are aspirational. The underwater items are evidence of the work already done across 36 weeks.

Step 3: Reflect (2 min): Write a one-sentence reflection at the bottom of the iceberg: "Looking at my underwater work, the most important thing I learned about career exploration is _____."

Facilitation Tip

Have students count the items they put underwater. If a student has fewer than 5, send them back through each six-weeks block and ask for one project, one piece of research, or one skill from each. The page should show the work that sits underneath the final presentation.

DOK 4: In what ways do the things underneath your iceberg AFFECT the things on top? Use a specific example from your iceberg.

docs.title: Activity 2: Rung 4 Debrief — Make Meaning of Your Strengths Interview (25 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 287-289: "Rung 4: Strengths Interview")

Rung 4 is the one rung the ladder cannot build in class, because it needs an adult outside the room. It was assigned as a take-home two weeks ago: interview a trusted adult (a family member, a teacher, a coach, or a mentor) using the workbook's five questions plus at least two of the student's own, and record the answers in the Interview Notes box (FYF p. 288). Today the class does the half that has to happen here, which is deciding what the interview meant.

Step 1: Make Meaning of What You Heard (15 min). Students answer the five prompts on page 289:

  1. What is one strength they mentioned that you agree with?
  2. What is one strength or idea that surprised you?
  3. Did they suggest a career you had not thought about before?
  4. How does this connect to your career choice from Rung 2?
  5. Will this change your thinking about your future? Yes or no, and why or why not?

Questions 4 and 5 are the ones that matter for the rest of the week, because they are where a student either confirms the career goal they have been building since January or names the reason they are adjusting it. Both answers are legitimate. Neither is a failure.

Active Monitoring: walk a fixed pathway three times, one target per lap. Lap 1, the interview notes are actually written on page 288 rather than remembered. Lap 2, all five Make Meaning prompts are answered. Lap 3, the answer to question 4 names the Rung 2 career by name. Have the feedback ready before class for the two predictable problems: a student who copied the adult's words without saying whether they agree, and a student who answers question 5 with a bare yes or no. The pivot: if more than a handful stall on question 4, pause the room and model one connection out loud using a career nobody in the class picked.

Step 2: Check the ladder (10 min). Students open their workbooks and confirm that the rungs built earlier are actually filled in: Rungs 1-3 (FYF pp. 281-286) from the mid-year career-planning week, Rung 5 (FYF pp. 290-291) from last week, and Rungs 6-7 (FYF pp. 292-296) from the course-mapping week. Anything blank gets a sticky flag. Day 2 is when those gaps get filled, so the point today is finding them, not fixing them.

[H&L PLATFORM] Students open the Hats & Ladders app and click on Career Plan, which is the app step Rung 2 sends them to (FYF p. 283). They confirm the plan still names the career they are presenting this week, and update it if the Rung 4 interview moved their thinking.

Facilitation Tip. The students who have no interview

Some students will arrive with nothing. Do not spend the period chasing them. Send them to the ladder check first, then run a single group interview during Activity 3 with whatever adult you lined up, a counselor, a coach, or a fellow teacher. Five minutes with a real adult who knows them produces a usable Rung 4. A student who still has no interview by the end of the period can conduct it tonight and write the Make Meaning answers during Day 2's work time.

DOK 3: Your interview adult named a strength you did not expect. What evidence from your own year supports it, or argues against it?

docs.title: Activity 3: Optional Core Personality Retake (5 min)
docs.text:
Source: H&L app, Profile → Discover Your Core (taught in Week 0)

Optional for students who finish the Make Meaning page early. Students took Discover Your Core in Week 0 and wrote the result in their engineering notebook. They compare that result to how they would answer today.

[H&L PLATFORM] Students retake the Discover Your Core activity in the H&L app under Profile if the app allows it. If it does not, they read their Week 0 notebook entry and write one sentence saying whether it still describes them.

The growth comparison is powerful. A student who came out a Doer in September and reads more like an Analyzer in May has not made a mistake; they have collected 36 weeks of new evidence about themselves. The shift is the point.

[VERIFY IN H&L] Confirm with the H&L district admin whether the Discover Your Core activity supports a retake with a side-by-side comparison to the original result.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Venn Diagram) · Printable PDF:

Draw two circles labeled TOP OF ICEBERG (what people see) and UNDER THE ICEBERG (what people do not see). Place 2 items in each zone AND 1 item in the OVERLAP (something that is both visible and hidden work).

TOP OF ICEBERG (2 items I listed today):

UNDER THE ICEBERG (2 items I listed today):

OVERLAP (1 item that is both visible to others AND took hidden work):

Bottom line:

My career goal from Rung 2: _____

One strength my interview adult named that I agree with: _____

(d(8)(A))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Pre-fill the iceberg with 5 example underwater items so students only add 5 more, or hand out the workbook's printed Electrician frame (FYF p. 7) as a lower-lift alternative to a personal iceberg. Provide sentence stems for the five Make Meaning prompts ("One strength she named was _. I agree because ___.").
  • Extension: Students fill in both printed career icebergs, Electrician (FYF p. 7) and Nurse (FYF p. 8), and answer the page 8 class discussion questions in writing: how did your thinking change after researching these careers, and which career had the most surprising responsibilities underneath the iceberg? Or they retake Discover Your Core and write a one-paragraph comparison to Week 0.
  • ELL: Pre-teach: Iceberg = Iceberg, Strength = Fortaleza, Career Plan = Plan de carrera. Allow iceberg labels in Spanish or bilingual format. The Rung 4 interview was very likely conducted in Spanish; the notes and the Make Meaning answers may stay in Spanish. Pair ESL students with bilingual peers for the app navigation.

docs.title: Day 2: Check Your Ladder + Choose Your Presentation
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Audit all eight rungs against the workbook's completion check and fill the gaps; transfer the ladder onto the written Career Plan; choose one of the seven presentation formats and plan the presentation against the 32-point rubric TEKS d(8)(A), d(8)(B), d(8)(C), d(4)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explore: Ladder check and written Career Plan · Explain: Format menu and rubric · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Written Career Plan (eight rung sections) + chosen presentation format + presentation plan Materials Find Your Future workbook pp. 278-280 and p. 299, students' completed Rungs 1-7, printed Career Plan template, Chromebooks, H&L accounts, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (3 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: In ONE sentence, what is your career goal? In ONE more sentence, what is your first step toward it?

Take 4-5 student responses. This forces clarity. If a student can't answer in 2 sentences, they need the work time today. Their career goal is Rung 2 and their first step is the short-term goal in Rung 6, so both sentences are already somewhere in their book.

docs.title: Activity 1: Check Your Ladder and Write the Career Plan (25 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 299: "Prepare & Present") + (FYF p. 278: "Capstone Project Requirements")

Step 1: Check Your Ladder (5 min). The workbook opens Prepare & Present with a three-question audit of the whole project (FYF p. 299). Students answer it honestly:

  1. Did you complete all 8 rungs?
  2. Did you fully answer each section with effort and detail?
  3. Is your work neat, organized, and easy to understand?

Anything marked "not yet" is the first thing that gets fixed today. Rung 8 is the one rung students should expect to be blank, because it is written on Day 4. The eight rungs and what each one holds are previewed on page 278: Rung 1 Who Are You, Rung 2 Career Goal, Rung 3 Career Deep Dive, Rung 4 Strengths Interview, Rung 5 Local Connection, Rung 6 Goal Setting, Rung 7 High School Plan, Rung 8 Stay Motivated.

Step 2: Write the Career Plan (20 min). Distribute the printed Career Plan template (or share a Google Doc version). This is the one-document version of the ladder, the copy that goes home and to the 9th-grade counselor. Its eight sections follow the eight rungs, so every answer already exists in the workbook and students are transferring and tightening rather than starting over.

Chunking: release the template in three chunks and say what each chunk is for before students start it. Model Section 2 out loud first, using a career nobody in the room chose, so students hear how much detail a rung section is supposed to carry. Chunk 1 is Sections 1-3, who you are and the career you chose. Chunk 2 is Sections 4-5, what a trusted adult sees in you and what an employer actually asks for. Chunk 3 is Sections 6-7, your goals and your high school plan. Close each chunk with a thumbs check before releasing the next.

Section 1: Who You Are (Rung 1, FYF pp. 281-282)

  • My top core personality type, my top 2 work values, 3 Building Blocks
  • Two strengths I am confident about

Section 2: Career Goal (Rung 2, FYF pp. 283-284)

  • "My career goal is to become a _ in the ___ cluster."
  • Where someone in this career works, and whether the work is mostly with people, ideas, data, or tools
  • One perk and one quirk of the job

Section 3: Career Deep Dive (Rung 3, FYF pp. 285-286)

  • Education or training required, plus any certification or license
  • Estimated starting salary and the average in our area
  • Growing, stable, or declining

Section 4: What Others See in Me (Rung 4, FYF pp. 287-289)

  • One strength my interview adult named that I agree with
  • Whether the interview changed my plan, and why

Section 5: Local Connection (Rung 5, FYF pp. 290-291)

  • One real job posting: the title, where I found it, and two things the employer is asking for

Section 6: My Three Goals (Rung 6, FYF pp. 292-293)

  • Short-term (now to the end of 8th grade): _____
  • Medium-term (high school): _____
  • Long-term (after high school): _____
  • Each goal SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-Bound), each with the support I need to reach it
  • My after-high-school path, pick ONE: 4-year university, 2-year community college (Dallas College / TCC), trade school, military, apprenticeship, or direct employment with certification

Section 7: High School Plan (Rung 7, FYF pp. 294-296)

  • "I will pursue this career through the _ pathway at ___ High School."
  • One club, CTSO, or special program at that campus, and how it helps
Year Required Courses CTE / Pathway Course Electives 9th English I, Algebra I, Biology, World Geography, PE/Health 10th English II, Geometry, Chemistry, World History 11th English III, Algebra II, Physics, US History 12th English IV, Math elective, Science elective, Government/Econ

Section 8: Stay Motivated (Rung 8, FYF pp. 297-298)

  • Left blank today. Students write it on Day 4 and add it to the plan before it goes home.

The Career Plan should be 1-2 pages. Students who finish early start planning their presentation format.

Facilitation Tip

Walk around with the template visible. Students get stuck on the Time-Bound part of the Rung 6 goals because they have never attached a date to an intention. Coach them: "When exactly? Before winter break? Before registration in the spring? Write that date down." A goal without a date is a wish, and the rubric's Goal Setting row is looking for specific and realistic.

DOK 4: Look at your three goals. If you actually reach all three, how will your life be different by the end of 9th grade?

docs.title: Activity 2: Choose Your Format and Read the Rubric (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 279: "Presentation Options") + (FYF p. 280: "Rubric") + (FYF p. 299: "Prepare & Present")

Students turn to page 279 and read the seven presentation formats the workbook offers:

Format What it looks like Comic or Storyboard Draw yourself climbing the ladder, with captions and speech bubbles "Unboxing My Future" Video Unbox an object for each rung and explain what it means TED Talk-Style Speech An inspiring talk about your career path, delivered on your feet Podcast: Interview Your Future Self An audio interview where you ask and answer your own questions Essay A clear, organized written version with paragraphs and details Slideshow Google Slides, PowerPoint, or Canva, presented live or recorded Website A simple site with a page or section for each rung

The page also invites a format the workbook did not list, discussed with the teacher first. Whatever the format, the workbook requires the same three things: all 8 rungs included, ideas clear and complete, and effort and creativity shown.

Match the format to the days you actually have

Students present on Day 3 or Day 4, so the format has to be buildable in the time left. The TED Talk-Style Speech, the Slideshow, the Comic or Storyboard, and the Essay are the in-class-feasible defaults and should be offered as such. The video, the podcast, and the website are worth offering to students who will finish them at home tonight or who already have the pieces. Say this out loud before students choose, not after one of them commits to a website.

Read the rubric together (FYF p. 280). The workbook prints its own eight-category rubric, scored at four levels for 32 total points: All 8 Rungs Completed, Career Research, Personal Connection, Goal Setting, Interview Reflection, Creativity and Design, Presenter Delivery, and Participation and Collaboration. Students already hold this page, so it is the scoring standard for the week. Do not hand out a second rubric.

Plan the presentation (FYF p. 299). The workbook lists what the presentation has to show, and it is simply the ladder in order: who you are (Rung 1), your career goal (Rung 2), what it takes (Rung 3), what others see in you (Rung 4), real-world connections (Rung 5), your goals (Rung 6), your high school plan (Rung 7), and your motivation plan (Rung 8). Students write one line per rung on the presentation planner, which becomes their notes on presentation day. Bullet points only, no scripts. The workbook's own delivery tips close the activity: speak clearly and at a steady pace, look up and engage the audience, show confidence even when nervous, and use the work to guide you instead of reading it word for word.

Facilitation Tip

Project a timer for any student who wants a 30-second test run during the last 5 minutes. Hearing yourself out loud once is better than reading silently 10 times.

DOK 3: What is the difference between a career goal and a goal from Rung 6? Why does a finished ladder need both?

DELIVERABLE: Written Career Plan + chosen presentation format + presentation planner with one line per rung.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (7 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Short Constructed Response) · Printable PDF:

  1. My career goal (one sentence): __________

  2. After high school I plan to (circle ONE): 4-year university / 2-year community college / trade school / military / apprenticeship / job with a certification

  3. My short-term goal, now to the end of 8th grade (say WHAT and say WHEN): __________

  4. My medium-term goal, during high school: __________

  5. My long-term goal, after high school: __________

  6. In one sentence, why this after-high-school path fits MY career goal (not a general answer):

(d(8)(B), d(8)(C))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Pre-fill the 4-year course plan grid with the standard required courses. Students only fill in the CTE pathway courses and electives. Provide sentence starters for every rung section ("My career goal is _. This fits me because ___."). For students whose Rung 5 job posting is missing, print one local posting per common career goal so the section can be completed today.
  • Extension: Students build the presentation artifact itself during the work time rather than only planning it, or they draft a Plan A and a Plan B ladder and write a paragraph on why a backup matters.
  • ELL: Bilingual Career Plan template with Spanish rung headers and sentence starters. Allow the written plan and the presentation to be in Spanish or bilingual. Pair ESL students with bilingual peers for the Rung 6 goal-writing section, which carries the most abstract vocabulary on the page.

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Present the eight-rung Career Ladder in the chosen format (first half of class); provide constructive Two Stars and a Wish feedback to peers TEKS d(4)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: Capstone presentations · Evaluate: Peer feedback and Exit Ticket Deliverable Capstone presentation delivered + scored on the workbook's 32-point rubric Materials Students' written Career Plans + presentation planners + presentation artifacts (slides, comic, essay, video, audio), Find Your Future workbook pp. 279-280 and p. 299, timer, projector, speakers

docs.title: Warm-Up (3 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Take 90 seconds. Read your presentation planner silently. Eye contact. Clear voice. Confident posture. This is YOUR ladder and YOUR future. Own it.

Quiet warm-up. No discussion. Project a 90-second timer. The energy this week should feel different from any other week. This is the year's most important presentation.

docs.title: Activity 1: Capstone Ladder Presentations (40 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 299: "Prepare & Present") + (FYF p. 280: "Rubric")

Today the FIRST HALF of the class presents. The remaining students present on Day 4. Splitting across two days lets every student present to the whole class without rushing.

Formats will vary, because students chose from the workbook's seven options on Day 2. A slideshow gets projected, a comic gets shown on the document camera, a video or podcast gets played, an essay gets read from in part. What does not vary is that the student stands up and walks the room through their ladder in their own words. The artifact is the vehicle, not the substitute.

What every presentation has to show (FYF p. 299):

  1. Who you are (Rung 1)
  2. Your career goal (Rung 2)
  3. What it takes (Rung 3)
  4. What others see in you (Rung 4)
  5. Real-world connections (Rung 5)
  6. Your goals (Rung 6)
  7. Your high school plan (Rung 7)
  8. Your motivation plan (Rung 8)

Format:

  • 5-minute time limit per student (visible timer projected; see the warning below for the realistic slot)
  • Teacher scores each presentation on the workbook's own rubric (FYF p. 280): eight categories, four levels, 32 points
  • After each presentation, the class gives Two Stars and a Wish (specific positive + specific suggestion)
  • Move quickly to keep momentum, applaud every speaker

Presentation timing: the math does not fit 5 min/student

Half a class of 25 = 12–13 students. At 5 min each, that is 60–65 min. EXCEEDS the 50-min period before warm-up, feedback, and transitions. Plan for 2.5–3 min per student as the realistic baseline; 5 min is the ceiling, not the expectation. Choose one compression approach before Day 3 begins:

  • 2.5–3 min per student: ~32–39 min presentations + 8–10 min Two Stars and a Wish + 3 min warm-up = ~45 min. Safe margin.
  • Corner rotation: Split class into 3 groups of 8–9. Teacher circulates between corners; each group presents to a smaller audience at 3–4 min each. Lower pressure, more speaking time.
  • Co-facilitator model: Invite an administrator or counselor. One adult scores Day 3 morning, the other facilitates warm-up, timer, and closing. Allows the named 5-min ceiling for some students.

First-time presenters run long. Build in buffer. Presentation quality matters more than rigid 5-min timers. If you compress, tell students which rungs to hit hardest rather than asking them to say all eight faster: Rungs 2, 3, and 7 carry the most rubric weight.

Time, Voice, Body: post the three blocks before the first presenter. Voice 0 while a slideshow, video, or audio file loads, Voice 3 for the presenter, Voice 1 for the Two Stars and a Wish talk. Run a visible countdown set to whichever slot length you chose. Say where the presenter stands and where the feedback slips go, so transitions do not eat presentation time.

Facilitation Tip

Treat this like a real event. Wear professional clothes and greet students at the door. If possible, invite an administrator, counselor, or parent for part of the day. Tell the audience when to applaud and keep the rubric visible; students should feel celebrated and still know the presentation is being assessed.

Class feedback after each presentation:

  • One student gives a SPECIFIC star ("I loved how the job posting you found in Rung 5 asked for the exact skill you named in Rung 1")
  • One student gives a SPECIFIC wish ("Your goals were strong. I wish you had said which 9th-grade course starts your pathway")
  • Move on quickly

DOK 4: As you watch your classmates present, evaluate which ladders are MOST realistic and well-researched. What specific evidence makes a ladder convincing?

DELIVERABLE: Capstone ladder presentation delivered live, scored on the workbook rubric.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (7 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Ranked Justification) · Printable PDF:

The workbook rubric scores eight things. Rank these FOUR of them from MOST important (1) to LEAST (4), based on what made today's STRONGEST ladder strong.

  • Career Research (real training, real pay, real outlook): rank ____
  • Personal Connection (why this career fits THEM): rank ____
  • Creativity and Design (the format was clear and engaging): rank ____
  • Presenter Delivery (eye contact, pace, confidence): rank ____

The ONE classmate's ladder that impressed me most today:

Classmate / career: _____

For the Rank 1 category (most important), ONE specific thing that classmate did:

For the Rank 4 category (least important), why it mattered LESS than the others:

(d(4)(C))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Allow note cards visible during the presentation. Allow a printed slide as a visual aid. Allow anxious students to present to a small group of 4-5 instead of the whole class. The very most anxious can present 1-on-1 to the teacher during a free period, or submit the essay or comic format and talk through only two rungs out loud.
  • Extension: Students who finish their presentation early prepare a 1-minute Q&A. They take questions from the audience about their ladder. Practices defending decisions under audience questions.
  • ELL: Allow Spanish or bilingual presentations. Pair ESL students with bilingual peers for audience feedback. Language flexibility lets ESL students show their ladder without language being a barrier.

docs.title: Day 4: Capstone Presentations Day 2 + Plan Download + Rung 8
Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Present the eight-rung Career Ladder in the chosen format (second half of class); download the finalized H&L Career Plan; write the Rung 8 motivation plan TEKS d(4)(C), d(8)(B), d(8)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: Capstone presentations · Extend: Career Plan download and motivation plan · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Capstone presentation delivered + downloaded H&L Career Plan + completed Rung 8 Materials Students' written Career Plans + presentation artifacts, H&L accounts, Find Your Future workbook pp. 297-298 and p. 280, timer, projector, speakers

docs.title: Warm-Up (3 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Yesterday you watched the first half of the class present. What was the BEST ladder presentation you saw, and what made it strong?

Take 2-3 student responses. This primes today's presenters to bring the same energy. Naming what worked yesterday makes it more likely to happen again today.

docs.title: Activity 1: Capstone Presentations Day 2 (30 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 299: "Prepare & Present") + (FYF p. 280: "Rubric")

The SECOND HALF of the class presents their eight-rung ladder. Same format and the same eight required rungs as Day 3.

Presentation timing: the math is tighter today than Day 3

Half a class of 25 = 12-13 students. At 5 min each, that is 60-65 min. DOUBLE the 30-min Activity 1 budget. Apply the same compression you picked on Day 3:

  • 2.5 min/student: 12-13 × 2.5 min = 30-32 min presentations. Fits with no margin. Exit ticket runs tight.
  • 2 min/student: 12-13 × 2 min = 24-26 min. Leaves ~4 min for Two Stars and a Wish batching.
  • Corner rotation: 2 corners of 6-7. Teacher circulates. Each student presents to a smaller audience at 3 min each.

Day 4 has less runway than Day 3 because Activities 2 and 3 (Career Plan download + Rung 8) together eat 17 min. Protect them. The download is the artifact that goes home, and Rung 8 is the last rung on the ladder.

  • 5-minute time limit per student (visible timer; see warning above for realistic slot)
  • Teacher scores on the workbook's rubric (FYF p. 280), the same eight categories used yesterday
  • Class gives Two Stars and a Wish after each
  • Applaud every speaker
  • Move quickly to keep momentum

The room should feel celebratory by now. Students who watched yesterday's presentations come in calmer because they know the format. Students who present today benefit from yesterday's models.

Facilitation Tip

Take quick photos (with permission) of presenters. These can be used for end-of-year slideshows, parent communications, and yearbook. The capstone presentation IS the most important moment of the course, capture it.

DOK 4: Looking at all the presentations across both days, what patterns do you see in the strongest ladders? What do they have in common?

docs.title: Activity 2: Download H&L Career Plan (7 min)
docs.text:
Source: H&L app Career Plan, the app step Rung 2 sends students to (FYF p. 283)

After all presentations are done, direct students to open H&L and download or export their finalized Career Plan.

[H&L PLATFORM] Students open Career Plan in the Hats & Ladders app and download or print it. The downloaded Plan is the app-side copy of the ladder they just presented. Confirm the export process with the H&L district admin; most H&L installations support a PDF export of the Career Plan or at least a print view.

[VERIFY IN H&L] Confirm the specific download/export workflow in the current H&L app version. If the app does not support direct PDF export, use Print → Save as PDF as a workaround. Day-of backup plan: if simultaneous PDF export fails for 24 students (most likely failure mode), have students print the H&L Career Plan directly to PDF via the Chromebook browser Print dialog, OR take full-page screenshots and email them to themselves for home and counselor sharing. Every student leaves with an artifact, paper, PDF, or screenshot.

Students save the Plan to:

  1. Their school Google Drive (digital backup)
  2. Print one copy to take home (for parents/guardians and the 9th-grade course registration meeting)

Every student leaves with a copy of the Career Plan to show a parent or guardian and bring to the 9th-grade course-registration meeting. Pair it with the written Career Plan from Day 2.

docs.title: Activity 3: Rung 8 — Stay Motivated (10 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF pp. 297-298: "Rung 8: Stay Motivated")

The last rung is about what happens after the presentation is over. The workbook's framing is plain: reaching your goals will not always be easy, and staying motivated is what keeps you climbing. Students build their own motivation plan on pages 297-298.

Your Affirmation. A short, powerful statement students can tell themselves when things get hard. It should sound positive, confident, and personal. The workbook's two examples are about growing through challenges and being capable of reaching goals. Push students past copying those: the affirmation should sound like them.

Your Hashtags. Two to four short, catchy hashtags that represent the student's mindset and goals. The workbook models the length with #KeepClimbing and #FutureReady. This is the fastest part of the page and it is worth protecting, because it is the part reluctant writers finish first.

Strategies to Stay on Track. Three prompts, and this is where the old Support System work now lives:

  1. What is one thing you can do when you feel stuck or discouraged?
  2. Who is someone you can go to for support?
  3. What is one habit you can build to stay consistent?

For question 2, students go back to the three-person career community they named in Week 0 (FYF p. 22: "Building a Career Community"). Nine months have passed. Some of those people are still right, some have been replaced by a teacher or a coach the student did not know in September, and some students now need a high school name they have not met yet. Students update the list to three current, real names.

Name How this person can help me How I will stay connected

Real names, not "a teacher" but "Mrs. Garcia, my science teacher." Real names mean they actually know who to ask.

Picture Your Future. Two closing prompts on page 298: what does success look like for you, and how will you feel when you get there. The page ends with a one-word answer to how the student feels about the future now.

Students add the finished Rung 8 to Section 8 of the written Career Plan before it goes home.

DOK 3: Why is having someone to go to for support more important than having the perfect plan? What does a person give you that a plan alone cannot?

DELIVERABLE: Capstone presentation delivered + downloaded Career Plan + completed Rung 8 with an affirmation, hashtags, three strategies, and three named people.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (5 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (Concept Map) · Printable PDF:

Draw a quick concept map. Place MY CAREER LADDER in the center and connect it to each of the FOUR items below. On each line, write ONE word showing how the item supports the ladder.

  1. My Irving ISD high school + pathway: _____

  2. My downloaded Career Plan file (where I saved it): _____

  3. One summer action I will take with the downloaded Plan (share with a parent, bring to a counselor, save for 9th-grade registration):

  1. ONE person I can go to for support (real name, not "a teacher"): _____

How they will help (one phrase): _____

My affirmation, in my own words: _____

(d(8)(B), d(8)(C))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Help students navigate the H&L download/export process at the device level. Provide a printed Career Plan summary as a backup if the app export fails. Pre-fill the support table with example role categories (Parent, Teacher, Mentor) so students fill in just the names, and offer two affirmation sentence frames ("I can _ even when ." / "I am the kind of person who __.").
  • Extension: Students answer the workbook's "Being a Career Thinker and Doer" discussion question in writing (FYF p. 22): what is the difference between thinking about a goal and taking action toward it? They tie the answer to one of the three strategies they just wrote. Students who chose the Comic or Storyboard presentation format (FYF p. 279) can add a final panel showing where the affirmation gets used.
  • ELL: Bilingual support table with Spanish column headers. Allow the affirmation, hashtags, and "how they help" descriptions to be in Spanish. Many ESL students have strong family support systems, encourage them to list family members who have wisdom even if they speak limited English.

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Time 50 minutes Objectives Complete the workbook's Final Reflection inside a comprehensive 36-week review; celebrate the completion of the CCE course; preview the 8th-to-9th grade transition TEKS d(8)(A), d(8)(C) 5E Phases Engage: Warm-Up · Explain: Six-weeks review and Final Reflection · Extend: Eighth-to-ninth grade preview · Evaluate: Exit Ticket Deliverable Final Reflection complete + (optional) Certificate of Completion Materials Chromebooks, H&L accounts, Find Your Future workbook p. 300, printed End-of-Year Reflection handout, optional Certificates of Completion, snacks if available, projector

docs.title: Warm-Up (5 min)
docs.text:
WARM-UP: Finish this sentence in writing, "On the first day of CCE, I thought career planning was _. Now I think career planning is ___."

Stop and Jot: 90 seconds, prompt on screen, written before anyone talks. Then take 4-5 student responses. This is the perfect emotional opener for the last day. Most students will say something like "I thought it was about picking ONE job. Now I know it's about exploring."

docs.title: Activity 1: Final Reflection (25 min)
docs.text:
Source: (FYF p. 300: "Final Reflection") + 36-week course summary

Distribute the End-of-Year Reflection handout. It wraps the workbook's four closing questions inside a review of the whole year, so students have their evidence in front of them before they answer.

Section 1: What I Explored (7 min)

For each six weeks block, list one specific thing the student learned:

  • 1st Six Weeks (IT, Manufacturing): I learned _____
  • 2nd Six Weeks (Law, Health Science, Powerskills): I learned _____
  • 3rd Six Weeks (Ag, Hospitality, Human Services, Business): I learned _____
  • 4th Six Weeks (Career Plan intro, Transportation, Engineering): I learned _____
  • 5th Six Weeks (Architecture, Civil Eng, Construction, Trades, Budgeting, Real Estate): I learned _____
  • 6th Six Weeks (Education, Arts, Marketing, Sales, Job Skills, Capstone): I learned _____

Section 2: What I Learned About Myself (3 min)

The workbook's first closing question. "The most valuable thing I learned about MYSELF in 36 weeks of CCE is _. This will affect my career decisions because ___." Then the book's last line: how do you feel about your future now?

Section 3: The Rung That Mattered Most (3 min)

The workbook's second closing question. "The rung that mattered most to me was Rung _, because ___." Any of the eight is a legitimate answer, and the reason matters more than the number.

Section 4: Skills I Built (5 min)

List 5 specific career-readiness skills from this year:

  • (Example: I can write a resume, present a career ladder, design a billboard ad, sit a mock interview, write a cover letter)

For each skill, write a one-sentence explanation of HOW you will use it.

Section 5: My Next Step in Real Life (5 min)

The workbook's third closing question, asked concretely. "In 8th grade, I will _. In 9th grade, I will start the pathway at High School. The one thing I will actually do after this project is _. I am most excited about . I am most worried about ."

Section 6: Advice to Next Year's Students (2 min)

Write a 1-paragraph letter to NEXT year's CCE class. What is your single best piece of advice for them about career exploration?

Facilitation Tip

Make this a quiet writing moment. Play soft instrumental music if appropriate. The reflection is the year's most personal artifact. Resist the urge to fill silence with talk, let students think.

DOK 4: Looking back at all 36 weeks, what is the ONE most important thing you learned about YOURSELF? Not about a career, about you.

docs.title: Activity 2: Celebration + Certificates (15 min)
docs.text:
Source: Course completion + Optional certificates

Distribute Certificates of Completion if available. Even a simple printed certificate (your school logo, "CCE Course Completion 2026," teacher signature) means a lot.

Whole-class celebration moment:

  • Each student shares ONE highlight from the year, favorite cluster, favorite activity, favorite project, biggest growth moment. Quick, 10-15 seconds each. Keep moving.
  • Applaud after each share
  • Teacher takes a class photo if appropriate

8th-to-9th grade preview (5 min):

Walk through what happens next:

  • End of 8th grade (next school year): Students register for 9th-grade courses. They should bring their Career Plan to the registration meeting. The high school counselor will use it to recommend a CTE pathway.
  • Start of 9th grade: Students begin their selected CTE pathway. The work they did this year IS the foundation for that pathway choice.
  • Through high school: The ladder is a LIVING document. They can change it. They can add Plan B and Plan C. They can switch pathways. Rung 2 says so on its own page: this does not have to be a forever decision.

docs.title: Activity 3: Final H&L Update + Goodbye (3 min)
docs.text:
Source: H&L app Career Plan

One last task: students log into H&L one more time and confirm their Career Plan is finalized and downloaded. They should be able to access it from home over the summer.

[H&L PLATFORM] Students confirm their Career Plan is saved in their H&L account. The downloaded copy from Day 4 is the artifact that goes home. The H&L account stays active. Students can log in any time to keep building.

docs.title: Exit Ticket (2 min)
docs.text:
EXIT TICKET (3-2-1 Reflective) · Printable PDF:

3 things I learned about MYSELF across 36 weeks (not about a career, about me):

2 things I will DO between now and 9th-grade registration:

1 piece of advice I would give next year's CCE students:

My top career choice as of TODAY: _____

(d(8)(A), d(8)(C))

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
• Support: Provide a simplified Final Reflection with guided yes/no questions and pick-from-list options instead of open prompts. Allow students to dictate answers to a peer or teacher if writing is challenging.
  • Extension: Students write a letter to their FUTURE SELF (to open in 12th grade) describing where they hope to be. Seal it in an envelope. The teacher mails it to them at graduation through the school office or a parent.
  • ELL: Bilingual Final Reflection with Spanish prompts throughout. Allow the entire reflection to be written in Spanish, English, or bilingual. Bilingual Certificates of Completion. Pair ESL students with bilingual peers for the celebration share-out.

docs.title: Final Notes for Teachers
docs.text:
This is the last day of a 36-week course. Students have grown enormously. Even students who were disengaged in September have a career ladder, a resume, and a downloadable artifact they can show their family. Even students who arrived with no career idea now have at least ONE direction they could pursue.

The Career Plan they downloaded yesterday is the most important thing they take home from this course. Encourage them to share it with their parents, bring it to high school registration, and revisit it whenever they need to remember who they wanted to be in 7th grade.

Thank you for teaching CCE. The work matters.

docs.title: Week 6: The Grand Finale — My Career Ladder Capstone
docs.text: 6th Six Weeks | Cross-Cluster Capstone | 5 class periods (50 min each)

docs.title: Lesson Objective
docs.text:
Students complete and present the Find Your Future Capstone Project, an eight-rung Career Ladder built across the whole year. This week they debrief the Rung 4 Strengths Interview assigned as a take-home two weeks earlier, audit all eight rungs against the workbook's own completion check, transfer the ladder onto a written Career Plan, choose one of the workbook's seven presentation formats, deliver that presentation to the class against the workbook's 32-point rubric, download the finalized H&L Career Plan, write the Rung 8 motivation plan, and close the course with the workbook's Final Reflection.

Learning Target: I can build all eight rungs of my Career Ladder, present my ladder in the format I choose, and explain what I learned about myself this year.

Success Criteria: I will know I am successful when all eight rungs in my workbook are filled in, when my written Career Plan names my career goal, my training and pay research, my three goals, and my Irving ISD pathway and campus, when my presentation shows all eight rungs in the format I chose, and when my Final Reflection names the rung that mattered most to me and one real step I will take next.

Adapt to your end-of-year schedule

The original scope-and-sequence left this week blank for a reason: it is the last week of school, and end-of-year events (yearbook, field day, awards, early release) reshape it unpredictably. Nothing here is critical to year-end TEKS coverage. Every standard 6SW Wk6 claims is already covered upstream:

  • d(4)(C) oral presentation → 6SW Wk4 Sales/Presentations
  • d(8)(A) select pathway → 4SW Wk1 Career Planning
  • d(8)(B) courses + postsecondary → 4SW Wk1 and 4SW Wk2
  • d(8)(C) write individual plan → 4SW Wk2 Course Mapping

Adapt using these verbs: cut (the optional core personality retake, the celebration), compress (Days 3-4 into one day with 90-second ladder walk-throughs), substitute (a written Final Reflection instead of the celebration), skip entirely (let students finish the ladder at home). Any subset is fine. Zero days is fine.

docs.title: Demonstration of Learning
docs.text: "I can present all eight rungs of my Career Ladder: who I am, my career goal, what the career takes, what a trusted adult sees in me, a real local job posting, my three goals, my Irving ISD high school plan, and how I will stay motivated."

docs.title: TEKS Alignment
docs.text:
• d(8)(A): Select a career pathway related to personal interests.
  • d(8)(B): Document high school courses, postsecondary education, and training requirements.
  • d(8)(C): Write an individual plan to start a career.
  • d(4)(C): Prepare and deliver an oral presentation (capstone ladder presentation).

This is the capstone pass, not the artifact week. The official d(8) and d(4)(C) artifacts are locked upstream in 4SW Wk1 / 4SW Wk2 / 6SW Wk4 per the admonition above. Students who complete this week assemble the ladder they have been building since January, present it, and bring the downloaded Career Plan to their 9th-grade counselor.

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Chromebooks with internet access (1 per student)
  • Hats & Ladders student accounts (Career Plan)
  • Find Your Future workbook, Capstone chapter (printed pp. 277-300) and the Career Iceberg (printed pp. 6-8)
  • Students' completed Rungs 1-7, including the Rung 4 interview notes assigned as a take-home two weeks earlier
  • Week 0 My Career Journey reflections, retrieved from the class folder
  • Printed Career Plan template, eight sections mirroring the eight rungs (CCE artifact)
  • The workbook's own Capstone rubric (FYF p. 280) as the scoring standard. Do not print a second CCE rubric.
  • Printed End-of-Year Reflection handout built on (FYF p. 300: "Final Reflection")
  • Texas OnCourse: texasoncourse.org
  • Irving ISD CTE Pathways guide (PATHWAYS.md printed)
  • Presentation supplies for students choosing the comic or storyboard format: paper, markers, rulers
  • Optional: Certificates of Completion
  • Projector for modeling

docs.title: Career Connection
docs.text:
Over 36 weeks students have explored every CTE cluster: Manufacturing, IT, Law & Public Service, Health Science, Agriculture, Hospitality, Human Services, Business / Marketing / Finance, Aviation, Automotive, Skilled Trades, Architecture, Civil Engineering, Construction, Real Estate, Education, Arts & A/V, and Sales. By this week they have a resume, a cover letter, a thank-you letter, a mock interview, references identified, a personal budget, and dozens of researched career profiles. The capstone chapter opener puts three more Hats in front of them, Air Traffic Controller, Dentist, and Cement Mason, and asks the question the whole project answers: how can you prepare for your future career (FYF p. 277)?

What is Happening at Irving ISD? Students select and present the SPECIFIC Irving ISD CTE pathway they want to begin in 9th grade. Any pathway from any Irving ISD high school explored during the year is valid. The Capstone chapter prints no district page of its own; the local detail lands in Rung 7's "What's Available to Me?" prompt (FYF p. 296), which asks students what their own high school offers that connects to their goals.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text:
• Career Ladder: The workbook's name for the capstone project. Eight rungs, each one a part of the student's career journey, presented as one project.
  • Rung: One numbered part of the Career Ladder. Rung 1 is who you are. Rung 8 is how you stay motivated.
  • Capstone: A culminating project demonstrating everything learned throughout a course.
  • Career Plan: The H&L app tool and the written document that hold the career goal, the pathway, the high school course sequence, the postsecondary requirements, and the goals.
  • Postsecondary Goal: Plan for after high school: 4-year university, 2-year community college, trade school, military service, apprenticeship, or direct employment with certification.
  • SMART Goal: A goal that is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-Bound. Rung 6 asks for three of them.
  • Affirmation: A short, positive statement students tell themselves when the work gets hard. Written in Rung 8.

docs.title: Bridge to Theory (Hats & Ladders)
docs.text:
The Find Your Future Capstone chapter runs printed pages 277 through 300. It is one project rather than a set of separate activities: students build a Career Ladder with eight rungs and then present it. The chapter opener frames a career as a ladder that may be straight, may twist and turn, and may have a few broken steps to fix along the way (FYF p. 277).

  • Capstone Project Requirements (FYF p. 278): a one-page preview of all eight rungs, with a two-sentence description of each. Rung 1 Who Are You, Rung 2 Career Goal, Rung 3 Career Deep Dive, Rung 4 Strengths Interview, Rung 5 Local Connection, Rung 6 Goal Setting, Rung 7 High School Plan, Rung 8 Stay Motivated.
  • Presentation Options (FYF p. 279): seven named formats plus an open option. Comic or Storyboard, "Unboxing My Future" Video, TED Talk-Style Speech, Podcast Interviewing Your Future Self, Essay, Slideshow, Website, and "have another idea, discuss with your teacher." Whatever the format, all eight rungs must be included, the ideas must be clear and complete, and the work must show effort and creativity.
  • Rubric (FYF p. 280): eight categories scored at four levels for 32 total points. All 8 Rungs Completed, Career Research, Personal Connection, Goal Setting, Interview Reflection, Creativity and Design, Presenter Delivery, and Participation and Collaboration. This is the published rubric students hold in their own books, so it is the scoring standard for the week.
  • Rung 4: Strengths Interview (FYF pp. 287-289): the interview itself is a take-home assigned two weeks earlier. The "Make Meaning of What You Heard" page (FYF p. 289) is the classroom half and it lands on Day 1.
  • Rung 8: Stay Motivated (FYF pp. 297-298): an affirmation, two to four hashtags, three Strategies to Stay on Track including who to go to for support, and a Picture Your Future prompt.
  • Prepare & Present (FYF p. 299): a three-question completion check across the whole ladder plus the list of what the presentation has to show and four delivery tips.
  • Final Reflection (FYF p. 300): four closing questions that end the book and the course.
  • The Career Iceberg (FYF pp. 6-8): a World of Work activity that opens the workbook rather than closing it. The printed example is a sports trophy, and pages 7 and 8 are blank iceberg frames labeled Electrician and Nurse for students to research and fill in.

This week does not rebuild every rung. Rungs 1-3 (FYF pp. 281-286) return from mid-year, Rung 5 (FYF pp. 290-291) from last week, and Rungs 6-7 (FYF pp. 292-296) from the course-mapping week. This week covers the requirements page, the rubric, the Rung 4 debrief, Rung 8, Prepare & Present, and the Final Reflection.

The Career Plan students download from H&L this week updates the d(8) artifact produced in 4SW Wk1-Wk2. Students can share it with families and Irving ISD high school counselors during the 8th-to-9th grade transition.

docs.title: IISD Instructional Strategies
docs.text:
• Think-Pair-Share: Day 1, Activity 1, the printed trophy iceberg the workbook asks partners to read together (FYF p. 6). Distinguished: pose the book's own question to the whole group, hold a silent 30 second Think, then time Partner A for 30 seconds and Partner B for 30 seconds, and post two stems at different levels: "On top I see _, underneath I see " and "Winning first place is really about __ because _____." Ask two pairs to share, not one. Listen while pairs talk for who can name something underneath that is not practice time. If most pairs only name the visible prize, add three items from your own career to the projected iceberg before releasing Step 2, so the personal icebergs do not come back with two words under the water line.
  • Stop and Jot: Day 5, Activity 1, the written warm-up sentence and the Final Reflection sections (FYF p. 300). Distinguished: give 90 seconds for the warm-up with the prompt on screen, name the time box for each reflection section before students start it, and offer two stems for the hardest section: "The rung that mattered most to me was _ because " and "My next step in real life is __, and I will do it by _____." Read the "what I learned about myself" answers over shoulders while students write, mark three that are specific, and ask those three students first during the celebration share-out so the room hears strong models rather than one-word answers.
  • Active Monitoring: Day 1, Activity 2, the Rung 4 debrief and the ladder check. Distinguished: walk a fixed pathway three times with one target per lap, carrying a second device with the H&L app dashboard open so Career Plan completion is visible as you go. Lap 1, interview notes are actually on page 288. Lap 2, all five Make Meaning prompts on page 289 are answered. Lap 3, Rungs 1-3 and 5-7 are filled in and the blanks are flagged for Day 2. Have feedback ready before class for the two predictable problems: a student who copied the adult's words without answering whether they agree, and a student whose Rung 5 job posting is a national listing rather than a local one. If more than a handful arrive with no interview at all, pull that group to one table and run the interview questions with an available staff adult during Activity 3 instead of coaching them one desk at a time.
  • Chunking: Day 2, Activity 1, the eight sections of the written Career Plan. Distinguished: release the plan in three chunks rather than all eight sections at once, and say what each chunk is for before students start it. Chunk 1 is Rungs 1-3, who you are and the career you chose. Chunk 2 is Rungs 4-5, what a trusted adult sees in you and what an employer actually asks for. Chunk 3 is Rungs 6-7, the three goals and the high school plan. Model Section 2 out loud with a career nobody in the class chose before releasing Chunk 1, so students hear the level of detail the rubric's Career Research row asks for, and close each chunk with a thumbs check before releasing the next. Note which chunk stalls the most, because that chunk becomes a three minute re-teach at the start of Activity 2, and students who cleared all three chunks start planning their presentation format early instead of waiting.
  • Time, Voice, Body (TVB): Days 3 and 4, Activity 1, the capstone presentations. Distinguished: post the three blocks before the first presenter, Voice 0 while a slideshow or video loads, Voice 3 for the presenter, Voice 1 for the two stars and a wish talk, and run a visible countdown for every presenter set to whichever slot length you chose. Define where presenters stand and where feedback slips go so transitions do not eat presentation time. Narrate the students who are meeting the expectation rather than correcting the ones who are not. If the rotation is running long by the third presenter, trim the peer talk to one star only and announce the change before the next presenter begins.

Pre-Capstone Teacher Checklist (only if you can run this week)

  • H&L access: Test login with 2–3 student accounts. Confirm SSO, account refresh, and Climber Profile access on at least one Chromebook.
  • Rung 4 interviews: The Strengths Interview was assigned as a take-home two weeks ago. Count how many are done before Day 1 and line up a counselor, coach, or fellow teacher who can sit for a five-minute interview with the students who arrive with nothing.
  • Core personality retake: Confirm whether the app's Discover Your Core activity supports a retake with a side-by-side comparison to the Week 0 result. If not, students self-assess against the Week 0 entry in their engineering notebook.
  • Career Plan PDF export: Walk through the download workflow yourself. If direct PDF export is unavailable, confirm Print → Save as PDF works from the Chromebook browser. Document the exact steps to project on Day 4.
  • Chromebook fleet: Coordinate with your tech team to avoid OS updates during presentation days. Spot-check 5 devices for battery/keyboard/touchpad.
  • Wk0 reflection folder: Retrieve the class folder of Week 0 My Career Journey reflections you saved per the 1SW Wk0 Day 5 Persistent Portfolio admonition. These are the Week 0 baseline students reference all week.
  • Presentation math: Review the Day 3/4 timing admonition (24 students × 5 min does not fit 50 min). Pick your compression approach before Day 3.

Addressing these early prevents 24-student simultaneous failures mid-week.

docs.title: Formative Assessment
docs.text:
• Personal career iceberg + Rung 4 Make Meaning answers (Day 1): d(8)(A)
  • Ladder completion check + written Career Plan (Day 2): d(8)(A), d(8)(B), d(8)(C)
  • Format choice + presentation plan (Day 2): d(4)(C)
  • Capstone presentation scored on the workbook's 32-point rubric (Days 3-4): d(4)(C)
  • Career Plan download + Rung 8 motivation plan (Day 4): d(8)(B), d(8)(C)
  • Final Reflection (Day 5): d(8)(A), d(8)(C)

docs.title: Summative Assessment
docs.text:
Three-Part Capstone Assessment:

  1. Written Career Plan, eight sections mirroring the eight rungs (d(8)(A), d(8)(B), d(8)(C)): submitted Day 2
  2. Capstone presentation in the student's chosen format, scored on the workbook's eight-category, 32-point rubric (d(4)(C)): delivered Days 3-4
  3. Final Reflection (FYF p. 300) demonstrating self-awareness growth across 36 weeks, submitted Day 5

The H&L downloadable Career Plan is the capstone-week polish of an artifact already produced in 4SW Wk1-Wk2. Students who complete this week take home the polished download for 9th-grade course registration; students whose end-of-year week is disrupted still have the 4SW Career Plan on file.

docs.title: Scaffolded Learning
docs.text:
• Career Plan template with sentence starters for every rung section
  • Allow note cards (or a printed slide deck) during the capstone presentation
  • Option to present 1-on-1 to the teacher instead of the whole class for very anxious students
  • Simplified Final Reflection with guided questions instead of open prompts
  • Pre-built iceberg with example items in each zone, or the workbook's printed Electrician frame (FYF p. 7) as a lower-lift alternative to a personal iceberg

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
• Create a visual career roadmap poster from 8th grade to age 25 with milestones marked
  • Write a letter to your future self (to open in 12th grade)
  • Build the presentation in one of the workbook's higher-production formats: the "Unboxing My Future" video, the podcast interview with your future self, or the website (FYF p. 279)
  • Present TWO career plans (Plan A and a backup Plan B) and explain why having a backup matters

docs.title: ELL Language Support
docs.text:
• Bilingual Final Reflection with Spanish prompts
  • Capstone presentation can be delivered in English, Spanish, or bilingual format
  • Bilingual Career Plan template with Spanish rung headers
  • Bilingual Certificates of Completion
  • The Rung 4 Strengths Interview can be conducted in Spanish and the notes kept in Spanish. Bilingual ESL students should name bilingual capability as a Career Plan strength, because it is one of the most marketable skills in DFW.

docs.title: Facilitation Strategies
docs.text: Use these discussion and reading structures when a daily plan calls for students to read together or discuss as a class, but the default routine is not working. The daily plan supplies the content and time; this page gives the teacher a way to organize the talk or reading without changing the activity.

docs.title: How to Pick a Strategy
docs.text:
• By activity type. Partner talk: Think-Pair-Share, RallyRobin. Dense reading: Talk-Read-Talk-Write, Jigsaw. Accountable check: QSSA. Seat-mixer: Stand Up Hand Up Pair Up.
  • By time budget. Under 5 min: RallyRobin or QSSA. 5 to 10 min: Think-Pair-Share, RoundRobin. 15+ min: Talk-Read-Talk-Write, Jigsaw.
  • By rigor target. DOK 1 recall: RallyRobin, Think-Pair-Share. DOK 2 analysis: Talk-Read-Talk-Write, Jigsaw. DOK 3 application: QSSA with a scenario stem.

docs.title: QSSA (Question, Signal, Stem, Answer)
docs.text:
Time: 3 to 5 min | Group size: whole class | Best for: accountable talk, quick formative check, a DOK 2 question mid-activity

  1. Question. Ask a question aligned to the lesson objective.
  2. Signal. Students signal when they have an answer (thumb at chest, pencil down, hand up).
  3. Stem. Provide a sentence stem ("One reason is _ because ___").
  4. Answer. Students share with a partner using the stem. Cold-call 1 to 2 students to repeat their partner's answer using the stem.

CCE fit: warm-ups where every student needs time to think, exit-ticket pre-checks, and DOK 2 questions inside a daily plan.

docs.title: Think-Pair-Share
docs.text:
Time: 4 to 6 min | Group size: partners | Best for: warm-ups, low-risk participation, vocabulary introduction

  1. Think (60 sec). Students silently think and jot a bullet or one word.
  2. Pair (90 to 120 sec). Partners share. Each partner must contribute before anyone talks twice.
  3. Share (1 to 2 min). Cold-call or take volunteers. Students may share their partner's idea, not only their own.

CCE fit: most warm-ups, introducing H&L vocabulary (Climber, Hat, cluster), DOK 2 questions mid-activity.

docs.title: Talk-Read-Talk-Write
docs.text:
Time: 15 to 25 min | Group size: partners or quads | Best for: dense reading passages where students tend to skim, H&L chapter openers, pathway readouts

  1. Talk (3 to 5 min). Partners predict what a passage will say based on the title, headings, or a preview image.
  2. Read (8 to 15 min). Students read silently or in pairs (alternating paragraphs).
  3. Talk (3 to 5 min). Partners discuss: what matched our prediction? What surprised us?
  4. Write (3 to 5 min). Students write individually (exit ticket, stop-and-jot, journal reflection).

CCE fit: H&L chapter openers, the six-pathway readouts (e.g., Ch 14 p. 230), Powerskills modules that students otherwise skim.

docs.title: Jigsaw
docs.text:
Time: 15 to 20 min | Group size: expert groups of 4 to 6, then mixed home groups | Best for: parallel content where each sub-section has the same structure (6 pathways, 14 clusters, 6 personality types)

  1. Assign (1 min). Divide students into expert groups. Assign each group ONE sub-section (one Manufacturing pathway, one core personality type, one cluster).
  2. Expert (6 to 8 min). Groups read and discuss their sub-section. Each member writes 2 to 3 key points in their workbook.
  3. Remix (1 min). Re-sort students so every new home group has one expert from each original group.
  4. Teach (6 to 8 min). Experts teach their sub-section to the home group. Peers take notes.

CCE fit: 1SW Wk1 Day 1 (6 Manufacturing pathways), any week teaching parallel H&L chapter lists.

Differentiation note: Pair ELL students with a bilingual peer in the expert group so they can process in L1 before teaching in L2. For students with reading-level gaps, assign them the sub-section with the most visual support in the workbook.

docs.title: Kagan: RallyRobin
docs.text:
Time: 2 to 3 min | Group size: partners | Best for: a quick brainstorm in which both partners answer

  1. Pose a question with many possible answers ("Name a career in Manufacturing", "Name a daily object that was manufactured").
  2. Partners alternate answers, one at a time, back and forth, until time is called.
  3. Cold-call 2 to 3 pairs to share the best answer they heard.

CCE fit: warm-ups asking for examples, rapid recall of career clusters, Work Values brainstorm.

docs.title: Kagan: RoundRobin
docs.text:
Time: 4 to 6 min | Group size: quads | Best for: a discussion in which each student gets a turn

  1. Pose a question.
  2. Students in each table group of 4 share one answer in order, clockwise. No interruptions.
  3. After one full round, the group picks the best answer and one student reports out.

CCE fit: Work Values discussion, cluster favorites, reflection on a Hat that students researched.

docs.title: Kagan: Stand Up Hand Up Pair Up
docs.text:
Time: 3 to 5 min | Group size: whole class, random partners | Best for: mixer, finding a partner outside the usual seat group

  1. Students stand, hand up, and walk the room. The first classmate they meet with hand up becomes their partner.
  2. Partners discuss the teacher's question (pair with Think-Pair-Share or QSSA).
  3. Call time. Students return to their seats.

CCE fit: Week 0 classroom community building, mid-year cluster check-ins, any week where the seat-partner pattern has gone stale.
